Q1:
## Introduction

Between 1946 and 1949, the Constituent Assembly consciously borrowed institutional forms from Britain, the USA, Ireland, Canada, Australia and the USSR. Yet these borrowings were never transplanted mechanically — each was reshaped to serve India's specific needs of unity, social transformation and mass democracy, producing a document comparative in origin but original in synthesis.

- **Source** — Feature Borrowed · Indian Adaptation / Example
- **Britain** — Parliamentary govt., Rule of Law, single citizenship · Cabinet accountable to Lok Sabha, but entrenched in a written, supreme Constitution unlike Britain's unwritten one
- **USA** — Fundamental Rights, Judicial Review · Part III rights are subject to reasonable restrictions, unlike the largely absolute US Bill of Rights
- **Ireland** — Directive Principles of State Policy · Made effectively co-equal with Fundamental Rights post-Minerva Mills (1980), going beyond Ireland's model
- **Canada** — Strong Centre, residuary power (Art. 248) · Unlike Canada's federation of equals, India is a ‘Union of States’ (Art. 1) that Parliament can reorganise (Art. 3)
- **USSR** — Fundamental Duties (42nd Amendment, 1976) · Made moral, non-justiciable obligations (Art. 51A) unlike the USSR's legally enforceable duties

Indianisation in practice The Andhra State Act, 1953 — creating India's first linguistic State after Potti Sriramulu's fast-unto-death — shows Article 3's borrowed ‘unitary’ power (Parliament can alter State boundaries by simple majority, unlike the USA where States are indestructible) being used for India's own linguistic-federal accommodation. The later Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 shows the same borrowed mechanism still shaping India's federal map. Critical examination

- Strength: The Basic Structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) lets courts protect the borrowed rights/federal core from majoritarian erosion — a corrective absent in Britain, where parliamentary sovereignty is near-absolute.
- Tension: Selective borrowing produced a ‘quasi-federal’ polity where Centre-State friction recurs, e.g., the prolonged Governor-Bill litigation culminating in the Supreme Court's 2025 Presidential Reference — showing borrowed federal forms sitting uneasily with a centralising design.

## Conclusion

The Constitution is thus neither wholly borrowed nor wholly original — it is a deliberate synthesis where global constitutional experience was filtered through India's own struggle for freedom and social justice. This is what Granville Austin meant by calling it a ‘seamless web,’ and why it remains familiar to comparative lawyers yet unmistakably Indian in spirit and application.

## Value addition
- B.R. Ambedkar described the Constitution as ‘both unitary and federal according to the requirements of time and circumstances.’
- Granville Austin called it a ‘seamless web’ of rights, principles and structures, blending global best practice with indigenous needs.
- The Constituent Assembly deliberated for 2 years, 11 months and 18 days, drawing on nearly 60 world constitutions via B.N. Rau's comparative notes.
- The 106th Amendment, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam), reserving 33% of Lok Sabha/Assembly seats for women, shows the Constitution's continuing capacity for indigenous innovation beyond its original borrowings.
Q2:
## Introduction

K.C. Wheare's description of India as ‘quasi-federal’ captures a design that divides power (federal form) while equipping the Centre with overriding authority in defined circumstances (unitary spirit). Unlike the USA's ‘coming together’ federation of pre-existing sovereign states, India is a ‘holding together’ federation (Alfred Stepan) — a single, indivisible Union that devolved power to States — which explains why the unitary strand runs so deep.

- **Federal Features** — Unitary Features
- **Division of powers — Seventh Schedule** — Residuary powers with Parliament (Art. 248)
- **Dual polity — separate Union & State executives/legislatures** — Single Constitution and single citizenship
- **Rajya Sabha safeguards State interests** — All-India Services ensure uniform administration
- **Independent judiciary for Centre-State disputes (Arts. 131, 136)** — Union's financial dominance; States depend on Finance Commission transfers
- **Rigid amendment procedure for federal provisions (Art. 368)** — Emergency provisions (Arts. 352, 356, 360) let the Union assume State functions

In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held federalism to be part of the basic structure, curbing arbitrary use of Article 356; yet in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963), it held Indian federalism not strictly comparable to classical federations, since Parliament can legislate even on State matters in defined situations. The Governor's-assent saga (2023–25): federalism tested in real time In State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu (8 April 2025), the Supreme Court held Governors cannot exercise a ‘pocket veto,’ set assent timelines, and deemed 10 pending Bills assented under Article 142. But on a Presidential Reference under Article 143, a five-judge Bench (20 November 2025, 2025 INSC 1333) recalibrated this: it held that courts cannot read fixed timelines into Articles 200/201 and that Governor/President discretion is largely non-justiciable, while still confirming a Governor cannot indefinitely ‘sit’ on a Bill without acting. This judicial oscillation itself illustrates the unresolved federal-unitary tension. AP-specific instance The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, bifurcating the State under Article 3, required only the State Assembly's non-binding opinion — Parliament could, and did, override it — a textbook illustration of ‘unitary in spirit’ territorial power.

## Conclusion

India's Constitution is thus consciously ‘holding together’ — federal enough to accommodate diversity, unitary enough to preserve unity in crises. The 2023-25 Governor-Bill litigation shows this balance is not settled once and for all but continuously renegotiated between courts, Centre and States — a live federalism suited to a country as vast and plural as India.

## Value addition
- Alfred Stepan's typology: the USA is a ‘coming together’ federation; India is a ‘holding together’ federation — a high-value conceptual line for a ‘Discuss’ answer.
- Delimitation, due after the 2026 freeze ends, worries southern States, including Andhra Pradesh, about reduced Lok Sabha representation despite better population control — a live federal-equity debate.
- The GST Council's three-fourths weighted voting (Centre 1/3, States 2/3 combined) is a rare instance of States holding a collective veto over the Centre.
- The November 2025 advisory opinion (2025 INSC 1333) was only the 16th Presidential Reference under Article 143 since 1950 — a rare constitutional event.
Q3:
## Introduction

The Basic Structure Doctrine, coined in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) and first actually applied just two years later in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), limits Parliament's Article 368 amending power by protecting core features like democracy, secularism, federalism and judicial review. Critics call it a ‘myth’ because it has no textual basis and its contents are entirely judge-defined.

## Why it is called a ‘myth’
- No explicit constitutional mention — the doctrine is a judicial invention, not a textual provision.
- The Supreme Court has never given an exhaustive list of what constitutes the basic structure, leaving its scope indeterminate.
- Seen by some as judicial overreach into Parliament's amending domain.
- Applied selectively — not every constitutional change is tested against it.

## Testing the claim against post-1973 amendments
- 39th Amendment (1975): Struck down in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain for immunising the Prime Minister's election from judicial review — the doctrine's founding proof of concept.
- 42nd Amendment (1976), the ‘Mini-Constitution’: Struck down in part by Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), which held the FR-DPSP balance and limited amending power to be basic features.
- 99th Amendment (2014): Struck down in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) for compromising judicial independence via the NJAC.
- 97th Amendment (2011): Partly struck down in Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021) for infringing State legislative competence over cooperatives.
- 103rd Amendment (2019, EWS reservation): By contrast, upheld 3:2 in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022) — economic-criteria reservation was held not to breach the basic structure, even while excluding SC/ST/OBC citizens from its ambit.

This mixed record — some amendments struck down, a comparably radical one (103rd) upheld — is precisely what fuels the ‘myth’ charge: outcomes appear to hinge on the Bench and era, not a fixed, predictable list.

## Conclusion

The Basic Structure Doctrine has undeniably blocked authoritarian drift (Indira Gandhi, Minerva Mills, NJAC), yet its judge-made, undefined and unevenly applied character keeps the ‘myth’ label alive. As then-CJI B.R. Gavai remarked in 2025 that rewriting the Constitution is ‘against democracy,’ the doctrine's paradox persists: an indispensable safeguard whose exact boundaries even the judiciary declines to fix in advance.

## Value addition
- Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), the pre-Kesavananda precursor, had held Fundamental Rights entirely un-amendable — a position Kesavananda later moderated into the basic structure formula.
- Justice Rohinton Nariman notes Parliament itself implicitly recognised the doctrine by amending Article 359(1) so Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended, even during an Emergency.
- I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007): even Ninth Schedule laws enacted after 1973 remain open to basic-structure review.
- The Supreme Court's November 2025 Presidential Reference on the Governor's powers (2025 INSC 1333) shows ‘federalism as basic structure’ remains a live, contested frontier.

## Introduction

Free and fair elections are the bedrock of India's parliamentary democracy and were held in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) to be part of the Constitution's basic structure — meaning not even a constitutional amendment can dilute them. The Election Commission of India (ECI), an independent constitutional authority under Article 324, is the institution that translates this promise into practice.

## Constitutional & judicial basis
- Articles 324–329: Vest superintendence, direction and control of elections in the ECI.
- Representation of the People Acts, 1950 & 1951: Regulate electoral rolls, qualifications/disqualifications and corrupt practices.
- Judicial interpretation: Mohinder Singh Gill v. CEC (1978) affirmed the ECI's plenary residuary powers; ADR (2002) and PUCL (2003) mandated candidates' asset/criminal disclosure; Subramanian Swamy v. ECI (2013) introduced VVPATs.

## Significant roles of the ECI
- Superintending poll schedules, symbols and deployment of security forces.
- Maintaining pure electoral rolls under Article 325.
- Enforcing the Model Code of Conduct against hate speech, paid news and misuse of official machinery.
- Curbing malpractice via cVIGIL, which resolved complaints with 98% accuracy within the target response time during the 2025 Delhi Assembly polls (ECI, 2025).
- Deploying EVM-VVPAT, webcasting and booth-wise turnout data for transparency.
- Voter outreach through SVEEP, and accessibility measures for PwD and elderly voters.

Current flashpoint: Special Intensive Revision (SIR) Since June 2025, the ECI has conducted a nationwide Special Intensive Revision (SIR) to purge deceased, duplicate and ineligible entries and enrol left-out citizens, beginning with Bihar and extending to Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Kerala, Gujarat and other States/UTs (ECI, Nov 2025). Challenged as risking mass disenfranchisement, the exercise was upheld on 27 May 2026 in Association for Democratic Reforms v. Election Commission of India, the Supreme Court holding it a valid exercise of the ECI's power under Article 324 read with Section 21(3) of the RPA, 1950, undertaken to protect the ‘integrity, accuracy and credibility’ of electoral rolls. Andhra Pradesh instance The 2024 Andhra Pradesh Assembly election (175 seats), held simultaneously with the Lok Sabha poll on 13 May 2024, recorded an 81.86% turnout (ECI, 2024); the ECI also took firm follow-up action against post-poll violence reported in the State, illustrating Model Code enforcement on the ground.

## Conclusion

Free and fair elections are thus not a policy preference but a non-negotiable, judicially protected constitutional guarantee. Through its constitutional authority, evolving technology and, most recently, the judicially affirmed SIR exercise, the ECI continues to safeguard electoral integrity — even as debates over roll-purification methods show that the mechanics of ‘free and fair’ remain a living, contested constitutional conversation.

## Value addition
- The ECI's Green Elections initiative, AI-based MCC monitoring, and expanded home voting for 80+/PwD electors show its evolving inclusive and environmental role.
- The ECI released 42 statistical reports for the 2024 Lok Sabha polls and 14 each for the simultaneous Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim Assembly elections (PIB, 2024) — a transparency-by-data initiative.
- Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) remains the origin point for treating free elections as basic structure.
- SIR 2025-26 was upheld by a Bench led by CJI Surya Kant, which also directed pan-India safeguards for the security of Booth Level Officers.

## Introduction

Moved by Jawaharlal Nehru as the Objectives Resolution in December 1946 and adopted on 26 November 1949, the Preamble is the Constitution's introductory declaration of its source, nature, objectives and date of adoption. N.A. Palkhivala famously called it the Constitution's 'identity card.' Its legal status, however, has been contested — and settled — in two landmark rulings four decades apart.

## Significance of the Preamble
- Declares the source of authority: 'We, the People of India' establishes popular sovereignty — the Constitution derives not from the Crown or the British Parliament but from Indians themselves, an assertion of decolonised self-rule.
- States the nature of the polity: 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic' — the words 'Socialist,' 'Secular' and 'Integrity' were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
- Sets the objectives: Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty, Equality and Fraternity — the sequence itself echoes the French Revolution, while the Justice formulation is drawn from the Russian Revolution.
- Serves as an interpretive key: Courts use it to resolve ambiguity; in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Preamble's ideals were treated as evidence of the Constitution's basic structure.
- Is amendable but not destructible: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Court held the Preamble amendable under Article 368, but not so as to destroy its basic features.
- **Issue** — Berubari Union Case (1960) · Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
- **Is the Preamble part of the Constitution?** — No — it is a key to the makers' minds, but not an operative part · Yes — it is an integral part of the Constitution
- **Can it be amended?** — Question did not arise · Yes, under Article 368, subject to basic structure
- **Is it a source of power?** — No — it confers no powers, imposes no limitations · Reaffirmed — it guides, but does not grant, power

Is the Preamble a source of constitutional power? No. Both Berubari and Kesavananda agree that the Preamble is declaratory, not substantive — it says what the Constitution seeks to achieve, not how power is conferred. Powers flow only from the operative Articles: legislative power from Articles 245–246 and the Seventh Schedule, executive power from Articles 53 and 154, judicial power from Articles 124 and 214. Nor is the Preamble by itself enforceable in court. Its authority is directive and moral, not the fount of legal competence.

Current relevance In Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (25 November 2024), the Supreme Court dismissed petitions seeking deletion of 'socialist' and 'secular,' holding that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 extends to the Preamble, that both terms have acquired settled meanings in Indian jurisprudence, and that the Constitution is a living document — a ruling that simultaneously reaffirms the Preamble's amenability and its constitutional centrality.

## Conclusion

The Preamble is the Constitution's philosophical charter — it names the source of authority, declares the polity's character and fixes its goals — but it is not the legal source of constitutional power, which rests in the operative provisions. Judicially, it has travelled from being merely 'a key to the makers' minds' to being an integral, amendable yet basic-structure-protected part of the Constitution, and remains its most quoted moral compass.

## Value addition
- Only the 42nd Amendment, 1976 has ever amended the Preamble — inserting 'Socialist,' 'Secular' and 'Integrity.'
- K.M. Munshi described the Preamble as the 'horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic'; Thakur Das Bhargava called it the Constitution's 'most precious part' and its 'soul.'
- Sir Ernest Barker opened his Principles of Social and Political Theory by quoting India's Preamble — a rare instance of an Indian text framing Western political theory.
- In LIC of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995), the Court used the Preamble's socialist ideal to read social justice obligations into state instrumentalities.
- The Preamble carries the date 26 November 1949, though most provisions came into force on 26 January 1950.

## Introduction

Article 1 deliberately describes India as a 'Union of States,' not a federation — Ambedkar explained the phrase signified that the Union is indestructible and that States derive their existence from it, not the reverse. India therefore possesses the essential machinery of federalism — dual polity, division of powers, written supreme Constitution, independent judiciary — but operates it with a pronounced central tilt.

## Federal features present
- Dual polity and division of powers: The Seventh Schedule allocates subjects across three Lists; at present the Union List has 98 subjects, the State List 59 and the Concurrent List 52 (Laxmikanth, 6th ed.). States legislate autonomously on police, public health and agriculture.
- Written, supreme, partly rigid Constitution: Federal provisions can be amended only with ratification by half the State legislatures (Article 368).
- Independent judiciary and bicameralism: Article 131 gives the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction over Centre-State disputes; the Rajya Sabha (Article 80) represents States in Parliament.

## Unitary features that qualify it
- Union List outweighs the State List, and residuary powers rest with Parliament (Article 248) — the reverse of the USA.
- Single Constitution and single citizenship (Articles 5–11), unlike the USA's dual citizenship.
- Emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360) can convert the federal system into a unitary one.
- Governors are appointed by the President (Article 155); All-India Services (Article 312) are centrally controlled.
- Parliament can alter State boundaries, names and areas by simple majority (Article 3) — as it did through the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, over the objection of the then State Assembly.

Judicial verdict and evolving practice In State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963), the Court held States are not sovereign in the classical federal sense; in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), it declared federalism part of the basic structure, curbing misuse of Article 356. More recently the Court has expanded State space: in Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India (25 July 2024), a nine-judge Bench held 8:1 that royalty is not a tax and upheld States' power to tax mineral rights and mineral-bearing land under Entries 49 and 50 of the State List, overruling India Cement (1990). Institutionally, NITI Aayog (cooperative federalism through the Governing Council and Aspirational Districts Programme) and the GST Council (Article 279A, three-fourths weighted voting) show federalism operating through negotiation rather than command.

## Conclusion

India is therefore a federation in substance but not of the classical American type — a 'quasi-federal' polity in K.C. Wheare's phrase, or in D.D. Basu's formulation, neither purely federal nor purely unitary. The Constitution supplies federal machinery; how federal India actually is depends at any moment on judicial interpretation, fiscal arrangements and the political balance between Centre and States.

## Value addition
- Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly: the term 'Union' was chosen deliberately because the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among States, and no State has a right to secede.
- The Sarkaria Commission (1988) recommended sparing use of Article 356 and revival of the Inter-State Council; the Punchhi Commission (2010) proposed 'localised emergency' in place of State-wide President's Rule.
- State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024) permitted States to sub-classify Scheduled Castes for reservation, expanding State legislative space in social justice.
- India is often classed as a 'holding together' federation (Alfred Stepan), unlike the USA's 'coming together' model.

## Introduction

The framers built centripetal safeguards into the Constitution — residuary powers with Parliament, an appointed Governor, All-India Services, and emergency provisions permitting a unitary conversion. Yet seven decades on, federalism has not merely survived but deepened. The explanation lies less in constitutional text than in judicial interpretation, party-system change and the growth of negotiating institutions.

## The unitary pull
- Union List dominance, residuary powers (Article 248), and the Centre's fiscal pre-eminence with conditional grants under Article 282.
- Emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360); Article 356 was used over 100 times before 1994, most notoriously in 1977 and 1980 when nine State governments were dismissed at a stroke.
- Integrated administration through Governors (Articles 153–156) and All-India Services (Article 312).

## Why federalism nonetheless survived
- Judicial guardianship: S.R. Bommai (1994) made Article 356 proclamations justiciable and mandated a floor test, collapsing its casual use. In Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India (July 2024), a nine-judge Bench upheld States' power to tax mineral rights; State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024) permitted State sub-classification of SCs.
- Party-system transformation: The end of one-party dominance and the rise of regional parties from the late 1980s turned Centre-State relations from hierarchical to bargained; coalition governments (1989–2014) institutionalised State leverage, and regional parties remain pivotal in current NDA coalition arithmetic.
- Institutionalised negotiation: The Finance Commission (Article 280), GST Council (Article 279A, with States holding two-thirds of the weighted vote), Inter-State Council (Article 263) and NITI Aayog's Governing Council create standing forums where States bargain rather than petition.
- Fiscal stability of States: The 14th FC raised devolution sharply to 42%; the 15th set it at 41%; the 16th Finance Commission (Chair: Dr. Arvind Panagariya), whose report was tabled in Parliament on 1 February 2026 for 2026-31, retained the States' share of the divisible pool at 41% — continuity that preserved State fiscal space.

Live frontiers The Governor's assent controversy shows the balance still being negotiated: State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu (8 April 2025) barred the pocket veto and set timelines, but the Supreme Court's advisory opinion on the Presidential Reference (20 November 2025, 2025 INSC 1333) held that courts cannot read fixed timelines into Articles 200/201, while affirming that a Governor cannot indefinitely refuse to act. Delimitation after the 2026 freeze, and southern States' concern — Andhra Pradesh included — that demographic performance should not cost them Lok Sabha seats, is the next federal test.

## Conclusion

Federalism survived in India not because the Constitution guaranteed it but because courts protected it, politics demanded it, and institutions gradually made bargaining the default. The unitary provisions remain fully intact on paper; what has changed is the political and judicial cost of using them. The task now is to make negotiation more transparent and time-bound — through a functioning Inter-State Council and clearer fiscal rules — so that federal balance rests on institutions rather than on political arithmetic alone.

## Value addition
- K.C. Wheare: the Constitution of India is quasi-federal, not strictly federal. D.D. Basu: neither purely federal nor unitary, but a combination of both.
- Cesses and surcharges are excluded from the divisible pool, a standing State grievance since they reduce the effective share below the headline 41%.
- Article 356 usage has fallen dramatically post-Bommai (1994) — the single clearest empirical proof that judicial doctrine can restrain constitutional text.
- Punchhi Commission (2010) recommended a 'localised emergency' confined to a district or region instead of dismissing an entire State government.

## Introduction

The Inter-State Council is a constitutional body created under Article 263, which permits the President to establish such a Council whenever it appears that the public interest would be served. Acting on the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation, it was constituted by Presidential Order dated 28 May 1990 and functions under the Ministry of Home Affairs through a dedicated Inter-State Council Secretariat.

## Formation and composition
- **Element** — Detail
- **Constitutional basis** — Article 263 — Presidential Order, not a statute; hence not a permanent body
- **Trigger** — Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State Relations (1983–88) recommendation
- **Date of establishment** — Presidential Order, 28 May 1990 (V.P. Singh government)
- **Chairman** — Prime Minister
- **Members** — CMs of all States, CMs of UTs with legislatures, Administrators of other UTs, and six Union Cabinet Ministers nominated by the PM
- **Standing Committee** — Chaired by the Union Home Minister; select Union Ministers and Chief Ministers; does preparatory and follow-up work
- **Secretariat** — Inter-State Council Secretariat, Ministry of Home Affairs (also services the five Zonal Councils)

## Functions under Article 263
- Clause (a) — Inquiry into disputes: Advisory inquiry into disputes that have arisen between States; distinct from the Supreme Court's binding original jurisdiction (Article 131) and water-dispute tribunals (Article 262).
- Clause (b) — Investigation and discussion: Examines subjects in which some or all States, or the Union and one or more States, have a common interest — internal security, GST implementation, disaster management.
- Clause (c) — Recommendations: Recommends measures for better coordination of policy and action; recommendations are persuasive, not binding, which is the source of both its flexibility and its weakness.
- Oversight: The Standing Committee monitors implementation of decisions and processes recommendations of commissions such as Sarkaria and Punchhi.

## Developments in recent years
- Reconstitution (November 2024): MHA reconstituted the ISC with the Prime Minister as Chairman, nine Union Ministers as members and thirteen as permanent invitees; the Standing Committee was reconstituted under the Union Home Minister, including the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh among eight State CMs.
- ISC dormancy: Despite reconstitution, no full session has been held since the 11th meeting on 16 July 2016, which had considered the Punchhi Commission recommendations, Aadhaar-based subsidy delivery and education outcomes.
- Zonal Councils as the active mechanism: Southern Zonal Council met at Chennai on 31 January 2025; the Central Zonal Council's 25th meeting was held at Varanasi on 24 June 2025 (PIB, June 2025); the Eastern Zonal Council met at Ranchi in July 2025 and the Northern Zonal Council at Faridabad in November 2025.
- Measurable performance: Zonal Council meetings rose from 25 during 2004–2014 to 63 during 2014–2025, with the issue-resolution rate improving from 43% to 64% (Ministry of Home Affairs / PIB, 2025).
- Andhra Pradesh-specific: At the 30th Southern Zonal Council meeting (Thiruvananthapuram, September 2022), 26 issues were discussed and 9 resolved; of the 17 carried forward, 9 concerned Andhra Pradesh's reorganisation — asset division, Polavaram and resource-gap funding (PIB, 2022).

## Conclusion

The Inter-State Council was designed as the Constitution's premier forum for executive federalism, and its 1990 creation, 2024 reconstitution and active Secretariat show the architecture is in place. What is missing is regularity: with no full sitting since 2016, the burden of coordination has shifted to Zonal Councils. Mandating periodic meetings, publishing action-taken reports and giving the Secretariat research capacity would restore the ISC to the role Sarkaria envisaged.

## Value addition
- Zonal Councils: Northern (Haryana, HP, Punjab, Rajasthan, Delhi, J&K, Ladakh, Chandigarh); Central (UP, MP, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand); Eastern (Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal); Western (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu); Southern (AP, Telangana, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry).
- Zonal Councils are chaired by the Union Home Minister; the Chief Ministers of member States serve as Vice-Chairman by annual rotation.
- Article 262 empowers Parliament to bar courts from inter-State water disputes — hence the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, amended in 2019 to propose a single permanent tribunal.
- The ISC is a non-permanent constitutional body: since it exists by Presidential Order rather than statute, it can be reconstituted or left dormant at executive discretion.

## Introduction

India's quasi-federal design creates a structural mismatch: States shoulder the bulk of welfare and developmental functions, while the Union commands the more buoyant tax handles. This vertical fiscal imbalance is not accidental – it lets the Centre pursue macroeconomic stability and inter-State equity – but it leaves States perennially dependent on transfers, making the “functions with States, resources with Centre” critique substantially valid, though partially corrected each Finance Commission cycle.

Functional load on States: The State List's 66 subjects (public order, police, health, agriculture, irrigation, local government) force States to execute most welfare delivery. States' consolidated gross fiscal deficit stood at 3.3% of GDP in 2025-26, driven largely by committed revenue spending on salaries, pensions and subsidies (RBI, State Finances: A Study of Budgets of 2025-26, January 2026). Resource concentration: The Union List's 97 subjects give Parliament the more elastic sources – corporate tax, customs, and (via the GST Council) a decisive say over the common consumption tax. Articles 268–272 and 275 make States reliant on devolution and grants-in-aid. Corrective architecture, updated: The 16th Finance Commission (Chair: Dr Arvind Panagariya) submitted its report to the President on 17 November 2025; it was tabled in Parliament on 1 February 2026 alongside the Union Budget, and the Government has retained States' vertical share at 41% of the divisible pool, unchanged from the 15th FC (PIB, 1 February 2026). Significantly, the 16th FC has discontinued Revenue Deficit Grants and State-/sector-specific grants that had cushioned deficit States – a shift from “entitlement” to “compliance/performance”-based transfers. AP-specific instance: Andhra Pradesh was among the States that received the Post-Devolution Revenue Deficit Grant under the 15th FC to help meet AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 resource-gap commitments (PIB, 2022). With RDG now discontinued and AP's divisible-pool share rising only marginally, the State's reliance on its own resource mobilisation and central capex loans is set to grow further.

Suggested exam diagram – a quick two-column comparison table:

- **Feature** — 15th FC (2021-26) · 16th FC (2026-31)
- **Vertical devolution** — 41% of divisible pool · 41% (retained – PIB, Feb 2026)
- **Revenue Deficit Grant** — Recommended to States incl. AP · Discontinued (16th FC Report, 2025)
- **Key new criterion** — Tax & fiscal effort (2.5%) · Contribution to GDP (10%)
- **AP's divisible-pool share** — ≈4.05% · ≈4.22% (marginal rise)

The Constitution deliberately concentrates resources with the Union for reasons of macro-stability and equalisation, but this has hardened into a chronic vertical imbalance. While Finance Commission devolution and GST partially bridge the gap, the 16th FC's compliance-driven shift raises the stakes for fiscally stressed States like Andhra Pradesh. Rationalising CSS, protecting untied transfers, and honouring reorganisation-linked commitments are essential to keep cooperative federalism fiscally credible.

## Value addition
- 16th FC's “grand bargain”: States accept the status-quo 41% share if the Centre merges more cesses/surcharges into the divisible pool (16th FC Report, 2025-31).

## Introduction

Cooperative federalism is a governance model in which the Union and States function as partners, not rivals, in policy formulation and implementation, pooling resources and expertise for shared national goals. In India's asymmetric federal structure, where the Centre holds constitutional primacy, cooperative mechanisms are what make federalism workable in practice rather than merely a paper guarantee.

Definition & features: Shared policy formulation, joint implementation (e.g., PMGSY, Swachh Bharat Mission), institutionalised dialogue platforms, and formula-based resource sharing. Constitutional basis: The Concurrent List enables joint legislative competence; Article 282 lets both levels make grants for public purposes; Articles 263 and 280 institutionalise coordination and devolution. Institutional architecture, current: NITI Aayog's Governing Council – its 10th meeting, chaired by the Prime Minister on 24 May 2025 at Bharat Mandapam on the theme “Viksit Rajya for Viksit Bharat@2047” – was attended by 24 States and 7 UTs, including Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu (NITI Aayog, May 2025), showing States actively shaping national vision documents. The GST Council (Art. 279A) takes rate decisions largely by consensus, embodying fiscal cooperative federalism; Zonal Councils, including the Southern Zonal Council (Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry), resolve inter-State and regional issues. Fiscal cooperation, updated: The 16th Finance Commission's report (submitted 17 November 2025, tabled in Parliament 1 February 2026) retained the 41% vertical devolution and introduced a new “contribution to GDP” criterion (PIB, February 2026) – evidence that fiscal federalism keeps evolving through consultative Finance Commission cycles rather than unilateral central diktat. Judicial recognition: In S.R. Bommai (1994), the Supreme Court held federalism to be part of the basic structure, reinforcing cooperative rather than confrontational Centre–State conduct.

Suggested exam diagram – a classification table of institutions:

- **Institution** — Constitutional/Legal Basis · Function
- **Inter-State Council** — Article 263 · Investigates & discusses Centre-State/inter-State disputes
- **Finance Commission** — Article 280 · Vertical & horizontal tax devolution, grants-in-aid
- **GST Council** — Article 279A · Consensus-based indirect-tax rate setting
- **NITI Aayog Governing Council** — Cabinet resolution, 2015 · Shared vision, Viksit Bharat/Rajya planning

- **Institution** — Constitutional/Legal Basis · Function
- **Zonal Councils** — States Reorganisation Act, 1956 · Regional coordination (AP in Southern Zonal Council)

India's federalism, though unitary-tilted in structure, functions cooperatively in practice through constitutional provisions, fiscal devolution and standing institutions like NITI Aayog, the GST Council and Zonal Councils. States such as Andhra Pradesh actively use these platforms – from Governing Council meetings to the Southern Zonal Council – making cooperative federalism a practical, evolving necessity rather than a static ideal.

## Introduction

Articles 256 to 263 in Part XI of the Constitution govern administrative relations between the Union and the States, ensuring policy coherence within India's quasi-federal design. While States enjoy executive autonomy over State List subjects, the Union retains directive and supervisory powers to preserve national unity. Water, though a State subject (Entry 17, List II), routinely triggers inter-State friction, for which Article 262 provides a distinct constitutional mechanism of adjudication.

Administrative Relations between Union and States — reproduce as a flowchart: Executive Power Distribution → Centre's Directive Powers → Cooperative Mechanisms → Emergency Control.

- Distribution of Executive Power: Union executive power runs coextensive with Parliament's legislative power (mainly the Union List); States exercise it over the State List; on Concurrent List matters, Union executive direction prevails in conflict.
- Centre's Directive Powers: Article 256 obliges States to comply with Union laws; Article 257 lets the Union direct States on matters of national/military importance (communication networks, railway protection); non-compliance can trigger Article 365, opening the route to President's Rule under Article 356.
- Cooperative Mechanisms: All-India Services (IAS/IPS/IFS) preserve administrative uniformity; the Inter-State Council (Art. 263) and Zonal Councils offer deliberative platforms; NITI Aayog enables Centre–State consultation on planning.
- Emergency Control: National Emergency (Art. 352) lets the Union direct States on any matter; President's Rule (Art. 356) and Financial Emergency (Art. 360) further expand central control.

Resolution of Inter-State Water Disputes (reproduce as a 3-step flow: Negotiation → Dispute Resolution Committee → Water Disputes Tribunal):

- Article 262 bars ordinary courts from adjudicating notified river disputes; Parliament enacted the Inter-State River Water Disputes (ISRWD) Act, 1956.
- The 2019 Amendment envisaged a single permanent Tribunal with multiple benches to replace ad hoc bodies; however, implementation remains partial — the Ministry of Jal Shakti records four active tribunals (Krishna-II, Ravi-Beas, Vansadhara and Mahadayi/Mahanadi) functioning individually alongside five already-dissolved ones (PIB, December 2025).
- AP illustration: The Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal-II, constituted in 2004, was given fresh Terms of Reference after the 2014 bifurcation to adjudicate the Krishna-water dispute between Andhra Pradesh and Telangana; its term was most recently extended by one year to 31 July 2026 (PIB, July 2025). Godavari waters remain without a final sharing agreement between the two States (PIB, Apex Council meeting, October 2020).
- The Krishna and Godavari River Management Boards (KRMB/GRMB), constituted under Sections 85–87 of the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 and given project-wise jurisdiction in July 2021, regulate specified projects under an Apex Council chaired by the Union Jal Shakti Minister — showing how administrative relations and water-dispute machinery intersect in a bifurcated State.

## Conclusion

Administrative relations under Part XI let India's federal structure function with unity of purpose, while Article 262 offers a specialised, court-excluding route for inter-State water conflicts. Yet persistent delays — the Krishna dispute has run for over two decades — show that statutory timelines alone cannot substitute for political will. A genuinely single, depoliticised, data-transparent tribunal remains essential to operationalise the spirit of cooperative federalism.

## Introduction

Though India is described as a Union of States rather than a strict federation, the Constitution deliberately tilts the balance towards the Centre. Several provisions let the Union legislate on, direct, fund, or even take over State administration under defined conditions. These instruments — legislative, administrative, financial and emergency — are meant to safeguard national unity, not to routinely override State autonomy, as the Supreme Court clarified in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994).

- Reproduce as a 4-box classification chart: Legislative
- Administrative
- Financial
- Emergency.
- Legislative Control: Article 248 read with Entry 97 (Union List) gives Parliament residuary power; Article 249 lets Parliament legislate on a State subject if the Rajya Sabha passes a two-thirds resolution “in national interest”; Article 250 extends this during a National Emergency; Article 253 empowers Parliament to legislate on any subject to implement international treaties.
- Administrative Control: Articles 256–257 let the Union direct States on compliance and on matters of national/military importance; Article 355 obliges the Union to protect States from external aggression and internal disturbance; Article 312 permits creation of All-India Services, binding State cadres to central service rules.
- Financial Control: Articles 275 and 282 allow conditional Union grants-in-aid; Article 279A gives the Union a decisive voice in GST Council decisions — State fiscal autonomy is pooled rather than eliminated.
- Emergency Provisions: Article 356 allows President's Rule when constitutional machinery fails; Article 360 permits Union direction over State finances during a Financial Emergency.

Current illustration: President's Rule was imposed in Manipur on 13 February 2025 under Article 356(1) following a constitutional breakdown after the Chief Minister's resignation; Parliament approved a further six-month extension from 13 August 2025 under Article 356(4) (PIB, 2025) — the requirement of parliamentary ratification itself illustrates the constitutional checks built into this “control” power.

AP-specific instance: Article 371D — inserted by the 32nd Amendment (1973) and extended to residuary Andhra Pradesh and Telangana after the 2014 bifurcation — lets the President mandate local cadres and reservation in

State employment/education, and constitute a special Administrative Tribunal for service matters. The Presidential-Order framework required fresh State legislation after the ten-year sunset written into the AP Reorganisation Act, and the resulting local-candidate rules were recently upheld by the Supreme Court in State of Telangana v. Kalluri Naga Narasimha Abhiram Medical College (2025).

## Conclusion

These provisions confirm that Indian federalism carries a deliberate unitary bias, activated to protect national integrity rather than to subordinate States routinely. Judicial review — from Bommai to the 2025 Article 371D ruling — has consistently required that such powers rest on objective, justiciable grounds, ensuring that “control” does not slide into arbitrary central overreach.

## Value addition
- Sarkaria (1988) & Punchhi (2010) Commissions: recommended Article 356 be used as a “measure of last resort,” with a prior warning to the State government.
- Bommai case (1994): made presidential satisfaction under Art. 356 subject to judicial review and floor-test verification, checking arbitrary use.
- Article 371D is constitutionally unique — the only provision creating a permanent, State-specific Union-ordained cadre/reservation and tribunal architecture, distinct from the general Article 371 family covering the North-East and Maharashtra/Gujarat.
- GST Council (Art. 279A): decisions by three-fourths weighted majority illustrate “pooled” rather than unilateral central control — a softer, cooperative form of Union influence.

## Introduction

The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, in force from 24 April 1993, gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs), operationalising Article 40 of the Directive Principles and Mahatma Gandhi's vision of Gram Swaraj. By mandating elections, reservation and fiscal devolution across over 2.5 lakh Gram Panchayats, it converted local self-government from an administrative convenience into a constitutionally protected third tier of democracy.

Key Provisions (reproduce as a labelled diagram): Part IX (Arts. 243–243O) + 11th Schedule (29 subjects) → three-tier structure (Village → Intermediate → Zilla Parishad) → 5-year term, elections via State Election Commission (Art. 243K) → 1/3rd reservation for women, proportionate for SC/ST → State Finance Commission (Art. 243I) → District Planning Committee.

## Significance in Strengthening Grassroots Democracy
- Decentralised Governance: Kerala's People's Plan Campaign remains the classic model of PRI-led participatory budgeting.
- Inclusive Participation: Women's reservation produced leaders like Chhavi Rajawat (Rajasthan); nationally, women now hold about 1.4–1.45 million PRI seats — roughly 46% of all elected representatives, well above the mandatory one-third (PIB, 2024–25).
- Accountability: Social audits under MGNREGS in Andhra Pradesh remain a benchmark for PRI-driven transparency.
- Data-driven Monitoring: The Ministry of Panchayati Raj's Panchayat Advancement Index (PAI) 2.0, released on National Panchayati Raj Day (24 April 2026), scored 2.6 lakh Gram Panchayats across 33 States/UTs on 9 SDG-linked themes, with 3,635 GPs emerging as “Front Runners” (PIB, 2026) — giving grassroots governance an evidence-based report card for the first time.
- Fiscal Deepening: The 16th Finance Commission recommended Rs. 4,35,236 crore for Rural Local Bodies for 2026–31, against just Rs. 65,160 crore under the 13th Finance Commission (PIB, 2025) — a near seven-fold rise within a decade.
- AP Illustration: Andhra Pradesh was among the original pilot States of the SVAMITVA scheme (2020–21) and has achieved full drone-survey coverage, giving rural households legally recognised property cards (PIB, April 2025); the State also reorganised Gram Panchayat staffing and grading through G.O.Ms.No.91 (4 November 2025).

Challenges: incomplete devolution of the “3 Fs” — Funds, Functions, Functionaries; capacity gaps among elected representatives; political and bureaucratic interference.

## Conclusion

The 73rd Amendment has institutionalised participatory democracy at a scale unmatched globally, converting formal representation into measurable outcomes through tools like PAI. Yet its promise remains only partly realised: unless States complete genuine devolution of funds, functions and functionaries, Panchayats will continue to implement rather than author local development — the next frontier of Gram Swaraj.

## Introduction

The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992–93) inserted Parts IX and IX-A, converting Panchayats and Municipalities from creatures of state statute into a constitutionally mandated third tier with assured elections, reservations and finance commissions. Their real test, however, is not the creation of structures but the transfer of the ‘3Fs’ — functions, funds and functionaries. Measured on that test, the MoPR–IIPA Status of Devolution to Panchayats report puts national devolution at just 43.9% (PIB, February 2025): a tier that is widely elected but narrowly empowered.

## Where implementation has genuinely delivered
- Representation at unmatched scale: India has 2,62,738 PRIs with roughly 31 lakh elected representatives, of whom 14.5 lakh (46%) are women, and 21 States/2 UTs now legislate 50% reservation (PIB, MoPR, 2025–26). Reservation has thus moved from a constitutional floor to a political norm.
- Fiscal deepening: the per-capita grant to rural local bodies has risen from ₹176 under the 13th FC to ₹953 under the 16th FC, which awarded ₹4,35,236 crore to RLBs for 2026–31 — an 84% jump (PIB, MoPR, July 2026). Panchayats are no longer token spenders.
- Auditable local finance: eGramSwaraj integrated with PFMS, AuditOnline, SabhaSaar (used by 1.17 lakh GPs as on 11.03.2026) and SVAMITVA (3.10 crore property cards prepared) have made panchayat accounts traceable and created a property-tax base (PIB, March 2026).
- Outcome measurement: the Panchayat Advancement Index 2.0 scored 2,59,867 GPs (97.3% participation) across nine LSDG themes, with 3,635 rated Front Runners (PIB, April 2026) — shifting monitoring from expenditure to results.

## Where implementation has stalled
- Devolution is permissive, not obligatory: Articles 243G and 243W say the legislature “may” endow local bodies with powers, so outcomes diverge sharply — Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu top the Devolution Index while Andhra Pradesh sits in the 50–55 ‘medium’ band (PIB, February 2025).
- The urban tier is the weaker twin: Metropolitan Planning Committees (Art. 243ZE) remain largely unconstituted and most States have not vested ward delimitation in the State Election Commission, so parastatal development authorities — not elected Mayors — effectively plan cities.
- Financial dependence persists: own-source revenue remains thin, which is why the MoPR is now drafting a Model OSR Rules Framework and has tied ₹87,048 crore of 16th FC performance grants to OSR and audited accounts (PIB, July 2026).
- Proxy representation: the ‘Sarpanch-pati’ practice hollows out women’s reservation; following a Supreme Court direction of 06.07.2023 an Advisory Committee under Shri Sushil Kumar was constituted to examine it (PIB, MoPR, 2024).
- **Constitutional promise** — Delivered (Form) · Pending (Substance)
- **Regular elections (Art. 243E/243U)** — Held across 2.6 lakh PRIs · 61% of ULBs face delayed polls
- **Funds (Art. 243I/280(3)(bb))** — ₹953 per capita, 16th FC · OSR negligible; grant-dependent
- **Functions (11th/12th Schedule)** — Activity mapping begun · Devolution only 43.9%
- **Functionaries** — Staff recruited under RGSA · Control still with line departments

## Conclusion

Judged by form, the amendments are a success: elections are regular, representation is the most inclusive in the world, and grants are at a historic high. Judged by substance, devolution has plateaued at 43.9% precisely because Articles 243G and 243W left it to State discretion. Effectiveness will follow only when a Framework Law makes activity mapping mandatory (2nd ARC, 6th Report), State Finance Commissions are constituted on time, and urban bodies acquire a directly accountable executive.

## Introduction

The phrase echoes the 1949 anthology The God That Failed, in which disillusioned writers renounced a creed they had once revered. Applied to Panchayati Raj, the charge is that an institution invested with Gandhian moral authority — Gram Swaraj — produced ritual elections without real power. Evaluating it fairly requires separating a failure of design from a failure of delivery. The evidence points to the latter: Panchayati Raj is not a failed god, but an under-empowered one.

## The case for the charge
- Under-powered by constitutional design: Article 243G merely permits the State legislature to endow Panchayats with powers. Optional devolution has produced a national Devolution Index of only 43.9%, with the functions and finances dimensions lagging worst (MoPR–IIPA, PIB, February 2025).
- Fiscal impotence: PRIs subsist on Finance Commission and State grants with negligible own-source revenue — a gap so structural that the MoPR is itself drafting a Model OSR Rules Framework (PIB, July 2026). A government that cannot tax cannot prioritise.
- Capture and proxy rule: the ‘Sarpanch-pati’ phenomenon substitutes male relatives for elected women; the Supreme Court’s order of 06.07.2023 prompted the Sushil Kumar Advisory Committee on proxy representation (MoPR, 2024).
- Bureaucratic supremacy: line departments retain control over staff and schemes, leaving Panchayats as implementing agencies. The 2nd ARC’s own colloquium concluded that the three-tier system is “over-structured and under-powered”.

## The case against the charge
- A representational revolution: 14.5 lakh women out of roughly 31 lakh elected representatives (46%) — a scale of transfer of political power to women unmatched anywhere in the world, sustained across three decades (PIB, February 2025).
- Finance has moved decisively: per-capita RLB grants rose from ₹176 (13th FC) to ₹953 (16th FC), and 95% of the 15th FC’s allocation (₹2,82,632 crore of ₹2,97,555 crore) was actually released — the highest release ratio for local bodies under any Finance Commission (PIB, July 2026).
- Demonstrated outcomes, not just structures: under PAI 2.0, 3,635 GPs are Front Runners (PIB, April 2026). AP’s Bokkasam Palem GP (Tirupati) recorded zero crimes against women, zero maternal and neonatal deaths, zero child marriages and 100% institutional deliveries over five years (PIB Vijayawada, May 2026) — a failed god does not produce this.

## Charge Evidence for Evidence against Verdict

No real power Devolution 43.9%; Art. 243G permissive

Activity mapping under way in leading States

## Largely upheld

No money OSR negligible ₹176 → ₹953 per capita Partly rebutted

No genuine representation

Sarpanch-pati 46% women; SC-mandated committee

## Contested

No delivery Uneven across States 3,635 Front Runner GPs (PAI 2.0) Rebutted

## Conclusion

The metaphor mistakes an unfinished transfer of power for a discredited idea. Panchayati Raj has succeeded almost everywhere the Constitution made a duty mandatory — elections, reservations, State Election Commissions — and underperformed precisely where the Constitution left devolution discretionary. The corrective is therefore legal rather than theological: mandatory activity mapping, timely State Finance Commissions, real taxation powers and a Framework Law as urged by the 2nd ARC. A god not yet given its powers cannot fairly be said to have failed.

## Introduction

The Fourteenth Finance Commission (2015–20), chaired by Dr Y.V. Reddy, marked a doctrinal turn in the treatment of the third tier. It deliberately abandoned the expression ‘local bodies’ in favour of ‘local governments’, and it routed money to the Gram Panchayat itself rather than through intermediate tiers. That principle — untied, formula-based money delivered directly to the elected village government — remains the benchmark against which the 15th and 16th Commissions are judged.

## Recommendations of the 14th FC on devolution to PRIs
- Enlarged fiscal space: the States’ share of the divisible pool was raised from 32% to 42% — the largest single increase ever recommended — widening the pool from which States finance Panchayats and reducing dependence on tied central schemes.
- Direct grant to Gram Panchayats: ₹2,00,292 crore for 2015–20, equal to roughly 3% of the divisible pool against 2.5% under the 13th FC. Crucially, only Gram Panchayats constituted under Part IX were eligible — intermediate and district Panchayats were bypassed, forcing money to the point of delivery.

The 13th FC’s six conditionalities were relaxed so that weaker Panchayats could actually qualify — incentive rather than punishment.

Political parties are registered by the Election Commission under Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, but recognised under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968. Recognition is not honorific: it determines who holds a reserved symbol, how many star campaigners a party may field, and access to free broadcast time on Doordarshan and All India Radio. - **Criteria (any one)** — (i) 6% of valid votes in Lok Sabha or Assembly polls in 4 or more States plus 4 Lok Sabha seats; or (ii) 2% of Lok Sabha seats (11 seats) from at least 3 States; or (iii) recognised as a State party in 4 or more States. · (i) 6% of valid votes in the State Assembly poll plus 2 Assembly seats; or (ii) 6% of valid votes in the State at a Lok Sabha poll plus 1 Lok Sabha seat; or (iii) 3% of Assembly seats or 3 seats, whichever is higher; or (iv) 1 Lok Sabha seat for every 25 allotted to the State; or (v) 8% of total valid votes in the State (added 2011), even without winning a seat.
- **Symbol** — Reserved across the whole of India · Reserved only within that State
- **Present list** — BJP, INC, BSP, CPI(M), AAP, NPP (6) · 67 parties — e.g. TDP, YSRCP and Jana Sena in Andhra Pradesh; DMK, BJD, JD(U)
- **Review** — Since 2016, status is reviewed after two consecutive elections, not after every election — a cushion against a single bad result. · Same rule applies; recognised parties (national and State alike) may name 40 star campaigners against 20 for unrecognised parties (Sec. 77, RP Act).

## Features of the Indian party system
- A multi-party system with a shifting core: India has moved from Congress dominance (1952–67) through fragmentation and coalition (1989–2014) to a BJP-centred system since 2014 — yet State politics remains genuinely multipolar, so the national and State party systems no longer mirror each other.
- Federalisation of party competition: regional parties are decisive actors, not junior partners — they shape outcomes in the Rajya Sabha, the GST Council and Chief Ministers’ conferences. Andhra Pradesh’s TDP illustrates how a State party can determine national coalition arithmetic while retaining a purely regional base.
- Identity and welfare-based mobilisation: parties organise around language, caste, region and welfare delivery — the DMK around Tamil identity, the BRS around Telangana statehood, the BSP around Dalit assertion. This has widened participation rather than narrowing it, drawing previously excluded groups into electoral politics.
- Personalisation and defection: leader-centred organisations with weak internal democracy coexist uneasily with the Tenth Schedule’s anti-defection regime, upheld in Kihoto Hollohan (1992); factional splits are adjudicated by the ECI under Para 15 of the Symbols Order.
- Tightening regulation: the Commission delisted 808 registered-unrecognised parties in two rounds in 2025 for having contested no election since 2019 (PIB, September 2025), and now holds structured consultations with all recognised parties — 4,719 such meetings were held in a single month in 2025 (PIB, April 2025).

## Conclusion

The national–regional distinction is a legal classification of electoral reach, not a hierarchy of legitimacy: a State party can govern a State of 50 million while a national party governs none. Its real significance is federal — it institutionalises the reality that Indian democracy is contested simultaneously at two levels. Whether the system stays representative as well as competitive now depends on internal party democracy, transparent funding after the Supreme Court struck down the Electoral Bonds Scheme in 2024, and continued cleaning of the register.

- Landmark judgments:ADR v. Union of India (February 2024) struck down the Electoral Bonds Scheme as violative of the right to information under Article 19(1)(a); Kihoto Hollohan v. ADR (2002) mandated disclosure of candidates’ criminal, financial and educational antecedents.
- Andhra Pradesh angle (paper-specific): TDP (founded 1982), YSRCP (2011) and Jana Sena (2014) are ECI-recognised State parties; AP is a textbook case of a State where no national party has formed a government on its own since 1983 — useful evidence for the federalisation argument.

## Introduction

Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission of India (ECI), and Section 61A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 supplies the statutory authority for voting by machine. India’s EVM journey therefore runs on two tracks – a technological one, from the first experimental use in Kerala in 1982 to a fully EVM-VVPAT system, and a legal one, in which every expansion of the machine’s role has been tested and refined by the Supreme Court. The current controversy is not about whether the machine can count, but about whether the citizen can independently verify that it counted correctly – a question of demonstrable rather than merely technical integrity.

## Milestones in EVM Usage — A Legally Driven Evolution
- Draw this as a single horizontal timeline arrow with year-markers above and the corresponding judgment or statute below each marker. It shows the examiner at a glance that EVM policy in India has been court-shaped, and costs under a minute to reproduce.
- **Year** — Milestone · Why it mattered
- **1982** — First experimental use at the Parur (North Paravur) Assembly by-election, Kerala, on 50 polling stations. · Established technical feasibility, but the exercise had no statutory backing.
- **1984** — A.C. Jose v. Sivan Pillai (1984) 2 SCC 656 – the Supreme Court set aside the poll. · Held that the ECI’s plenary power under Article 324 cannot override the statutory ballot procedure; machine voting needed express legislative sanction.
- **1989** — Parliament inserted Section 61A in the RPA, 1951 (amendment of 1988, in force 15 March 1989). · Converted EVMs from an administrative experiment into a legally recognised mode of polling.
- **1998–2004** — Phased rollout – 25 Assembly constituencies in Delhi, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan (1998); complete coverage in the 2004 Lok Sabha election. · India became the first large democracy to conduct a national election entirely on EVMs, ending invalid votes and booth-capturing by ballot-stuffing.
- **2013** — Subramanian Swamy v. ECI (2013) – paper trail held an “indispensable requirement of free and fair elections”. VVPAT first used at the Noksen by-election, Nagaland (September 2013). · Added voter-verifiability: the elector now sees a printed slip confirming the vote.
- **2019** — N. Chandrababu Naidu v. Union of India (8 April 2019) – petition led by the then Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh with 21 parties; VVPAT counting raised from 1 to 5 polling stations per Assembly constituency/segment. · The single largest expansion of statistical audit in Indian elections – and an Andhra Pradesh-led reform, worth citing in an APPSC answer.
- **2024** — ADR v. ECI (26 April 2024) – 100% VVPAT counting and a return to ballot papers were refused, but two directions issued: seal and store Symbol Loading Units for 45 days; allow burnt-memory verification by BEL/ECIL engineers on the written request of the 2nd or 3rd-placed candidate within 7 days of the result. · Created, for the first time, a candidate-triggered right of verification – a shift from institutional assurance to individual remedy.
- **2025–26** — Supreme Court order of 7 May 2025 accepted the ECI’s amended Technical SOP (self-diagnosis, mutual authentication, no erasure or reloading of polled data, certification by ECIL/BEL engineers) and ordered the verification fee reduced; ECI issued the revised SOP on 17 June 2025. · Closed the loophole that verification itself was wiping the very data to be verified.

## Analysing the Tampering Allegations — Evidence Versus Perception
- The ECI’s empirical record is strong. In the Bihar Assembly election of 2025, mandatory VVPAT slip verification was carried out at five randomly selected polling stations in each of the 243 constituencies – 1,215 stations in all – with no discrepancy found anywhere, and not a single losing candidate applied for burnt-memory verification across those 243 seats or the 8 bypoll seats (Election Commission of India, December 2025). A remedy that exists and is not used weakens the tampering thesis considerably.
- The technical architecture is genuinely hard to subvert. The microcontroller is one-time programmable and physically inaccessible; the units have no wireless, network or serial interface; mutual authentication means a Ballot Unit will not communicate with an unpaired Control Unit; and mock polls are conducted before candidates’ agents on poll day. The Supreme Court in ADR (2024) expressly cautioned that “blindly distrusting” the system breeds unwarranted scepticism.
- But the transparency deficit is real, and this is the honest half of the answer. Three gaps recur: (i) the system is not software-independent – no audit can prove a result correct without trusting the burnt firmware; (ii) polling-station-wise Form 17C data is given only to agents, not published, so independent reconciliation is impossible; and (iii) the Symbol Loading Unit, an ordinary device that touches the VVPAT, sat outside any published protocol until the 2024–25 orders. The ADR litigation of 2025 was driven precisely by the ECI’s own SOPs providing only for a diagnostic check and mock poll rather than an examination of the burnt memory.
- Andhra Pradesh instance: after the simultaneous Lok Sabha and Assembly polls of 2024, the ECI received applications for burnt-memory verification in respect of the Assembly elections in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha alongside eight applications for the Lok Sabha poll (All India Radio / ECI, June 2024). The verification mechanism was thus used and tested in the State, and no count was disturbed.

## Solutions — From Assurance to Verifiability
- Adopt Risk-Limiting Audits (RLAs). Replace a fixed count of five stations with a statistically determined sample that scales with the victory margin – a landslide needs a token audit, a 500-vote margin needs a deep one. This gives a measurable confidence level at lower total cost than blanket counting.
- Publish what is already collected. Uploading scanned Form 17C and mock-poll results constituency-wise on ECINET – the unified platform launched by the CEC on 22 January 2026 at the India International Conference on Democracy and Election Management, integrating over 40 apps in all 22 scheduled languages – would cost nothing and remove the single biggest grievance at almost no administrative burden.
- Make verification affordable and prompt. The Court itself found the Rs 40,000 per-unit fee “too high” (order of 11 February 2025). A graded fee, refundable if a discrepancy is established, would convert a symbolic right into a usable one.
- Institutionalise adversarial scrutiny. Reconstitute the Technical Experts Committee with independent computer scientists, permit supervised source-code and hardware review by nominees of recognised parties, and revive the all-party consultative mechanism – trust in elections is built politically, not only technically.

## Conclusion

Every strengthening of the EVM – statutory sanction in 1989, the paper trail in 2013, the fivefold audit won on an Andhra Pradesh petition in 2019, and candidate-triggered burnt-memory checks in 2024–25 – has come from a dialogue between the Commission and the Court rather than from abandoning the machine. The evidence does not support the tampering charge; the perception gap, however, is a real democratic cost. The task ahead is to move from “trust us, it is secure” to “check for yourself, here is the data”, because in an electoral democracy the legitimacy of a result rests as much on being seen to be verified as on being accurate.

## Value addition
- Machine architecture: an EVM has a Control Unit with the Presiding Officer and a Balloting Unit inside the voting compartment, joined by a five-metre cable; one Balloting Unit takes 16 candidates and up to four units can be linked, giving a ceiling of 64 candidates plus NOTA. M3-generation units carry tamper-detection that self-disables the machine on intrusion.
- Manufacture is public-sector and one of the two units is in the Telugu States: Electronics Corporation of India Limited (ECIL), Hyderabad and Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL), Bengaluru – both Government of India undertakings, which is itself a safeguard against private capture.
- NOTA was introduced on the ballot unit following PUCL v. Union of India (2013); the VVPAT slip is displayed for seven seconds before being cut into a sealed drop box.
- Key numbers for the exam hall: ECI told the Supreme Court in April 2024 that over 41,600 random VVPAT verifications had been conducted and more than four crore slips matched, without a single mismatch; the Indian Statistical Institute had advised that a sample of 479 EVMs nationwide yields over 99% confidence.
- Committees and law: Article 324 (superintendence), Article 326 (adult suffrage), Section 61A RPA 1951 (voting machines); the 255th Report of the Law Commission (2015) on electoral reforms recommended greater audit transparency and stronger anti-paid-news provisions.

## Introduction

Article 324 creates a single, all-India Election Commission and vests in it the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, the State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. A permanent body since 25 January 1950 and multi-member since 1 October 1993, it today comprises Chief Election Commissioner Shri Gyanesh Kumar (in office since 19 February 2025) with Election Commissioners Dr. Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Dr. Vivek Joshi, appointed under the CEC and other ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 enacted after Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023). Its constitutional significance lies in a simple proposition: representative government is legitimate only if the act of representation is itself honestly ascertained.

## Powers and Functions — A Three-Fold Classification
- Reproduce as a three-branch tree: a single box “ECI – Article 324” at the top branching into Administrative / Quasi-Judicial / Advisory, with two examples under each branch. Classification plus one live example per branch is what separates a listed answer from an analysed one.
- **Head of power** — Content · Live illustration (sourced)
- **Administrative** — Preparation and revision of electoral rolls; delimitation of polling areas; notification of the poll schedule; deployment of observers; countermanding a poll for booth capturing or bribery. · Special Intensive Revision (SIR) – in Andhra Pradesh, enumeration forms were distributed to 4.16 crore electors through 46,397 Booth Level Officers; the draft roll published on 31 July 2026 carried 3.71 crore electors after 44.89 lakh deletions (15.22 lakh deceased, 22.30 lakh shifted, 7.37 lakh duplicate), with the final roll due 3 October 2026 (Office of the CEO, Andhra Pradesh, July 2026).
- **Quasi-judicial** — Registration of parties under Section 29A RPA 1951; recognition as national or State party; adjudication of symbol and split disputes under Para 15 of the Symbols Order, 1968; disqualification for failure to lodge election expenses. · The Commission’s symbol-dispute jurisdiction is judicially settled since Sadiq Ali v. ECI (1972); its orders are quasi-judicial and appealable only by writ, which is why the power to freeze a party symbol is one of the most consequential it holds.

- **Head of power** — Content · Live illustration (sourced)
- **Advisory / regulatory** — Opinion to the President and Governor on post-election disqualification of sitting members under Articles 103 and 192; enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct; ceilings on candidate expenditure; regulation of campaign conduct and paid news. · The MCC operates from the date of announcement of the schedule; expenditure ceilings stand at Rs 95 lakh for a Lok Sabha seat and Rs 40 lakh for an Assembly seat in larger States (Ministry of Law and Justice notification, 2022).

## How These Powers Protect Representative Democracy
- It converts consent into an auditable fact. A government’s claim to speak for the people is only as good as the roll and the count behind it. The Supreme Court, upholding the SIR on 27 May 2026 in Association for Democratic Reforms v. ECI (W.P. (C) 640 of 2025), held that roll revision falls within the ECI’s statutory mandate under the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and flows from its Article 324 obligation to secure free and fair elections – judicial confirmation that roll purity is a democratic, not merely clerical, function.
- It equalises the contest. The Model Code restrains the incumbent’s ability to convert State resources into electoral advantage – no new schemes after announcement, no official machinery for campaigning. Enforcement is now crowd-sourced: the cVIGIL facility lets any citizen photograph a violation for action within 100 minutes.
- It widens the franchise in practice, not just in law. Article 326 grants adult suffrage; SVEEP, home voting for electors above 85 and persons with disabilities, and accessible polling stations make it usable. ECINET, launched on 22 January 2026, consolidates over 40 separate applications – voter registration, roll search, e-EPIC download, grievance redress – into one platform in all 22 scheduled languages, which matters most to the migrant and first-time voter.
- It disciplines the parties that populate the legislature. Mandatory contribution reports, expenditure statements and periodic de-listing of registered-unrecognised parties that never contest keep the party system from becoming a shell – a precondition for meaningful representation.

## Structural Limitations — The Analytical Edge
- Dependence in appointment and security of tenure. Only the CEC enjoys removal protection equivalent to a Supreme Court judge; an Election Commissioner may be removed on the CEC’s recommendation. The 2023 Act placed appointment with a committee of the Prime Minister, a Union Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, replacing the Chief Justice contemplated in Anoop Baranwal – an unresolved autonomy question.
- No independent secretariat and no power to de-register a party for violating its own constitution or failing to hold internal elections; the ECI can only refuse recognition. The Model Code, similarly, rests on moral and administrative authority rather than statute.
- Jurisdictional limit worth stating in an APPSC answer: the ECI does not conduct local body elections. Panchayat and municipal polls in Andhra Pradesh are conducted by the Andhra Pradesh State Election Commission under Articles 243K and 243ZA – a distinct constitutional authority students routinely conflate with the ECI.

## Conclusion

The Election Commission is the institution through which the abstract promise of Article 326 becomes the concrete fact of a government that can be voted out. Its authority, as T.N. Seshan’s tenure demonstrated, has always been drawn less from added statutory power than from the willingness to use Article 324 fully and impartially. Strengthening it further – a collegium-based appointment, a statutory Model Code, an independent secretariat and full disclosure of poll-level data – would ensure that the Commission continues to be trusted not merely as the manager of elections but as the guarantor of representative government itself.

## Value addition
- Constitutional scaffolding: Articles 324 to 329 constitute Part XV. Article 325 bars a separate roll on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex; Article 326 provides adult suffrage; Article 329(b) bars judicial interference once the election process has begun, save by an election petition – the reason courts decline mid-poll intervention.
- Composition facts: permanent body established 25 January 1950 (observed as National Voters’ Day); single-member till 16 October 1989, briefly three-member, and multi-member permanently since 1 October 1993; decisions by majority; CEC and ECs enjoy equal say, affirmed in T.N. Seshan v. Union of India (1995).
- Landmark judgments to cite:Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner (1978) – Article 324 is a reservoir of residuary power where the law is silent; Union of India v. ADR (2002) – the voter’s right to know candidates’ assets and criminal antecedents; PUCL v. Union of India (2013) – NOTA; Anoop Baranwal (2023) – appointment process.
- Institutional capacity: the India International Institute of Democracy and Election Management (IIIDEM), New Delhi, trains Indian and foreign election officials; the ECI hosted the India International Conference on Democracy and Election Management in January 2026 with participating Election Management Bodies from several countries, reflecting India’s soft-power role in electoral administration.
- Reform proposals on record: the 255th Law Commission Report (2015) and the Second ARC recommended a broad-based collegium for appointments, statutory backing for the Model Code, state funding of elections and de-registration powers – useful as the “way forward” in any ECI question.
