## Introduction

Dr. Ambedkar described the Comptroller and Auditor-General as probably the most important officer under the Constitution. Appointed under Article 148 and drawing duties from Article 149, the CAG submits Union accounts to the President and State accounts to the Governor under Article 151; once laid before the House, the reports stand automatically referred to the Public Accounts Committee. That mechanism is the whole basis of the metaphor: the PAC, a committee of twenty-two lay legislators serving one-year terms, possesses neither the technical capacity nor the access to records to detect financial irregularity on its own. The CAG supplies the evidence, the method and the interpretation – hence friend, philosopher and guide.

- Draw a simple accountability cycle as five boxes in a closed loop: Parliament grants funds → Executive spends → CAG audits (Art. 149–151) → PAC examines and reports → Ministry files Action Taken Notes → back to Parliament. Marking the CAG box as the only independent node makes the argument visually before you write it.

## Friend — The Committee’s Only Independent Source of Fact
- The PAC cannot summon records or conduct field verification; the CAG can, and does so with statutory access under the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. The Committee’s agenda is therefore literally written by the audit report.
- Andhra Pradesh illustration: the CAG’s performance audit of the Polavaram Irrigation Project (Report No. 4 of 2025, covering 2017-18 to 2022-23) found that against 213 planned rehabilitation colonies costing Rs 13,262 crore, only 26 stood completed as of March 2023, and just 11,677 of 1,06,006 project-displaced families had been shifted; budget utilisation ranged between 21 and 66 per cent, largely because of the damaged diaphragm wall and the incomplete earth-cum-rock-fill dam. No legislator could have assembled that picture unaided – which is exactly what “friend” means here.

## Philosopher — Supplying the Standard of Scrutiny
- The CAG has shifted legislative oversight beyond the question “was the money legally spent?” to “was it well spent?”. Performance audit under the Regulations on Audit and Accounts, 2007 (revised 2020) applies the three Es – economy, efficiency and effectiveness – and thereby teaches the PAC a vocabulary of value for money rather than mere regularity.
- Andhra Pradesh illustration: the Information Systems Audit of the Andhra Pradesh Comprehensive Financial Management System (Report No. 1 of 2024) examined not a transaction but a system – the design and controls of the platform through which the entire State treasury operates. Auditing the architecture of spending, rather than individual vouchers, is precisely the conceptual leadership the word “philosopher” captures.

## Guide — Technical Interpretation Through the Examination
- Officers of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department attend PAC sittings, brief members before departmental secretaries are examined, and help frame the questions put to witnesses. The Committee thus borrows both the CAG’s findings and its professional judgement.
- Andhra Pradesh illustration: the CAG’s report on the Functioning of the Mines and Geology Department (Report No. 1 of 2025) and the Revenue Department report for the period ended March 2023 (Report No. 6 of 2025) translate complex questions of royalty assessment and revenue leakage into examinable audit paragraphs – without which a legislature committee would have no purchase on the subject at all.
- Institutional link worth naming: the Public Accounts Committee for 2026-27, reconstituted with effect from 1 May 2026, is chaired by Shri K.C. Venugopal, by the convention followed since 1967 that the chair goes to the Opposition; it includes the Andhra Pradesh members Shri Magunta Sreenivasulu Reddy (TDP) and Shri Balashowry Vallabhaneni (Jana Sena) (Lok Sabha Secretariat, May 2026).

## Where the Relationship Falls Short
- **Limitation** — Consequence
- **Audit is entirely post facto** — By the time an irregularity is reported, the money is spent and the contract executed; the Polavaram findings surfaced two decades into the project.
- **CAG reports and PAC recommendations are recommendatory** — Enforcement depends on Action Taken Notes from ministries, which are frequently delayed beyond the six-month norm and rarely tested for compliance.
- **Time and capacity mismatch** — A 22-member committee with a one-year term cannot examine more than a fraction of the audit paragraphs laid before it, creating a large residue of unexamined findings.
- **Coverage gaps** — Public-private partnerships, special purpose vehicles and off-budget borrowing by State entities sit at the edge of the audit mandate even though they carry contingent liability for the exchequer.
- **The PAC cannot question policy** — It may only examine the execution of an approved policy, so a wasteful decision that was properly authorised largely escapes its reach.

## Conclusion

The metaphor holds, but only as a description of potential. The CAG makes legislative financial control possible; it cannot make it effective, because audit ends where political will begins. Statutory timelines for Action Taken Notes, a dedicated research secretariat for the PAC and its State counterparts, real-time or concurrent audit of large national projects, and the long-standing proposal for a multi-member CAG would convert audit findings into consequences. Until then, as the Polavaram report suggests, the friend advises, the philosopher instructs and the guide points – but the executive is free to walk on.

## Value addition
- Constitutional and statutory frame: Article 148 (appointment, oath, salary charged on the Consolidated Fund, removal only in the manner of a Supreme Court judge); Article 149 (duties as prescribed by Parliament); Article 150 (form of accounts on CAG’s advice); Article 151 (submission of reports). Tenure is six years or age 65, whichever is earlier. Shri K. Sanjay Murthy was sworn in as the 15th CAG on 21 November 2024 (Office of the CAG).
- PAC essentials: instituted in 1921 under the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms; constituted annually under Rule 308 of the Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure; 22 members – 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha, elected by proportional representation through the single transferable vote; a Minister cannot be a member; excess expenditure it examines is regularised under Article 115.
- Types of audit to name precisely: regularity (compliance), financial attest, performance, and information systems audit; supplementary audit of government companies flows from Section 19A of the DPC Act, 1971. Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly ranked the CAG above even the judiciary in importance to financial probity.
- State-level parallel for APPSC: the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly has its own Public Accounts Committee examining the Principal Accountant General (Audit), Andhra Pradesh reports tabled at Vijayawada; the State Finances Audit Report is the annual instrument for testing compliance with the Andhra Pradesh Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2005 (last amended December 2021).
- Reform benchmarks: the Second ARC’s report on Strengthening Financial Management Systems urged outcome-based audit and timely Action Taken Notes; the 15th and 16th Finance Commissions have both flagged off-budget borrowing by States as an audit and transparency concern.
Q21:
## Introduction

Article 368 confers on Parliament the constituent power to amend the Constitution by way of addition, variation or repeal, and 106 amendments in seventy-six years show how freely it has been used. Yet the power is not plenary. Granville Austin called the Indian Constitution neither rigid nor flexible but responsive, and that responsiveness is engineered through limits: a demanding procedure inside Parliament, a federal veto for entrenched provisions, a judicially enforced core, and the political arithmetic of assembling a super-majority. To say the power is “limited”, therefore, is not merely to invoke Kesavananda Bharati.

- Draw four concentric arcs (or four locks on a single gate) labelled Procedural → Federal → Judicial → Political, with one example written beside each. This instantly signals to the evaluator that you have classified the limitation rather than merely narrated case law.

## Procedural Limit — The Special Majority Is a Real Barrier
- An amendment bill must be passed in each House separately by a majority of the total membership and a two-thirds majority of those present and voting; there is no joint sitting to break a deadlock, and since the 24th Amendment (1971) the President has no discretion to withhold assent. The Rajya Sabha is therefore a co-equal chamber for constituent purposes, unlike its position on money bills.
- Decisive contemporary example: the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, which sought to enlarge the Lok Sabha and operationalise women’s reservation through an earlier delimitation, was negatived in the Lok Sabha on 17 April 2026 – 298 members voted for it and 230 against out of 528 voting, short of the two-thirds requirement of Article 368(2). The dependent Delimitation Bill, 2026 and Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 were consequently not proceeded with (PIB, Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, 18 April 2026). A government commanding a working majority still could not amend the Constitution – the clearest possible proof that the procedural limit bites.

## Federal Limit — The States Hold a Veto Over the Core Structure
- Amendments touching the election of the President, the extent of Union and State executive power, the High Courts, distribution of legislative powers under Articles 245–255, the Seventh Schedule, representation of States in Parliament, or Article 368 itself additionally require ratification by the legislatures of not less than one-half of the States by simple majority. Federalism thus operates as a structural, not merely sentimental, restraint.
- Examples: the 101st Amendment (GST, 2016) and the 99th Amendment (NJAC, 2014) both went through State ratification. The 101st reshaped fiscal federalism and survived; the 99th was ratified by sixteen States and still fell,

which shows that clearing the federal lock does not clear the judicial one.

## Judicial Limit — The Basic Structure Doctrine
- **Case** — Holding and its significance
- **Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965)** — Amending power held wide enough to abridge Fundamental Rights – the starting position the doctrine later displaced.
- **Golak Nath (1967)** — Reversed course: Parliament held unable to abridge Fundamental Rights. Provoked the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments in response.
- **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)** — A thirteen-judge Bench held 7:6 that Parliament may amend any provision but cannot destroy the basic structure – supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism and judicial review. The single most important limit on Article 368.
- **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)** — Article 329A, inserted by the 39th Amendment to place the Prime Minister’s election beyond judicial scrutiny, was struck down – free and fair elections and judicial review are part of the basic structure.
- **Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)** — Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368, inserted by the 42nd Amendment to confer unlimited amending power and bar review, were void. Limited amending power is itself a basic feature; harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles must be preserved.
- **Waman Rao (1981)** — Fixed 24 April 1973 – the date of Kesavananda – as the cut-off from which Ninth Schedule entries become testable.
- **S.R. Bommai (1994)** — Secularism affirmed as a basic feature, constraining both amendment and the exercise of Article 356.
- **I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)** — Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to review if they damage the basic structure – closing the last route to insulate legislation from Part III.
- **SCAORA v. Union of India (NJAC, 2015)** — The 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act were struck down for impairing judicial independence – proof that the doctrine is live and not merely of historical interest.
- **Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024)** — The insertion of “socialist” and “secular” in the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment was upheld; the amending power extends to the Preamble, and its valid exercise is equally part of the story.

## The Limit Runs Both Ways — Judicial Restraint as Its Mirror
- If Parliament cannot rewrite the Constitution’s core, neither may the judiciary rewrite it by interpretation. In its advisory opinion of 20 November 2025 on Special Reference No. 1 of 2025 under Article 143, a five-judge Bench headed by CJI B.R. Gavai held that courts cannot prescribe timelines for the Governor or the President under Articles 200 and 201 where the Constitution lays down none, and rejected the device of “deemed assent” under Article 142. The message is symmetrical: textual change to the Constitution must travel through Article 368 alone.

## Political Limit — Consensus as an Unwritten Requirement
- Because a super-majority in both Houses is rarely available to a single party, constitutional change in practice demands cross-party agreement. This is why the Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, 2025 – providing for a Minister, Chief Minister or Prime Minister to demit office after thirty consecutive days in custody on a charge punishable by five years or more – was referred to a Joint Committee of both Houses rather than pushed to a vote, and why the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 on simultaneous elections has been before a 41-member Joint Parliamentary Committee chaired by Shri P.P. Chaudhary since December 2024.

## Conclusion

Parliament’s amending power is wide but bounded on four sides: it must clear a super-majority in each House separately, obtain the States’ concurrence where the federal core is touched, respect a judicially guarded basic structure, and command a political consensus wider than a governing majority. The defeat of the 131st Amendment Bill in April 2026 and the striking down of the NJAC in 2015 show the first and third of these operating in living memory. Together they ensure that the Constitution can be adapted to changing needs without any transient majority being able to alter what it fundamentally is.

## Value addition
- Three amending procedures (only the latter two fall under Article 368 proper): simple majority for matters like creation of new States, abolition of a State Legislative Council or changes to citizenship; special majority; and special majority with ratification by half the States. An amendment bill may be introduced in either House, by a Minister or a private member, and needs no prior Presidential recommendation.
- Illustrative basic features to list if asked: supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, judicial review and Article 32, separation of powers, federalism, secularism, sovereign democratic republican structure, free and fair elections, harmony between Parts III and IV, parliamentary system, and the limited amending power itself.
- Amendments to keep at your fingertips: 24th (1971) – assent made obligatory; 42nd (1976) – the “mini Constitution”; 44th (1978) – right to property moved to Article 300A and Emergency safeguards restored; 73rd and 74th (1992) – local self-government; 101st (2016) – GST; 103rd (2019) – EWS reservation, upheld in Janhit Abhiyan (2022); 106th (2023) – Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, one-third reservation for women, to take effect after the next census and delimitation.
- Comparative note that adds depth: the basic structure doctrine is not unique to India – its lineage runs through the German Basic Law’s eternity clause (Article 79(3)) and it has since been cited by courts in Bangladesh, Pakistan and Kenya, making India an exporter of constitutional doctrine.
- Andhra Pradesh link: the reorganisation of Andhra Pradesh in 2014 was effected under Article 3 by a simple majority, not Article 368 – a reminder that alteration of State boundaries is not a constitutional amendment even though the First Schedule changes as a consequence (Article 4).

## Introduction
Legislators enjoy **privileges and immunities** (Articles 105 and 194) to function fearlessly, but the claim of **absolute immunity** from all proceedings has no constitutional basis — as leading cases demonstrate.

## The privilege architecture
- **Freedom of speech in the House** (Articles 105(1)/194(1)) and **immunity from court proceedings** for anything said or any vote given in the legislature (105(2)/194(2)).
- Immunity from arrest in civil cases during and around sessions; the House's power to punish for contempt.

## Why immunity is not absolute
- The immunity attaches to **proceedings of the House**, not to a member's every act. Courts have delineated its limits:
  - **Keshav Singh (1965)**: privileges are subject to Fundamental Rights and judicial scrutiny of jurisdiction.
  - **Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: expulsion of members (cash-for-query) upheld but held **judicially reviewable**.
  - **Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024)**: a seven-judge bench **overruled *P.V. Narasimha Rao* (1998)**, holding that legislators who take **bribes have no immunity** under Articles 105(2)/194(2) — a decisive rejection of absolute immunity.

## Conclusion
Privileges protect the **integrity of legislative functioning**, not the criminality of individual members. The trend, culminating in *Sita Soren* (2024), confirms that parliamentary immunity is **functional and bounded, never absolute**.

## Introduction
The **declining quality and quantity of legislative debate** is one of the most worrying trends in Indian parliamentary democracy, weakening the legislature's core functions of deliberation and oversight.

## Evidence of decline
- **Fewer sitting days** — far below the 120–130 days a year of the 1950s–60s.
- **Bills passed with little discussion**, often amid disruptions, and **declining reference to Standing Committees**.
- Frequent use of the **Money Bill route** and **ordinances** bypasses deliberation; the **guillotine** puts un-discussed demands to vote.
- Rising **disruptions and adjournments** substitute spectacle for scrutiny.

## Causes
- Anti-defection discipline (Tenth Schedule) muffling individual voice; executive dominance; weak committee culture; and the incentive of disruption over debate.

## Consequences
- Poorly scrutinised laws, eroded accountability, and diminished public trust in the institution.

## Remedies
- A **minimum number of sitting days**, mandatory committee scrutiny of bills, protected time for opposition and private members, disruption-limiting rules, and stronger research support for members.

## Conclusion
A legislature that debates less **legislates worse and checks the executive less** — reversing the decline is essential to keeping Parliament a genuine forum of deliberation rather than a rubber stamp.

## Introduction
When the two Houses of a **bicameral State legislature** — the Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) and the Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) — disagree over a bill, the Constitution provides a conflict-resolution mechanism heavily weighted toward the **directly elected Assembly**.

## The mechanism (Article 197)
- On an **ordinary bill** passed by the Assembly and sent to the Council, the Council may reject it, take no action, or return it with amendments.
- If the Council **rejects, delays beyond the prescribed periods, or the Assembly disagrees with its amendments**, the **Assembly may pass the bill a second time**.
- If the Council again obstructs it (or lets the **specified periods — about three months plus one month** — lapse), the **bill is deemed passed** in the form the Assembly approved.

## Key features
- **No joint sitting** at the State level (unlike Article 108 for Parliament) — the deadlock is resolved simply by the Assembly's persistence.
- The Council can only **delay an ordinary bill by up to about four months in total**; on **Money Bills** its role is purely recommendatory (14 days).
- Hence the Council is a **revising and delaying chamber**, not a co-equal one.

## Conclusion
The design ensures the **primacy of the popularly elected Assembly** while giving the Council a limited revising role — a deliberate constitutional choice that prevents an unelected second chamber from blocking the popular will.

## Introduction
**Legislative privileges** (Article 194 for States, 105 for Parliament) are special rights enabling legislatures and their members to discharge functions independently; they remain **uncodified**, drawn from those of the House of Commons at the Constitution's commencement.

## Privileges and immunities
- **Individual privileges**: freedom of speech in the legislature; immunity from court proceedings for anything said or voted; freedom from arrest in civil matters during sessions.
- **Collective privileges**: the House's right to publish proceedings, exclude strangers, regulate internal affairs, and **punish for contempt or breach of privilege**.

## Judicial interference — how far?
- Privileges are **not above the Constitution**. Courts have asserted the power to review:
  - **Keshav Singh (1965)**: the House's power to commit for contempt is subject to judicial examination of jurisdiction and Fundamental Rights.
  - **Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: expulsion of members is **judicially reviewable**.
  - **Sita Soren (2024)**: bribe-taking legislators enjoy **no immunity** — a major limit.
- Courts generally respect the **internal autonomy** of the House (Article 212 bars questioning proceedings on grounds of procedural irregularity) but intervene on **illegality, unconstitutionality and violation of rights**.

## Conclusion
Privileges protect legislative independence, but **the judiciary retains the power to prevent their misuse** — striking a balance between House autonomy and the rule of law. The unresolved debate over **codification** continues, balancing certainty against House self-governance.

## Introduction
The **principles of natural justice** — the twin pillars of *nemo judex in causa sua* (no one a judge in his own cause) and *audi alteram partem* (hear the other side) — are the bedrock of fair adjudication, and they play an especially significant role before **administrative tribunals**, which decide disputes outside the ordinary court hierarchy.

## The principles
- **Rule against bias** (*nemo judex*): the adjudicator must be impartial and free of personal, pecuniary or institutional interest.
- **Right to a fair hearing** (*audi alteram partem*): notice, opportunity to present one's case, disclosure of evidence, and a **reasoned/speaking order**.

## Their role in administrative tribunals
- Tribunals (created under **Articles 323A/323B** — CAT, NGT, NCLT, etc.) exercise quasi-judicial functions and are **bound by natural justice** even where not bound by strict procedure.
- They ensure **flexibility with fairness** — technical expertise and speed without sacrificing due process.
- Judicial safeguards: *A.K. Kraipak* (1969) blurred the line between administrative and quasi-judicial, extending natural justice broadly; *Maneka Gandhi* (1978) infused fairness into Article 21; *L. Chandra Kumar* (1997) preserved **High Court judicial review** over tribunals as basic structure.

## Conclusion
Natural justice makes tribunal adjudication **legitimate and fair**, guarding against arbitrariness. Its observance — impartiality, hearing and reasoned decisions — is what distinguishes a lawful tribunal from an executive fiat.

## Introduction

The basic structure doctrine is a judicially-evolved implied limitation on Parliament’s constituent power under Article 368: certain foundational features may be amended in form but never damaged, emasculated or abrogated in substance. Laid down by a 13-judge Bench in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) by a narrow 7:6 majority, it overruled Golak Nath (1967) — which had held Fundamental Rights wholly unamendable — while simultaneously denying Parliament the unlimited power asserted through the 24th Amendment (1971). The Court has deliberately never given an exhaustive list, keeping the doctrine open-textured.

## What Constitutes the Basic Structure — Four Thematic Clusters

The Supreme Court has never defined the basic structure exhaustively; features are declared case by case as challenges arise. Roughly twenty have crystallised, best grouped as follows:

- Constitutional identity: supremacy of the Constitution; the sovereign, democratic and republican character of the polity; secularism; unity and integrity of the nation. In Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024) the Court upheld the 42nd Amendment’s insertion of ‘socialist’ and ‘secular’ into the Preamble, confirming that these are descriptive of an already-existing constitutional identity.
- Governance architecture: federalism, separation of powers, the parliamentary system, and rule of law. These matter because they distribute power — strip any one away and majoritarian capture becomes structurally possible.
- Rights and justice: harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, the principle of equality, freedom and dignity of the individual, effective access to justice, and the essence (not every clause) underlying Fundamental Rights.
- Guardianship mechanisms: judicial review, independence of the judiciary, the powers of the Supreme Court under Articles 32, 136, 141 and 142 and of High Courts under Articles 226 and 227, free and fair elections, and the limited nature of the amending power itself.

## II. Landmark Judgments — the Doctrinal Chain
- **Case (Year)** — Contribution to the Doctrine
- **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** — 13-judge Bench, 7:6. Amendments valid under Art. 368 but may not ‘damage or destroy’ the basic structure. Upheld the 24th Amendment while limiting it.
- **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)** — Struck down cl. 4 of the 39th Amendment insulating the PM’s election from judicial scrutiny — free and fair elections and judicial review declared basic features.
- **Minerva Mills (1980)** — Struck down Art. 368(4) & (5) and the expanded Art. 31C. Chandrachud CJ: ‘the donee of a limited power cannot convert it into an unlimited one’.
- **Waman Rao (1981)** — Doctrine applies prospectively — only to amendments made after 24 April 1973, protecting settled land-reform legislation.
- **Kihoto Hollohan (1992)** — Para 7 of the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection) struck down for want of ratification — judicial review of High Courts held part of the basic structure.
- **S.R. Bommai (1994)** — Federalism, secularism and democracy declared basic features; Art. 356 proclamations made justiciable.
- **I.R. Coelho (2007)** — Laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after 24.4.1973 are testable against the ‘rights test’ and basic structure — Art. 31B is no longer an absolute shield.
- **NJAC / SCAORA (2015)** — 99th Amendment struck down; independence of the judiciary and primacy in appointments held inviolable.
- **Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021)** — Part IXB (97th Amendment, 2011) struck down for cooperative societies operating within a State — enacted without ratification under the proviso to Art. 368(2).

## III. The Contemporary Frontier — Where the Doctrine Stops
- The doctrine binds constituent power, not ordinary legislative power. In Anjum Kadari v. Union of India (2024 INSC 831, 5 November 2024), a three-judge Bench upholding the UP Board of Madarsa Education Act, 2004 held that an ordinary statute cannot be struck down merely for violating the basic structure; the challenger must show breach of a specific constitutional provision or want of legislative competence. The reasoning is that concepts like secularism and federalism are ‘undefined’ and would inject unacceptable uncertainty into adjudication.
- The doctrine keeps generating fresh consequences decades later. In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024 INSC 835, 5 November 2024), a nine-judge Bench unanimously held that the original Article 31C revived once Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment’s expansion of it — a direct downstream effect of basic-structure review 44 years on.
- It continues to police institutional design. In its 19 November 2025 tribunals ruling (2025 INSC 1330), the Court reaffirmed L. Chandra Kumar (1997): High Court superintendence under Articles 226/227 is basic structure, and tribunals may supplement but never substitute constitutional courts.

## IV. Andhra Pradesh Connect

AP’s own constitutional history illustrates the doctrine’s boundary. The bifurcation of the State by the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, and the AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Act, 2026 declaring Amaravati the sole capital (passed by Rajya Sabha on 2 April 2026; Akashvani/News on AIR, 2 April 2026) were both ordinary laws under Articles 3 and 4, not amendments under Article 368 — and therefore, after Anjum Kadari, cannot be tested against the basic structure at all. Territorial reorganisation, however politically fraught, sits outside the doctrine’s reach.

## Conclusion

The basic structure doctrine is India’s answer to the paradox of a written Constitution that must both endure and evolve. It permits Parliament to amend freely at the periphery while placing the constitutional core — democracy, secularism, federalism, judicial review, the rule of law — beyond the reach of any transient majority. Its recent trajectory shows a Court simultaneously consolidating the doctrine against constituent overreach and disciplining it against indiscriminate use on ordinary statutes. That dual movement is precisely what keeps the doctrine credible rather than a roving commission to strike down inconvenient laws.

## Value addition
- Intellectual origin: the doctrine draws on German constitutional scholar Dieter Conrad’s 1965 Banaras Hindu University lecture on implied limitations, itself inspired by Article 79(3) of the German Basic Law (the ‘eternity clause’) — useful for showing comparative depth.
- Key contrast: Article 79(3) of Germany’s Basic Law and Article 89 of the French Constitution expressly entrench unamendable provisions; India achieved the same result judicially, which is why the doctrine is criticised as counter-majoritarian.
- Standard criticisms to deploy: (i) no exhaustive list, hence unpredictable; (ii) unelected judges determine the ‘spirit’ of the Constitution; (iii) it inverts Article 368’s plain text. Note the Court itself conceded in Anjum Kadari (2024) that these are ‘undefined concepts’.
- Comparative note: Bangladesh (Anwar Hossain Chowdhury, 1989) and Pakistan (District Bar Association Rawalpindi, 2015) have expressly adopted Indian basic-structure reasoning — evidence of the doctrine’s export value.
- Live debates (2025–26): the simultaneous-elections proposal and the November 2025 advisory opinion on gubernatorial assent (In re Assent, 2025 INSC 1333, 20 November 2025) both raise federalism-as-basic-structure questions currently unresolved.

## Introduction

India’s Constitution creates a system of divided legislative competence: Article 246 read with the Seventh Schedule distributes subjects across the Union List (98 entries), State List (59) and Concurrent List (52), while Article 246A (101st Amendment, 2016) creates simultaneous power over GST. Overlap is therefore structural, not accidental. Where two valid laws collide irreconcilably, Article 254 supplies the constitutional tie-breaker, and the courts have layered onto it a set of interpretive doctrines designed to save legislation wherever possible and strike it down only where unavoidable.

## The Doctrine of Repugnancy — Article 254(1)

Where a State law on a Concurrent List subject is inconsistent with a Union law, the Union law prevails and the State law is void only to the extent of the repugnancy — an application of severability that preserves the valid remainder. Two tests govern:

- M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979): repugnancy arises only on direct and irreconcilable collision — where obedience to one law necessarily means disobedience to the other; where both occupy the same field; or where Parliament intended its law to be a complete and exhaustive code.
- Innoventive Industries v. ICICI Bank (2018): the governing modern statement. The Maharashtra Relief Undertakings Act was held repugnant to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, since the IBC is an exhaustive code on insolvency — establishing that repugnancy can arise from coverage of the field, not merely textual contradiction.
- Forum for People’s Collective Efforts v. State of West Bengal (2021): the West Bengal Housing Industry Regulation Act, 2017 was struck down in its entirety as repugnant to the central RERA, 2016 — a State cannot enact a parallel statute in a field Parliament has fully occupied.

## II. The Presidential Assent Exception — Article 254(2)

A State law repugnant to an existing Union law survives within that State if it is reserved for the President’s consideration and receives assent. But the proviso preserves Parliament’s power to legislate afresh on the same matter and override it — so the protection is conditional, not permanent.

- AP illustration: the Andhra Pradesh Disha Act (Criminal Law AP Amendment), 2019 — prescribing investigation in 7 days, trial in 14 and enhanced sentencing for offences against women — amended the IPC and CrPC (Concurrent List, Entries 1 and 2). It was accordingly reserved for Presidential assent, which has remained pending for over six years. With the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replacing the IPC from 1 July 2024, much of the Act has been overtaken. This is the sharpest available demonstration that Article 254(2) offers States a route that is legally available but politically and practically fragile.

## III. Doctrines that Save Legislation
- **Doctrine** — What the Court Asks · Leading Authority
- **Pith and substance** — What is the true nature and character of the law? Incidental encroachment on another List does not invalidate it. · State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951); Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee (1947, PC)
- **Occupied field** — Has Parliament covered the entire field, leaving no room for State legislation? · Ch. Tika Ramji v. State of U.P. (1956); Hoechst Pharmaceuticals (1983)
- **Harmonious construction** — Can both laws be read so as to operate together? Conflict is a last resort, not a first reading. · Calcutta Gas Co. v. State of West Bengal (1962)
- **Colourable legislation** — Is the legislature doing indirectly what it cannot do directly? · K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953)
- **Union supremacy** — On irreconcilable Union List vs State List conflict, the non obstante clause in Art. 246(1) gives Parliament primacy. · Ch. Tika Ramji (1956)

## IV. Recent Application
- In Anjum Kadari v. Union of India (2024), while upholding the UP Madarsa Act, the Court struck down its provisions on higher-education degrees as repugnant to the UGC Act, 1956 (Entry 66, Union List) — a textbook use of severability to save the statute while excising the repugnant part.
- In Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India (2024), a nine-judge Bench upheld States’ power to levy taxes on mineral rights (Entry 50, List II), holding royalty is not a tax — a reminder that clarifying legislative fields, not just applying Article 254, is often the real judicial task.

## Conclusion

The judicial approach to Centre-State legislative conflict is deliberately conservative. Courts begin from a presumption of constitutionality, apply pith and substance to sustain incidental overlap, attempt harmonious construction, and reach Article 254 only when conflict is truly irreconcilable — then striking down only the offending portion. This calibrated method secures Parliament’s primacy in the concurrent sphere without reducing States to legislative subordinates, and it explains why the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions both urged prior Centre-State consultation as a cheaper alternative to litigation.

## Value addition
- Committee positions: the Sarkaria Commission (1988) recommended that the Centre consult States before legislating on Concurrent List subjects and that Presidential assent under Art. 254(2) be decided within a reasonable time. The Punchhi Commission (2010) went further, urging that Concurrent List legislation be preceded by consultation through the Inter-State Council (Art. 263).
- Related override provisions to cite: Art. 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution, 2/3 majority, on a State List subject in national interest); Art. 250 (during a National Emergency); Art. 252 (two or more States request Parliament to legislate); Art. 253 (international treaties). Art. 251 clarifies these do not restrict State power — State law is merely in abeyance.
- Doctrine of severability flows from Art. 13 and R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India (1957) — explains why Art. 254(1) voids the State law only ‘to the extent’ of repugnancy.
- GST as a structural innovation: Art. 246A creates simultaneous rather than concurrent power. In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022) the Court held GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding — a significant reaffirmation of fiscal federalism.

## Introduction

Article 1 describes India as a ‘Union of States’ — a formulation Dr. Ambedkar defended in the Constituent Assembly precisely because it signals that the Union is not the result of an agreement among States and that no State has a right to secede. The corollary is that States are destructible units of an indestructible Union: their names, boundaries and very existence lie in Parliament’s hands. Articles 2, 3 and 4 operationalise this, giving India one of the most flexible territorial frameworks among federal constitutions.

## The Constitutional Scheme — Articles 2 to 4
- **Article** — Scope and Significance
- **Article 2** — Empowers Parliament to admit into, or establish, new States on such terms as it thinks fit. It deals with territory not already part of India — e.g. Sikkim’s admission as an associate State (35th Amendment, 1974) and later as a full State (36th Amendment, 1975).
- **Article 3** — Deals with territory already within India: forming a new State by separation or union, increasing or diminishing a State’s area, and altering boundaries or names. Two safeguards apply — (i) the Bill may be introduced only on the President’s recommendation, and (ii) it must first be referred to the legislature of the affected State for its views within a specified period.
- **Article 4** — The decisive provision: laws under Articles 2 and 3 may amend the First Schedule (States and territories) and Fourth Schedule (Rajya Sabha seat allocation), and such laws ‘shall not be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of Article 368’. A simple majority therefore suffices.

## II. The Consultative — Not Consensual — Safeguard
- The State legislature’s views are not binding. In Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay (1960), the Court held that Parliament need not make a fresh reference if the Bill is subsequently amended, and that the President may fix any time limit he thinks fit — after which Parliament may proceed regardless. This is the single largest asymmetry in Indian federalism.
- The AP experience proves it. The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly rejected the draft Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Bill in January 2014, yet Parliament enacted the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 (Act 6 of 2014) creating Telangana with effect from 2 June 2014. Constitutionally, the rejection had no legal consequence — only political weight.

## III. The Direct Question — Is an Amendment Necessary?
- For internal reorganisation: NO. Article 4 expressly removes such laws from Article 368. Mangal Singh v. Union of India (1966) confirmed that reorganisation laws are valid even though they alter constitutional Schedules, provided the resulting State retains the essential machinery of a democratic parliamentary government. This is why the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, the creation of Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand (2000) and Telangana (2014) all proceeded by ordinary legislation.
- For cession of Indian territory to a foreign State: YES. In In re Berubari Union (1960), an advisory opinion under Article 143, the Court held that Article 3 permits reorganisation within India but does not authorise ceding territory to another country — that alters Article 1 and the First Schedule and requires an Article 368 amendment. Hence the 9th Amendment (1960) for Berubari and the 100th Amendment (2015) giving effect to the India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement affecting Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya and Tripura.
- A refinement: in Ram Kishore Sen v. Union of India (1966), the Court held that mere settlement of a boundary dispute is not cession and may be effected by executive action — the amendment requirement is triggered only by actual transfer of sovereign territory.

## IV. Andhra Pradesh — A Live Application (2026)

On 2 April 2026 Parliament passed the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation (Amendment) Act, 2026, amending Section 5 of the 2014 Act to declare that ‘Amaravati shall be the new capital’, with retrospective effect from 2 June 2024 (Bill No. 105 of 2026, Gazette of India; Lok Sabha 1 April, Rajya Sabha 2 April 2026, per Akashvani/News on AIR). It followed a resolution of the AP Legislative Assembly on 28 March 2026. Constitutionally, the point to note is that a matter as consequential as the permanent seat of a State’s government was settled by an ordinary parliamentary statute — no special majority, no State ratification — exactly as Article 4 contemplates. V. An Unresolved Frontier In In Re Article 370 (2023), the Court upheld the carving out of Ladakh as a Union Territory under Article 3(a) read with Explanation I, but expressly left open whether an entire State may be converted into Union Territories — relying on the Union’s assurance that J&K’s statehood would be restored. As of 10 October 2025 the Supreme Court granted the Centre four weeks to respond to pleas seeking that restoration (News on AIR, 10 October 2025). The scope of Article 3 thus remains an open constitutional question with direct implications for federalism.

## Conclusion

State formation in India is a legislative, not constituent, function. Parliament may redraw the political map by simple majority under Articles 3 and 4, with the State’s views sought but never controlling — a design the framers chose deliberately to prevent territorial rigidity from becoming a source of national instability. The one firm limit is external: territory cannot be ceded to another country without an Article 368 amendment. The framework has proved genuinely adaptive, absorbing linguistic reorganisation in 1956, statehood demands in 2000 and 2014, and the settlement of Andhra Pradesh’s capital in 2026 — but its asymmetry remains the strongest evidence for describing India as a federation with a unitary bias.

## Value addition
- Constituent Assembly context: Ambedkar explained that ‘Union’ was preferred over ‘Federation’ to convey that India was not formed by agreement among States and that no unit may secede. Article 3’s flexibility was a conscious response to the 1947 experience of Partition.
- Commissions on reorganisation: the Dhar Commission (1948) rejected linguistic reorganisation; the JVP Committee (1949, Nehru-Patel-Sitaramayya) concurred; the death of Potti Sriramulu in December 1952 led to Andhra State in 1953 — the first linguistic State. The Fazl Ali Commission (1955) then produced the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
- Pending AP Reorganisation Act commitments remain a recurring examination theme — Special Category Status, the Polavaram Multipurpose Project (a National Project under Section 90), the Kadapa steel plant, the Dugarajapatnam port, and division of institutions under the Ninth and Tenth Schedules of the 2014 Act.
- Article 3 vs comparative practice: under Article IV, Section 3 of the US Constitution, no new State may be formed within an existing State without the consent of that State’s legislature. India’s merely consultative requirement is a deliberate departure — a strong point for any federalism answer.
Q30:
## Introduction

The Constitution (42nd Amendment) Act, 1976 — enacted during the Emergency and dubbed the ‘Mini-Constitution’ — inserted clauses (4) and (5) into Article 368 through Section 55. Their combined object was to place constitutional amendments permanently beyond judicial reach and to convert Parliament’s limited amending power into an unlimited constituent power. This was not an isolated measure but the culmination of a decade-long institutional contest, and it was aimed squarely at neutralising Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

## The Sequence Leading to Clauses (4) and (5)

The clauses make sense only as the last move in an escalating exchange:

- Golak Nath (1967): a constitutional amendment is ‘law’ under Article 13 and cannot abridge Fundamental Rights. Response — 24th Amendment (1971): inserted Article 13(4) and Article 368(1) and (3), declaring that Article 13 does not apply to amendments and that assent is obligatory.
- Kesavananda Bharati (1973): upheld the 24th Amendment but evolved the basic structure doctrine. Response — 39th Amendment (1975): placed the Prime Minister’s election beyond judicial scrutiny; struck down in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975).
- Final response — 42nd Amendment (1976): having failed to overcome the doctrine case by case, Parliament attempted to abolish the power of review itself.

## II. How the Two Clauses Were Designed to Operate Together
- **Clause** — Text and Purpose · Intended Effect
- **Art. 368(5)** — ‘For the removal of doubts… there shall be no limitation whatever on the constituent power of Parliament to add, vary or repeal the provisions of this Constitution.’ · The substantive move — removes the implied limitation on which the basic structure doctrine rests.
- **Art. 368(4)** — No amendment, including one affecting Part III, ‘shall be called in question in any court on any ground’. · The procedural move — ousts the forum in which any limitation could be enforced.
- **Combined** — Parliament grants itself unlimited power and simultaneously bars any court from examining whether the grant is valid. · A self-referential bootstrap: the amendment insulates the very instrument that created it.

## III. The Judicial Response — Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
- A five-judge Bench struck down both clauses by 4:1. Chandrachud CJ held: ‘the donee of a limited power cannot by the exercise of that power convert the limited power into an unlimited one.’ Limited amending power and judicial review are themselves basic features, so clause (5) destroyed what it purported to enlarge and clause (4) removed the mechanism by which the limit could be enforced.
- The Court also struck down Section 4 of the 42nd Amendment, which had extended Article 31C’s immunity from Articles 39(b) and (c) to all Directive Principles — holding that the harmony and balance between Parts III and IV is itself basic structure. Parts III and IV, the Court said, are ‘like two wheels of a chariot’.
- Bhagwati J. dissented on the Article 31C point, holding the expanded provision valid since implementing Directive Principles could not damage the basic structure. Citing the dissent shows genuine familiarity with the judgment.

## IV. Two Nuances Most Answers Miss
- The clauses were never repealed. Judicial invalidation does not delete text. Article 368(4) and (5) still appear in the printed Constitution, marked by footnotes recording that they were declared void. The 44th Amendment (1978) reversed much of the 42nd — restoring judicial review of Emergency proclamations, deleting the right to property from Part III, and protecting Articles 20 and 21 from suspension — but did not remove these clauses. The lesson: a provision may be constitutionally dead yet textually alive.
- The consequences were still being worked out in 2024. In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024 INSC 835, 5 November 2024), a nine-judge Bench unanimously held that the original Article 31C (as upheld in Kesavananda) revived once Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment’s expansion of it — the Court reasoning that Parliament had intended only to widen the immunity, not to repeal the provision. Forty-four years after Minerva Mills, the 42nd Amendment was still generating constitutional litigation.

## The Doctrine’s Boundary Today

Minerva Mills confirmed that constituent power is limited. But in Anjum Kadari v. Union of India (2024 INSC 831), the Court clarified that ordinary legislative power is not policed by the same doctrine — a statute must be challenged for want of legislative competence or breach of a specific provision, not for offending the basic structure at large. The doctrine is thus a shield against constitutional subversion, not a general standard of legislative validity.

## Conclusion

Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 represent the most direct assault ever mounted on judicial review in India, and their failure defines the Indian constitutional settlement. Minerva Mills established that Parliament holds a delegated and limited constituent power which it cannot enlarge into sovereignty over the Constitution. The episode also demonstrates the resilience of institutional checks: a provision drafted expressly to be unreviewable was, within four years, reviewed and struck down. That outcome — more than any single doctrine — is why constitutional supremacy rather than parliamentary supremacy remains India’s governing principle.

## Value addition
- Scale of the 42nd Amendment: it amended the Preamble (adding ‘Socialist’, ‘Secular’ and ‘Integrity’), added Part IVA (Fundamental Duties, on the Swaran Singh Committee’s recommendation), inserted Articles 323A and 323B (tribunals), moved five subjects from the State to the Concurrent List (education, forests, weights and measures, wildlife, administration of justice), and extended Lok Sabha and Assembly terms to six years.
- Article 323A(2)(d) and 323B(3)(d), also inserted by the 42nd, were later struck down in L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) for excluding High Court jurisdiction — reaffirmed by the Supreme Court on 19 November 2025 (2025 INSC 1330).
- Preamble litigation: in Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (2024) the Court dismissed challenges to the words ‘socialist’ and ‘secular’, holding that Article 368 permits amendment of the Preamble and that these terms are integral to constitutional identity.
- Later basic-structure strike-downs to cite:Kihoto Hollohan (1992, Tenth Schedule para 7), I.R. Coelho (2007, Ninth Schedule), SCAORA v. Union of India (2015, 99th Amendment/NJAC), Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021, Part IXB of the 97th Amendment).

## Introduction

The framers rejected both the near-immutability of the American Constitution — which has been amended only 27 times in 235 years — and the unlimited flexibility of the unwritten British constitution. Article 368, drawing on the South African model, creates a graded procedure in which the difficulty of amendment rises with the constitutional significance of the provision. Dr. Ambedkar defended this as making the Constitution ‘as solid and as flexible as circumstances may require’. India has since seen 106 constitutional amendments, the most recent being the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam of 2023.

## The Three Routes
- **Route** — Majority Required · Provisions Covered · Illustration
- **Outside Article 368** — Simple majority of members present and voting (as for an ordinary Bill) · Arts. 2, 3 and 4 (new States, names, boundaries); creation or abolition of Legislative Councils (Art. 169); Second, Fifth and Sixth Schedules; citizenship; salaries and quorum · AP Reorganisation Act, 2014; AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Act, 2026 declaring Amaravati the capital
- **Art. 368 — special majority** — Majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of members present and voting · Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, and all provisions not in the other two categories · 42nd Amendment (1976); 44th Amendment (1978); 86th Amendment (2002); 103rd Amendment (2019)
- **Art. 368 — special majority + State ratification** — Special majority in Parliament plus ratification by legislatures of half the States by simple majority · Federal provisions: election of the President (Arts. 54, 55), executive power of Union and States (Arts. 73, 162), the Supreme Court and High Courts, distribution of legislative powers, Seventh Schedule, representation of States, and Art. 368 itself · 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992); 101st Amendment (GST, 2016)

## II. The Procedural Steps
- Initiation: only by a Bill in either House of Parliament — State legislatures cannot initiate. The Bill may be moved by a minister or a private member and needs no prior recommendation of the President.
- Passage: each House must pass the Bill separately by the requisite majority. There is no provision for a joint sitting under Article 108 to resolve deadlock — a structural risk of permanent stalemate.
- Ratification (where required): by the legislatures of half the States, by simple majority. There is no time limit, and once given, ratification cannot be withdrawn.
- Assent: since the 24th Amendment (1971), Article 368(2) provides that the President ‘shall give his assent’ — he can neither withhold assent nor return the Bill for reconsideration.

## III. Criticism of the Procedure
- No separate constituent body. Unlike the US (conventions) or Ireland and Australia (referendum), the ordinary legislature exercises constituent power. A single party or coalition with a two-thirds Lok Sabha majority can reshape the Constitution — the 42nd Amendment, passed during the Emergency when Opposition members were detained, is the standing warning.
- The federal safeguard is thin. Ratification is required for only a limited category, is by simple majority, and carries no deadline. The Constitution is also silent on whether a State may reconsider — a gap that has never been judicially settled.
- States cannot initiate amendments at all, except indirectly by resolution under Article 169 (Legislative Councils). Compare Article V of the US Constitution, where two-thirds of State legislatures may compel a convention.
- No joint sitting means an evenly divided Rajya Sabha can block reform indefinitely — the Women’s Reservation Bill of 2010 passed the Rajya Sabha but lapsed for want of Lok Sabha passage.
- Vagueness of the basic structure limit. Because no exhaustive list exists, Parliament legislates without knowing what is amendable. The Court itself acknowledged in Anjum Kadari (2024) that these are ‘undefined concepts’ whose open-ended application would create uncertainty.

## IV. Two Recent Illustrations that the Safeguards Bite
- The special majority is a real brake, not a formality. The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 — seeking to raise the Lok Sabha ceiling from 550 to 850 seats and to advance women’s reservation by delinking it from a post-2026 census — was introduced on 16 April 2026 and defeated in the Lok Sabha on 17 April 2026: 298 votes in favour and 230 against out of 528 voting, against a required threshold of 352. The linked Delimitation Bill, 2026 and Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 were consequently not proceeded with (PIB, 17 April 2026; Akashvani/News on AIR, 16–17 April 2026). It is the clearest modern demonstration that Article 368 requires cross-party consensus, not merely a governing majority.
- The ratification requirement is judicially enforced. In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Court struck down Part IXB inserted by the 97th Amendment (2011) insofar as it applied to cooperative societies operating within a State, because it curtailed State power over Entry 32 of List II without ratification under the proviso to Article 368(2). Part IXB survives only for multi-State cooperatives.

## Conclusion

Article 368 has largely vindicated the framers’ judgment. Its graded design has allowed the Constitution to absorb transformative change — panchayati raj, GST, the right to education, women’s reservation — without the paralysis that afflicts more rigid constitutions. Its weaknesses are real: the absence of a distinct constituent body, a thin federal veto, and the exclusion of States from initiating change. Yet the 2021 ratification ruling and the 2026 defeat of the 131st Amendment Bill together show that the procedure’s safeguards, both judicial and political, still function. The case for reform therefore lies not in redesigning Article 368 but in strengthening deliberation — through mandatory referral of amendment Bills to the Inter-State Council and to parliamentary committees.

## Value addition
- Numbers worth quoting: 106 amendments in 76 years, against 27 in the United States since 1789. Article 368 as it stands is itself the product of amendment — the 24th (1971) made assent obligatory, the 42nd (1976) added clauses (4) and (5), and Minerva Mills (1980) voided them.
- The 106th Amendment (2023), Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, reserving one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies (Arts. 330A, 332A, 334A), came into force on 16 April 2026, but implementation remains tied to delimitation following the next census, with the reference date for the ongoing census set at 1 March 2027.
- Comparative models to cite: Australia and Ireland require a referendum; the US requires ratification by three-fourths of States; Switzerland permits citizen-initiated amendment. India has none of these participatory mechanisms — the core of the ‘no popular sanction’ criticism.
- Committee recommendations: the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (Venkatachaliah Commission, 2002) recommended that amendments affecting federal provisions be referred to an Inter-State Council under Article 263 before introduction — an argument directly usable in the conclusion.
- AP angle: Andhra Pradesh has been affected by both categories — ordinary reorganisation laws in 2014 and 2026, and ratified amendments such as the 101st (GST, 2016), which the AP Assembly ratified in 2016, requiring the State to surrender autonomous taxing powers over entry tax and VAT.

## Introduction

Part III (Articles 12–35) has been the most contested terrain in Indian constitutional history because it sits at the intersection of two competing imperatives — the protection of individual liberty and the pursuit of social and economic transformation under Part IV. Of the 106 amendments so far, a substantial proportion touch Part III directly. Their trajectory is not random: the early amendments curtailed rights to enable land reform, the middle period fought over whether rights could be amended at all, and the modern phase has largely expanded them.

## The Threshold Question — Are Fundamental Rights Amendable?
- Sankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) held that an amendment is not ‘law’ under Article 13(2), so Part III was amendable.
- Golak Nath (1967) reversed this, holding Fundamental Rights ‘transcendental and immutable’ and wholly beyond amendment.
- The 24th Amendment (1971) — the hinge of the entire story — inserted Article 13(4) and Article 368(1) and (3), expressly declaring that Article 13 does not apply to amendments under Article 368.
- Kesavananda Bharati (1973) settled the position: Parliament may amend any Fundamental Right, but not so as to damage the basic structure. Confirmed for the Ninth Schedule in I.R. Coelho (2007), which made post-1973 insertions testable against the ‘rights test’.

## II. Three Phases of Amendment
- **Phase** — Key Amendments · Effect on Part III
- **Phase I (1951–64) Social reform vs property and equality** — 1st (1951), 4th (1955), 17th (1964) · The 1st Amendment added Art. 15(4) (reversing Champakam Dorairajan), widened Art. 19(2) to include public order and incitement (reversing Romesh Thappar), and inserted Arts. 31A and 31B with the Ninth Schedule to shield land reform. The 4th and 17th expanded that shield further.

- **Phase** — Key Amendments · Effect on Part III
- **Phase II (1971–76) The contest over amendability** — 24th (1971), 25th (1971), 42nd (1976) · The 24th restored Parliament’s power to amend Part III. The 25th replaced ‘compensation’ with ‘amount’ for acquisition and inserted Art. 31C, immunising laws implementing Arts. 39(b) and (c). The 42nd extended 31C to all Directive Principles — struck down in Minerva Mills (1980) as destroying the FR–DPSP balance.
- **Phase III (1978–2023) Restoration and expansion** — 44th (1978), 86th (2002), 93rd (2005), 97th (2011), 103rd (2019), 106th (2023) · The 44th deleted Art. 19(1)(f) and Art. 31, converting property into a legal right under Art. 300A, and amended Art. 359 so that Arts. 20 and 21 can never be suspended even during an Emergency. The 86th added Art. 21A (free and compulsory education, 6–14 years) and Art. 51A(k). The 93rd added Art. 15(5), upheld in Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008). The 103rd added Arts. 15(6) and 16(6) for 10% EWS reservation, upheld 3:2 in Janhit Abhiyan (2022).

## III. A Correction Most Answers Get Wrong

The 97th Amendment (2011) is routinely cited as having added ‘co-operative societies’ to Article 19(1)(c) and inserted Article 43B and Part IXB. Two of the three survive. In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Supreme Court struck down Part IXB insofar as it applies to cooperative societies operating within a State, because it curtailed State legislative power over Entry 32 of List II without ratification under the proviso to Article 368(2). Part IXB now operates only for multi-State cooperatives; the amendments to Article 19(1)(c) and Article 43B were unaffected. Stating this accurately distinguishes a top-band answer from a textbook reproduction. IV. Analysing the Net Direction

- From property to social rights. The right to property was the principal casualty — from a Fundamental Right in 1950 to a constitutional legal right by 1978. The Court has nonetheless kept Art. 300A meaningful, and in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024) a nine-judge Bench held 8:1 that not all private property is a ‘material resource of the community’ under Art. 39(b), rejecting the expansive Krishna Iyer formulation.
- From negative liberty to positive entitlement. Article 21A (2002) marked a shift from restraining the State to obliging it — giving rise to the Right to Education Act, 2009 and, through judicial interpretation of Article 21, to rights to livelihood, privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017) and a clean environment.
- Judicial review as the balance-wheel. Every major curtailment has been checked — the 42nd by Minerva Mills, the Ninth Schedule by Coelho, the 97th by Rajendra N. Shah — while genuine social-justice amendments (86th, 93rd, 103rd) have been sustained. The pattern shows the Court policing method and structure, not policy.

## Andhra Pradesh Application

AP implements the 103rd Amendment’s 10% EWS reservation in State services and in AP EAPCET/EDCET admissions, alongside SC (15%), ST (6%) and BC quotas. AP’s land-ceiling legislation — notably the AP Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973 — sits in the Ninth Schedule; being pre-24 April 1973 it retains I.R. Coelho’s protection, whereas any post-1973 insertion would now be open to challenge. Andhra Pradesh also has a live stake in the 106th Amendment (2023): with 175 Assembly seats, roughly 58 would be reserved for women once delimitation follows the next census.

## Conclusion

The amendment history of Part III is best read not as a series of attacks on liberty but as a continuing negotiation between rights and redistribution. Parliament has repeatedly recalibrated Fundamental Rights to advance land reform, educational access and social justice; the judiciary has responded by fixing an outer boundary rather than a policy preference. The result is a Part III that looks materially different from 1950 — leaner on property, richer in social entitlement — yet whose core has never been surrendered. That equilibrium, secured by the basic structure doctrine and the ratification requirement, is the real achievement of seventy-six years of constitutional amendment.

## Introduction

Articles 352 to 360 in Part XVIII are the Constitution’s crisis architecture, drawn largely from Section 93 and the emergency scheme of the Government of India Act, 1935. Dr. Ambedkar defended them in the Constituent Assembly on the ground that India would be “federal in normal times and unitary in emergency” – a design that makes India the only major federation able to convert into a unitary State without amending its Constitution. That very flexibility is the source of both their utility and their abuse. The year 2025 marked fifty years of the 1975 Emergency, making a critical appraisal of these powers directly examinable.

## The Three-Fold Constitutional Architecture
- **Type** — Ground & Article · Approval and duration · Record of invocation
- **National Emergency** — War, external aggression or armed rebellion (Art. 352). “Armed rebellion” replaced “internal disturbance” by the 44th Amendment, 1978. · Special majority of both Houses within 1 month; renewable every 6 months. · Thrice – 1962 (China), 1971 (Pakistan), 1975 (internal disturbance).
- **President’s Rule / State Emergency** — Failure of constitutional machinery in a State (Art. 356); Art. 365 deems failure where a State ignores a Union direction. · Simple majority within 2 months; 6 months at a time; beyond one year only if a National Emergency is in force in that State and the ECI certifies elections cannot be held; maximum 3 years. · About 134 times since 1950 across 29 States and UTs. Most recent: Manipur, imposed 13 February 2025, revoked 4 February 2026.
- **Financial Emergency** — Threat to the financial stability or credit of India (Art. 360). · Simple majority within 2 months; no maximum duration. · Never invoked – not in the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis, nor in 2020.

2. Why the Powers Are Necessary IWartime capacity to legislate and mobilise. During the 1962 and 1971 emergencies, Article 250 let Parliament legislate on State List subjects and Article 354 allowed the Centre to alter the tax-sharing formula – without which the Defence of India Act, 1962 and wartime resource redirection would have been constitutionally impossible. IFilling a genuine governance vacuum. Article 356 is defensible where no alternative government can be formed. In Manipur, President’s Rule followed the Chief Minister’s resignation with no party staking a claim; Parliament confirmed the proclamation in April 2025 and it was revoked on 4 February 2026 the moment a ministry could be sworn in (Ministry of Home Affairs notifications, reported by newsonair.gov.in, February 2025 and February 2026). IPreserving the Union’s duty under Article 355. Emergency powers give operative content to the Union’s obligation to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance, converting a duty into an enforceable competence.

3. The Record of Misuse – and Its Constitutional Mechanics IThe 1975–77 Emergency was political, not existential. It was proclaimed on 25 June 1975 on the ground of “internal disturbance” days after the Allahabad High Court voided the Prime Minister’s election in State of U.P. v. Raj Narain, against a backdrop of the JP Movement and inflation of 23% (1973) and 30% (1974). Lakhs were detained under MISA and press censorship was imposed. IRights were suspended through Articles 358 and 359, not Article 352 alone. Article 358 automatically suspended Article 19; Article 359 empowered the President to suspend enforcement of the remaining rights. In ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976) the Court held that even Article 21 was unenforceable – a holding expressly overruled by the nine-judge bench in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017). IJudicial review itself was extinguished by amendment. The 38th Amendment (1975) made the President’s satisfaction under Articles 352, 356 and 360 final and non-justiciable; the 39th placed the Prime Minister’s election beyond court scrutiny; the 42nd extended the Lok Sabha term to six years. Misuse, in other words, required constitutional capture – which is why the safeguards had to be constitutional too. IArticle 356 has been the routine instrument of abuse. Kerala (1959), the wholesale dismissals of 1977 and 1980 after changes of government at the Centre, and nine State governments in 1992 were political rather than constitutional. Andhra Pradesh is a compact case study: President’s Rule in Andhra State in 1954 after the Prakasam ministry lost its majority; from 11 January to 10 December 1973 during the Jai Andhra agitation following P.V. Narasimha Rao’s resignation; and again in March 2014 pending bifurcation. Only the 1973 spell was a plausible breakdown of machinery.

4. The Correctives – Constitutional, Judicial and Institutional I44th Amendment Act, 1978 (acting on the Shah Commission, 1977): ground narrowed to “armed rebellion”; written advice of the Union Cabinet made mandatory; approval by special majority within one month; six-monthly renewal; the Lok Sabha may revoke by simple majority on a requisition by one-tenth of its members; Articles 20 and 21 made non-suspendable under Article 359; Lok Sabha term restored to five years. IJudicial:S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) restored justiciability – the proclamation is reviewable, majority is tested only on the floor of the House, the Assembly cannot be dissolved before both Houses approve, and secularism and federalism are basic structure. Rameshwar Prasad (2006) struck down the Bihar dissolution as mala fide; Nabam Rebia (2016) restored the Arunachal Pradesh government. IInstitutional memory as a check: the MHA gazette notification of 12 July 2024 declared 25 June as Samvidhaan Hatya Diwas, observed annually since 2025 (newsonair.gov.in, June 2025) – keeping the 1975 experience politically salient.

## Conclusion

Emergency powers are not a constitutional defect; they are an insurance policy that a diverse federation cannot do without. The defect lay in a design that once allowed the insured to certify his own claim. The 44th Amendment and Bommai together converted an unreviewable executive prerogative into a reviewable constitutional act, and the Manipur cycle of 2025–26 – proclamation on a Governor’s report, Parliamentary confirmation, Assembly kept in suspended animation rather than dissolved, and prompt revocation – shows the corrected model working. The remaining safeguard is not textual but political: emergency powers survive best when they are least used.

## Value addition
- Article 358 vs Article 359 – the standard distinguishing question. Article 358 suspends Article 19 automatically, and after the 44th Amendment only when the emergency is declared on external grounds (war or external aggression). Article 359 requires a separate Presidential order, may be for the whole or part of India, and now cannot cover Articles 20 and 21. IEffects of a Financial Emergency (Art. 360), never yet tested: the Centre may direct States to reduce salaries of all persons serving under them, may require all State Money Bills to be reserved for the President’s consideration, and may reduce the salaries of Supreme Court and High Court judges. ## Introduction

The Right to Property was originally guaranteed twice over – by Article 19(1)(f), the freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property, and by Article 31, protection against deprivation save by authority of law and on payment of compensation. It was the only Fundamental Right that operated as a direct restraint on the State’s redistributive power, and it triggered India’s longest constitutional conflict: the First, Fourth, Seventeenth and Twenty-fifth Amendments, the Ninth Schedule, and the line of cases from Shankari Prasad (1951) through Golaknath (1967) to Kesavananda Bharati (1973). The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 ended that conflict by relocating the right outside Part III.

1. What the 44th Amendment Actually Did IOmitted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 and inserted Article 300A in a new Chapter IV of Part XII: “No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.” The right thus became a constitutional and legal right rather than a Fundamental Right. IThe remedial consequence is the crux. Article 32 is no longer available, since it lies only for Part III rights; the aggrieved owner must move the High Court under Article 226 or file an ordinary suit. Yet the right did not become weak – in Vidya Devi v. IWhat survived is as important as what went. Articles 31A, 31B, 31C and the Ninth Schedule were retained, so protection for agrarian reform legislation continues – though I.R. Coelho (2007) held that Ninth Schedule entries made after 24 April 1973 are testable against the basic structure. Two express compensation guarantees also survive: the proviso to Article 31A (land under personal cultivation within the ceiling) and Article 30(1A) (property of minority educational institutions).

## Introduction

Judicial review is a power the Constitution confers; judicial activism is a posture the judiciary adopts. Review is the authority under Articles 13, 32 and 226 to test the validity of legislative and executive action against the Constitution. Activism describes an expansive, purposive exercise of that authority – relaxing standing, reading new content into rights, and issuing directions to fill vacuums left by the other organs. The two are related but not identical: all activism is exercised through review, but not all review is activist.

## Judicial Review and Judicial Activism Distinguished
- **Basis** — Judicial Review · Judicial Activism
- **Source of authority** — Express constitutional grant – Articles 13, 32, 131–136, 226, 227; declared basic structure in Kesavananda (1973). · No textual basis; evolved through interpretation, chiefly by expanding Article 21 and relaxing locus standi.
- **Nature and trigger** — Essentially reactive – the Court acts when a law or action is challenged before it by an aggrieved party. · Essentially proactive – often initiated through PIL, suo motu cognisance or a letter petition.
- **Function performed** — Validity-testing: preserves constitutional supremacy and legislative competence. · Gap-filling: supplies norms and remedies where the legislature or executive has not acted.
- **Remedial reach** — Ordinarily declaratory – the impugned law or order is struck down, quashed or read down. · Directive and supervisory – guidelines, continuing mandamus, court-monitored committees, Article 142 orders.
- **Characteristic risk** — Countermajoritarian criticism – unelected judges voiding the will of an elected legislature. · Judicial overreach – the Court assuming functions that are institutionally legislative or executive.
- **Restraining doctrine** — Presumption of constitutionality; process not merits (Tata Cellular, 1994); political-question restraint. · Self-restraint; institutional competence; the caution in Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass (2008) against “judicial adventurism”.

2. Important Decisions – Judicial Review IKesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): Parliament’s amending power under Article 368 does not extend to destroying the basic structure – the foundational exercise of review over a constitutional amendment. Raj Narain (1975) and Minerva Mills (1980): struck down, respectively, Clause 4 of the 39th Amendment which had immunised the Prime Minister’s election, and Articles 368(4) and (5) inserted by the 42nd Amendment – establishing that limited amending power and judicial review are themselves basic features.

- S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): a proclamation under Article 356 is justiciable and majority must be tested on the floor of the House – review applied to the highest executive act in the federal scheme. Union of India (February 2024): the Electoral Bonds Scheme and the accompanying amendments to the Representation of the People Act, the Companies Act and the Income-tax Act were struck down as violating the voter’s right to information under Article 19(1)(a) – classic review, testing a statute against Part III. Union of India (19 November 2025): key provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 were struck down for reproducing provisions already invalidated, amounting to a legislative override that compromised tribunal independence and the separation of powers.

Union of India (1981): the first read a right to speedy trial and free legal aid into Article 21 for undertrials; the second relaxed locus standi to permit any public-spirited person to approach the Court – jointly the birth of PIL. IUnni Krishnan J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993): an Andhra Pradesh case in which the Court read a right to free and compulsory education up to the age of 14 into Article 21 by reading Articles 41 and 45 into it. Its significance is that activism here proved catalytic rather than final – Parliament constitutionalised the holding through the 86th Amendment (2002), inserting Article 21A, followed by the Right to Education Act, 2009. Fletcher, and later built the polluter-pays and precautionary principles – judicial creation of substantive environmental law. IVishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997): in the absence of legislation, the Court framed binding guidelines on sexual harassment at the workplace under Article 32, drawing on CEDAW. Judicial review is the Constitution’s own device for keeping power within limits; judicial activism is the judiciary’s response when those limits are observed but the constitutional promise is not met.
