## Introduction

The modern administrative State makes rules, applies them and adjudicates disputes arising from them – a concentration that the classical separation of powers cannot by itself restrain. Judicial review of administrative action supplies that restraint, testing whether an authority acted within its powers, fairly and reasonably. Its constitutional foundations are Articles 13, 14, 21, 32, 226, 227, 136 and 300A. Crucially, it is review and not appeal: as the Supreme Court held in Tata Cellular v. Union of India (1994), the court examines the decision-making process, not the correctness of the decision.

## Grounds of Review

The classification is drawn from Lord Diplock’s formulation in Council of Civil Service Unions v. Minister for the Civil Service (the GCHQ case, 1985) – illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety – which Indian courts adopted and then supplemented with proportionality and legitimate expectation.

- 1. Illegality. The authority must correctly understand the law that empowers it and give effect to it. Review lies where action is ultra vires the parent statute, where power is exercised for an improper purpose or on irrelevant considerations, where relevant considerations are ignored, where discretion is fettered by rigid rules or abdicated to another body, or where the action is mala fide. Delegated legislation exceeding the rule-making power in the parent Act is the commonest instance. I2. Irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness). From Associated Provincial Picture Houses v. Wednesbury Corporation (1948): a decision so outrageous in its defiance of logic or accepted moral standards that no sensible authority could have arrived at it. In India this has been fortified by Article 14 – E.P. Royappa (1974) equated arbitrariness with inequality, and Shayara Bano (2017) established manifest arbitrariness as a free-standing ground. I3. Procedural impropriety. Two elements: failure to observe the procedure expressly laid down by statute, and breach of natural justice – nemo judex in causa sua (no one a judge in his own cause) and audi alteram partem (hear the other side). A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India (1969) extended natural justice from quasi-judicial to purely administrative action; Maneka Gandhi (1978) required that the procedure itself be just, fair and reasonable. I4. Proportionality. The means must be suitable to the object, necessary in the sense that no less restrictive alternative exists, and balanced against the right infringed. Applied to disciplinary punishment in Om Kumar v. Union of India (2001) and formulated as a four-prong test in Modern Dental College (2016) and K.S. Puttaswamy (2017). Andhra Pradesh illustration: in Kaka Ramakrishna v. State of Andhra Pradesh (AP High Court, 12 May 2023) the Court struck down G.O. Rt. No. 1 dated 2 January 2023, issued under Section 30 of the Police Act, 1861, which had effectively barred meetings on State and national highways. The Court held the power was regulatory, not prohibitory, and that a total ban dressed as regulation was arbitrary, excessive and failed the tests of reasonableness and proportionality under Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(b) and 21.
- 5. Legitimate expectation. A settled past practice or a clear promise generates an expectation that cannot be defeated without a hearing and an overriding public interest – Navjyoti Co-operative Group Housing Society (1992) and Food Corporation of India v. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries (1993). This is the doctrine under which assurances of return plots and annuities to farmers under a land-pooling scheme become legally cognisable.

## Modes of Review
- **Mode** — Provision and reach · Illustration
- **Writ jurisdiction** — Article 32 (Supreme Court, only for Fundamental Rights) and Article 226 (High Courts, wider – for FRs “and for any other purpose”). Five writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto. · Certiorari quashes a completed quasi-judicial decision; mandamus compels performance of a public duty – the remedy the Supreme Court held available against gubernatorial inaction in Special Reference No. 1 of 2025 (20 November 2025).
- **Supervisory and appellate routes** — Article 227 superintendence over all courts and tribunals in a High Court’s territory; Article 136 special leave; plus statutory appeals and revisions under the parent Act. · Statutory appeals must ordinarily be exhausted first – the alternative-remedy rule is a self-imposed limit on writ jurisdiction.
- **Tribunals, with residual High Court review** — Articles 323A and 323B (inserted by the 42nd Amendment) and the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985. L. Chandra Kumar (1997): tribunal decisions remain subject to review by a Division Bench of the High Court under Articles 226 and 227. · AP: the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal was abolished by the Union at the State’s request (DoPT notification G.S.R. 30(E), 14 January 2020), so AP service matters now go directly to the High Court under Article 226. Tribunal independence was reinforced in Madras Bar Association (19 November 2025), striking down parts of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021.
- **Public Interest Litigation and continuing mandamus** — Relaxed locus standi under Articles 32 and 226 permits any public-spirited person to move the court; the court may retain the matter and supervise compliance over time. · Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1998) supervised a stalled investigation through continuing mandamus and led to statutory status for the CVC in 2003.

- Non-judicial complements matter, because litigation is slow and expensive. CAG audit under Article 148, the Lokpal and State Lokayuktas, the Central Vigilance Commission, and statutory grievance machinery perform the same accountability function ex ante. The Second ARC’s Twelfth Report, Citizen Centric Administration – The Heart of Governance (February 2009), recommended a robust internal grievance-redress architecture and the Sevottam service-delivery model precisely so that citizens are not forced into court for ordinary administrative failure.

## Conclusion

Judicial review of administrative action is the constitutional answer to the discretion that modern governance necessarily requires. By insisting on legality, rationality, fair procedure and proportionality, and by making these enforceable through writs, supervisory jurisdiction, tribunals and public interest litigation, it converts administrative power into accountable power. Its limits are equally important: the court reviews the process rather than the wisdom of a decision, defers to specialised expertise in policy, and declines relief where an efficacious alternative exists. Sustained accountability therefore requires that judicial review be complemented by internal grievance redress, audit and vigilance institutions – so that the citizen’s first remedy is administrative, and the court remains the last.

**Judicial review** in India has evolved well beyond the classical striking down of unconstitutional laws; several **novel trends** have expanded its reach, reflecting the judiciary's growing role as guardian of rights and governance.

These trends empower citizens but raise concerns of **judicial overreach** into policy and administration.

- Deepening from calories to nutrition: The Union Cabinet approved universal supply of fortified rice (iron, folic acid, vitamin B12) across PMGKAY, ICDS and PM POSHAN from July 2024 to December 2028, at Rs. 17,082 crore fully Centre-funded (PIB, October 2024) — a response to the NFHS-5 finding of widespread anaemia.

- AP dimension: Andhra Pradesh layers state action on the statutory floor — doorstep delivery of rice through Mobile Dispatch Units, and the revival of Anna Canteens on 15 August 2024 offering subsidised meals to the urban poor, who are typically the group least able to convert a ration entitlement into a cooked meal.

## Conclusion

The NFSA is genuinely paradigmatic in the legal sense: it created a justiciable claim, a remedy for default, and an institutional forum, moving India from charity to entitlement. It remains incomplete in the nutritional sense, being cereal-centric and anchored to a 2011 population base. Updating coverage after the next Census, widening the basket to pulses and millets, and converging NFSA with POSHAN 2.0 would carry the shift from food security to genuine nutrition security — the substance of SDG 2 (Zero Hunger).

## Value addition
- Key sections to cite by number: Sec. 3 (entitlement), Sec. 4–6 (women and children), Sec. 8 (food security allowance), Sec. 13 (eldest woman as head of household), Sec. 14–16 (grievance redressal, State Food Commission), Sec. 24 (Centre–State obligations).
- Constitutional and judicial hooks: Article 21 (right to life includes right to food, PUCL v. Union of India, 2001); Article 47 (DPSP — duty to raise nutrition levels); Article 15(3) for special provisions for women and children.
- Convergent schemes: PMGKAY (free grain extended to December 2028), PM POSHAN, POSHAN 2.0/Saksham Anganwadi, PMMVY, ONORC, and the Price Stabilisation Fund — useful to show that NFSA is the statutory floor, not the whole edifice.
- Committee memory: Wadhwa Committee (Supreme Court-appointed, on PDS reform) and the Shanta Kumar Committee (2015), which recommended narrowing coverage to 40% and cash transfers — a counterpoint worth naming when arguing fiscal sustainability.
- Global frame: SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 1 (No Poverty); India’s SDG India Index composite score rose to 71 in 2023-24 from 66 in 2020-21 (NITI Aayog, July 2024), with Zero Hunger flagged as a lagging goal.

## Introduction

Indian health records have historically been fragmented across paper prescriptions and siloed hospital systems, forcing repeat diagnostics and breaking continuity of care. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission — piloted as the National Digital Health Mission in six UTs on 15 August 2020 and launched nationwide on 27 September 2021, implemented by the National Health Authority with a Rs. 1,600 crore outlay for 2021-22 to 2025-26 — is India’s attempt to build Digital Public Infrastructure for health, doing for medical records what UPI did for payments.

- **Building block** — What it is · Problem it solves · Status (MoHFW/NHA, July 2026)
- **ABHA** — 14-digit unique health ID · No portable patient identity · 93.95 crore created; 105 crore records linked
- **HFR** — Health Facility Registry · No verified list of facilities · 5.33 lakh facilities registered
- **HPR** — Healthcare Professionals Registry · Unverifiable practitioner credentials · 9.85 lakh professionals registered
- **UHI** — Unified Health Interface · Closed, non-interoperable apps · Open protocol; teleconsultation and e-pharmacy

## Assessing the claim of a ‘robust digital health ecosystem’
- Scale achieved is genuinely transformative: ABDM has crossed 93.95 crore ABHA numbers, 105 crore linked health records, and 2.72 lakh facilities using ABDM-enabled software (Mission Steering Group, 3rd meeting, MoHFW, July 2026). ABHA creation has climbed steadily from 14.7 crore in 2021 to over 90 crore by May 2026 (PIB, 30 May 2026) — a genuine population-scale digital public good.
- Measured service-delivery gains, not just enrolment: The Scan and Share service lets a patient generate an OPD token by scanning a QR code; an IIHMR study cited by the Ministry found waiting times fell from about one hour to 2–5 minutes, with roughly 24 crore tokens generated (PIB, July 2026). This is the strongest evidence that ABDM is changing experience, not merely counting IDs.
- Consent-based portability as the core design principle: Records move only with patient consent through the Health Information Exchange, which preserves autonomy while enabling continuity — the migrant construction worker treated in Vijayawada and later in Visakhapatnam no longer starts diagnostics from zero.
- Integration with flagship programmes: ABDM now interlinks with AB PM-JAY, CGHS, ESIC and Ni-kshay, and expands through Model Districts and Model Facilities, so digitisation rides on existing service delivery rather than running parallel to it (MoHFW, July 2026).
- New AI layer, new governance questions:Aarogya Setu 2.0 was launched on 29 June 2026 as a unified citizen gateway, alongside AI-governance initiatives SAHI and BODH announced in February 2026. Capability is expanding faster than the accountability framework around algorithmic decisions in clinical settings.
- Binding constraints: Health data is the most sensitive personal data, and operationalising the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 rules is the precondition for public trust; the digital divide persists, mitigated only partly by assisted and offline ABHA creation; and record linkage still lags record creation, especially among small private providers who bear the software cost without a visible return.

## Conclusion

ABDM has convincingly built the rails of a digital health ecosystem — identity, registries and an open interface at population scale. The next test is utilisation: whether linked records actually change clinical decisions and reduce out-of-pocket expenditure. That depends on enforceable data-protection rules, deeper private-provider onboarding, and Centre–State convergence. Handled well, ABDM becomes the delivery backbone for Universal Health Coverage under SDG 3; handled poorly, it becomes the largest health database with the thinnest safeguards.

## Introduction

Urban poverty differs qualitatively from rural poverty: it is characterised less by absolute food scarcity than by informality of work, insecurity of tenure and invisibility in official records. NITI Aayog estimates multidimensional poverty at 11.28% in 2022-23, with about 24.82 crore people exiting multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23 (NITI Aayog Discussion Paper, 2024). Notably, Andhra Pradesh was the first Indian State to adopt a State-level Multidimensional Poverty Index (2018), ahead of the national baseline report of 2021.

- **Pillar** — Flagship instrument · Achievement (official) · Residual gap
- **Shelter** — PMAY-Urban & PMAY-U 2.0 · 13.61 lakh houses sanctioned under 2.0 by Feb 2026, incl. AP · Land cost; peripheral siting away from work
- **Livelihood** — DAY-NULM; skilling under PMKVY · SHGs, self-employment credit, shelters for urban homeless · No urban employment guarantee analogous to MGNREGA
- **Micro-credi t** — PM SVANidhi · 96 lakh loans, Rs. 13,797 crore to 68 lakh vendors · Working-capital scale still small per vendor
- **Social security** — AB PM-JAY, e-Shram, NFSA-ONORC · Portable health cover and portable rations · Registration depends on documents migrants lack

## Why the programmes have, on balance, delivered
- Shelter converts residence into an asset: Under PMAY-U, over 1.18 crore houses were sanctioned and more than 95 lakh completed; PMAY-U 2.0 (Cabinet approval, August 2024) targets one crore additional urban homes, and the 6th Central Sanctioning and Monitoring Committee sanctioned 2.88 lakh more houses in February 2026, taking the total to 13.61 lakh across 16 States/UTs including Andhra Pradesh (MoHUA, February 2026). A titled house ends eviction risk and unlocks formal credit — the single largest asset transfer to the urban poor.
- Street vendors moved from the informal moneylender to the formal system:PM SVANidhi has disbursed about 96 lakh loans worth Rs. 13,797 crore, and the Cabinet restructured and extended it to 31 March 2030 with a Rs. 7,332 crore outlay covering 1.15 crore beneficiaries including 50 lakh new vendors (Cabinet decision, August 2025). Nearly 47 lakh digitally active vendors have built transaction histories — the credit record that formal finance requires.
- Livelihood and skilling reach the urban informal worker: DAY-NULM supplies skill training, self-employment credit, SHG formation and shelters for the urban homeless. Andhra Pradesh delivers this through MEPMA (Mission for Elimination of Poverty in Municipal Areas), one of India’s longest-running dedicated urban poverty agencies, which gives the State an institutional depth many others lack.
- Portability makes entitlements follow the migrant: One Nation One Ration Card and AB PM-JAY allow a worker who has moved from Srikakulam to Visakhapatnam to draw rations and hospitalisation cover without re-registration — directly addressing the mobility that made the urban poor invisible to welfare.
- State-level food and income supplements: AP revived Anna Canteens on 15 August 2024 offering subsidised meals, launched Stree Shakti free bus travel for women, girls and transgender persons on 15 August 2025 covering about 2.62 crore beneficiaries at roughly Rs. 1,942 crore annually (G.O.Ms.No.27, Transport R&B Dept.), and pays Rs. 4,000 per month old-age pension under NTR Bharosa — transfers that materially raise the disposable income of the urban poor.
- Honest limitations: There is no urban counterpart to MGNREGA, leaving urban unemployment without a statutory fallback; poverty lines still rest on Tendulkar/Rangarajan methodology with no post-2011 Census enumeration; urban local bodies remain fiscally weak and dependent on transfers, limiting their capacity to implement; and beneficiary identification systematically excludes undocumented migrants.

## Conclusion

The verdict is a qualified affirmative. Urban poverty programmes have demonstrably improved shelter security, credit access and social protection, and the multidimensional poverty data confirm real movement. But they remain a set of vertical schemes rather than an integrated urban poverty strategy. Convergence under empowered ULBs, an urban employment guarantee, and updated enumeration would convert incremental relief into structural exit — the ambition behind Andhra Pradesh’s P4 ‘Zero Poverty’ model and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities).

- AP’s signature intervention:P4 — Public, Private, People Partnership (‘Zero Poverty’), launched on Ugadi, 30 March 2025 under Swarnandhra Vision 2047. The richest 10% (Margadarsis) adopt the poorest 20% (Bangaru Kutumbam) through ‘Adopt a Family’, ‘Adopt a Village’ or ‘Fund a Need’; the State acts only as facilitator and verifier — a rare co-production model in Indian poverty policy.
- Measurement debate to display: Tendulkar (2009) vs Rangarajan (2014) poverty lines; NITI Aayog National MPI (12 indicators, three dimensions, NFHS-based); AP as the first State with its own MPI (2018).

## Introduction

The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 defines a senior citizen as a person aged 60 or above. India is ageing rapidly: the India Ageing Report 2023 (UNFPA–IIPS) projects the elderly share rising from about 10.5% of the population in 2022 to roughly 20.8% by 2050, when the elderly will outnumber children under 15. With shrinking joint families and a largely uncovered informal workforce, State support has moved from optional charity to constitutional obligation under Article 41.

- **Need** — Central intervention · Andhra Pradesh counterpart
- **Income security** — IGNOAPS under NSAP; Atal Pension Yojana; Senior Citizens’ Savings Scheme · NTR Bharosa Pension — Rs. 4,000/month for old age (G.O.Ms.No.43, 13.06.2024)
- **Health security** — Ayushman Vay Vandana Card (70+); NPHCE; Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana · Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva; Ayushman Arogya Mandirs
- **Care & dignity** — AVYAY umbrella — Senior Citizen Homes, Elder Line 14567, SAGE, SACRED portal · Doorstep pension delivery by secretariat staff; Anna Canteens
- **Legal protection** — MWPSC Act, 2007 — Maintenance Tribunals; Article 41 (DPSP) · District Maintenance Tribunals under the 2007 Act

## Analysis of the principal interventions
- Health security — the decisive recent shift: On 29 October 2024 AB PM-JAY was extended to all citizens aged 70 and above irrespective of income, through the Ayushman Vay Vandana Card giving Rs. 5 lakh annual cover (with a separate top-up for seniors already in PM-JAY families). Over 1.14 crore cards had been issued by 28 February 2026 (MoHFW reply to Rajya Sabha, March 2026). This breaks the income-test principle and treats old age itself as the qualifying vulnerability — conceptually the most significant elderly-welfare reform in years.
- Income security remains the weakest link: Under IGNOAPS the central contribution is only Rs. 200 per month for those aged 60–79 and Rs. 500 for those 80 and above, unrevised for well over a decade; adequacy therefore depends almost entirely on State top-ups. Andhra Pradesh’s NTR Bharosa pension of Rs. 4,000 per month is among India’s highest, with a budget of Rs. 32,143 crore for FY 2025-26 (Govt. of AP) — showing that the binding constraint is State fiscal capacity, not central design.
- Care infrastructure and loneliness: The Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana (AVYAY) umbrella funds Senior Citizen Homes, the national Elder Line (14567) helpline, and the SAGE (Seniorcare Ageing Growth Engine) start-up platform, while SACRED connects elderly job-seekers to employers. These address isolation and purposelessness, which the India Ageing Report identifies as major determinants of elderly mental health.
- Assistive devices and geriatric care:Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana distributes hearing aids, walkers and spectacles to BPL elderly, and NPHCE creates geriatric wards at district hospitals and regional geriatric centres — a small but high-return intervention, since mobility loss is the trigger for dependency.
- Legal and rights architecture: The 2007 Act makes maintenance a legally enforceable obligation on children and heirs, with summary Maintenance Tribunals and a provision allowing transfer of property to be voided where the transferee neglects the elderly transferor — a powerful remedy that remains under-used because awareness is low.
- Persisting gaps:Feminisation of ageing means elderly women, more likely to be widowed and without independent income, face compounded vulnerability; the rising old-age dependency ratio strains a pay-as-you-go system; elder abuse is under-reported; and increasingly digital-only interfaces exclude precisely those with the lowest digital literacy.

## Conclusion

India’s elderly welfare architecture is now reasonably comprehensive in design — income, health, care and legal protection are all addressed — but uneven in adequacy. The universalisation of health cover for the 70+ cohort is a genuine advance; the stagnant central pension share is a genuine failure. Indexing IGNOAPS to inflation, building geriatric capacity at the primary level, and pairing digital delivery with assisted access would turn a scheme portfolio into dignified ageing, consistent with SDG 3 and SDG 10.

## Value addition
- Data points that carry weight: India Ageing Report 2023 (UNFPA–IIPS) — elderly share 10.5% (2022) rising to about 20.8% by 2050; Ayushman Vay Vandana Cards crossed 1.14 crore by 28 February 2026 (MoHFW); West Bengal joined AB PM-JAY in 2026, completing national coverage.
- Policy and legal instruments: National Policy on Older Persons, 1999; National Policy for Senior Citizens, 2011 (draft); Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007; Section 125 CrPC / Section 144 BNSS maintenance provisions; Article 41 (DPSP) and Article 21 (dignity in old age).
- Institutional map: Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (AVYAY, RVY, Elder Line, SAGE, SACRED); Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (NPHCE, AB PM-JAY 70+); Ministry of Rural Development (NSAP/IGNOAPS); National Council of Senior Citizens as the apex advisory body.
- AP specifics worth quoting exactly: NTR Bharosa Pension enhanced by G.O.Ms.No.43 dated 13.06.2024 — Rs. 4,000 (old age, widows, weavers, single women, transgender persons), Rs. 6,000 (disabled), Rs. 10,000 (fully disabled and chronic conditions including dialysis); doorstep delivery through Village and Ward Secretariat staff.

## Introduction

The National Education Policy 2020 is India’s first comprehensive education policy since 1986, targeting 100% gross enrolment in school education by 2030 and a 50% GER in higher education by 2035. Because education sits on the Concurrent List (moved there by the 42nd Amendment, 1976), NEP is not self-executing — it is a framework whose success depends on State adoption, teacher capacity and money. Implementation, not intent, is the variable.

- **Stage** — Ages / Grades · Curricular anchor · Delivery instrument
- **Foundational (5)** — 3–8 / Anganwadi–Gr. 2 · NCF-FS 2022; Jadui Pitara · NIPUN Bharat; Balvatika; Saksham Anganwadi
- **Preparatory (3)** — 8–11 / Gr. 3–5 · NCF-SE 2023; new NCERT texts · Samagra Shiksha; mother-tongue instruction
- **Middle (3)** — 11–14 / Gr. 6–8 · Vocational exposure from Gr. 6 · PM SHRI exemplar schools; internships
- **Secondary (4)** — 14–18 / Gr. 9–12 · Subject flexibility; no stream silos · Holistic Progress Card; twice-a-year boards

## Implementation pathway
- Get the foundation right first — and treat it as unfinished: NIPUN Bharat targets universal foundational literacy and numeracy. But PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024 — covering 21.15 lakh students in 74,229 schools across 781 districts (NCERT, national report July 2025) — found only 55% of Class 3 students could order numbers up to 99 and only 53% of Class 6 students knew tables up to 10. The mission must be deepened with remedial teaching, not declared complete.
- Curriculum and assessment reform must move together: NCF-FS 2022 and NCF-SE 2023 have been operationalised through new NCERT textbooks; PARAKH has been set up as the National Assessment Centre, developing the Holistic Progress Card and moving boards toward two attempts a year. Without assessment reform, a competency-based curriculum collapses back into rote learning at the exam gate.
- Teacher capacity is the binding constraint: The four-year Integrated Teacher Education Programme (ITEP) is being rolled out by NCTE as the single-track qualification, supported by NISHTHA training on DIKSHA. Filling vacancies matters as much as training: Andhra Pradesh’s Mega DSC-2025 was the State’s largest teacher recruitment in years, and the litigation around it underlines that transparent recruitment is itself an implementation task.
- Higher education needs regulatory follow-through: Multiple entry and exit, the Academic Bank of Credits, the National Credit Framework integrating general, vocational and experiential learning, and UGC’s 2023 regulations permitting foreign university campuses are in place. The unfinished item is the single regulator, HECI, which requires parliamentary legislation.
- Equity, language and demand-side support:PM SHRI exemplar schools, the Gender Inclusion Fund, Special Education Zones and ULLAS Nav Bharat Saksharta for adult literacy address supply. Demand-side retention matters equally — AP’s Talliki Vandanam transfers Rs. 15,000 per child per year to mothers, sanctioned at Rs. 10,090.74 crore for 67.27 lakh students and 42.69 lakh mothers in 2025-26 (AP School Education Dept. G.O., June 2025), with Rs. 2,000 retained for school upkeep — a direct attack on the cost barrier to attendance.
- Financing and federal comity decide the outcome: NEP reiterates the long-standing target of 6% of GDP on education; combined Centre–State spending has persistently hovered well below it. Equally, disputes with some States over the three-language formula and PM SHRI conditionalities show that on a Concurrent List subject, implementation requires negotiated consent, not directive.

## Conclusion

NEP 2020 can meet India’s educational requirements only if implementation is sequenced rather than simultaneous: foundational literacy first, assessment and teacher capacity next, structural higher-education reform thereafter. The instruments — NIPUN Bharat, PARAKH, ITEP, ABC, PM SHRI — already exist; what is scarce is money at 6% of GDP, trained teachers in classrooms, and Centre–State trust. Delivered well, NEP converts India’s demographic dividend into human capital and advances SDG 4 (Quality Education).

## Value addition
- Hard targets to quote: 100% GER in school education by 2030; 50% GER in higher education by 2035; universal foundational literacy and numeracy; public spending of 6% of GDP; vocational exposure for at least 50% of learners; mother tongue as medium of instruction at least to Grade 5, preferably to Grade 8.
- Institutions created or repurposed: PARAKH (National Assessment Centre under NCERT); National Higher Education Regulatory Council and the proposed HECI; National Research Foundation (now Anusandhan NRF); National Curriculum Frameworks FS-2022 and SE-2023; Academic Bank of Credits; National Credit Framework.
- Flagship missions: NIPUN Bharat, Samagra Shiksha, PM SHRI, PM POSHAN, ULLAS Nav Bharat Saksharta, PM Vidyalaxmi, PM-USHA for State universities, and the ITEP four-year integrated teacher degree.
- Evidence base: PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024 — 21.15 lakh students, 74,229 schools, 781 districts; UDISE+ for enrolment and infrastructure; ASER for independent corroboration of foundational learning levels.
- AP anchors: Talliki Vandanam (Rs. 15,000 per child; Rs. 10,090.74 crore, 2025-26); Mega DSC-2025 teacher recruitment; bilingual textbooks and CBSE alignment in government schools; Mana Mitra delivery of student certificates and hall tickets.

Q79 │ Section B — Q15 National Education Policy (2020) has been criticised as denuding the autonomy of States. In this connection, examine the rationale behind the transfer of matters from the State List to the Concurrent List.

Education originally stood as Entry 11 of the State List, reflecting the Government of India Act, 1935 and the Constituent Assembly's belief that schooling is culturally rooted and must be locally governed. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, acting on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation, deleted Entry 11 and inserted education into Entry 25 of the Concurrent List, making it a shared responsibility. Nearly five decades later, the National Education Policy, 2020 — reviewed at the Akhil Bharatiya Shiksha Samagam on its fifth anniversary (PIB, July 2025) — has reopened the question of whether concurrency has quietly become centralisation.

## Rationale Behind the Transfer to the Concurrent List
- Uniform standards and comparability of qualifications. A fragmented system produces degrees that States cannot recognise across borders. Note that Entry 66 of the Union List already vested the Union with 'coordination and determination of standards' in higher education; Entry 25 merely extended a comparable logic to school education. The Academic Bank of Credits, with 1,667 institutions onboarded and 2.75 crore students registered (PIB, December 2023), is unworkable without a single national credit grammar.
- Labour mobility in an integrated national market. India has an internally migrant workforce; a child moving from Srikakulam to Surat should not lose an academic year. Concurrency permits a common structural spine — NEP 2020's 5+3+3+4 design and the National Credit Framework — while leaving curricular content to States, so that transfers are administratively survivable.
- Equalising fiscal capacity across unequal States. School education is capital-hungry and poorer States cannot fund it alone. Samagra Shiksha, with an outlay of Rs 2,94,283 crore (Central share Rs 1,85,398 crore) for 2021-22 to 2025-26, and PM SHRI (Rs 27,360 crore; 13,076 exemplar schools selected as of July 2025 — PIB) transfer resources that only a Union-level pool can generate. Concurrency is the constitutional gateway for that transfer.
- National integration and constitutional literacy. Education transmits shared citizenship. Concurrency allows a common floor of civic and constitutional content — the ground on which Article 51A(k) and the RTE Act, 2009 (Article 21A, 86th Amendment) operate uniformly.

## The Autonomy Critique — Why the Criticism Has Force
- Article 254 makes concurrency asymmetric. In a repugnancy, Union law prevails; a State law survives only with Presidential assent under Article 254(2). Shared competence therefore functions as a Union veto in reserve, which is why the Sarkaria Commission (1988) and the Punchhi Commission (2010) both urged prior consultation with States before legislating on Concurrent List entries.
- Conditionality converts persuasion into leverage. NEP 2020 is a policy, not a statute, and is not legally binding on States — yet access to Samagra Shiksha and PM SHRI funds is tied to adoption. Tamil Nadu's refusal of the three-language formula and the consequent fund dispute (2025) is the clearest illustration; the Ministry of Education clarified in the Rajya Sabha (March 2025) that no language would be imposed and that the choice of the three languages rests with States and students, provided two are Indian.
- Cultural and linguistic distinctiveness. Language, textbook content and teacher recruitment are identity-bearing. A single national framework risks flattening Telugu-medium pedagogy, local history and tribal-language instruction in Scheduled Areas — precisely what Entry 11 was meant to protect.

## Andhra Pradesh — Concurrency Working Cooperatively
- AP illustrates the constructive face of shared competence. The State has aligned school reform with NEP's foundational-stage design while designing its own demand-side instrument: Talliki Vandanam (launched June 2025) transfers Rs 15,000 per school-going child annually, covering about 67 lakh students and 43 lakh mothers — a State-conceived scheme layered on Union-funded infrastructure. AP's score of 74 in the SDG India Index 2023-24 (NITI Aayog), in the Front Runner band, reflects this dual-track effort. Concurrency here is complementarity, not capture.
- **Dimension** — Pre-1976 (Entry 11, State List) · Post-1976 (Entry 25, Concurrent List)
- **Legislative competence** — States alone (Union limited to Entry 66) · Union and States; Article 254 gives Union primacy
- **Financing** — Largely State budgets · Large centrally sponsored schemes (Samagra Shiksha, PM SHRI)
- **Standards** — State boards, varied · PARAKH, NCrF, ABC — national benchmarking
- **Risk** — Inter-State disparity in quality · Homogenisation and conditional transfers

## Conclusion

The transfer of education to the Concurrent List was a defensible response to a real problem — inter-State inequality of educational capacity and the incomparability of qualifications in a mobile national economy. The criticism, however, is not about the entry but about its method of exercise: concurrency was designed as a partnership and is increasingly practised as conditionality. The corrective is institutional rather than constitutional — reviving the Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) as a genuine deliberative forum, delinking scheme funds from policy conformity, and reading the Sarkaria–Punchhi consultation norm into every Concurrent List intervention. Only then will NEP 2020 be a national consensus rather than a Union prescription.

- Constitutional map: Entry 11 (State List, deleted 1976) → Entry 25 (Concurrent List); Entry 63–66 (Union List) on national institutions and standards; Article 21A and Article 51A(k) inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002; Article 350A on mother-tongue instruction at the primary stage.
- NEP 2020 targets: 100% GER from pre-school to secondary by 2030; higher-education GER from 26.3% (2018) to 50% by 2035; public investment in education to reach 6% of GDP (PIB, Ministry of Education).
- Delivery architecture: PARAKH (national assessment centre), NCrF and National Higher Education Qualification Framework, Academic Bank of Credits, NIPUN Bharat, DIKSHA, SWAYAM PRABHA (200 DTH channels, 30 languages — PIB, July 2025).
- Outcome data (UDISE+ 2025-26, Ministry of Education, July 2026): dropout at the preparatory stage fell from 2.3% to 1.8% and at the secondary stage from 8.2% to 7.0%; PTR now 10/12/17/21 across foundational, preparatory, middle and secondary stages, against NEP's 30:1 norm; teachers crossed 1 crore in 2024-25.
- Committee memory: Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended the shift; Sarkaria Commission (1988) and Punchhi Commission (2010) both cautioned against unilateral Union legislation on Concurrent List subjects; Kothari Commission (1964-66) first proposed the 6%-of-GDP benchmark.
- AP hook: Talliki Vandanam (Rs 15,000 per child; ~67 lakh students, 43 lakh mothers, 2025); AP scored 74 on the SDG India Index 2023-24 (NITI Aayog), placing it in the Front Runner category.

Q80 │ Section B — Q16 Government's intervention in development has come a long way with impressive outcomes in India. In this connection, discuss the Atmanirbhar Bharat Mission aimed at making India self-reliant.

Launched in May 2020 amid pandemic-induced supply-chain collapse, the Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan reframed self-reliance not as import substitution of the 1960s variety but as strategic autonomy with global competitiveness — building domestic capacity in critical sectors while remaining embedded in world value chains. Its architecture rests on five pillars: Economy, Infrastructure, System, Vibrant Demography and Demand. Six years on, the mission is best assessed not by its Rs 20 lakh crore launch package but by measurable industrial outcomes, which have now accumulated.

## The Five Pillars and Their Operating Instruments
- Economy — scale-linked incentives. The Production Linked Incentive scheme, with an outlay of Rs 1.91–1.97 lakh crore across 14 sectors, ties public money to verified output rather than to capacity creation. As on 31 December 2025, it had drawn cumulative investment exceeding Rs 2.16 lakh crore, generated sales of Rs 20.41 lakh crore and exports of Rs 8.3 lakh crore, created 14.39 lakh direct and indirect jobs across 836 approved applications, with Rs 28,748 crore disbursed (PIB, February 2026).
- Infrastructure — logistics as competitiveness.PM GatiShakti National Master Plan (October 2021), a GIS platform integrating road, rail, port, waterway, telecom and power data layers, attacks the single largest drag on Indian manufacturing — logistics cost. It is operationalised through the National Infrastructure Pipeline and the National Logistics Policy, 2022.
- System — technology-led governance. GST, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, faceless assessment and the new Income-tax Act, 2025 (in force from April 2026) reduce compliance friction, which is what converts announced investment into realised investment.
- Vibrant Demography — skilling for the new lines. Capital without skilled labour idles. Under the semiconductor push alone, the Government initiated training for 85,000 engineers in advanced semiconductor and electronics manufacturing (PIB, 2025), alongside PMKVY and the apprenticeship route.
- Demand — protecting the MSME base. ECLGS, the Credit Guarantee Scheme for Micro and Small Enterprises (cover up to Rs 10 crore) and the Self-Reliant India Fund (Rs 50,000 crore equity corpus) sustain the enterprises that supply the assemblers. Budget 2026-27 announced a further Rs 2,000 crore top-up to the SRI Fund (PIB, 2026).

## Outcomes That Substantiate the Claim
- Defence. Indigenous defence production rose from Rs 46,429 crore in 2014-15 to a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26, and defence exports from Rs 686 crore in 2013-14 to Rs 38,424 crore in 2025-26, reaching over 80 countries (PIB, June 2026). Five Positive Indigenisation Lists covering 5,500+ items structurally closed the import route.
- Electronics and semiconductors. Electronics production rose from Rs 11.32 lakh crore (FY 2024-25) to Rs 13.11 lakh crore (FY 2025-26), a 15.8% increase (PIB, 2026); 99.2% of mobile phones sold in India are now domestically made, from 26% in 2014-15. Under the India Semiconductor Mission, 10 projects worth about Rs 1.60 lakh crore across six States stand approved (PIB, December 2025), with ISM 2.0 and an enhanced Rs 40,000 crore Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme announced in Budget 2026-27.
- Andhra Pradesh's stake. The Union Cabinet's approval of Advanced System in Package Technologies (ASIP) in Andhra Pradesh on 12 August 2025 — about Rs 468–480 crore, capacity of 96 million units a year, in technology partnership with APACT Co. Ltd, South Korea — places AP on the national semiconductor map for the first time (PIB). Combined with Sri City's electronics cluster and the Orvakal and Kopparthy industrial nodes, this converts Atmanirbharta from a slogan into a State-level industrial opportunity.
- **Pillar** — Flagship Instrument · Verified Outcome (latest)
- **Economy** — PLI, 14 sectors · Rs 2.16 lakh cr investment; Rs 20.41 lakh cr sales (31 Dec 2025)
- **Infrastructure** — PM GatiShakti, NLP 2022 · Multimodal integration; logistics-cost reduction
- **System** — GST, IBC, Income-tax Act 2025 · Compliance simplification; faceless assessment
- **Demography** — Skilling for chip/electronics · 85,000 engineers under training (2025)
- **Demand** — ECLGS, CGTMSE, SRI Fund · SRI Fund topped up by Rs 2,000 cr (Budget 2026-27)

## The Unfinished Agenda
- Assembly-stage value addition still masks component-level import dependence, particularly on China for electronic components, APIs and rare earths. PLI uptake has been uneven — strong in mobiles, pharmaceuticals and food processing, weak in textiles and advanced chemistry cells. Self-reliance must not slide into protectionism: sustained tariff walls raise input costs and erode export competitiveness, the very outcome the mission seeks to avoid.

## Conclusion

Atmanirbhar Bharat has moved decisively past the announcement stage: Rs 2.16 lakh crore of PLI investment, Rs 1.78 lakh crore of indigenous defence production and ten approved semiconductor projects are outcomes no earlier industrial policy episode produced at this speed. Its durability, however, will be settled by three tests — whether domestic value addition deepens beyond final assembly, whether MSMEs are absorbed into the supply chains rather than displaced by them, and whether incentives are withdrawn on schedule so that competitiveness, not subsidy, sustains the sector. Self-reliance succeeds only when it graduates into self-sustaining global competitiveness.

- Five pillars: Economy, Infrastructure, System, Vibrant Demography, Demand. Launch package of Rs 20 lakh crore, roughly 10% of GDP (May 2020).
- PLI at a glance (PIB, 31 December 2025): 14 sectors, outlay Rs 1.91 lakh crore, 836 approved applications, investment Rs 2.16 lakh crore, sales Rs 20.41 lakh crore, exports Rs 8.3 lakh crore, employment 14.39 lakh, incentives disbursed Rs 28,748 crore.
- Semiconductors: India Semiconductor Mission approved December 2021 with a Rs 76,000 crore outlay and fiscal support up to 50%; 10 approved projects worth Rs 1.60 lakh crore across six States; ISM 2.0 targets 3nm and 2nm nodes, with India expected to meet 70–75% of domestic chip demand by 2029 (PIB, February 2026).
- Defence: production Rs 1.78 lakh crore and exports Rs 38,424 crore in 2025-26; targets of Rs 3 lakh crore production and Rs 50,000 crore exports by 2029; enablers include DAP 2020, iDEX, SRIJAN/DEEP portal (41,000+ vendors, 2.7 lakh products as of May 2026), and UP and Tamil Nadu Defence Industrial Corridors.
- Supporting reforms: National Logistics Policy 2022, PM GatiShakti (2021), National Single Window System, Vivad se Vishwas, Income-tax Act 2025, and the corporate tax cut of 2019.
- AP hook: ASIP Technologies semiconductor unit approved for Andhra Pradesh, 12 August 2025 (Rs 468–480 crore, 96 million units per annum, with APACT Co. Ltd, South Korea) — cite it as evidence that the mission has a federal, not merely national, footprint.

Q81 │ Section B — Q17 Explain the major governmental interventions in the social sector with special reference to health and education.

The social sector is where the Constitution's promise of substantive equality is either delivered or defaulted upon. Article 47 obliges the State to raise nutrition and public health, Article 41 mandates public assistance in sickness and disablement, and Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) made elementary education a fundamental right. The Supreme Court, in Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996), read the right to emergency medical care into Article 21. Indian social-sector policy since has moved from discretionary welfare to justiciable entitlement — a shift best read through health and education.

## Health Sector Interventions
- Financial protection at the tertiary end.Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY (September 2018) offers Rs 5 lakh per family per year to roughly 12 crore families; over 42 crore Ayushman cards had been issued by October 2025, with more than 33,000 hospitals empanelled (17,685 public, 15,380 private). Its 2024 expansion to all citizens aged 70 and above, irrespective of income, had generated 96.73 lakh Ayushman Vay Vandana cards and authorised 10.33 lakh admissions worth Rs 2,154 crore by 31 December 2025 (PIB, February 2026).
- Primary care and infrastructure.Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (upgraded sub-centres and PHCs) shift the system from episodic curative care to continuous screening for hypertension, diabetes and cancers. PM-ABHIM commits Rs 64,180 crore for 2021-26 to critical-care blocks, public health labs and surveillance — the pandemic's principal institutional lesson.
- Digital public infrastructure in health. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission issues the ABHA health ID and links health facility and professional registries, enabling portability of records across States — decisive for a migrant workforce.
- Measured outcome. Per the National Health Accounts (2021-22), out-of-pocket expenditure fell from 62.6% to 39.4% of total health expenditure between 2014-15 and 2021-22, while Government health expenditure rose from 1.13% to 1.84% of GDP and its share of total health expenditure from 29% to 48%. This is the single most persuasive figure available on social-sector performance — memorise it.

## Education Sector Interventions
- Structural reform.NEP 2020 replaced the 10+2 design with 5+3+3+4, mandated mother-tongue instruction till at least Grade 5, and introduced multiple entry and exit with the Academic Bank of Credits in higher education.
- Universalisation and retention.Samagra Shiksha (Rs 2,94,283 crore, 2021-26) covers pre-primary to Class XII; PM POSHAN addresses classroom hunger; NIPUN Bharat targets foundational literacy and numeracy, the stage at which learning deficits become irreversible; PM SHRI has selected 13,076 exemplar schools (PIB, July 2025).
- Measured outcome.UDISE+ 2025-26 (Ministry of Education, July 2026) records the dropout rate falling from 2.3% to 1.8% at the preparatory stage and from 8.2% to 7.0% at the secondary stage, with the middle-to-secondary transition rate rising from 86.6% to 88.3%. The number of teachers crossed 1 crore for the first time in 2024-25, and PTR now stands at 21 at the secondary stage against NEP's 30:1 norm.

## The Andhra Pradesh Layer
- AP demonstrates how States thicken Union floors. Dr NTR Vaidya Seva, run by the Dr NTR Vaidya Seva Trust and co-branded with AB PM-JAY under the State's Universal Health Policy, extends cashless cover up to Rs 25 lakh per family per year across roughly 3,257 procedures — far above the national Rs 5 lakh floor. On the education side, Talliki Vandanam (2025) transfers Rs 15,000 per school-going child to about 43 lakh mothers, attacking the demand-side cost of schooling that infrastructure schemes cannot reach.
- **Sector** — Flagship Intervention · Indicator Movement (sourced)
- **Health — financing** — AB PM-JAY; Vay Vandana · OOPE 62.6% → 39.4% of THE (NHA 2021-22)
- **Health — public spend** — NHM, PM-ABHIM · GHE 1.13% → 1.84% of GDP (NHA 2021-22)
- **Education — retention** — Samagra Shiksha, PM POSHAN · Secondary dropout 8.2% → 7.0% (UDISE+ 2025-26)
- **Education — capacity** — Teacher recruitment · Teachers crossed 1 crore (UDISE+ 2024-25)
- **AP layer** — Dr NTR Vaidya Seva; Talliki Vandanam · Cover up to Rs 25 lakh; ~67 lakh students

## Persistent Gaps
- Government health expenditure at 1.84% of GDP remains well short of the 2.5% by 2025 target set by the National Health Policy, 2017 and endorsed by the Fifteenth Finance Commission; education spending likewise trails the 6%-of-GDP benchmark first proposed by the Kothari Commission. UDISE+ also records a fall in total school enrolment, and the NITI Aayog Fiscal Health Index 2026 places Andhra Pradesh among States facing fiscal stress — a reminder that entitlement expansion without fiscal space produces arrears, not access.

## Conclusion

India's social-sector story is one of genuine, measurable progress — out-of-pocket health spending has fallen by a third, secondary dropout is declining, and the teacher workforce has crossed a crore. But the binding constraints have shifted from access to quality and financing: an Ayushman card does not guarantee a specialist in a district hospital, and enrolment does not guarantee grade-level learning. Achieving SDG 3 and SDG 4 by 2030 will require raising public health spending towards 2.5% of GDP, closing teacher vacancies, and shifting monitoring from inputs disbursed to outcomes delivered.

- Constitutional and legal base: Articles 21, 21A, 39(e)&(f), 41, 42, 45, 47; RTE Act, 2009; National Food Security Act, 2013; Mental Healthcare Act, 2017; Code on Social Security, 2020.
- Health numbers (PIB / NHA): 42 crore Ayushman cards (October 2025); 96.73 lakh Vay Vandana cards (31 December 2025); 33,000+ empanelled hospitals; OOPE 39.4% and GHE 1.84% of GDP (NHA 2021-22); PM-ABHIM outlay Rs 64,180 crore (2021-26).
- Education numbers: Samagra Shiksha Rs 2,94,283 crore (2021-26); PM SHRI 13,076 schools; 5,269 Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas housing 7.58 lakh girls and 1,137 Netaji Subhash Avasiya Vidyalayas (PIB, July 2025); higher-education GER target of 50% by 2035.
- Benchmarks to cite: National Health Policy 2017 target of 2.5% of GDP by 2025; Kothari Commission's 6%-of-GDP education benchmark; Fifteenth Finance Commission's health-spending recommendation; NITI Aayog MPI decline from 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23).
- Social security spine: EPFO, ESIC, National Pension System, Atal Pension Yojana, PM-JAY, e-Shram registry for unorganised workers — the four-code labour reform consolidates nine earlier laws.
- AP hook: Dr NTR Vaidya Seva (cover up to Rs 25 lakh under AP's Universal Health Policy, co-branded with AB PM-JAY, ~3,257 procedures); Talliki Vandanam (Rs 15,000 per child, ~67 lakh students); AP scored 74 on the SDG India Index 2023-24 but is flagged for fiscal stress in NITI Aayog's Fiscal Health Index 2026.

Q82 │ Section B — Q18 Bring out the politics of the Women's Reservation Bill.

The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 — Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam — reserves one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha, the State Legislative Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly through new Articles 330A, 332A and 334A, with a fifteen-year sunset and rotation of reserved constituencies. It passed the Lok Sabha 454-2 and the Rajya Sabha unanimously. Yet the more revealing fact is that a measure commanding near-total declared support waited twenty-seven years to be enacted and remains unimplemented three years later — a gap that is entirely political, not constitutional.

A. The Legislative Graveyard, 1996–2010: Support in Principle, Resistance in Practice

- The Bill was introduced four times and died four times — as the 81st Amendment Bill in 1996 (Deve Gowda government), the 84th in 1998, the 85th in 1999 (Vajpayee government) and the 108th in 2008, which the Rajya Sabha actually passed in 2010 before it lapsed for want of Lok

Sabha consideration. The Geeta Mukherjee Joint Parliamentary Committee (1996) made seven recommendations; two — sub-reservation for OBC women and extension to the Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils — were never incorporated. This is the classic pattern of declaratory support with procedural burial.

## Three Political Fault Lines
- Incumbency and winnability. One-third reservation with rotation means roughly a third of sitting members lose their seats each cycle. Resistance is therefore not ideological but distributive, and it operates within parties rather than between them — which is precisely why floor votes and party manifestos diverge. Empirically, only 74 women were elected to the 18th Lok Sabha in 2024, about 13.6% of 543, down from 78 in the 17th (the Home Minister put the current strength at 75 — PIB, April 2026).
- The caste sub-quota question. Parties representing OBC and minority constituencies have argued since 1996 that an undifferentiated one-third quota would be captured by socially advantaged women, reproducing rather than dismantling hierarchy. The 106th Amendment provides sub-reservation for SC and ST women within reserved seats but not for OBC women — leaving the original objection live and available for renewed mobilisation.
- The delimitation linkage — the decisive design choice.Article 334A makes the reservation operative only after delimitation following the first census taken after the Amendment's commencement. Since the 42nd Amendment (1976) froze seats on the 1971 census and the 84th Amendment (2001) extended that freeze to the first census after 2026, implementation was effectively deferred well beyond the 2029 general election. Critics read this as converting an entitlement into a promise.

## April 2026 — The Politics Made Visible
- The 2023 Act was formally notified on 16 April 2026. On the same day the Government introduced a three-Bill package to advance implementation to 2029: the Delimitation Bill, 2026 (raising Lok Sabha strength from 543 to 850, comprising 815 from States and 35 from Union Territories), the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 (permitting delimitation on the 2011 census rather than awaiting the 2027 census), and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026.
- On 17 April 2026 the 131st Amendment Bill was defeated on the floor of the Lok Sabha — 298 votes in favour against 230, with 528 members present, short of the 352 required as a two-thirds majority of those present and voting under Article 368. The two companion Bills were consequently withdrawn. The Home Minister noted that 130 members participated in the debate, including 56 women (PIB, 17 April 2026). This was the first constitutional amendment defeated on the floor of the House in the present Government's tenure — a rare instance of Article 368's special-majority requirement operating as a real check.
- The federal fault line and Andhra Pradesh. Opposition centred not on women's reservation but on delimitation: southern States, having succeeded at population stabilisation, feared penalisation in seat reallocation. The Government countered that the five southern States would rise from 129 to about 195 seats, holding their share broadly stable near 23.8%. For Andhra Pradesh — 25 Lok Sabha and 175 Assembly seats — the episode links women's representation to the deeper question of the South's weight in the Union, a live concern since the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014.
- **Milestone** — Instrument · Outcome
- **1996** — 81st Amendment Bill · Lapsed; Geeta Mukherjee JPC constituted
- **2008-10** — 108th Amendment Bill · Passed Rajya Sabha 2010; lapsed in Lok Sabha
- **Sept 2023** — 106th Amendment Act · Enacted; Articles 330A, 332A, 334A inserted
- **16 Apr 2026** — Notification + 3-Bill package · Act notified; Delimitation route proposed

- **Milestone** — Instrument · Outcome
- **17 Apr 2026** — 131st Amendment Bill · Defeated 298-230 of 528; companion Bills withdrawn

## Conclusion

The politics of women's reservation is the politics of sequencing. Every actor endorses the principle; the contest is over the conditions attached to it — which census, how many seats, whose sub-quota, and by when. The 106th Amendment made the entitlement constitutional; the April 2026 defeat demonstrated that its operationalisation is hostage to an unrelated federal dispute over delimitation. The panchayat experience since the 73rd and 74th Amendments — over 14 lakh elected women, with several States including Andhra Pradesh legislating 50% reservation — establishes that the transformative effect is real once implementation begins. Delinking the quota from delimitation, and settling the OBC sub-quota question openly, is now the shortest route from symbolism to substance.

- Provisions: Articles 330A (Lok Sabha), 332A (State Assemblies), 239AA(2) (Delhi) and 334A (commencement); one-third of SC/ST reserved seats also reserved for women of those groups; rotation of reserved constituencies; sunset after fifteen years; does not extend to the Rajya Sabha or Legislative Councils.
- Passage: Introduced 19 September 2023 in the new Parliament building as the 128th Amendment Bill; passed Lok Sabha 454-2 and Rajya Sabha unanimously; enacted as the 106th Amendment Act, 2023; notified 16 April 2026.
- April 2026 package: Delimitation Bill, 2026 (543 → 850 seats: 815 States + 35 UTs); Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 (delimitation on 2011 census to enable the quota by 2029); Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026. The 131st was defeated 298-230 of 528 present on 17 April 2026, against the 352 required under Article 368; companion Bills withdrawn (PIB).
- Seat-freeze chronology: 42nd Amendment (1976) froze seats on the 1971 census; 84th Amendment (2001) extended the freeze to the first census after 2026; 87th Amendment (2003) permitted readjustment of constituencies on 2001 census figures without altering State seat totals.
- Representation data: 74 women elected to the 18th Lok Sabha (about 13.6%), against 78 in the 17th; average women's representation in State Assemblies is around 9%; India ranks low among 185 countries on Inter-Parliamentary Union comparisons of women in lower houses.
- Grassroots contrast: 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992-93) reserve not less than one-third of seats and chairperson posts for women; Andhra Pradesh and several other States raised this to 50%, producing over 14 lakh elected women representatives — the strongest empirical rebuttal to the 'proxy representation' objection.

Q83 │ Section B — Q19 Define 'development' as explained by Prof. Amartya Sen. Explain the characteristics of the new development thinking, and also mention the four areas where the government has to play a crucial role.

Classical development economics equated progress with GDP growth, industrialisation and per capita income. Prof. Amartya Sen, in Poverty and Famines (1981) and Development as Freedom (1999), recast development as the process of expanding the real freedoms that people enjoy. Income is instrumental; freedom is constitutive. Correspondingly, poverty is redefined as capability deprivation rather than low income — a person may be income-poor yet capable, or income-adequate yet unfree. Sen's collaboration with Mahbub ul Haq produced the UNDP Human Development Index (1990), translating this philosophy into global measurement.

## Sen's Conception of Development
- Capabilities and functionings.Functionings are actual achievements — being well nourished, literate, mobile, politically heard. Capability is the substantive freedom to achieve alternative combinations of them. Two people with identical incomes may possess radically different capabilities depending on health, gender, caste and public provisioning. Kerala's high literacy and life expectancy at modest per capita income remains the standard Indian illustration.
- The entitlement approach. Sen's study of the Bengal famine of 1943 showed that famines occur not from an absolute absence of food but from the collapse of exchange entitlements — the ability to command food through wages, production or transfers. This directly justifies rights-based instruments such as the National Food Security Act, 2013, which converts food access from availability into a legal entitlement for about two-thirds of the population.
- Freedom as both means and end. Development is pursued through freedom and evaluated by freedom. Sen's five instrumental freedoms — political freedoms, economic facilities, social opportunities, transparency guarantees and protective security — are mutually reinforcing. The Right to Information Act, 2005 is a transparency guarantee that makes MGNREGA's protective security enforceable: this interlocking is Sen's central insight.

## Characteristics of the New Development Thinking
- Human-centric rather than output-centric. The unit of evaluation shifts from national aggregate to individual capability. India's National Multidimensional Poverty Index operationalises this with twelve SDG-aligned indicators across health, education and living standards, rather than a single consumption line.
- Multidimensional and disaggregated. Averages conceal deprivation. NITI Aayog's MPI records the headcount ratio falling from 29.17% in 2013-14 to 11.28% in 2022-23, with about 24.82 crore people moving out of multidimensional poverty (NITI Aayog Discussion Paper, January 2024) — a claim only a multidimensional measure can make.
- Participatory — people as agents, not patients. Sen insists the poor are agents of their own development. Article 243G and the Gram Sabha, social audit under Section 17 of MGNREGA, and participatory planning under the Fifteenth Finance Commission's tied grants institutionalise agency.
- Inclusive and intergenerationally sustainable. Growth that degrades the commons borrows capability from the future. The Sustainable Development Goals and NITI Aayog's SDG India Index — on which Andhra Pradesh scored 74 in 2023-24, in the Front Runner band — embed this.

## The Four Areas of Crucial Government Role
- 1. Education. Sen treats schooling as the master capability, since it conditions access to all others. Samagra Shiksha (Rs 2,94,283 crore, 2021-26) and NIPUN Bharat address exactly the foundational stage at which capability deficits become irreversible.
- 2. Health and nutrition. Ill health destroys capability and assets simultaneously. AB PM-JAY and Poshan Abhiyaan operate here; the fall in out-of-pocket expenditure from 62.6% to 39.4% of total health expenditure (NHA 2021-22) is capability protection in measurable form.
- 3. Social security — protective security. Vulnerability, not merely poverty, is the capability threat. MGNREGA, NFSA 2013, the Code on Social Security, 2020 and the e-Shram registry cushion livelihood shocks for the unorganised workforce.
- 4. Infrastructure and opportunity — economic facilities. Capability requires reachable markets, power, irrigation, connectivity and credit. PM Gram Sadak Yojana, Jal Jeevan Mission and India's digital public infrastructure (Aadhaar-UPI-DBT) convert entitlements into usable freedoms.
- **Aspect** — GDP-centric view · Sen's capability view
- **Goal** — Rising national output · Expansion of substantive freedoms
- **Poverty** — Income below a line · Deprivation of basic capabilities
- **Person** — Beneficiary of growth · Agent of own development
- **Measure** — GDP, per capita income · HDI, MPI, SDG India Index

## The Andhra Pradesh Instance
- AP's P4 — Public-Private-People Partnership, launched on 30 March 2025 under the Swarna Andhra @2047 vision, is a capability-partnership model in Sen's sense: affluent citizens and diaspora ('Margadarsis') mentor and support poorer households ('Bangaru Kutumbams') through education sponsorship, healthcare access and enterprise capital, with the State acting only as facilitator and verifier through the zeropovertyp4.ap.gov.in platform. It targets zero poverty by 2029 and addresses capability rather than transfer alone — though NITI Aayog's Fiscal Health Index 2026, which flags AP for fiscal stress, is a reminder that voluntary partnership cannot substitute for public provisioning.

## Conclusion

Sen's contribution was to relocate the question of development from how much a nation produces to what its people are actually able to do and to be. Growth remains necessary — capability expansion requires fiscal capacity — but it is instrumental, never the objective. For India, and for Andhra Pradesh in particular, the practical implication is that public investment in education, health, social security and connectivity is not consumption competing with growth but the mechanism by which growth is converted into human freedom. Development, in Sen's formulation, is finally measured by the range of lives a person has reason to value and is genuinely able to choose.

- Key works:Poverty and Famines (1981, entitlement approach); Development as Freedom (1999); Hunger and Public Action (with Jean Drèze, 1989); The Idea of Justice (2009). Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 1998.
- Five instrumental freedoms (the highest-value point in this answer): political freedoms, economic facilities, social opportunities, transparency guarantees, protective security.
- Core concepts: capability, functioning, agency, entitlement failure, adaptive preference; poverty as capability deprivation; the 'missing women' hypothesis on sex-ratio deficits.
- Measurement lineage: Sen and Mahbub ul Haq designed the HDI (UNDP Human Development Report, 1990); later variants include the Inequality-adjusted HDI, Gender Inequality Index and the OPHI–UNDP global MPI, for which NITI Aayog is India's nodal agency.
- Indian data: MPI headcount fell 29.17% (2013-14) → 11.28% (2022-23); about 24.82 crore people escaped multidimensional poverty (NITI Aayog, January 2024); OOPE in health fell to 39.4% of THE (NHA 2021-22); AP scored 74 on the SDG India Index 2023-24.
- Debate to cite for balance: the Sen–Bhagwati exchange — Jagdish Bhagwati and Arvind Panagariya argue growth-first generates the resources for redistribution, while Sen and Drèze argue social investment is itself the engine of sustained growth. Referencing both sides signals analytical maturity.
- AP hook: P4 (Public-Private-People Partnership) Margadarsi–Bangaru Kutumbam, launched 30 March 2025 under Swarna Andhra @2047, targeting zero poverty by 2029 with the top 10% supporting the bottom 20%.

Q84 │ Section B — Q20 What do you understand by civil society in the Indian context? Discuss its key features and the limitations it faces in a democratic system.

Civil society denotes the associational space between the State, the market and the family — voluntary organisations, social movements, professional bodies, self-help groups, trade unions, faith-based welfare bodies and citizens' collectives that pursue public purposes without coercive power or the profit motive. Its constitutional foundation lies in Article 19(1)(c), the freedom to form associations, read with the freedoms of speech and assembly. In India, civil society long predates the Republic: the social reform movements of the nineteenth century and Gandhian constructive work established a tradition in which associational life is a source of democratic legitimacy, not merely a supplement to the State.

## Key Features of Indian Civil Society
- Pluralism and scale. Indian civil society spans caste associations, religious trusts, professional bodies, environmental collectives and over six million registered self-help groups. This heterogeneity gives it reach into constituencies the administrative State struggles to see — but it also makes coordinated national action difficult.
- Legislative agenda-setting. Civil society has authored, not merely lobbied for, major statutes. The Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan's jan sunwais in Rajasthan produced the demand that became the Right to Information Act, 2005; the campaign for employment guarantee shaped MGNREGA, 2005. This is norm-entrepreneurship — converting local grievance into national law.
- Watchdog and litigation function. The Association for Democratic Reforms' public interest litigation compelled the Supreme Court to require candidates to disclose criminal antecedents, assets and educational qualifications — an electoral-transparency reform no political party would have initiated. Public interest litigation gives civil society standing where it has no votes.
- Complementary service delivery. The Akshaya Patra Foundation operates centralised kitchens delivering PM POSHAN meals at a scale and unit cost the State would find difficult to replicate; SEWA organises informal-sector women workers; Pratham's ASER survey supplies learning-outcome data that shaped the foundational-literacy focus of NEP 2020.
- Deliberative and accountability role. Social audit under Section 17 of MGNREGA and the Meghalaya Community Participation and Public Services Social Audit Act, 2017 institutionalise citizen scrutiny of expenditure — the mechanism the Second ARC endorsed in its reports on Ethics in Governance and Citizen Centric Administration.

## Limitations in a Democratic System
- Regulatory tightening around foreign funding. This is now the dominant constraint. In 2024-25, about 16,200 associations were actively registered under the FCRA, receiving roughly Rs 22,963 crore in foreign contribution; over the last decade nearly 22,000 registrations were cancelled and about 15,000 deemed to have ceased (PIB Backgrounder, July 2026). The FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026 (introduced in the Lok Sabha on 25 March 2026) and the revised FCRA Rules notified on 22 June 2026 add provisional and permanent vesting of assets on non-restoration of registration, purpose- and State-specific certificates, a minimum utilisation threshold of Rs 10 lakh over two years for renewal, and ultimate-donor disclosure — while simultaneously reducing maximum imprisonment from five years to one and creating a right of appeal to the District Judge. The Supreme Court upheld the 2010 framework in Indian Social Action Forum v. Union of India (2020) and the 2020 amendments in Noel Harper v. Union of India (2022).
- Compliance burden displaces mission. Registration under multiple statutes, five-yearly renewal, the 20% ceiling on administrative expenditure and detailed annual returns impose costs that large professionalised NGOs absorb but small grassroots bodies cannot — producing a survivorship bias towards well-resourced urban organisations.
- Political co-option and the legitimacy question. Proximity to parties compromises the watchdog role; distance from them forfeits influence. Civil society bodies are also unelected, which makes 'whom do you represent?' a legitimate democratic challenge — one they can answer only through transparency and internal democracy, not by asserting moral authority.
- Urban and issue concentration. Organisational density clusters in metropolitan centres and around visible causes, leaving remote and tribal regions — precisely the areas of deepest deprivation — comparatively unserved.
- Fragmentation along social cleavages. Caste, religion and region frequently structure associational life itself, so civil society sometimes reproduces the divisions it seeks to bridge, weakening collective bargaining with the State.

## The Andhra Pradesh Instance
- AP's P4 (Public-Private-People Partnership), launched on 30 March 2025, is an attempt to channel voluntary and philanthropic energy through a State-run platform: 'Margadarsis' — affluent citizens, institutions and the Telugu diaspora — adopt 'Bangaru Kutumbam' households via the zeropovertyp4.ap.gov.in portal, choosing among 'Adopt a Family', 'Adopt a Village' and 'Fund a Need'. Government contributes no money and acts only as facilitator and verifier. It is an instructive hybrid — it lowers transaction costs for givers, but a civil society mediated entirely through a government platform necessarily trades some of the autonomy that gives the sector its watchdog value.
- **Function** — Illustration · Democratic Value Added
- **Agenda-setting** — MKSS → RTI Act, 2005 · Converts grievance into statutory right
- **Watchdog** — ADR public interest litigation · Electoral transparency
- **Service delivery** — Akshaya Patra under PM POSHAN · Scale and cost efficiency
- **Evidence generation** — Pratham's ASER survey · Independent outcome data
- **Accountability** — Social audit, MGNREGA s.17 · Citizen scrutiny of expenditure

## Conclusion

Civil society is not an adversary of the democratic State but its diagnostic organ — it detects failure earlier than administrative reporting does, and it converted that detection into the RTI Act, MGNREGA and mandatory electoral disclosure. Its limitations are real: dependence on external funding, an unelected mandate, urban concentration and a compliance burden that falls hardest on the smallest actors. The policy task, as the Second ARC framed it, is to distinguish regulating from disabling — retaining strict transparency on foreign funds while lowering the entry barrier for small domestic organisations, expanding CSR and NGO-Darpan channels, and institutionalising civil society in social audit. A democracy in which citizens act only on polling day is electoral; one in which they organise between elections is participatory.

- Constitutional and conceptual base: Article 19(1)(c) freedom of association, with reasonable restrictions under Article 19(4); Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b); Article 43B (co-operative societies, 97th Amendment). Conceptually, de Tocqueville's associational democracy and Gramsci's civil society as the sphere of consent rather than coercion.
- Registration statutes: Societies Registration Act, 1860 (minimum seven persons); Indian Trusts Act, 1882 and State public trust Acts; Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013; FCRA, 2010 as amended in 2016, 2018, 2020 and 2026; Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandating 2% of average net profit on CSR for qualifying companies.
- FCRA data (PIB Backgrounder, 22 July 2026): ~16,200 actively registered associations received about Rs 22,963 crore in 2024-25; nearly 22,000 registrations cancelled and about 15,000 deemed ceased over the decade; the Ministry estimates FCRA-registered bodies at under 1% of all NGOs operating in India; foreign contribution must be received in a single designated SBI New Delhi Main Branch account; administrative expenditure capped at 20%.
- Case law:Indian Social Action Forum v. Union of India (2020) upheld FCRA Section 5 while reading down 'organisation of a political nature'; Noel Harper v. Union of India (2022) upheld the 2020 amendments including the sub-granting bar and the single-account requirement.
- Institutional interface: NITI Aayog's NGO-Darpan portal for unique IDs; the National Policy on the Voluntary Sector, 2007; Second ARC's Fourth Report (Ethics in Governance) and Twelfth Report (Citizen Centric Administration) on partnership; the United Nations grants consultative status to NGOs through ECOSOC under Article 71 of the UN Charter.
- Landmark civil society outcomes to name: MKSS → RTI Act, 2005; Bachpan Bachao Andolan (Kailash Satyarthi) on child labour; SEWA on informal women workers; Naz Foundation litigation; Chipko and Narmada Bachao Andolan on environmental accountability.
- AP hook: P4 — Public-Private-People Partnership, launched 30 March 2025 (Margadarsi–Bangaru Kutumbam, zeropovertyp4.ap.gov.in), targeting zero poverty by 2029 under Swarna Andhra @2047 — cite as a State-facilitated model of organised voluntarism and note the autonomy trade-off.
