Q85 In what ways can the role of NGOs be enhanced in promoting women’s empowerment and welfare in India? Discuss, with a focus on the key challenges they encounter. (APPSC, 2025) — 10 Marks

Women’s empowerment is a constitutional mandate (Articles 15(3), 39(a) and 42) and India’s commitment under SDG-5. The State supplies scale and statutory backing; Non-Governmental Organisations supply proximity, trust and the ability to reach women whom formal machinery misses — widows, single women, migrant workers, and tribal households in Agency areas. Enhancing their role is therefore less about adding new actors and more about institutionalising an existing one — giving NGOs a defined, funded and accountable place inside the delivery chain rather than a discretionary one outside it.

## How the role of NGOs can be enhanced
- Formal empanelment as service providers under Mission Shakti: Mission Shakti (2021–22 to 2025–26) runs two verticals — Sambal (One Stop Centres, Women Helpline 181, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, Nari Adalat) and Samarthya (Shakti Sadan, Sakhi Niwas, PMMVY, Palna). 819 One Stop Centres have assisted 10.98 lakh women, and the Women Helpline has handled 214.78 lakh calls (PIB Factsheet, August 2025). Because OSCs need trained counsellors and 24x7 case-workers that district administrations cannot staff internally, empanelling audited NGOs as OSC operators under Collector supervision converts voluntarism into a costed, accountable service line. Andhra Pradesh already demonstrates the model: its Disha (Sakhi) One Stop Centres are co-located with Disha police stations in district hospitals at Kakinada, Kadapa, Chittoor and Vizianagaram, making the NGO counsellor the first point of contact for a survivor.
- Deepening the SHG–NGO convergence for economic agency: Under DAY-NRLM, 10.20 crore rural households are organised into 90.90 lakh SHGs (PIB, December 2025), and 1.48 crore members had crossed the Rs 1 lakh annual income threshold as Lakhpati Didis by March 2025 (PIB, June 2025) against a target of 6 crore. The binding constraint is not credit but enterprise capability, which is why the Ministry of Rural Development launched a National Campaign on Entrepreneurship in January 2026 to train 50 lakh SHG members through 50,000 Community Resource Persons. NGOs are the natural suppliers of these CRPs. Andhra Pradesh is the historic laboratory here — the DWCRA–Velugu–SERP lineage built the three-tier Mandal Samakhya federations that the national mission later replicated, so AP’s NGOs can be scaled as enterprise incubators rather than mere mobilisers.
- Legal literacy and community justice partnerships: Rights on paper fail without a forum a woman can actually walk into. Nari Adalat, the gram-panchayat-level women’s collective for mediating petty harassment and denial of entitlements, is operational in only 50 gram panchayats each in Assam and Jammu & Kashmir (Ministry of Women and Child Development, 2025) — a pilot begging for NGO-led scale-up. Similarly, the NCW’s Pre-Marital Counselling Centres (“Tere Mere Sapne”) are run in collaboration with voluntary organisations, the 284th such centre being inaugurated with an NGO partner (NCW, 2025–26). Tie-ups with District Legal Services Authorities under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 would give these efforts statutory footing.
- Evidence-based advocacy that feeds policy: NGOs generate the disaggregated field data that national surveys smooth over — on ICC compliance under the POSH Act, 2013, on deepfake and cyber abuse, and on female labour force participation. The NCW’s Final Review Consultation on Cyber Laws for Women at Vigyan Bhawan (NCW, March 2025) was built on exactly such civil-society input. Institutionalising NGO representation in State-level review committees and in NITI Aayog’s SDG monitoring converts anecdote into policy.
- Building compliance and governance capacity: Enhancement now depends as much on the ability to survive regulation as on programme skill. The NGO Darpan Unique ID (NITI Aayog, since 2015) is the gateway to government grants and to Section 12A/80G tax registration; a State-funded compliance helpdesk for small women-focused NGOs would prevent capable organisations from being disqualified on paperwork.

## Key challenges encountered
- Funding volatility and a tightening foreign-funding regime: As on 15 July 2026 there were 14,449 active FCRA registrations against 22,498 cancelled and 15,212 expired (MHA FCRA Portal Dashboard, 2026) — the attrition is the story. The FCRA (Amendment) Rules, 2026, notified on 22 June 2026, now tie registration to specified purposes and named States/UTs and require an NGO to show utilisation of at least Rs 10 lakh of foreign contribution over the preceding two years to renew (PIB Factsheet, July 2026). Small, single-district women’s NGOs are structurally the least able to meet such thresholds.
- Thin organisational capacity: Grassroots bodies typically lack chartered accountants, MIS staff and project-management systems. The 2020 amendment’s cut in the administrative-expense ceiling from 50% to 20% and the bar on sub-granting (PIB Factsheet, July 2026) squeeze precisely the overheads that fund such capacity, creating a compliance trap.
- Fragmentation and geographic blind spots: Effort clusters in accessible districts. In Andhra Pradesh, the Agency areas of Alluri Sitharama Raju and Parvathipuram Manyam — where maternal health and child-marriage indicators lag most — have the thinnest NGO presence, so duplication coexists with vacuum.
- Credibility and political friction: Instances of fund diversion, and the perception of NGOs as adversaries rather than partners, delay grant release and deter district officials from formal collaboration — an accountability deficit that must be cured by transparency, not by exit.
- **Enhancement lever** — Concrete instrument / illustration
- **Service delivery** — Empanelment in Mission Shakti OSCs — AP’s Disha (Sakhi) centres
- **Economic agency** — CRPs under DAY-NRLM; SERP federations, AP

- **Enhancement lever** — Concrete instrument / illustration
- **Access to justice** — Nari Adalat scale-up; DLSA and NCW PMCC tie-ups
- **Policy voice** — SDG-5 monitoring; NCW cyber-law consultations
- **Survival capacity** — NGO Darpan ID; FCRA compliance handholding

## Conclusion

NGOs cannot substitute for the State — they lack scale, coercive power and universal reach — but the State cannot substitute for them either, because trust at the doorstep is not administrable by fiat. The way forward is a partnership-with-accountability compact: predictable multi-year funding through NGO Darpan-verified channels, formal empanelment in Mission Shakti and DAY-NRLM delivery, and proportionate rather than punitive regulation. Andhra Pradesh, which pioneered the SHG federation and now runs the Disha–Sakhi model, is well placed to demonstrate that regulation and partnership are complements, not alternatives — turning women from beneficiaries of welfare into agents of development.

- Mission Shakti architecture:Sambal = OSC + Women Helpline 181 + BBBP + Nari Adalat; Samarthya = Shakti Sadan (ex-Swadhar Greh/Ujjwala) + Sakhi Niwas (ex-Working Women Hostel) + PMMVY + Palna. 15th FC cycle, 2021–22 to 2025–26 (MWCD).
- Constitutional hooks: Art. 15(3) special provisions for women; Art. 39(a) and (d); Art. 42 maternity relief; Art. 51A(e) fundamental duty to renounce practices derogatory to women; Art. 243D and 243T — one-third reservation in panchayats and municipalities.
- Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (106th Constitutional Amendment, 2023): reserves one-third of Lok Sabha and State Assembly seats for women, with SC/ST sub-reservation; operative after the census and delimitation.
- Data points: 10.20 crore households in 90.90 lakh SHGs (PIB, Dec 2025); 1.48 crore Lakhpati Didis, target 6 crore (PIB, 2025); 819 OSCs serving 10.98 lakh women (PIB, Aug 2025); 14,449 active FCRA registrations (MHA, July 2026).
- AP-specific: SERP (Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty) and its Mandal Samakhya federations; Disha (Sakhi) One Stop Centres; A.P. State Commission for Women under the A.P. Women’s Commission Act, 1998; AP Societies Registration Act, 2001 for NGO registration.
- Committee anchor: Second ARC, 12th Report on Citizen Centric Administration — recommends structured civil-society partnership in service delivery and citizen charters.

Q86 “NGOs play a critical role in promoting human rights, defending the marginalised, and creating a more just and equitable society.” Comment on the role of NGOs in India. (APPSC, 2023) — 10 Marks

Non-Governmental Organisations are voluntary, non-profit associations operating outside the State and the market. Their existence in India rests not on executive licence but on the fundamental right to form associations under Article 19(1)(c), and their reach into courts on the relaxation of locus standi in S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981), which allowed public-spirited bodies to litigate for those who cannot litigate for themselves. The quoted claim is largely sound — but its strength lies in a specific, demonstrable fact: several of India’s most important rights statutes began as NGO campaigns.

## Assessing the claim — what NGOs have actually produced
- They have converted advocacy into binding law: This is the strongest evidence for the proposition. The Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan’s Rajasthan campaign for muster-roll disclosure culminated in the Right to Information Act, 2005. Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), litigated by women’s groups, produced binding guidelines that Parliament later enacted as the POSH Act, 2013. The PUCL “right to food” petition (2001) generated the interim orders that hardened into the National Food Security Act, 2013. The Association for Democratic Reforms’ PIL (2002) established the voter’s right to know candidates’ criminal, educational and financial antecedents — now embedded in Form 26 affidavits filed with the Election Commission. Advocacy that ends in a statute is not lobbying; it is law-making by another route.
- They have defended constituencies that lack political weight: Bachpan Bachao Andolan’s litigation on trafficking and child labour, NALSA-supported advocacy culminating in NALSA v. Union of India (2014) recognising transgender persons as a third gender under Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21, and the Naz Foundation line of cases leading to Navtej Singh Johar (2018) all involved groups too small or too stigmatised to command electoral attention. This is the structural argument for NGOs: majoritarian politics under-supplies rights to minorities, and courts require a petitioner.
- They supply statutory institutions with capacity they lack: The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, Section 12(i) expressly directs the NHRC to encourage the efforts of non-governmental organisations working in the field of human rights — NGO partnership is written into the statute, not merely tolerated. NGOs also serve as implementing partners for schemes (Akshaya Patra under PM POSHAN) and as counsellors in Mission Shakti One Stop Centres, including Andhra Pradesh’s Disha (Sakhi) centres.
- They give India’s citizens a channel into international accountability: Under Article 71 of the UN Charter, ECOSOC consults NGOs; 6,494 NGOs held active consultative status as on 31 December 2024 (UN DESA, 2025). Indian organisations use this to file shadow reports in the Universal Periodic Review and before the CEDAW Committee — external scrutiny that domestic institutions alone cannot generate.
- The qualification — accountability of the accountability-holders: A watchdog claiming public trust must itself be transparent. India’s response has been regulatory. The FCRA (Amendment) Act, 2020 mandated Aadhaar identification of office-bearers, routed all foreign contributions through a single designated account at the SBI New Delhi Main Branch, prohibited sub-granting, and cut the administrative-expense ceiling from 50% to 20%. The Supreme Court in Noel Harper v. Union of India (2022) upheld these provisions, holding that no one has a fundamental right to receive foreign contributions. The FCRA (Amendment) Rules, 2026 (notified 22 June 2026) add purpose- and State-specific registration and a minimum utilisation threshold, while the FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026 (introduced in Lok Sabha on 25 March 2026) creates a Designated Authority over lapsed-registration assets, reduces maximum imprisonment from five years to one, and provides appeal to the District Judge (PIB Factsheet, July 2026). Critics counter that 22,498 cancelled and 15,212 expired registrations against 14,449 active ones (MHA, July 2026) chills legitimate work. Both propositions can be true: transparency is legitimate, and disproportionate compliance cost is a real cost.
- **NGO / movement** — Judicial milestone · Statutory outcome
- **MKSS** — Campaign for muster-roll disclosure · Right to Information Act, 2005
- **Women’s groups** — Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) · POSH Act, 2013
- **PUCL** — PUCL v. Union of India (2001) · National Food Security Act, 2013
- **ADR** — ADR v. Union of India (2002) · Mandatory candidate affidavits (ECI)
- **Trans-rights groups** — NALSA v. Union of India (2014) · Transgender Persons Act, 2019

## Conclusion

The claim is substantially valid but conditional. NGOs have demonstrably widened the content of Articles 14, 19 and 21 and delivered statutes that Parliament might not otherwise have enacted; that record cannot be dismissed. Yet legitimacy earned by holding others accountable is forfeited by resisting accountability oneself. The constructive settlement is proportionate regulation with a partnership presumption — disclosure standards uniform across sectors, timely and reasoned decisions on registration, and grievance mechanisms with judicial appeal, as the 2026 Bill now contemplates. A society becomes more just not when the State and civil society police each other into paralysis, but when each treats the other’s scrutiny as legitimate.

- Constitutional basis: Art. 19(1)(c) freedom of association, subject to reasonable restrictions under Art. 19(4); Art. 32 and 226 writ jurisdiction; S.P. Gupta (1981) and Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984) liberalised locus standi.
- Statutory recognition: Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, Sec. 12(i) — NHRC to encourage NGO efforts; Sec. 12(j) — human rights literacy. NHRC maintains a Core Group of NGOs and Human Rights Defenders.
- Key case law:Noel Harper v. Union of India (2022) upheld the FCRA 2020 amendments; Indian Social Action Forum (INSAF) v. Union of India (2020) read down “political nature” in the FCRA Rules to exclude ordinary advocacy.
- FCRA timeline: 1976 enacted → 2010 replaced (five-year renewal, vesting under Sec. 15) → 2020 major amendment → 2022 relatives’ limit raised Rs 1 lakh to Rs 10 lakh → Rules, 2026 notified 22 June 2026; Amendment Bill, 2026 introduced 25 March 2026.
- Comparative point (high-value): The PIB Factsheet (July 2026) situates FCRA alongside the US FARA (1938), Australia’s Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme (2018), the UK’s Foreign Influence Registration Scheme under the National Security Act 2023 (in force July 2025) and Canada’s FITAA (2024) — useful for arguing India is not an outlier.
- AP-specific: NGOs registered under the A.P. Societies Registration Act, 2001 (Act 35 of 2001); civil society engagement in Fifth Schedule Agency areas is mediated through PESA, 1996 and the Forest Rights Act, 2006.

Q87 Describe the role of NGOs and Civil Services in Democracy. (APPSC, 2020) — 10 Marks

Democracy requires two things that no single institution supplies: the capacity to implement and the capacity to contest. The civil service, constitutionally protected under Articles 309 to 311 and 312, provides permanence, neutrality and coercive reach; NGOs, resting on the associational freedom of Article 19(1)(c), provide voice, proximity and the willingness to challenge. Neither is a substitute for the other — an unchallenged bureaucracy drifts toward proceduralism, while unimplemented advocacy remains rhetoric. Their interaction, not their separation, is what makes democracy deliver.

- **Axis** — Civil Services · NGOs
- **Legitimacy** — Constitutional — Arts. 309–311, 312 (AIS) · Associational — Art. 19(1)(c); registration statutes
- **Core function** — Policy implementation, regulation, rule of law · Mobilisation, advocacy, last-mile innovation
- **Accountability** — Minister → legislature; CAG audit; RTI Act, 2005 · Donors and members; NGO Darpan; FCRA, 2010
- **Reach** — Territorial and universal, but thin at the last mile · Thematic and deep, but geographically patchy

## Comparing the two actors and their interlock
- Civil services — the implementing spine of democracy: Civil servants convert legislative intent into administrative reality: the District Collector as the hinge of scheme delivery, the Returning Officer under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the Public Information Officer under the RTI Act, 2005. Their constitutional protection under Article 311 exists precisely so that they can advise fearlessly and act impartially. Capacity reform is the current frontier — Mission Karmayogi (National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building, launched 2020) with the iGOT Karmayogi platform shifts training from rule-compliance to role-and-competency, so that officials can partner with non-state actors rather than merely regulate them.
- NGOs — the contesting and connecting layer: NGOs articulate demands before they reach the ballot box, generate evidence that administration does not collect, and reach populations that formal machinery misses. The RTI Act, 2005 itself originated in the MKSS movement — the clearest illustration that civil-society pressure can restructure the terms on which the civil service operates.
- Interlock 1 — co-production of services: The State finances and supervises; the NGO delivers at the point of contact. Akshaya Patra Foundation implements PM POSHAN; NGOs staff Mission Shakti One Stop Centres, of which 819 are operational and have assisted 10.98 lakh women (PIB Factsheet, August 2025). This is not outsourcing — accountability for outcomes remains with the Collector.
- Interlock 2 — social audit, the sharpest example:Section 17 of MGNREGA, 2005 mandates social audit of all works by the Gram Sabha, and Rule 4 of the MGNREG Audit of Scheme Rules, 2011 requires an independent Social Audit Unit. Andhra Pradesh pioneered this: the Society for Social Audit, Accountability and Transparency (SSAAT), established in 2009, was India’s first dedicated State social audit society and became the template for the national architecture. Here the civil service supplies records and enforcement while civil society supplies verification — neither could audit credibly alone.
- Interlock 3 — crisis response: In disasters the State commands resources and legal authority under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, while NGOs supply speed and local knowledge. After Cyclone Michaung struck coastal Andhra Pradesh in December 2023, district administrations coordinated evacuation and compensation while voluntary bodies ran relief camps and community kitchens — a division of labour neither could have performed alone.
- Points of friction — stated honestly: Three tensions recur. Regulatory suspicion: as on 15 July 2026 there were 14,449 active FCRA registrations against 22,498 cancelled (MHA, 2026), which conditions how officials view partnership. Co-option: NGOs dependent on government grants lose the independence that made them valuable. Elite capture: articulate urban NGOs crowd out the tribal and remote constituencies most in need — visible in the thin voluntary presence in AP’s Alluri Sitharama Raju district.

## Conclusion

NGOs and the civil services are best understood as the voice and the hand of democratic governance — the first ensures that the right problems reach the agenda, the second ensures that decisions reach the ground. The Second Administrative Reforms Commission’s 12th Report on Citizen Centric Administration made this structural, recommending citizen charters, service-delivery standards and institutionalised civil-society partnership rather than ad hoc collaboration. Andhra Pradesh’s SSAAT model shows what the synergy looks like when it is designed rather than improvised: a State-funded body that audits the State itself. Deepening democracy therefore means neither bureaucratising civil society nor privatising administration, but building durable, rule-bound interfaces between them.

- Second ARC anchors: 12th Report, Citizen Centric Administration (2009) — Sevottam framework, citizen charters, grievance redress; 4th Report, Ethics in Governance — civil society as an external accountability check; 10th Report, Refurbishing of Personnel Administration — domain competence and performance management.
- Constitutional provisions on civil services: Art. 309 (recruitment and service conditions), Art. 310 (doctrine of pleasure), Art. 311 (safeguards — no dismissal without inquiry), Art. 312 (All India Services on a Rajya Sabha resolution under Art. 249-type special majority), Art. 315–323 (UPSC and State PSCs).
- Capacity reform: Mission Karmayogi (2020) and iGOT Karmayogi; Karmayogi Bharat (Section 8 company); Capacity Building Commission; the shift from ‘rules’ to ‘roles’.
- Social audit framework: MGNREGA Sec. 17; MGNREG Audit of Scheme Rules, 2011; CAG-issued Auditing Standards for Social Audit (2016); Meghalaya Community Participation and Public Services Social Audit Act, 2017 — the first State law making social audit statutory across departments.
- AP-specific: SSAAT (2009), India’s first State social audit society; AP Real Time Governance Society (RTGS), Amaravati, for data-driven monitoring; Grama and Ward Sachivalayams with village volunteers as the last-mile interface.
- Sharp line for the conclusion: Civil services provide legitimacy of process; NGOs provide legitimacy of participation. Democracy needs both to be credible.

Q88 Give the reason for the UN to partner with civil society. Explain the importance of civil societies. Under which Acts are the NGOs in India legally registered? (APPSC, 2020) — 10 Marks

Civil society comprises voluntary associations, NGOs, community groups and social movements operating between the family, the market and the State. Its partnership with the United Nations is not a matter of goodwill but of constitutional design within the UN system: the Charter itself provides for it. Domestically, Indian NGOs acquire juridical personality only through specific registration statutes, and it is that legal form which determines their governance, taxation and access to funds.

## Part 1 — Why the UN partners with civil society
- An express Charter mandate:Article 71 of the UN Charter empowers the Economic and Social Council to “make suitable arrangements for consultation with non-governmental organisations”. This is operationalised through ECOSOC Resolution 1996/31 and the Committee on NGOs (established 1946, composed of 19 Member States), which recommends grant of consultative status in three categories — General, Special and Roster. The scale of the relationship has transformed: from 41 NGOs in 1946 to 6,494 holding active consultative status as on 31 December 2024 (UN DESA, 2025).
- Delivery of the 2030 Agenda:SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals), Target 17.17, expressly calls for effective public, public-private and civil society partnerships. Civil society participates through the Major Groups and Other Stakeholders mechanism at the High-Level Political Forum and contributes to Voluntary National Reviews — India’s VNRs to the HLPF have drawn on civil-society inputs, and NITI Aayog’s SDG India Index localises the same logic to States and districts.
- Legitimacy and the ‘leave no one behind’ principle: The Charter opens with “We the Peoples”, not “We the Governments”. Since States negotiate at the UN but citizens bear the consequences, civil society is the mechanism through which affected populations — indigenous groups, persons with disabilities, women in conflict zones — obtain a seat that inter-governmental structures would otherwise deny them.
- Independent monitoring and expertise: Governments report on their own compliance, which creates an obvious verification problem. NGOs supply shadow reports in the Universal Periodic Review before the Human Rights Council and to treaty bodies such as the CEDAW and CRC Committees, and technical expertise on climate, health and humanitarian standards. Operational agencies — UNICEF, WFP, UNHCR — additionally rely on NGOs as implementing partners for last-mile delivery.

## Part 2 — Importance of civil society
- Democratisation of governance: It extends participation beyond the five-yearly vote into continuous engagement — consultations, public hearings, and pre-legislative scrutiny — making governance deliberative rather than merely representative.
- Filling delivery gaps: Voluntary organisations reach populations administration finds costly to serve. In Andhra Pradesh, NGOs staff Disha (Sakhi) One Stop Centres attached to district hospitals, and 819 such centres nationally have assisted 10.98 lakh women (PIB Factsheet, August 2025).
- Protection of rights and accountability: Civil society converts grievance into enforceable claims — the RTI Act, 2005 emerged from the MKSS movement, and PIL by voluntary bodies has expanded the content of Article 21. The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, Section 12(i) statutorily directs the NHRC to encourage NGO efforts.
- Innovation and crisis response: Small organisations pilot models that governments later scale — self-help group federations, community-managed nutrition and disaster relief — and mobilise faster than procurement rules permit in emergencies.

## Part 3 — Acts under which NGOs are registered in India
- **Legal form** — Governing statute · Registering authority
- **Society** — Societies Registration Act, 1860; in Andhra Pradesh, the A.P. Societies Registration Act, 2001 (Act 35 of 2001) · Registrar of Societies / District Registrar
- **Trust** — Indian Trusts Act, 1882 (private); public charitable trusts under State law · Sub-Registrar / Charity Commissioner
- **Non-profit company** — Section 8, Companies Act, 2013 · Registrar of Companies, MCA
- **Foreign funding** — Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010; FCRA (Amendment) Rules, 2026 · Ministry of Home Affairs
- **Tax exemption** — Sections 12A/12AB and 80G (recast in the Income-tax Act, 2025, in force 1 April 2026) · Income Tax Department
- **Government grants / CSR** — NGO Darpan Unique ID (NITI Aayog); Form CSR-1 under Sec. 135, Companies Act, 2013 · NITI Aayog / MCA

Note the AP-specific point: the A.P. Societies Registration Act, 2001 repealed the application of the Societies Registration Act, 1860 in the Andhra area and the A.P. (Telangana Area) Public Societies Registration Act, 1350 Fasli in the Telangana area — so an AP-based NGO today registers under the 2001 State Act, not the 1860 Central Act. Examiners reward this precision.

## Conclusion

Civil society is not an adjunct to the UN system but a component of it, written into Article 71 of the Charter and now expressed through 6,494 accredited organisations and the partnership mandate of SDG 17.

Domestically, India’s layered legal architecture — registration under societies, trusts or company law, regulation of foreign funds under the FCRA, tax recognition under the Income-tax Act, 2025, and transparency through NGO Darpan — seeks to combine legitimacy with accountability. The measure of success is whether these frameworks remain enabling rather than merely restrictive, for civil society’s value to both the United Nations and the Indian State lies precisely in its independence.

- UN framework: Art. 71 UN Charter → ECOSOC Resolution 1996/31 → Committee on NGOs (19 Member States, since 1946); three statuses — General, Special, Roster; separate accreditation with the UN Department of Global Communications (DGC, formerly DPI).
- Numbers: 41 NGOs accredited in 1946; over 700 by 1992; 6,494 with active consultative status as on 31 December 2024 (UN DESA, February 2025).
- SDG hook: SDG 17 — Partnerships; Target 17.17 on multi-stakeholder partnerships; Major Groups and Other Stakeholders at the HLPF; India’s Voluntary National Reviews (2017, 2020, 2025); NITI Aayog SDG India Index for sub-national localisation.

Q89 Which constitutional provisions empower the formation of quasi-judicial authorities in India? Explain with suitable examples. (APPSC, 2025) — 10 Marks

A quasi-judicial authority is a body which, though not a court, determines the rights of parties by applying law to facts, is bound by the principles of natural justice, and issues decisions enforceable in law. The Constitution does not create such bodies directly; it empowers legislatures to create them and simultaneously subjects them to judicial review. Understanding both halves — the enabling provisions and the controlling provisions — is essential, because Indian tribunal jurisprudence has been shaped precisely by the tension between them.

## Constitutional provisions enabling quasi-judicial authorities
- Article 323A — Administrative Tribunals: Inserted along with Article 323B in Part XIV-A by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. It empowers Parliament alone to provide for administrative tribunals for service matters of the Union and the States, giving rise to the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 and the Central Administrative Tribunal (1985). AP anchor: the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal, constituted on 26 October 1989, was abolished by DoPT notification G.S.R. 30(E) dated 14 January 2020 at the State Government’s request with the High Court’s concurrence — a vivid illustration that Article 323A tribunals are creatures of statute; service matters in AP now go directly to the High Court at Amaravati.
- Article 323B — Tribunals for other matters: Unlike 323A, this empowers both Parliament and State legislatures, and it enumerates the permissible subjects: taxation, foreign exchange, industrial and labour disputes, land reforms, ceiling on urban property, elections to Parliament and State legislatures, foodstuffs, and rent and tenancy. Example: the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (established 1941, the final fact-finding authority in direct tax appeals) and State sales tax and rent control tribunals.
- Article 246 read with the Seventh Schedule — the general legislative basis: Most modern regulators and tribunals are created not under Part XIV-A but under ordinary legislative competence, chiefly Entry 11A of the Concurrent List (administration of justice; constitution and organisation of all courts except the Supreme Court and High Courts) and Entry 46. Examples: the National Company Law Tribunal under the Companies Act, 2013; the Competition Commission of India under the Competition Act, 2002; the Central Information Commission under the RTI Act, 2005; and Consumer Commissions under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The National Green Tribunal (NGT Act, 2010) additionally draws on Article 253, Parliament’s power to legislate to implement international agreements — here the Stockholm (1972) and Rio (1992) Declarations.
- Article 262 — Inter-State river water dispute tribunals: Parliament may provide for adjudication of disputes over inter-State rivers and may bar the jurisdiction of all courts, including the Supreme Court — the sole express ouster of its kind. This produced the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956. AP anchor: the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal-II, constituted on 2 April 2004 under Section 5(1) of the 1956 Act, received further Terms of Reference approved by the Union Cabinet in October 2023 to adjudicate between Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, and its tenure was extended to 31 July 2026. Alongside it, Section 84 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 constitutes the Apex Council of the Union Jal Shakti Minister and the two Chief Ministers.
- Constitutional bodies exercising quasi-judicial power: Several bodies created directly by the Constitution adjudicate. Article 324 — the Election Commission decides disputes on party recognition and symbols under Paragraph 15 of the Symbols Order, 1968. Articles 103 and 192 — the President and Governor decide disqualification of legislators, bound by the ECI’s opinion. Tenth Schedule, Paragraph 6 — the Speaker or Chairman acts as a tribunal in defection cases, as held in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), and is therefore subject to judicial review. Articles 338, 338A and 338B — the NCSC, NCST and NCBC have the powers of a civil court while inquiring into complaints. Article 280 — the Finance Commission is classically described as a quasi-judicial body. Article 311(2) — departmental disciplinary inquiries are quasi-judicial and must observe natural justice; Article 317 requires a Supreme Court inquiry before removal of a UPSC or State PSC member.

## Constitutional provisions controlling quasi-judicial authorities — the corrective
- Articles 136, 226 and 227: Article 136 permits special leave to appeal from any tribunal; Article 226 sustains writ jurisdiction; Article 227 vests High Courts with superintendence over all tribunals within their territorial jurisdiction. Tribunals are therefore supplemental to, not substitutes for, the constitutional courts.
- L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) — the governing authority: A seven-judge Bench struck down Articles 323A(2)(d) and 323B(3)(d) insofar as they excluded the jurisdiction of the High Courts and Supreme Court, holding that judicial review under Articles 226/227 and 32 is part of the basic structure. All tribunal decisions are now subject to appeal before a Division Bench of the jurisdictional High Court. This is the doctrinal point the standard answer usually misses.
- Continuing contestation — Madras Bar Association (2025): On 19 November 2025, a Bench of Chief Justice B.R. Gavai and Justice K. Vinod Chandran struck down key provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 relating to appointment, tenure and service conditions of tribunal members, holding that Parliament had re-enacted provisions already declared unconstitutional and thereby violated the separation of powers and judicial independence (Prasar Bharati / NewsOnAir, November 2025). Read with the earlier Madras Bar Association line of cases and Rojer Mathew (2019), it confirms that tribunal independence is itself a constitutional requirement.
- **Constitutional provision** — Enabling statute · Quasi-judicial body
- **Art. 323A (42nd Amdt., 1976)** — Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 · CAT; APAT (1989–2020)
- **Art. 323B** — Income-tax law; State tax and rent laws · ITAT; State Sales Tax Tribunals
- **Art. 246 + Sch. VII, Entry 11A** — Companies Act 2013; Competition Act 2002; RTI Act 2005 · NCLT; CCI; CIC
- **Art. 253** — National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 · NGT
- **Art. 262** — Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 · KWDT-II (AP–Telangana)
- **Art. 324; Tenth Sch., Para 6** — Symbols Order 1968; Anti-defection law · ECI; Speaker as tribunal
- **Arts. 136, 226, 227** — — (judicial review) · Supreme Court and High Courts

## Conclusion

Quasi-judicial authorities occupy the space between executive action and judicial remedy, delivering specialised, faster and cheaper adjudication that the regular courts cannot supply at scale. Their constitutional foundation lies principally in Articles 323A, 323B, 246 read with the Seventh Schedule, and 262, while their legitimacy is secured by Articles 136, 226 and 227 as interpreted in L. Chandra Kumar (1997). The unresolved question is institutional independence — chronic vacancies and executive control over appointments, censured again in Madras Bar Association (November 2025), continue to erode their credibility. Establishing an independent National Tribunals Commission, as repeatedly urged by the Supreme Court, would give these bodies the autonomy their adjudicatory function demands and complete the constitutional design.

- Distinguish three categories (examiners reward this): Constitutional bodies — ECI (Art. 324), UPSC (Art. 315), CAG (Art. 148), Finance Commission (Art. 280); Statutory bodies — NHRC, NCW, SEBI, CIC; Quasi-judicial bodies — those among the above which adjudicate rights (ECI, CIC, NGT, CCI, NCLT, consumer commissions).
- Tests of a quasi-judicial function (from Province of Bombay v. Khushaldas Advani, 1950): a lis or dispute between parties; a duty to act judicially; determination of rights by applying law to facts; and a reasoned, appealable order.
- Case-law chain:S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) upheld the 1985 Act → L. Chandra Kumar (1997) restored High Court jurisdiction → Union of India v. Madras Bar Association (2010) on NCLT → Rojer Mathew (2019) struck down Part XIV of the Finance Act, 2017 for excessive delegation → Madras Bar Association (2020, 2021) → Madras Bar Association (19 November 2025) striking down provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021.
- Article 323B subjects (learn the list): taxation; foreign exchange, import and export; industrial and labour disputes; land reforms under Art. 31A; ceiling on urban property; elections to Parliament and State legislatures; foodstuffs; rent and tenancy rights.
- Article 262 specifics: Art. 262(1) empowers Parliament to provide for adjudication; Art. 262(2) permits it to bar the jurisdiction of all courts including the Supreme Court — the only such express bar. Implemented by the ISRWD Act, 1956; the Inter-State River Water Disputes (Amendment) Bill proposes a single standing tribunal with a Dispute Resolution Committee.
- AP-specific: APAT (1989–2020, abolished by G.S.R. 30(E) of 14 January 2020); KWDT-II under Art. 262 with tenure extended to 31 July 2026; Apex Council under Sec. 84 of the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014; APERC under the Electricity Act, 2003; AP RERA under RERA, 2016; A.P. State Commission for Women (1998) as a State quasi-judicial body.

Q90 Under which Act was the National Commission for Women (NCW) established? Describe its main features and limitations. (APPSC, 2025) — 10 Marks

The National Commission for Women was established under the National Commission for Women Act, 1990 (Act No. 20 of 1990) and was constituted in January 1992, with Smt. Jayanti Patnaik as its first Chairperson. Its genesis lies in the recommendation of the Committee on the Status of Women in India in its report Towards Equality (1974) and the National Perspective Plan for Women (1988). Functioning under the Ministry of Women and Child Development, it is the apex national body mandated to review safeguards for women, recommend remedial legislation and facilitate redressal of grievances.

## Main features of the NCW
- Composition (Section 3): A Chairperson committed to the cause of women, five Members — of whom at least one each must belong to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes — and a Member-Secretary, all nominated by the Central Government for a term of three years. The present Chairperson, Smt. Vijaya Kishore Rahatkar, assumed office in October 2024.
- Statutory functions (Section 10): The Commission examines constitutional and legal safeguards and recommends remedial measures; reviews existing laws and suggests amendments; takes up cases of violation of women’s rights with the appropriate authorities; takes suo motu notice of matters relating to deprivation of women’s rights; funds litigation involving issues affecting a large body of women; inspects jails, remand homes and women’s institutions; and submits annual and special reports which, with action-taken memoranda, are laid before Parliament.
- Quasi-judicial powers (Section 10(4)): While inquiring into complaints, the Commission has the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 — summoning and enforcing attendance of any person and examining them on oath, requiring discovery and production of documents, receiving evidence on affidavits and requisitioning any public record from any court or office. This is what makes the NCW a genuine quasi-judicial authority rather than a mere advisory board.
- Grievance redressal and outreach: The Commission launched a 24x7 five-digit toll-free helpline, 14490, in November 2025, replacing the earlier ten-digit number, to link women in distress with police, One Stop Centres, hospitals, legal services authorities and counselling (NCW, 2025). It also runs Parivarik Mahila Lok Adalats for family disputes, Pre-Marital Counselling Centres under ‘Tere Mere Sapne’ in collaboration with NGOs, and an NRI Cell for women abandoned by overseas spouses.
- Policy and capacity work: The NCW conducts studies, gender sensitisation and legal awareness programmes; convened a Final Review Consultation on Cyber Laws for Women at Vigyan Bhawan in March 2025 to address deepfakes, cyberstalking and non-consensual imagery; and launched the Yashoda AI Abhiyan (2025) with Future Shift Labs to build AI, cybersecurity and digital-safety skills among rural and semi-urban women.

## Limitations of the NCW
- Statutory, not constitutional — the decisive weakness: The NCW derives authority from an ordinary Act of Parliament, which can be amended or repealed by a simple majority. By contrast the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (Article 338), the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A) and the National Commission for Backward Classes (Article 338B, inserted by the 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018) enjoy constitutional status, with the government obliged to consult them on major policy affecting their constituencies. Women, though roughly half the population, have no such constitutional commission — the strongest argument for conferring constitutional status on the NCW.
- Recommendations are not binding: The Commission recommends; it cannot enforce, prosecute or punish non-compliance. It must rely on State police and administrations to act on its findings, which introduces delay and, in politically sensitive matters, inaction.
- Questions of autonomy in appointment and funding: All members are nominated by the Central Government under Section 3(2), without a bipartisan or collegium-based selection process, and the Commission depends on grants from the Ministry of Women and Child Development — arrangements that expose it to the charge of executive dependence and constrain its capacity for last-mile outreach.
- A weak federal architecture: The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Empowerment of Women (Chairperson: Dr. Heena Vijaykumar Gavit), in its report on the Working of the National Commission for Women and State Commissions for Women submitted on 10 August 2023, found that many State Commissions were non-functional for want of chairpersons or funds, recommended a statutory linkage between the NCW and State Commissions, and urged a review of the 1990 Act to make the NCW more independent and effective, including a degree of accountability over the police with penalties for non-compliance.
- Overlapping jurisdiction: Complaints frequently straddle the NCW, the NHRC, the NCPCR and State Commissions for Women, producing duplication and diffused responsibility. AP anchor: Andhra Pradesh has its own quasi-judicial State Commission for Women under the A.P. Women’s Commission Act, 1998 (Act 9 of 1998, as amended by Act 9 of 2023), and its Disha (Sakhi) One Stop Centres attached to Disha police stations form the operational front line — confirming that the NCW’s real influence is normative rather than executive.
- **Commission** — Basis · Enforcement value
- **NCW** — Statutory — NCW Act, 1990 · Civil court powers (Sec. 10(4)); recommendations non-binding

- **Commission** — Basis · Enforcement value
- **NCSC** — Constitutional — Art. 338 · Civil court powers; mandatory consultation on policy
- **NCST** — Constitutional — Art. 338A · Civil court powers; reports laid before Parliament
- **NCBC** — Constitutional — Art. 338B (102nd Amdt., 2018) · Civil court powers; mandatory consultation
- **A.P. State Commission for Women** — State statute — A.P. Act 9 of 1998 · Quasi-judicial; operational front line in AP

## Conclusion

Over three decades the NCW has become the principal national forum for women’s grievances, driving legislative review, suo motu inquiry and, more recently, a digital-safety agenda through the 14490 helpline and the Yashoda AI initiative. Yet its authority ends where enforcement begins: it can summon, inquire and recommend, but it cannot compel. Strengthening it therefore requires three convergent reforms — constitutional status on the model of Articles 338 to 338B, a transparent, bipartisan appointment process with financial autonomy, and a statutory linkage with functional State Commissions, as the Standing Committee recommended in 2023. Only then will the Commission move from being the conscience-keeper of gender justice to becoming its guarantor, giving substance to the equality promised by Articles 14, 15 and 15(3).

- Statute at a glance: NCW Act, 1990 (Act No. 20 of 1990); Commission constituted January 1992; first Chairperson Smt. Jayanti Patnaik; nodal ministry — Ministry of Women and Child Development; Sec. 3 composition, Sec. 10 functions, Sec. 10(4) civil court powers, Sec. 16 annual report laid before Parliament with action-taken memorandum.
- Genesis: Committee on the Status of Women in India, Towards Equality (1974); National Perspective Plan for Women (1988); recommended in line with the UN Commission on the Status of Women’s call for national machinery for women.
- Current initiatives (2025–26): 24x7 helpline 14490 (November 2025); Pre-Marital Counselling Centres ‘Tere Mere Sapne’; Yashoda AI Abhiyan with Future Shift Labs; Final Review Consultation on Cyber Laws for Women, Vigyan Bhawan (March 2025); NRI Cell; Parivarik Mahila Lok Adalat.
- Committee anchor: Standing Committee on Empowerment of Women (Chair: Dr. Heena Gavit), report on the Working of the NCW and State Commissions for Women, 10 August 2023 — review the 1990 Act; statutory linkage with State Commissions; accountability over police with penalty for non-compliance; NCW has reviewed and suggested amendments to about 161 laws.
- Supporting constitutional and statutory framework: Arts. 14, 15(1), 15(3), 16, 39(a) and (d), 42, 51A(e); 106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam), 2023 reserving one-third of seats; POSH Act, 2013; Domestic Violence Act, 2005; Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961; Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 (26 weeks’ leave).

Q91  |  Section B — Question 27 Describe the work of the statutory bodies with examples and mention in which countries they are set up. Explain quasi-judicial bodies, providing two examples from India. (APPSC, 2020)

A statutory body owes both its existence and its powers to an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature. This distinguishes it from a constitutional body created by the Constitution itself (Election Commission, CAG, UPSC) and from an executive body set up by a mere government resolution (NITI Aayog). The legislature creates such bodies when a function demands technical expertise, continuity and insulation from routine executive control — the defining institutional feature of the modern administrative state. Quasi-judicial bodies form a specialised subset that decides disputes without being courts.

## Work of Statutory Bodies — Three Functional Roles
- Regulatory work: SEBI, under the SEBI Act, 1992, frames binding regulations, investigates market abuse and imposes penalties. The rationale is speed — securities markets move faster than legislatures can legislate, so rule-making is delegated to an expert regulator. TRAI (TRAI Act, 1997) and FSSAI (FSS Act, 2006) perform the same role in telecom and food safety.
- Welfare and advisory work: The NCW (NCW Act, 1990; constituted 31 January 1992) reviews laws and advises government on all policy matters affecting women; the NHRC (Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993) inquires into violations. AP anchor: the AP State Commission for Women functions under the A.P. Women's Commission Act, 1998 (as amended by Act No. 9 of 2023), and the AP State Human Rights Commission under Section 21 of the same central Act of 1993.
- Adjudicatory work: A statutory body may itself be quasi-judicial. The Central Information Commission, under the RTI Act, 2005, decides second appeals and may impose a penalty of up to Rs. 25,000 on a defaulting Public Information Officer — a binding, enforceable order.
