## II. Comparable Bodies Across Countries
- **Country** — Statutory / independent body · Domain
- **United States** — Federal Trade Commission; Securities and Exchange Commission · Competition; securities
- **United Kingdom** — Ofcom; Equality and Human Rights Commission · Communications; equality
- **Australia** — Australian Human Rights Commission · Human rights ('A' status, GANHRI)
- **India** — SEBI, UGC, NHRC, NCW, FSSAI · Multi-sector regulation and welfare

III. Quasi-Judicial Bodies: Meaning and Two Indian Examples

- Meaning: bodies empowered to determine rights and impose liabilities by applying law to facts, bound by natural justice — notice, hearing, an unbiased decision-maker and a reasoned order — but free of the Civil Procedure Code's rigidity. Article 323A authorises administrative tribunals for service matters and Article 323B tribunals for taxation, land reforms, elections and similar subjects.
- Central Administrative Tribunal (Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985): 19 benches, a filing fee of only Rs. 50, and no compulsory lawyer — deliberate design choices to make service justice cheap. Since 1985 it has received 9,88,738 cases, of which 9,19,157 were disposed of up to 31 January 2026, leaving 69,581 pending (PIB / DoPT reply in Parliament, March 2026). Its Hyderabad Bench serves Andhra Pradesh.
- National Green Tribunal (NGT Act, 2010): a specialised environmental tribunal applying the polluter-pays, precautionary and sustainable-development principles, with power to award compensation and restitution of the environment. Correction to a common error: in the Sterlite Copper matter the NGT in 2013 permitted the plant to restart; the 2018 permanent closure was ordered by the TN Pollution Control Board, the Supreme Court set aside the NGT's contrary order in February 2019 for want of jurisdiction, and in February 2024 declined reopening.
- The outer limit: in L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) a seven-judge bench held that judicial review by High Courts under Articles 226/227 is part of the basic structure and cannot be excluded. Tribunals therefore supplement the higher judiciary; they do not substitute it.

## Conclusion

Statutory bodies allow a large democracy to combine democratic legitimacy with technical competence — the legislature sets the mandate, experts execute it. Quasi-judicial bodies extend this logic to dispute resolution, delivering speedy, low-cost and specialised justice. Their credibility, however, rests on independent appointments, timely filling of vacancies and financial autonomy; without these, specialisation degenerates into executive convenience, which is precisely what L. Chandra Kumar guarded against.

- Fourfold classification by source of power: Constitutional (Art. 324 ECI, Art. 148 CAG, Art. 338 NCSC) · Statutory (SEBI, NHRC, NCW, NCBC after the 102nd Amendment became constitutional under Art. 338B) · Executive/Non-statutory (NITI Aayog, 2015 Cabinet Resolution) · Regulatory (SEBI, TRAI, IRDAI, CCI, RERA).
- NGT structure: Principal Bench at New Delhi with four zonal benches; the Southern Zone Bench at Chennai has jurisdiction over Andhra Pradesh. Composed of judicial members and expert members — the expert member is the institutional innovation.
- A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India (1969): the Supreme Court held that the line between administrative and quasi-judicial functions is thin, and natural justice applies to administrative decisions affecting rights.
- AP regulatory instance: the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (APERC) under the AP Electricity Reform Act, 1998 (now read with the Electricity Act, 2003) fixes tariffs through a quasi-judicial public-hearing process.
- Exam line: 'A statutory body can be quasi-judicial (CIC), but a quasi-judicial body need not be statutory in origin — the NCSC is constitutional yet exercises civil-court powers under Art. 338(8).'

Q92  |  Section B — Question 28 What are the Constitutional guarantees given to women? Explain the role of the National Commission for Women in protecting the rights of women. (APPSC, 2012)

The Preamble's guarantee of justice — social, economic and political — and of equality of status and opportunity is the source from which every specific safeguard for women flows. The framers recognised that formal equality would be inadequate against centuries of structural disadvantage; hence Article 15(3) expressly permits protective discrimination. These guarantees operate at four levels — enforceable rights, directive principles, a fundamental duty, and political representation — while the National Commission for Women, a statutory body created in 1992, is the institutional machinery that monitors them.

## Constitutional Guarantees — A Four-Layer Architecture
- **Layer** — Provisions · What it guarantees
- **Fundamental Rights** — Arts. 14, 15(1), 15(3), 16, 23 · Equality before law; no discrimination on sex; enabling clause for special provisions; equal opportunity in public employment; prohibition of trafficking
- **Directive Principles** — Arts. 39(a), 39(d), 39(e), 39A, 42, 43 · Equal right to livelihood; equal pay for equal work; protection of health; free legal aid; just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
- **Fundamental Duty** — Art. 51A(e) · Duty of every citizen to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women

- **Layer** — Provisions · What it guarantees
- **Political representation** — Arts. 243D(3), 243T(3); 106th Amendment, 2023 · One-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities; one-third in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies

- The judicial layer matters equally:Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) read Articles 14, 19(1)(g) and 21 together to lay down binding workplace guidelines, later codified as the POSH Act, 2013. Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) struck down the adultery provision as treating a wife as her husband's property. Secretary, Ministry of Defence v. Babita Puniya (2020) secured permanent commission for women Army officers, rejecting 'physiological limitations' as a ground.
- Currency: the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act — Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023 — was formally notified on 16 April 2026, with reservation operationalising after the delimitation exercise (PIB, New India Samachar, May 2026). At the grassroots, nearly half of all elected Panchayati Raj representatives are already women (PIB, March 2026); Andhra Pradesh is among the States that reserve 50% of local-body seats for women. Female Labour Force Participation rose from 23.3% (2017–18) to 41.7% (2023–24) — PLFS, MoSPI.

## II. Role of the National Commission for Women
- Statutory watchdog, not a constitutional body: created under the NCW Act, 1990 and constituted on 31 January 1992, it enjoys the powers of a civil court while inquiring (Section 10(4)) — summoning witnesses, requisitioning records, receiving affidavit evidence. Its Foundation Day in January 2026 marked 34 years (PIB, January 2026); Smt. Vijaya Rahatkar has been Chairperson since October 2024 (PIB).
- Grievance redressal: complaints on domestic violence, dowry, workplace harassment and cyber abuse are received through an online portal and the 24x7 helpline 7827170170, and are pursued with State police through the Legal and Investigation Cells — giving a complainant national-level leverage when local machinery stalls.
- Legal reform and policy influence: NCW inputs shaped the POSH Act, 2013 and the Criminal Law (Amendment) Acts of 2013 and 2018. Complaints filed on the relaunched SHe-Box portal are now auto-routed to the relevant Internal Committee, with a nodal officer in every organisation (PIB, November 2025).
- AP anchor: Andhra Pradesh legislated the Disha Act — the A.P. Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2019 — mandating investigation within 7 working days and trial within 14 working days, backed by Disha police stations, the Disha SOS mobile app and Disha One Stop Centres run by the Women Development and Child Welfare Department (wdcw.ap.gov.in). Because it amends central criminal law, it required Presidential assent under Article 254(2) — a textbook illustration of the federal limits on State-led reform.
- Honest limitation: the NCW's recommendations are advisory, it cannot enforce its own findings, and several State Commissions function with vacancies — so constitutional promise still outruns institutional capacity.

## Conclusion

The Constitution supplies an unusually generous framework for gender justice — rights, directives, a citizen's duty and now reserved political space. The NCW converts that framework into everyday redress. Yet the persistence of gender-based violence, wage disparity and low female workforce participation shows that the binding constraint is enforcement, not entitlement. Strengthening the NCW with binding powers, filling State Commission vacancies and time-bound trials on the Disha model are the logical next steps.

- Article 15(3) jurisprudence: upheld protective discrimination in Government of A.P. v. P.B. Vijayakumar (1995), where the Supreme Court sustained a 30% reservation for women in State services — an Andhra Pradesh case, directly quotable in APPSC answers.
- Nirbhaya Fund: Rs. 7,712.85 crore allocated up to FY 2024–25, of which Rs. 5,846.08 crore (about 76%) was utilised, funding One Stop Centres, ERSS-112, Women Helpline 181, Fast Track Special Courts and Anti-Human Trafficking Units (PIB, March 2025).
- One Stop Centres: over 10.61 lakh women assisted since inception up to December 2024 (PIB, February 2025) — integrated medical, legal, police and psychosocial support under one roof.
- Statutory ecosystem beyond the Constitution: Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 · PC&PNDT Act, 1994 · Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 · POSH Act, 2013 · Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 (26 weeks' leave) · BNS, 2023 (in force 1 July 2024), which raises punishments for sexual offences.
- AP schemes: DISHA One Stop Centres · Mahila Police / Disha Patrols · AP State Commission for Women under the 1998 Act as amended in 2023 · 50% reservation for women in local bodies.
- SDG link: SDG-5 (Gender Equality) — India's composite SDG India Index score is tracked annually by NITI Aayog; gender remains among the weaker-performing goals, a useful evaluative line.

Q93  |  Section B — Question 29 What are the functions of the National Commission for Women? (APPSC, 2011)

The National Commission for Women is a statutory body constituted on 31 January 1992 under the National Commission for Women Act, 1990, following the recommendation of the Committee on the Status of Women in India (Towards Equality, 1974). Its mandate under Section 10 combines four roles that are rarely housed in one institution — reviewer of law, investigator of grievances, adviser on policy and generator of public awareness. That combination makes it a watchdog with quasi-judicial teeth but advisory reach.

## Functions under Section 10(1) of the NCW Act, 1990 — Four Families
- (a) Reviewing legal and constitutional safeguards: the Commission examines existing provisions, recommends amendments and reports on gaps in implementation. It has reviewed the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 and the PC&PNDT Act, 1994, and has engaged with the gender-related provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (in force from 1 July 2024). This is the highest-value function because a single legislative change protects millions, whereas a single complaint protects one.
- (b) Investigating complaints and suo motu cognizance: Section 10(1)(f) empowers it to act on its own motion where there is deprivation of women's rights, non-implementation of protective laws or non-compliance with policy. The Legal Cell, Investigation Cell and NRI Cell handle domestic violence, dowry, trafficking, workplace harassment and transnational abandonment cases, coordinating with the Ministry of External Affairs for the last.
- (c) Grievance redressal, mediation and legal aid: it conducts Parivarik Mahila Lok Adalats for family disputes, funds litigation involving a large body of women (Section 10(1)(l)), and refers cases to State Commissions. It also inspects jails, remand homes and women's institutions under Section 10(1)(k) and recommends remedial action.
- (d) Research, awareness and capacity building: gender-sensitisation workshops, the monthly Rashtra Mahila newsletter, and campaigns such as Digital Shakti against cyber harassment and

Yashoda AI (2025), an AI-literacy and cyber-safety programme for rural and semi-urban women including SHG members, ASHA workers and elected representatives.

✎ Infographic tip: Infographic: a simple 2x2 grid — Review Law | Investigate Complaints | Redress & Legal Aid | Research & Awareness — with one named example inside each quadrant. Fast to draw, and it visibly demonstrates grouping.

## II. Powers That Make These Functions Effective
- Under Section 10(4) the Commission has the powers of a civil court while inquiring — summoning and examining witnesses on oath, requisitioning any public record, receiving evidence on affidavit and issuing commissions. It must present reports to the Central Government, which are laid before Parliament with an action-taken memorandum, creating a parliamentary accountability loop.
- AP anchor: the NCW works alongside the AP State Commission for Women constituted under the A.P. Women's Commission Act, 1998 (as amended by Act No. 9 of 2023), and complaints arising in Andhra Pradesh are frequently routed through the State's Disha One Stop Centres and Disha police stations for time-bound investigation.
- Structural limitation: the Commission's findings are recommendatory, it depends on the Union Government for funds and staff, and its jurisdiction overlaps with State Commissions, the NHRC and the NCSC where a complainant is both a woman and a member of a Scheduled Caste — a coordination gap the 2nd ARC flagged for national commissions generally.

## Conclusion

The NCW's functions span the full life-cycle of a right — writing it better, enforcing it in individual cases, and building the awareness that makes citizens claim it. Its influence on the POSH Act, 2013 and on successive criminal-law amendments shows that a well-run advisory body can shape statute. To convert influence into guarantee, the Commission needs binding follow-up powers on its recommendations, an assured budget and a formal protocol with State Commissions.

- Origin: recommended by the Committee on the Status of Women in India in Towards Equality (1974); given effect by the NCW Act, 1990; first Chairperson Smt. Jayanti Patnaik (1992). Present Chairperson: Smt. Vijaya Rahatkar, since October 2024 (PIB).
- Composition: a Chairperson, five Members (at least one each from the SCs and STs), and a Member-Secretary, all nominated by the Central Government — the nomination route, rather than a collegium, is the principal criticism of its independence.
- Section 10(1) at a glance: examine safeguards → report to Government → recommend measures → review laws → take up violations → act suo motu → conduct studies → promote research → participate in planning → evaluate progress → inspect custodial institutions → fund litigation → report periodically.
- Distinguish carefully: NCW is statutory (Act of 1990) · NCSC and NCST are constitutional (Arts. 338 and 338A) · NCBC became constitutional through the 102nd Amendment, 2018 (Art. 338B) · NCPCR is statutory (CPCR Act, 2005). Mixing these up is the single commonest error in this topic.
- Supporting architecture: Mission Shakti (2021–22 onwards) with its Sambal and Samarthya sub-schemes · One Stop Centres · Women Helpline 181 · SHe-Box portal · Fast Track Special Courts under the Nirbhaya Fund.

Q94  |  Section B — Question 30 Explain the powers and functions of the Human Rights Commission. (APPSC, 2011)

The National Human Rights Commission was constituted under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 to protect rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in international covenants and enforceable by Indian courts. It is a statutory body — not constitutional — designed to meet the UN's Paris Principles on independence, pluralism and effectiveness. Its authority is therefore moral and investigative rather than coercive, which explains both its reach and its recurring criticism.

## Composition (as amended by the Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019)
- Chairperson: a former Chief Justice of India or a former Judge of the Supreme Court — the 2019 Amendment widened this from CJI-only, easing recruitment. Members: a sitting or former Supreme Court Judge, a sitting or former High Court Chief Justice, and three members with human rights knowledge, of whom at least one must be a woman. Seven ex-officio members: the chairpersons of the NCM, NCSC, NCST, NCW, NCBC, NCPCR and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities. Tenure was reduced from five years to three, with reappointment permitted.

## II. Powers
- Civil court powers (Section 13): while inquiring, the Commission may summon and examine witnesses on oath, require discovery and production of documents, receive evidence on affidavit and requisition any public record from any court or office. This is what allows it to extract information from a reluctant State Government rather than merely request it.
- Suo motu and intervention powers (Section 12): it may inquire on its own motion or on a petition, and may intervene in any proceeding involving an allegation of human rights violation pending before a court, with that court's approval. It may also visit any jail or State-controlled institution to study living conditions.
- Recommendatory and approach-to-court powers (Sections 18 and 20): it may recommend payment of compensation, initiation of prosecution or disciplinary action, and grant of immediate interim relief; it may approach the Supreme Court or a High Court for directions. Its annual report goes to the President and is laid before Parliament together with a memorandum of action taken — the accountability hook.

## III. Functions and Their Statutory Limits
- **Function** — Statutory basis · Built-in limitation
- **Inquiry into violations or negligence by public servants** — Sec. 12(a) · Sec. 36(2): no inquiry into an event more than one year old
- **Matters concerning the armed forces** — Sec. 19 · Only a report may be sought from the Central Government; no independent investigation
- **Recommending relief, prosecution, compensation** — Secs. 18, 20 · Recommendations are not binding on government
- **Prison visits, research, human rights literacy, treaty study** — Sec. 12(c)–(h) · Dependent on State cooperation and budgetary support

- Accreditation — the accurate current position: GANHRI's Sub-Committee on Accreditation, at its 45th session in March 2025, recommended downgrading NHRC-India from 'A' to 'B' status, citing the deployment of police officers in its investigations, government control over appointment of the Secretary-General, and insufficient pluralism. The NHRC challenged this; the GANHRI Bureau rejected the challenge in December 2025 and referred the matter back, with the final alteration-of-status review now deferred to the SCA's November 2026 session (GANHRI Accreditation Status Chart, 4 December 2025). 'A' status means full compliance with the Paris Principles and carries voting and speaking rights in UN human rights fora; 'B' status means partial compliance and the loss of those privileges.
- AP anchor: the Andhra Pradesh State Human Rights Commission functions under Section 21 of the same Act with its seat at Kurnool, and Section 30 requires a Human Rights Court in each district for speedy trial of offences arising out of violations. The NHRC has taken suo motu cognizance of Andhra Pradesh matters, including an assault on a woman by a moneylender in Kuppam, Chittoor district.

## Conclusion

The NHRC's strength lies in investigation, publicity and moral suasion — it can compel disclosure, expose State failure and place its findings before Parliament. Its weakness is structural: it cannot enforce, cannot independently probe the armed forces, and cannot look back beyond a year. The pending GANHRI review makes reform urgent rather than optional — a transparent, pluralistic appointment process, an independent investigative wing, and a statutory duty on governments to respond within a fixed period.

- Paris Principles (endorsed by the UN General Assembly, 1993): six benchmarks for a national human rights institution — broad mandate, autonomy from government, independence guaranteed by statute or Constitution, pluralism, adequate resources, and adequate powers of investigation.
- Accreditation grades: 'A' = fully compliant, with voting rights and speaking privileges at the UN Human Rights Council; 'B' = partially compliant, may attend but not vote or speak. As of December 2025 GANHRI had accredited 119 NHRIs.
- Appointment committee: Prime Minister (Chair), Speaker of the Lok Sabha, Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, Leaders of the Opposition in both Houses, and the Union Home Minister — an executive-dominated composition that is the core pluralism objection.
- State Human Rights Commissions: Sec. 21 permits a State to constitute an SHRC, which may inquire only into matters in List II and List III. Sec. 30 provides for Human Rights Courts in every district.
- 2nd ARC (5th Report, Public Order) recommended strengthening the NHRC's investigative machinery and making State compliance with its recommendations mandatory unless reasons are recorded.
- Key judicial support:D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) laid down custodial arrest safeguards that the NHRC routinely enforces through its custodial-death reporting requirement — every custodial death must be reported to the Commission within 24 hours.

Q95  |  Section B — Question 31 Analyse the functions and functioning of National Commission for Scheduled Castes. (APPSC, 2008)

The National Commission for Scheduled Castes is a constitutional body under Article 338, comprising a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. Its lineage runs from the Special Officer envisaged in the original Article 338, through the multi-member Commission created by the 65th Amendment Act, 1990, to the bifurcation effected by the 89th Amendment Act, 2003, which established the NCSC under Article 338 and the NCST under the new Article 338A with effect from 19 February 2004.

## Functions under Article 338(5)
- **Function** — Constitutional clause · Analytical significance
- **Investigate and monitor all safeguards for SCs** — 338(5)(a) · Converts paper safeguards into a monitored obligation
- **Inquire into specific complaints of deprivation of rights** — 338(5)(b) · Individual redress with civil-court backing
- **Participate in and advise on socio-economic development planning** — 338(5)(c) · Entry point into the budget process
- **Present annual and special reports to the President** — 338(5)(d) · Laid before Parliament with action-taken memorandum
- **Recommend measures for effective implementation** — 338(5)(e) · The Commission's main lever, but non-binding

## II. How It Actually Functions
- Civil court powers — Article 338(8): while investigating or inquiring, the Commission has all the powers of a civil court trying a suit — summoning witnesses on oath, requiring discovery and production of documents, receiving affidavit evidence and requisitioning public records. This is why a summons from the NCSC to a District Collector carries real weight even though its final recommendation does not bind.
- The consultation duty — Article 338(9): the Union and every State Government shall consult the Commission on all major policy matters affecting Scheduled Castes. This is the Commission's most under-used constitutional lever; in practice consultation is often post-facto or skipped, which is itself a strong analytical point.
- Reporting in practice: the Commission submitted its Annual Report for 2023–24 to the President in 2025, reviewing atrocities, reservation compliance and welfare-scheme implementation on the basis of spot visits and consultations with Central and State governments (PIB, 2025). Reports are, however, habitually tabled years late, blunting their policy impact.
- Institutional accompaniment: the Commission reviews the working of institutions such as NSFDC, which recorded its highest-ever disbursement of Rs. 775.26 crore in FY 2025–26, covering 59,002 beneficiaries — a 41% expansion over the previous year (PIB, April 2026).
- AP anchor: Andhra Pradesh gave statutory force to sub-plan budgeting through the A.P. Scheduled Castes Sub-Plan and Tribal Sub-Plan (Planning, Allocation and Utilisation of Financial Resources) Act, 2013, which ring-fences allocations proportionate to SC population — precisely the kind of measure the NCSC recommends nationally. The State also runs Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Study Circles (for example at Tirupati) for SC/ST civil services aspirants and offers cash incentives of Rs. 1 lakh and Rs. 50,000 to candidates clearing UPSC Prelims and Mains respectively (Social Welfare Department, Government of Andhra Pradesh).

## III. Structural Limitations
- Advisory character: recommendations bind no one; the Commission can expose but cannot compel. Delayed reporting: annual reports reach Parliament years after the period they cover. Capacity deficit: a five-member body with limited staff must monitor safeguards across 28 States. Jurisdictional overlap: where a complainant is a Dalit woman, or an SC forest-dweller, mandates of the NCSC, NCW, NCST and NHRC collide, causing duplication and delay.

## Conclusion

The NCSC is constitutionally powerful in process and weak in outcome — it can investigate like a court but can only recommend like an adviser. Its real value lies in the Article 338(9) consultation duty and in the parliamentary visibility of its reports. Making consultation demonstrable before policy is notified, mandating a time-bound action-taken reply from every government, filling vacancies promptly, and agreeing a written protocol with the NCST, NCW and NHRC would turn a monitoring body into an effective guarantor of social justice.

- Constitutional evolution — memorise the sequence: original Art. 338 (Special Officer, popularly the Commissioner for SCs and STs) → 65th Amendment Act, 1990 (multi-member National Commission for SCs and STs) → 89th Amendment Act, 2003 (bifurcation; NCSC under Art. 338, NCST under Art. 338A, effective 19 February 2004).
- Related constitutional bodies: NCBC under Art. 338B (102nd Amendment, 2018) · Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities under Art. 350B. The NCSC also discharges functions relating to the Anglo-Indian community and, on reference, other backward classes under Art. 338(10).
- Key safeguards it monitors: Arts. 15(4), 16(4), 16(4A) and 16(4B) (reservation and consequential seniority)
- Art. 17 (abolition of untouchability) · Art. 46 (educational and economic promotion) · Arts. 330 and 332 (reserved seats) · Art. 335 (claims to services consistent with efficiency).
- Statutory framework: Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 · SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, as strengthened in 2015 and 2018 (exclusive Special Courts, defined timelines, and the reversal of Subhash Kashinath Mahajan by the 2018 Amendment).
- Recent jurisprudence:State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024) — a seven-judge bench upheld sub-classification within Scheduled Castes for reservation purposes, a development the NCSC is now required to monitor in State implementation.
- AP institutions: A.P. SCSP and TSP Act, 2013 · A.P. Scheduled Castes Co-operative Finance Corporation · Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Study Circles · A.P. Commission for Scheduled Castes.

Q96  |  Section B — Question 32 Public servants often face situations where personal values conflict with public responsibilities. Examine how a strong ethical foundation can help resolve such dilemmas while maintaining accountability. (APPSC, 2025)

Every civil servant takes an oath under the Third Schedule to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and to discharge duties without fear or favour, affection or ill-will. The dilemma arises because public office is exercised by a person with private beliefs, family ties and human sympathies. A strong ethical foundation does not eliminate this friction; it supplies a defensible ordering of loyalties — constitutional duty first, institutional rules next, personal preference last — and, crucially, makes that ordering visible on record.

## Typology of Value Conflicts
- **Type of conflict** — Illustration · Resolving anchor
- **Personal belief vs constitutional duty** — An officer's religious or caste view vs enforcing a secular law · Oath under the Third Schedule; Art. 51A(e) and (h)
- **Compassion vs rule of law** — Evicting poor encroachers from public land · Proportionality; rehabilitation under the LARR Act, 2013
- **Political loyalty vs public interest** — Instruction to favour a particular contractor · Rule 3, AIS (Conduct) Rules, 1968 — integrity, devotion to duty, political neutrality
- **Private interest vs public office** — A family firm bidding for a departmental contract · Disclosure and recusal; 2nd ARC on conflict of interest

## II. How an Ethical Foundation Resolves Them
- It converts intuition into a reviewable process. A workable five-step protocol: identify all affected stakeholders → test the options against constitutional values (equality, dignity, due process) → confirm legality and jurisdiction → choose the least-harm option → record the reasons on file. The fifth step is decisive: a written justification is what makes discretion contestable under the RTI Act, 2005 and reviewable in court, so ethics and accountability become the same act rather than competing ones.
- It substitutes institutional values for private judgement. The 2nd ARC's Fourth Report, Ethics in Governance, recommended that 'Public Service Values' towards which all public servants should aspire be defined and made applicable to every tier of government and to parastatals, with any transgression treated as misconduct inviting punishment; it further recommended that conflict of interest be comprehensively covered in the codes of ethics and conduct, and that serving officials not be nominated to boards of public undertakings.
- It is teachable, not merely innate. Conduct Rules prohibit; a code of ethics guides. Mission Karmayogi and the iGOT Karmayogi platform embed behavioural and ethical competencies in the civil servant's continuous learning path, shifting training from rule-recall to judgement under pressure — the exact capacity a value conflict tests.

## III. Maintaining Accountability Through Ethical Conduct
- Legal accountability: judicial review, the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, the Prevention of Corruption Act as amended in 2018, and CVC oversight. AP anchor: the A.P. Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act, 1983 provides the State-level forum against maladministration.
- Administrative accountability: Citizen's Charters, RTI disclosure under Section 4, performance appraisal and social audit. AP anchor: Andhra Pradesh institutionalised third-party verification through its Society for Social Audit, Accountability and Transparency (SSAAT) for MGNREGS, and uses the Real Time Governance Society (RTGS) dashboard to track grievance disposal — accountability designed into the system rather than left to individual virtue.
- Moral accountability: where law and rule run out, conscience and peer scrutiny remain. Satyendra Dubey's exposure of corruption in the Golden Quadrilateral project in 2003 and his subsequent murder led directly to the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 — which nonetheless remains substantially unoperationalised, a candid reminder that individual courage is not a substitute for systemic protection.

## Conclusion

An ethical foundation does not tell a public servant which feeling to suppress; it tells her which loyalty ranks highest and obliges her to say so on record. Constitutional values order the conflict, codified public service values give the ordering institutional force, and documented reasoning converts a private moral choice into a publicly accountable decision. Enacting enforceable Public Service Values as the 2nd ARC urged, and giving real effect to whistleblower protection, would ensure that integrity is a system property rather than an act of individual heroism.

- Nolan Committee — Seven Principles of Public Life (UK, 1995): selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership. Quote as the international benchmark against which India's Conduct Rules are judged.
- 2nd ARC, Fourth Report (Ethics in Governance): India has Conduct Rules but no Code of Ethics for civil servants; the draft Public Service Bill proposed statutory values — allegiance to the Preamble, apolitical functioning, objectivity and impartiality, accountability and transparency, merit in selection, economy in expenditure — enforced through a Public Service Authority.
- Rule 3, All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968: every member shall maintain absolute integrity, devotion to duty and political neutrality, and shall do nothing unbecoming of a member of the Service — the operative legal hook to cite.
- Instruments for conflict of interest: mandatory annual declaration of assets and liabilities · Section 4(1)(b) RTI proactive disclosure · recusal protocols · cooling-off period for post-retirement employment · Register of Interests, as discussed by the 2nd ARC.
- Ethical competence beyond rules: emotional intelligence, moral courage, empathy and foresight — the qualities Mission Karmayogi's competency framework seeks to build, moving the civil service from rule-compliance to role-fitment.
- Illustrative cases (use one, not four): Satyendra Dubey (2003) · Ashok Khemka (2012) · Armstrong Pame's community-funded 'People's Road' in Manipur · Lal Bahadur Shastri's resignation after the 1956 Ariyalur rail accident, the classic Indian example of assuming moral responsibility without legal fault.
- AP institutions to name: A.P. Lokayukta (Act of 1983) · SSAAT social audits · Real Time Governance Society (RTGS) · Dr. MCR HRD Institute lineage for administrative training.

Q97  |  Section-B, Q33 “The Mission Karmayogi initiative of the Government of India will revitalize the Civil Services in India and equip them to face the challenges of Governance.” Examine. (TGPSC, 2024 — 10 Marks)

Mission Karmayogi — the National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building (NPCSCB), approved by the Union Cabinet on 2 September 2020 — responds to a specific diagnosis: an Indian bureaucracy recruited for generalist administration but now asked to regulate artificial intelligence, price carbon and defend critical digital infrastructure. Its central promise is a shift from ‘rule-based’ to ‘role-based’ functioning, delivered through the iGOT Karmayogi platform. Whether that promise revitalizes the services depends less on the architecture, which is sound, than on whether learning translates into changed administrative behaviour.

## How the Mission Seeks to Revitalize the Civil Services
- Rule-based to role-based functioning — the conceptual core.

–Under the FRAC framework (Functions–Roles–Activities–Competencies), posts are mapped to the competencies they actually demand, so training follows the job rather than seniority. The Cabinet approval covered around 46 lakh Central Government employees at a cost of ₹510.86 crore over five years (PIB, Cabinet Decision, 2 September 2020). –Why this matters: a Deputy Secretary handling procurement and one handling disaster response

previously sat through the same generic mid-career course. Role-mapping ends that mismatch — the difference between a trained officer and a merely senior one. GiGOT Karmayogi as Digital Public Infrastructure for learning. –The platform crossed 1.5 crore registered learners with over 8 crore course completions and more than 4,600 courses in multiple languages, alongside 130+ Capacity Building Plans developed by Ministries and States (PIB, Sādhana Saptah 2026, 4 April 2026). –Scale is the point: 3 lakh users in January 2023 to over 1 crore by May 2025 is a 30-fold rise in about two years (PIB, 20 May 2025) — no classroom system could have reached peons, drivers and multi-tasking staff, who are now among the platform’s top learners. GAn institutional spine, not a one-off scheme. –The Capacity Building Commission (2021) harmonises standards and exercises functional supervision

over Central Training Institutions; Karmayogi Bharat, a Section 8 SPV (2022), owns and runs iGOT; and a PM-led Public Human Resources Council approves Annual Capacity Building Plans. Courses are aligned to an indigenous Karmayogi Competency Model rooted in Indic wisdom (PIB, 20 May 2025).

## II. How It Equips Officers for 21st-Century Governance Challenges
- Emerging-technology competence is being built deliberately, not incidentally.

–At the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (Bharat Mandapam, 16–20 February 2026), the CBC and Karmayogi

Bharat showcased AI-enabled, role-based and multilingual learning tools embedded in iGOT, with courses on AI fundamentals, AI in governance and emerging technology risks (PIB, February 2026). GContinuous, on-demand learning suits crisis governance. –Structured national learning weeks institutionalise the habit — the first Karmayogi Saptah (19–27 October 2024) alone produced over 32 lakh course completions, and Sādhana Saptah (2–8 April 2026) marked five years of the Mission (PIB, 2024; 2026). An officer can now acquire a flood-response or vaccine-logistics module in days rather than waiting for the next mid-career slot. GFederalisation — and the Andhra Pradesh anchor. –Karmayogi Bharat and the CBC have signed tripartite MoUs with 28 States/UTs; over 60% of registered users are from States/UTs, and Andhra Pradesh is among the top five States by registered civil servants on iGOT (PIB, 20 May 2025). –AP is also one of only four States (with Assam, Gujarat and Odisha) in the CBC’s pilot extending Mission

Karmayogi to 60 Gram Panchayats, and hosted one of five State-level workshops on ULB capacity building in 2025 (PIB, CBC Year End Review 2025, 24 December 2025). The State’s own institution, APHRDI Bapatla, is the natural delivery arm.

## III. Why the Claim Must Be Qualified
- Course completions are an input, not an outcome.

–Eight crore completions measure consumption of content, not improved decisions. The Mission itself

acknowledges this: the new iGOT Learning Assessment Framework, introduced in 2026, is explicitly designed to test whether learning is applied in real workplace situations (PIB, 4 April 2026) — an admission that the earlier metric was insufficient. GCapacity is not the binding constraint on integrity. –Training cannot neutralise political interference, arbitrary transfers or the absence of fixed tenure — the very problems the 2nd ARC and the Supreme Court in T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013), which directed fixed minimum tenure and a Civil Services Board, identified as structural. A well-trained officer transferred every eight months delivers no more than an untrained one. GThe frontline is reached last.

–Over 1.75 lakh ULB officials have been onboarded and 125 designations mapped under the RACE framework (PIB, CBC Year End Review 2025) — significant, but small against India’s 2.64 lakh Gram Panchayats, where the citizen actually meets the State.

## IV. Verdict
- The statement is directionally correct but overstated as certainty. Mission Karmayogi supplies a capacity architecture India previously lacked; it does not supply the tenure security, performance consequences and political restraint that convert capacity into performance. It is a necessary condition for revitalization, not a sufficient one.

## Conclusion

Mission Karmayogi has done what no previous training reform managed — it has built a national, competency-anchored, federally shared learning infrastructure and made lifelong learning a routine expectation rather than an occasional privilege. Its revitalizing potential will be realised only when learning outcomes are hard-wired into appraisal and posting decisions, when the assessment framework matures beyond completion counts, and when the same rigour reaches the panchayat secretary as it does the Deputy Secretary. Capacity building is the foundation of civil service reform; it is not a substitute for it.

- Six Pillars of NPCSCB: Policy Framework; Institutional Framework; Competency Framework; Digital Learning Framework (iGOT-Karmayogi); electronic HRMS (e-HRMS); Monitoring & Evaluation Framework.
- Institutional trio to memorise: PM-led Public Human Resources Council (apex) → Capacity Building Commission, 2021 (standards, supervision over CTIs) → Karmayogi Bharat, Section 8 SPV, 2022 (runs iGOT, owns IPR for GoI).
- Key data line (PIB, April 2026): 1.5 crore+ learners; 8 crore+ completions; 4,600+ courses; 130+ Capacity Building Plans; MoUs with 28 States/UTs.
- Named initiatives worth citing: FRAC
- Karmayogi Competency Model (KCM)
- Karmayogi Saptah (National Learning Week, from October 2024)
- Sādhana Saptah 2026
- iGOT Learning Assessment Framework
- RACE Framework for ULBs
- Karmayogi Kshamata Connect (frontline functionaries).
- AP anchors: among top-5 States on iGOT registrations; one of four States in the CBC Gram Panchayat capacity pilot (60 GPs); APHRDI, Bapatla as the State ATI.
- Global comparators the Mission studied: Singapore Civil Service College; UK Civil Service Learning. Several Caribbean countries have sought to adopt the iGOT DPI framework.
- Committee/report hooks: 2nd ARC 10th Report, ‘Refurbishing of Personnel Administration’ (2008); Surinder Nath Committee (performance appraisal); Hota Committee (2004).

Q98  |  Section-B, Q34 Explain the scope of civil service reforms in India with a brief note on Mission Karmayogi. (APPSC, 2023 — 10 Marks)

Civil service reform in India is best understood not as a set of schemes but as an intervention across the employment life cycle — recruitment, training, deployment, appraisal, accountability and exit. The case for it is structural: a service designed in 1947 for revenue collection and law and order now delivers welfare to over 80 crore people, regulates digital markets and manages climate risk. The 2nd ARC’s 10th Report, ‘Refurbishing of Personnel Administration’ (2008), framed this as the shift from an authority-centric to a citizen-centric service; Mission Karmayogi (2020) is the most consequential recent instalment.

## Scope of Civil Service Reforms — A Life-Cycle Map
- Recruitment: from rewarding recall to testing judgement.

–The introduction of CSAT (2011) and the Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude paper (GS-IV, 2013) shifted selection toward reasoning and moral judgement. The Baswan Committee (2016) reviewed the examination pattern and age/attempt limits, while the Hota Committee (2004) urged reduced entry age.

–Lateral entry brings domain specialists at Joint Secretary and Director level for fixed tenures — valuable

for technical regulation, but contested for bypassing reservation and the career stream, a tension the answer should acknowledge rather than gloss. GTraining: from episodic courses to continuous competency building. –LBSNAA, the national academies and State ATIs — including APHRDI, Bapatla — have moved to blended and role-based learning under a common national framework, ending the earlier position where each department trained to its own standard. GPerformance appraisal: from confidential opinion to evidenced assessment. –The Surinder Nath Committee recommended replacing the closed Annual Confidential Report with a disclosed, competency-based PAR; 360-degree feedback now informs empanelment. The principle is that an officer must know, and be able to contest, what is said about them. GDeployment and tenure: the reform most often ignored. –In T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013) the Supreme Court directed a fixed minimum tenure and Civil Services Boards, and held that oral instructions from political superiors should be reduced to writing. Compliance across States remains uneven — which is why capacity reforms alone under-deliver. GAccountability and integrity. –The RTI Act, 2005 opened the file to the citizen; the Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 2018 criminalised bribe-giving and set a two-year norm for trial, while inserting Section 17A (prior approval for inquiry) as a shield for honest decision-making. The Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 received assent but has not been brought into force, and the 2015 Amendment Bill lapsed — a genuine gap worth naming. GService delivery and citizen interface. –Citizens’ Charters and the Sevottam model, statutory service-guarantee laws, and digital delivery form

the outward face of reform. Andhra Pradesh’s Mana Mitra WhatsApp Governance platform, launched in January 2025 with 161 services (Government of Andhra Pradesh, ITE&C; / CDMA portals), and the Grama-Ward Sachivalayam network of secretariats delivering services within notified timelines, are the State’s working examples.

## II. Brief Note on Mission Karmayogi (NPCSCB, 2020)
- What it is: a Central Sector Scheme of the DoPT, approved on 2 September 2020, covering about 46 lakh Central Government employees at ₹510.86 crore over five years, since extended to States and UTs (PIB, 2 September 2020).
- Its core shift: rule-based to role-based functioning, operationalised through FRAC (Functions–Roles–Activities–Competencies) and the Karmayogi Competency Model, so that training is matched to the post rather than to seniority.
- Its delivery: the iGOT Karmayogi platform — 1.5 crore+ registered learners, 8 crore+ course completions and 4,600+ courses, with MoUs signed with 28 States/UTs (PIB, 4 April 2026). Andhra Pradesh ranks among the top five States by registrations (PIB, 20 May 2025).
- Its institutions: PM-led Public Human Resources Council (apex approval), Capacity Building Commission (2021) for standards and supervision over Central Training Institutions, and Karmayogi Bharat SPV (2022) to run the platform.

## III. The Unfinished Agenda
- **Reform Frontier** — Present Position · What Remains
- **Tenure security** — Court-directed CSBs exist on paper · Statutory fixed tenure; oral orders recorded in writing
- **Whistle-blower cover** — 2014 Act un-notified; 2015 Bill lapsed · Bring the Act into force with anonymity safeguards
- **Right to Services** — State laws only (e.g. Karnataka Sakala, 2011) · A national service-guarantee framework with compensation

- **Reform Frontier** — Present Position · What Remains
- **Performance exit** — FR 56(j) periodic review · Objective, contestable criteria to avoid misuse

## Conclusion

The scope of civil service reform therefore runs from the examination hall to the exit interview, and its Indian record is uneven — strong on recruitment, training and transparency, weak precisely where political cost is highest, namely tenure security, whistle-blower protection and performance-linked exit. Mission Karmayogi has convincingly closed the capacity gap; the accountability gap remains. Article 311’s protections were designed to secure fearless advice, not to shield non-performance, and a mature reform agenda must honour both halves of that bargain if the services are to remain, in Sardar Patel’s phrase, the steel frame of a democratic and citizen-centric State.

- Committee ladder (memorise in order): Santhanam Committee (1964, corruption) → Surinder Nath Committee (performance appraisal) → Hota Committee (2004) → 2nd ARC 10th Report, ‘Refurbishing of Personnel Administration’ (2008) → Baswan Committee (2016, exam pattern).
- Case law: T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013) — fixed minimum tenure, Civil Services Boards, oral instructions to be recorded; Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006) — the parallel directions for police insulation.
- Legal instruments: RTI Act, 2005; Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 2018 (bribe-giving criminalised; Section 17A prior approval; two-year trial norm); Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013; FR 56(j) periodic review; Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 — not yet in force.
- 2nd ARC’s draft Public Service Bill values: allegiance to the Preamble, apolitical functioning, objectivity and impartiality, accountability and transparency, merit in selection, economy in expenditure.
- AP anchors: APHRDI, Bapatla (State ATI); Mana Mitra WhatsApp Governance (January 2025, 161 services); Grama-Ward Sachivalayam network; Real Time Governance Society (RTGS), 2017; Swarna Andhra@2047 vision plan and the P4 (Public–Private–People Partnership) model.
- Sharp closing line for any civil-services question: reform must move the service from ‘authority-centric’ to ‘citizen-centric’ — the 2nd ARC’s own formulation.

Q99  |  Section-B, Q35 What are the reasons for the decline of integrity in civil services? Also, discuss the institutional mechanisms to check corruption in India. (APPSC, 2023 — 10 Marks)

Integrity in public service means more than staying inside the rules; it is conduct that would withstand disclosure even where no rule has been broken. Its erosion in Indian administration is rarely a matter of individual venality alone — it is produced by systems that concentrate discretion, obscure decisions and impose no cost for delay. The Santhanam Committee (1964) warned that deteriorating standards in public life would outlast any single scandal, and the 2nd ARC’s ‘Ethics in Governance’ Report (2007) reached the same conclusion: India’s problem is less a shortage of anti-corruption agencies than an abundance of corruption-prone processes.

## Why Integrity Declines — Four Causal Layers
- Structural: wide discretion joined to low visibility.

–Where an official can grant or withhold a licence, mutation or clearance without a recorded reason, rent extraction becomes possible without rule-breaking. The 2nd ARC identified reducing discretion, simplifying transactions and promoting competition as the primary antidote — corruption is designed out of a process more reliably than it is policed out of a person.

–Illustration: land records and building approvals remain the highest-friction interfaces in most States,

which is precisely why SVAMITVA titling and online single-window building permissions are anti-corruption measures, not merely convenience measures. GInstitutional: tenure insecurity and toothless appraisal. –An officer who can be transferred at will has every incentive to accommodate and none to resist. The Supreme Court in T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013) directed fixed minimum tenure and Civil Services Boards precisely because arbitrary transfer is the cheapest instrument of pressure available to a political superior. –Seniority-driven promotion compounds this: where the honest and the compliant advance at the same pace, integrity becomes a private preference rather than a career strategy. GSocietal and political economy. –The cost of contesting elections, the demand for patronage postings, and public tolerance of ‘speed money’ all transmit pressure downward into the administration. The 2nd ARC treated ethics in politics as logically prior to ethics in administration for this reason. GEthical preparation: procedure taught, judgement not. –Training long emphasised rules over reasoning, leaving officers unequipped for genuine dilemmas —

tribal displacement against project timelines, for instance. Mandatory ethics modules on iGOT Karmayogi are the corrective, though their behavioural effect is not yet independently measured.

## II. Institutional Mechanisms to Check Corruption — Four Layers
- **Layer** — Institution & Legal Basis · Core Function & Limitation
- **Preventive** — Central Vigilance Commission — created by executive resolution in February 1964 on the Santhanam Committee’s recommendation; made statutory by the CVC Act, 2003 · Supervises vigilance administration and CVOs; advisory jurisdiction only — it recommends, it cannot punish
- **Investigative** — CBI — Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946; Enforcement Directorate — PMLA, 2002 · Investigates major corruption; requires State consent under Section 6, and faces chronic sanction and case-load delays
- **Ombudsman** — Lokpal — Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013; operational from March 2019, Foundation Day 16 January · Inquires into complaints against public functionaries including the PM (with exclusions); has an Inquiry Wing and a Prosecution Wing
- **Substantive law** — Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, as amended in 2018 · Criminalises bribe-giving; Section 17A requires prior approval before inquiry; two-year norm for trial
- **Audit & Adjudication** — CAG (Articles 148–151); Special Courts under the PC Act; judiciary through PILs · Detects financial irregularity ex post; conviction rates remain the weak point
- **Citizen-led** — RTI Act, 2005; social audit under MGNREGA Section 17; CPGRAMS · Converts citizens into auditors; depends on record quality and freedom from intimidation

- The Andhra Pradesh layer — essential for APPSC.

–The Institution of Lokayukta was set up under the A.P. Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayuktas Act, 1983 (in force from 1 November 1983), with the Lokayukta appointed by the Governor after consultation with the Chief Minister, Speaker, Leaders of Opposition in both Houses and the Chairman of the Legislative Council. –The State’s Vigilance and Enforcement Department and the Anti-Corruption Bureau handle preventive checks and trap cases, while the Public Grievance Redressal System (PGRS), run by the Real Time Governance Society, provides a tracked complaint channel — grievance redress and anti-corruption reinforcing each other.

## III. Why the Machinery Under-Delivers
- Sanction and delay: prosecution requires clearances at multiple stages; DoPT introduced a Single Window System in 2014 and additional Special Courts were sanctioned to compress timelines, yet the interval between detection and conviction remains the system’s weakest link (PIB, DoPT replies).
- Protection gaps: the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 has not been brought into force and the 2015 Amendment Bill lapsed, leaving disclosure informal and risky — the case of officers facing repeated punitive transfers after exposing irregularities illustrates the cost.
- Capacity and vacancies: anti-corruption bodies depend on timely appointments and specialist skills in forensic accounting and cyber investigation, which the Lokpal itself has identified as a recruitment priority.

## Conclusion

The decline of integrity is therefore a systems failure before it is a moral one: discretion without record, tenure without security, and disclosure without protection together make dishonesty rational and honesty expensive. India’s institutional response — CVC, CBI, Lokpal and Lokayuktas, the amended Prevention of Corruption Act, CAG and RTI — is architecturally complete but operationally slow. The 2nd ARC’s decisive insight remains the way forward: reduce discretion, digitise transactions, publish decisions and protect the honest officer, so that integrity ceases to require courage and becomes simply the path of least resistance.

- CBI — the three judgments to cite: Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997) — selection by a high-powered committee and a fixed two-year tenure for the Director; Subramanian Swamy v. Director, CBI (2014) — struck down Section 6A of the DSPE Act, removing prior approval for investigating senior officials; Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) — upheld the selection committee of PM, Leader of Opposition and CJI (or nominee).
- Statutory timeline: PC Act, 1988 → CVC Act, 2003 (statutory status) → Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 → Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 (not in force) → PC (Amendment) Act, 2018 → Lokpal operational, March 2019.
- Key 2nd ARC ‘Ethics in Governance’ recommendations: bring State Anti-Corruption Bureaus under the State Vigilance Commission; a Code of Ethics distinct from Conduct Rules; integrity pacts in procurement; confiscation of illegally acquired property; partial funding of elections.
- Constitutional and institutional handles: Article 311 (protection in dismissal/removal) — a safeguard for fearless advice, not a shield for misconduct; Articles 148–151 (CAG); All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968 and CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964.
- AP anchors: A.P. Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayuktas Act, 1983; Vigilance and Enforcement Department; Anti-Corruption Bureau; PGRS under the Real Time Governance Society.
- Preventive-vigilance vocabulary that impresses evaluators: integrity pacts, risk-based vigilance, systemic improvement measures, e-procurement, decision-mapping. The CVC’s annual Vigilance Awareness Week (in the week of Sardar Patel’s birth anniversary) is anchored on a three-month preventive-vigilance campaign — the 2024 theme was ‘Culture of Integrity for Nation’s Prosperity’.

Q100  |  Section-B, Q36 Define good governance. How does the Right to Information (RTI) Act promote the principles of good governance in India? (APPSC, 2025 — 10 Marks)

Good governance is the exercise of public authority in a manner that is transparent, accountable, participatory and responsive. UNESCAP identifies eight characteristics — participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, consensus orientation, equity and inclusiveness, effectiveness and efficiency, and accountability — while the 2nd ARC defines governance as the exercise of power in managing a country’s economic and social resources for development. The Right to Information Act, 2005 is India’s principal statutory instrument for realising these characteristics, because it converts transparency from an administrative courtesy into an enforceable citizen entitlement.

## RTI’s Constitutional Foundation — A Right Codified, Not Created
- The Supreme Court read the right to know into the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) long before the Act: in State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975) it held that the people are entitled to know what their government does, and in Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) it required electoral candidates to disclose assets, liabilities, education and criminal antecedents.

–Why an Act was still necessary: a fundamental right binds the State but supplies no machinery. The RTI

Act furnishes what the Constitution could not — PIOs, a 30-day deadline, an appellate hierarchy, penalties up to ₹25,000 on a PIO, and independent Information Commissions. Rights need plumbing. GThe Act emerged from a grassroots campaign — the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan’s jan sunwais in Rajasthan demanding muster rolls — which is why it is properly described as legislation demanded from below rather than conferred from above.

## II. Mapping RTI to the Principles of Good Governance
- **Principle** — RTI Mechanism · Illustration / Evidence
- **Transparency** — Section 4 mandatory proactive (suo motu) disclosure of 17 categories; Section 3 right of access · Budgets, beneficiary lists and norms of subsidy must be published without any application being filed
- **Accountability** — Section 20 penalty on the PIO; Section 19 two-tier appeal · The official who withholds information faces personal, not institutional, liability
- **Rule of law** — Section 8 exemptions are exhaustive; Section 8(2) public-interest override · CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011) upheld student access to evaluated answer scripts, narrowing the ‘fiduciary relationship’ exemption
- **Participation** — Citizen-initiated access without locus standi · Gram Sabhas have used RTI to obtain muster rolls and works estimates before social audits
- **Equity & inclusiveness** — Fee waiver for BPL applicants; Section 6(1) oral requests assisted by the PIO · Entitlement claims under PDS and MGNREGA by applicants who cannot draft a formal request
- **Effectiveness** — 30-day limit; 48 hours where life or liberty is involved · Converts a discretionary favour into a time-bound obligation

## III. Performance and Present Strain
- The system works better than it is credited for on refusals.

–The rejection rate for RTI applications fell to 3.26% in 2024–25 from 7.21% in 2013–14 (DoPT reply in

Parliament, PIB, February 2026) — evidence that disclosure has become the administrative default rather than the exception. GBut delay at the appellate stage blunts the remedy. –As on 1 February 2026, 29,034 second appeals and 3,577 complaints were pending before the Central Information Commission (PIB, February 2026). The Act sets no time limit for disposal of a second appeal — the single most consequential drafting gap. Information delayed past the decision it was sought to influence is information denied. –Compounding this, Section 12(2) permits up to ten Information Commissioners besides the Chief; the Commission has functioned well below that strength, and DoPT advertised for up to eight Commissioners in August 2024 (PIB, December 2024). GInstitutional independence was diluted in 2019. –The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019, read with the RTI Rules, 2019, replaced the fixed five-year term of the CIC and Information Commissioners with a term prescribed by the Central Government (notified as three years) and shifted salary-setting to the executive — removing the earlier statutory parity with the Chief Election Commissioner. GThe most consequential current change — Section 8(1)(j). –Section 44(3) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 substituted Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act,

exempting personal information as a category. The Government’s position is that this codifies existing judicial reasoning after Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India and that Section 8(2)’s public-interest override survives (PIB, Ministry of Electronics and IT, 2025). Critics argue the express ‘larger public interest’ test within Section 8(1)(j) itself has gone. With the DPDP Rules, 2025 notified on 14 November 2025, the amendment is now fully operational — the live constitutional question of transparency versus privacy, and a near-certain examination theme.

## IV. The Andhra Pradesh Dimension
- The Andhra Pradesh Information Commission functions as the State-level appellate authority under Section 15, covering State departments, panchayats and municipalities.
- Transparency is increasingly delivered without an application being filed: the State’s Mana Mitra WhatsApp Governance platform (January 2025, 161 services) and the Public Grievance Redressal System run by the Real Time Governance Society allow citizens to obtain certificates and track complaints directly — the logical extension of Section 4’s proactive-disclosure philosophy into service delivery.

## Conclusion

The RTI Act advances good governance because it relocates the burden of justification: the State must now explain its silence, rather than the citizen justify her curiosity. Measured against UNESCAP’s characteristics, it has strengthened transparency, accountability and participation, and its falling rejection rate suggests genuine cultural change within the bureaucracy. Its unfinished tasks are equally clear — a statutory deadline for second appeals, full-strength Information Commissions, restored independence in tenure and salary, and a principled reconciliation of the new privacy regime with the public-interest override. The 2nd ARC’s prescriptions point the way: an oath of transparency in place of the oath of secrecy, professional Public Records Offices, and a single portal for all suo motu disclosures — because the truest measure of the Act is not how many applications are filed, but how few need to be.

- UNESCAP’s eight characteristics of good governance — participation; rule of law; transparency; responsiveness; consensus orientation; equity and inclusiveness; effectiveness and efficiency; accountability. (Consensus orientation is the one most students forget.)
- Judicial line on the right to know: State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975) → S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) → Union of India v. ADR (2002) → CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011) → Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), which supplies the privacy counterweight.
- Structural provisions worth naming precisely: Section 4 (suo motu disclosure), Section 6 (request), Section 7 (30 days; 48 hours for life and liberty), Section 8 (exemptions), Section 8(2) (public-interest override), Section 19 (appeals), Section 20 (penalty up to ₹25,000), Section 24 with the Second Schedule (exempt organisations), Section 22 (overriding effect).
- Current data to quote: CIC pendency — 29,034 second appeals and 3,577 complaints as on 1 February 2026; rejection rate down to 3.26% in 2024–25 from 7.21% in 2013–14 (PIB/DoPT, February 2026).
- Legislative timeline: RTI Act, 2005 → RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 with RTI Rules, 2019 (tenure and salary to the executive) → DPDP Act, 2023, Section 44(3) amending Section 8(1)(j) → DPDP Rules notified 14 November 2025 (18-month phased compliance).
- 2nd ARC, First Report — ‘Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance’ (2006): substitute an oath of transparency for the oath of secrecy (amend Articles 75(4) and 164(3) and the Third Schedule); establish independent Public Records Offices under CIC/SIC supervision; a single NIC portal for all suo motu disclosures; include the Armed Forces in the Second Schedule with PIOs in all exempt organisations.
- AP anchors: Andhra Pradesh Information Commission; Mana Mitra WhatsApp Governance (161 services, January 2025); PGRS under the Real Time Governance Society, 2017; Mee Seva as the State’s single-window G2C precursor.

Q101  |  Section-B, Q37 Decentralisation is a necessary tool for good governance. Elaborate. (TGPSC, 2024 — 10 Marks)

Decentralisation is the transfer of authority, functionaries and finances from higher to lower tiers of government, and it operates in three dimensions — political (elected local bodies), administrative (functionaries answerable locally) and fiscal (assured funds and own-source revenue). The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) gave this constitutional form through Parts IX and IX-A, the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules and mandatory five-yearly elections under Articles 243E and 243K. The claim that it is necessary for good governance rests on a simple proposition: no distant authority can possess the local knowledge, or face the local accountability, that responsive government requires.

## How Decentralisation Delivers the Principles of Good Governance
- Participation — governance with a quorum of citizens, not merely of officials.

–The Gram Sabha is the only body in the Indian constitutional scheme where every adult voter is a member with a right to be heard; under PESA, 1996 it acquires powers over minor forest produce, land alienation and dispute resolution in Scheduled Areas.

–Andhra Pradesh’s Grama-Ward Sachivalayam system operationalises this: a secretariat for roughly every

2,000 households, staffed by functionaries of the local government and answerable to the Gram Panchayat, delivering notified services within fixed timelines (Government of Andhra Pradesh, GSWS Department). GTransparency and accountability — shorter feedback loops, digitally reinforced. –eGramSwaraj publishes plans, accounts and payments; integrated with PFMS, it enables real-time vendor payment. In FY 2025–26, as on 11 March 2026, 2,54,604 Gram Panchayats (96.36% of 2,64,211) had uploaded their Gram Panchayat Development Plans, and 2,42,871 (91.92%) had routed ₹38,491 crore through the eGramSwaraj–PFMS interface (PIB, Ministry of Panchayati Raj, March 2026). –Why this is more than a statistic: a published GPDP converts the sarpanch’s discretion into a document the village can read — the precondition for a meaningful social audit. GEffectiveness — decisions taken where the information is. –SVAMITVA uses drone and GIS survey to issue property cards in inhabited village areas, reducing title disputes and giving panchayats a defensible property-tax base — simultaneously a rights measure, a revenue measure and a conflict-reduction measure. GRule of law — the courts as guarantor of local democracy. –In Kishan Singh Tomar v. Municipal Corporation of the City of Ahmedabad (2006) the Supreme Court held that State Election Commissions must ensure municipal elections are held before the expiry of the five-year term, and that financial or administrative difficulty is no excuse — directly addressing the commonest method of hollowing out local government, namely simply not holding elections. –In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021) the Court struck down Part IX-B of the Constitution insofar as

it applied to co-operative societies within States, for want of ratification under the proviso to Article 368(2) — affirming that the federal-local architecture cannot be altered by ordinary majority.

## II. Fiscal Decentralisation — The Decisive Test
- The 16th Finance Commission (Chair: Dr Arvind Panagariya), whose award period runs from 1 April 2026 to 2030–31, made the largest local-body award yet.
- **Component** — Rural Local Bodies · Urban Local Bodies
- **Total grant, 2026–31** — ₹4,35,236 crore · ₹3,56,257 crore
- **Basic grant** — ₹3,48,188 crore — split equally tied / untied · Basic plus performance structure, with a raised urban share
- **Performance grants** — ₹43,524 cr (RLB) + ₹43,524 cr (State) — entirely untied · Performance component linked to own-source revenue effort
- **Tied purpose** — Sanitation and solid waste management, and/or water management, including O&M; · Same service priorities, reflecting urban service deficits

- Two shifts matter. The urban share of local-body grants rises to about 45%, recognising that service-delivery costs are concentrating in cities; and the Commission expressly insists that Union grants supplement, not substitute, State transfers, placing primary responsibility on States (16th Finance Commission Report, 2026–31; PIB, March 2026).
- The Commission also delivered a pointed criticism: many States fail to constitute State Finance Commissions in time, and their reports lack uniformity in approach, period covered and data quality — so much so that the Commission found them unusable for framing its recommendations (16th FC Report, paras 2.27 and 10.4). Article 243-I is being observed in form, not in substance.

## III. Where Indian Decentralisation Falls Short
- Devolution has improved, but slowly. The Ministry of Panchayati Raj’s report ‘Status of Devolution to Panchayats in States — An Indicative Evidence-Based Ranking, 2024’ (released 13 February 2025, prepared by IIPA) records overall devolution rising from 39.9% to 43.9% between 2013–14 and 2021–22

— after three decades, still under half.

- Andhra Pradesh’s position, which the answer must name: AP falls in the ‘medium scoring’ band with a Devolution Index score between 50 and 55, alongside Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha, below the top-ten group led by Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu (PIB, 13 February 2025). The State’s strength lies in service delivery through secretariats; its headroom lies in functional and fiscal devolution to elected panchayats themselves.
- Capacity remains the quiet constraint. The Capacity Building Commission has begun extending Mission Karmayogi to panchayats through a pilot in 60 Gram Panchayats across four States — Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Gujarat and Odisha — with 14 learning modules developed in 2025 (PIB, CBC Year End Review, December 2025). Devolving functions to untrained functionaries devolves failure.
- Parallel bodies dilute the elected tier: line-department societies and mission-mode structures often bypass panchayats, so functions listed in the Eleventh Schedule are exercised by agencies the Gram Sabha cannot question.

## Conclusion

Decentralisation is necessary for good governance because participation, responsiveness and accountability are all functions of proximity — no centralised apparatus can substitute for a villager’s knowledge of which handpump has failed, or for her ability to confront the person responsible. India has built the political tier convincingly and, with the 16th Finance Commission’s record award and digital platforms like eGramSwaraj and SVAMITVA, is strengthening the fiscal and transparency tiers. What remains is the hardest part: transferring functionaries along with functions, constituting State Finance Commissions on time and acting on them, building panchayat-level capacity, and dismantling the parallel bodies that hollow out the elected tier. Decentralisation is necessary; on the present evidence, it is not yet sufficient.

- Panchayat Devolution Index 2024 — correct Top 10 (DI score above 55), in order: Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Tripura, Rajasthan, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh. Medium band (50–55): ANDHRA PRADESH, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha. (The booklet’s list omits Karnataka, the top-ranked State.)
- Six dimensions of the Devolution Index: Framework, Functions, Finances, Functionaries, Capacity Enhancement, Accountability. Dimensional leaders — Kerala (Framework), Tamil Nadu (Functions), Karnataka (Finances and Accountability), Gujarat (Functionaries), Telangana (Capacity Enhancement). Notable movers: Uttar Pradesh 15th → 5th; Tripura 13th → 7th.
- Headline devolution data: 39.9% → 43.9% between 2013–14 and 2021–22; capacity enhancement 44% → 54.6% after RGSA (launched 21 April 2018); functionaries 39.6% → 50.9% (PIB, February 2025).
- 16th Finance Commission, 2026–31: ₹4,35,236 crore for RLBs and ₹3,56,257 crore for ULBs; urban share raised to about 45%; performance component fully untied; tied component for sanitation/solid waste and water; grants to supplement, not substitute, State transfers; sharp criticism of States’ failure to constitute and act on State Finance Commissions (Article 243-I).
- Constitutional articles to cite precisely: 243B (constitution of panchayats), 243D (reservations), 243E (five-year duration), 243G (powers, Eleventh Schedule), 243H (taxation powers), 243-I (State Finance Commission), 243K (State Election Commission), 243ZD (District Planning Committee), 243ZE (Metropolitan Planning Committee); PESA, 1996 for Fifth Schedule areas.
- Case law: Kishan Singh Tomar v. Municipal Corporation, Ahmedabad (2006) — timely local elections are mandatory; Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021) — Part IX-B struck down for want of State ratification under Article 368(2).
