Q102  |  Section-B, Q38 What are the different dimensions of governance? Briefly explain the administrative dimension of governance and its key components. (APPSC, 2023 — 10 Marks)

Governance is the process by which authority is exercised and decisions are made and implemented; the Second Administrative Reforms Commission describes it as the exercise of power in managing a country’s economic and social resources for development, while the World Bank frames it around accountability, rule of law and transparency. Because power is exercised in several arenas at once, governance is inherently multi-dimensional — political, economic, social, legal, environmental and administrative. Of these, the administrative dimension is pivotal, since it is the only one the citizen actually meets: a policy is, for its beneficiary, whatever the office window delivers.

## The Dimensions of Governance
- **Dimension** — Core Concern · Illustrative Instrument
- **Political** — Democratic legitimacy, electoral integrity, rule of law · Election Commission under Article 324; anti-defection under the Tenth Schedule

- **Dimension** — Core Concern · Illustrative Instrument
- **Economic** — Resource allocation, fiscal discipline, inclusive growth · FRBM Act, 2003; Finance Commission awards under Article 280
- **Social** — Equity, social justice, human development · Right to Education Act, 2009; National Food Security Act, 2013
- **Legal** — Access to justice, rights enforcement, procedural fairness · Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987; BNS/BNSS/BSA, 2023 in force from 1 July 2024
- **Environmental** — Sustainability, climate resilience, intergenerational equity · Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; India’s Net-Zero-by-2070 commitment; SDG-13
- **Administrative** — Implementation, service delivery, accountability of the executive · RTI Act, 2005; Citizens’ Charters and Sevottam; Mission Karmayogi

## II. The Administrative Dimension — Key Components
- 1. Policy implementation — converting statute into entitlement.

–The administrative machinery is what turns a legislative promise into a delivered good: Jal Jeevan Mission

into a functional household tap, PM Awas Yojana into a completed house. Failure here is invisible in the statute book and total in the household. G2. Efficiency and service delivery — measured in citizen time, not files cleared. –Digital delivery has compressed transaction costs — DigiLocker and UMANG at the Union level; in Andhra Pradesh, Mana Mitra WhatsApp Governance (January 2025) offers 161 services through a chat interface, and the Grama-Ward Sachivalayam network places a service point within roughly 2,000 households (Government of Andhra Pradesh). G3. Accountability and transparency — the citizen as auditor. –The RTI Act, 2005, statutory social audit under Section 17 of MGNREGA, and CAG audit under Articles 148–151 together create ex-ante and ex-post checks. In Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) the Supreme Court treated disclosure as integral to the citizen’s ability to hold power to account. G4. Responsiveness and grievance redress — the true test of administrative quality. –Comprehensive Guidelines issued on 23 August 2024 compressed the CPGRAMS redress timeline from 30 days to 21 days, with appeals in 30 days. In 2024–25, average disposal time was 15 days for Central Ministries but 64 days for States and UTs — a gap that identifies precisely where the citizen still waits (PIB, DoPT, February 2026). –Performance is now measured, not merely asserted: the Grievance Redressal Assessment and Index (GRAI) ranks Ministries on eleven indicators, including resolution within timeline and satisfaction with the outcome. G5. Rule of law and ethical administration — neutrality as a professional obligation. –Civil servants are expected to act impartially and to record reasons. In Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006) the Court issued binding directions — State Security Commissions, fixed two-year tenure for the DGP and key field officers, separation of investigation from law and order — to insulate administration from political direction. G6. Capacity building and administrative reform — the enabling condition. –The 2nd ARC’s 12th Report, ‘Citizen Centric Administration: The Heart of Governance’ (2009),

recommended the Sevottam model of service-delivery excellence and enforceable Citizens’ Charters. Mission Karmayogi operationalises the capacity half: 1.5 crore+ learners and 8 crore+ course completions on iGOT Karmayogi (PIB, April 2026), with 27,854 State/UT officials trained under Sevottam across 2022–25 (PIB, February 2026).

## III. Current Vectors Strengthening Administrative Governance
- Outcome-focused, area-based administration: the Aspirational Districts Programme (2018, 112 districts, 49 KPIs across five themes) and the Aspirational Blocks Programme (2023, extended to 513 blocks in

2025) rank on ‘delta’ — the pace of a district’s own improvement rather than its absolute standing — which is why weak districts compete instead of despairing. Sampoornata Abhiyan 2.0 (28 January to 14 April 2026) drives saturation of five KPIs in districts and six in blocks (PIB, NITI Aayog, January 2026).

- Real-time and data-driven administration: in Andhra Pradesh, the Real Time Governance Society (2017) integrates dashboards, CCTV surveillance of public works and the Public Grievance Redressal System, while Swarna Andhra@2047 and its P4 (Public–Private–People Partnership) model, including the Zero Poverty P4 initiative, frame the State’s administrative agenda (Government of Andhra Pradesh, Planning Department).
- Leakage control: the JAM trinity and Direct Benefit Transfer have shifted the administrative task from discretionary distribution to verified transfer — removing the intermediary is itself an administrative reform.

## Conclusion

The dimensions of governance are analytically separable but operationally interdependent: political legitimacy sets the mandate, economic and social policy set the priorities, law sets the limits, and administration determines whether any of it reaches the citizen. That is why the administrative dimension is the heart of governance, in the 2nd ARC’s phrase — it converts intent into outcome. As Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) held in reading the right to livelihood into Article 21 and requiring fair procedure before eviction, administrative efficiency can never be pursued at the cost of dignity or due process. A professional, transparent and capacitated administration, held accountable through RTI, social audit and measured grievance redress, is therefore not merely an instrument of good governance but its precondition.

- Definitional anchors: 2nd ARC — governance is the exercise of power in managing a country’s economic and social resources for development; World Bank (1992) — the manner in which power is exercised in managing a country’s resources; UNESCAP’s eight characteristics; UNDP’s framing of governance as the exercise of political, economic and administrative authority.
- 2nd ARC reports most quotable here: 1st — Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance (2006); 4th — Ethics in Governance (2007); 10th — Refurbishing of Personnel Administration (2008); 11th — Promoting e-Governance: The SMART Way Forward (2008); 12th — Citizen Centric Administration: The Heart of Governance (2009), which is the direct authority for this answer.
- SMART governance (from the 11th Report) — Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent. A one-line framework that fits almost any governance question.
- Current data to quote: CPGRAMS timeline cut from 30 to 21 days by guidelines of 23 August 2024; average disposal 15 days (Centre) against 64 days (States/UTs) in 2024–25; GRAI ranks Ministries on 11 indicators; 27,854 State/UT officials trained under Sevottam, 2022–25 (PIB, February 2026).
- Aspirational programmes: ADP (January 2018) — 112 districts, 49 KPIs, five themes (health and nutrition; education; agriculture and water; financial inclusion and skills; infrastructure); ABP (2023) — 500 blocks, raised to 513 in 2025; Champions of Change dashboard; delta ranking; Sampoornata Abhiyan 2.0 (28 January – 14 April 2026).
- Case law: Union of India v. ADR (2002) — disclosure and accountability; Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006) — insulating administration from political control; Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) — right to livelihood under Article 21 and fair procedure before eviction.

Q103   Discuss the significance of integrity, transparency, and accountability in leadership. How can public leaders demonstrate these values in their decision-making process? (APPSC, 2025)

Integrity, transparency and accountability form the operating triad of ethical public leadership. Integrity supplies the motive, transparency the visibility and accountability the consequence - each is incomplete without the other two. In Indian constitutional terms they give practical content to Article 14's bar on arbitrariness and to the doctrine of constitutional morality invoked in Manoj Narula v. Union of India (2014). Leadership that embodies them converts formal authority into legitimate authority.

1. Integrity: consistency between office and conduct

- Integrity means the public leader's decisions are traceable to the public interest alone. It is enforced, not merely exhorted: Rule 3 of the CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964 mandates absolute integrity and devotion to duty, and annual Immovable Property Returns place assets in the public domain.
- The Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 2018 sharpened this by criminalising bribe-giving and introducing Section 17A prior-approval - simultaneously protecting honest risk-taking and penalising venality, a balance the 2nd ARC's Ethics in Governance report had urged.
- Illustration: E. Sreedharan delivered the Delhi Metro on schedule and within cost, and made resignation-on-failure a personal norm - demonstrating that integrity is an operational asset, not a cost.

2. Transparency: decisions open to scrutiny

- Transparency substitutes reasoned disclosure for bureaucratic secrecy, thereby reducing rumour and discretion-shopping. Section 4 of the RTI Act, 2005 makes proactive, suo motu disclosure a duty, not a favour granted on request.
- Evidence that the culture is shifting: rejection of RTI applications by central public authorities fell to 3.26% in 2024-25 from 7.21% in 2013-14 (PIB, Ministry of Personnel, February 2026).

3. Accountability: answerability plus consequence

- Accountability is answerability backed by enforceable consequence. The CAG under Articles 148-151, examined by the Public Accounts Committee, supplies the external audit loop - as in the 2G Spectrum and Coal Block allocation reports.
- Citizen-facing accountability is now measurable: CPGRAMS recorded 1,88,969 grievances redressed by Central Ministries/Departments in April 2026 with an average disposal time of 13 days (DARPG, PIB, May 2026), down from 16 days in April 2025.

## Demonstrating the values in the decision-making process
- **Value** — Observable behaviour in decision-making · Instrument
- **Integrity** — Declare interest and recuse; refuse post-retirement conflicts · CCS Conduct Rules 1964; IPR disclosure
- **Transparency** — Record reasons on file; publish criteria before allotment; open data dashboards · RTI Sec. 4; e-Office
- **Accountability** — Set published targets; submit to audit and citizen feedback · CAG; social audit under MGNREGA Sec. 17

## Andhra Pradesh anchor
- AP institutionalises the triad through technology: the Real Time Governance Society (RTGS) runs live departmental dashboards, while Mana Mitra WhatsApp Governance (Govt. of AP, launched 30 January 2025) delivers certificates and grievance filing without an office visit - removing the discretionary counter where rent-seeking occurs.
- On integrity, the AP Anti-Corruption Bureau's toll-free 14400 helpline and 'ACB 14400' mobile app (acb.ap.gov.in) accept complaints with assured confidentiality of the complainant's identity.

## Conclusion

The three values are not parallel virtues but a single chain: integrity without transparency is unverifiable, transparency without accountability is merely informative, and accountability without integrity degenerates into procedural defensiveness. Public leaders demonstrate them less through declarations than through the ordinary discipline of recording reasons, declaring interests and submitting to audit. This is precisely what SDG Target 16.6 - effective, accountable and transparent institutions at all levels - asks of states, and what constitutional morality asks of every holder of public office in India.

- Nolan Committee's Seven Principles of Public Life (UK, 1995): selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership - the 2nd ARC drew on these for its Code of Ethics proposal.
- UN Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC), 2003 - adopted 31 October 2003, in force 2005; India ratified it in May 2011, binding it to Article 5 (preventive anti-corruption policies) and Article 8 (codes of conduct for public officials).
- SDG 16: Target 16.5 (substantially reduce corruption and bribery) and Target 16.6 (effective, accountable, transparent institutions) - quotable for any governance-ethics question.
- Case law: Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997) gave the CVC statutory footing and insulated investigative agencies; Manoj Narula v. Union of India (2014) developed constitutional morality as a standard for holders of public office.
- Institutional map worth memorising: CVC (statutory, 2003 Act) - preventive vigilance; Lokpal (2013 Act) -inquiry into public functionaries; CAG (Art. 148) - financial accountability; CIC/SIC (RTI 2005) - informational accountability.
- AP specifics: RTGS dashboards; Mana Mitra WhatsApp Governance; ACB toll-free 14400 and 'ACB 14400' app; AP Vigilance and Enforcement Department.

Q104   Whistle blowers are guardians of ethical accountability in governance. Discuss the ethical and institutional importance of whistle-blower protection in ensuring integrity in public service. (APPSC, 2025)

A whistleblower is an insider who discloses evidence of corruption, wilful misuse of power or danger to the public, through authorised channels, at personal risk. The description 'guardians of ethical accountability' is apt because ordinary oversight - audit, inspection, vigilance - reaches only what the record reveals; the whistleblower reaches what the record conceals. India recognises the value but, two decades after the Law Commission's 179th Report, still lacks an operative protection statute.

## Ethical importance
- Fiduciary duty over institutional loyalty: the public servant's ultimate obligation runs to the citizen, not the department. Whistleblowing resolves this dilemma in favour of the public, converting private knowledge into public accountability.
- Moral courage under asymmetric risk: Satyendra Dubey, an NHAI project director, exposed contract irregularities on the Golden Quadrilateral and was murdered in 2003; S. Manjunath, an IOC sales officer, was killed in 2005 for sealing a fuel outlet adulterating petrol. Both feature in the 2nd ARC's Ethics in Governance report as the human cost of an unprotected regime.
- Preventive ethical effect: credible protection changes the calculus for the potential wrongdoer, who must now assume any colleague may report. This deterrent operates before the loss occurs, unlike audit which operates after.

## Institutional importance - and the current Indian gap
- The statutory position must be stated precisely. The Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 (No. 17 of 2014) received assent on 9 May 2014 and was published in the Gazette on 12 May 2014, but under Section 1(3) it commences only on a date notified by the Central Government - and NO such notification has ever been issued. The Whistle Blowers Protection (Amendment) Bill, 2015, passed by the Lok Sabha on 13 May 2015, lapsed with the dissolution of the Sixteenth Lok Sabha (PIB, Ministry of Personnel, 11 December 2025).
- The live mechanism is therefore the Public Interest Disclosure and Protection of Informers (PIDPI) Resolution, 2004, under which the Central Vigilance Commission is the Designated Agency for disclosures against central government employees and CPSE/PSB staff.
- Rising usage evidences latent demand for protection, and that even a non-statutory channel can work if it is trusted:
- **Year** — PIDPI complaints (received + brought forward) · Disposed
- **2020** — 555 · 520
- **2022** — 1,907 · 1,887
- **2024** — 2,630 · 2,521

Source: Central Vigilance Commission data placed in Parliament, PIB, 11 December 2025.

- Sectoral protection already exists outside government: Section 177(9)-(10) of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates a vigil mechanism in listed companies; SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 require whistleblower policies; the RBI operates a Protected Disclosures Scheme for private and foreign banks. The anomaly is that the public sector - the very domain of the 2014 Act - is least protected.

## Balancing considerations
- Protection cannot be unconditional. PIDPI excludes anonymous complaints because unverifiable allegations enable score-settling; but insistence on identity is precisely what deters genuine disclosure - an unresolved tension. The Official Secrets Act, 1923 also overhangs disclosure; the 2nd ARC recommended its repeal and substitution by a chapter in the National Security Act.

## Andhra Pradesh anchor
- AP's Anti-Corruption Bureau runs a toll-free 14400 helpline and the 'ACB 14400' mobile app (acb.ap.gov.in), which accept complaints on assured confidentiality of identity - a state-level approximation of protected disclosure. The AP Vigilance and Enforcement Department performs the parallel preventive audit function.

## Conclusion

Whistleblowers can only be guardians of accountability if the state first guards them. India has the ethical consensus, the drafted law and a functioning administrative channel in PIDPI - what it lacks is commencement. Notifying the 2014 Act with the safeguards the government considers necessary, and enacting a False Claims-type law as the 2nd ARC recommended, would convert individual courage into systemic deterrence. Until then, integrity in public service continues to depend on individuals willing to bear costs the state has not agreed to share.

- 2nd ARC, Ethics in Governance (4th Report), para 3.6.4: whistleblowers exposing false claims, fraud or corruption must get confidentiality and anonymity, protection from career victimisation, and safeguards against bodily harm; harassment or retaliation should itself be a criminal offence with substantial penalty.
- 2nd ARC, para 5.2.5: enact a law on the lines of the U.S. False Claims Act allowing citizens and civil society to sue for recovery of the proceeds of corruption and to receive a share of the recovery - a market incentive to disclose.
- Comparative statutes worth naming: U.S. Whistleblower Protection Act, 1989 and Sarbanes-Oxley Act, 2002; U.K. Public Interest Disclosure Act, 1998; Australia's Public Interest Disclosure Act, 1994; New Zealand's Protected Disclosures Act, 2000.
- Law Commission of India, 179th Report (2001) proposed the Public Interest Disclosure (Protection of Informers) Bill - the direct ancestor of the 2014 Act.
- Key statutory numbers: Act No. 17 of 2014; assent 9 May 2014; gazetted 12 May 2014; commencement clause Section 1(3) - never notified. Competent authority against a Union Minister is the Prime Minister; maximum period for a complaint is seven years; SPG personnel are excluded.
- AP specifics: ACB toll-free 14400 and 'ACB 14400' app with identity confidentiality; AP Vigilance and Enforcement Department.

Q105   Define 'Accountability'. Discuss the factors that have led to the weakening of accountability in civil services. Suggest ways to improve the mechanisms for accountability in civil services. (APPSC, 2023)

Accountability is the obligation of a public servant to answer for the exercise of delegated authority and to bear consequence for its misuse. It has two limbs - answerability (giving reasons) and enforceability (facing sanction); a system with the first but not the second produces explanation without correction. In India it is constitutionally distributed rather than concentrated, which is its strength in design and its weakness in practice, because responsibility diffused across many holders is responsibility easily disclaimed.

## The five dimensions of accountability
- **Dimension** — Constitutional / legal anchor · Instrument in practice
- **Political** — Arts. 75(3) and 164(2) - collective responsibility · Question Hour; No-confidence motion
- **Financial** — Arts. 148-151 - CAG · PAC, Estimates Committee, audit reports
- **Legal / judicial** — Arts. 32 and 226; Art. 311 safeguards · Writs, PIL, judicial review
- **Administrative** — CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964; APAR · Hierarchy, disciplinary proceedings
- **Social** — RTI Act, 2005; MGNREGA Sec. 17 · Social audit, Jan Sunwai, citizen report cards

## Why accountability has weakened
- Political interference and tenure insecurity: arbitrary transfer is the cheapest sanction against an inconvenient officer. Sanjiv Chaturvedi, an IFS officer, faced repeated transfers after exposing irregularities. The Supreme Court in T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013) therefore directed a minimum assured tenure and Civil Services Boards, and barred action on oral instructions - a direction still unevenly implemented across states.
- Diffusion of responsibility in file-based decision-making: when a decision passes through six levels of noting, no single level owns the outcome. The 2nd ARC's central diagnosis was precisely this - authority is not fused with responsibility, so blame is always attributable elsewhere.
- Procedural insulation: Article 311's two-stage safeguard and Section 17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (inserted in 2018) requiring prior approval to investigate a public servant's official decisions are both defensible protections for honest risk-taking, but they lengthen the interval between misconduct and consequence, weakening deterrence.
- Opaque and inflated performance appraisal: an APAR system in which nearly all officers are graded 'outstanding' transmits no information and cannot support differential consequence - the 2nd ARC flagged this as a core flaw in personnel administration.
- Weak protection for internal reporting: with the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 still not notified, the officer who reports carries the entire risk - suppressing precisely the information accountability requires.

## Ways to strengthen accountability
- Institutional - competency-based capacity building: Mission Karmayogi's iGOT platform now has over 1.5 crore registered learners, more than 8 crore course completions and over 4,600 courses, with tripartite MoUs covering 28 States and UTs (PIB, February and April 2026). Capacity is a precondition for accountability: an officer cannot be held to a standard she was never trained to meet.
- Legal - convert charters into entitlements: over twenty states have Right to Public Services Acts imposing time limits and penalties. Following the Prime Minister's direction in the PRAGATI meeting of 5 March 2025, DARPG has begun integrating State RTS portals with CPGRAMS so that service-delivery failure and grievance data speak to each other (PIB, March 2025).
- Technological - measurable disposal: CPGRAMS recorded 1,88,969 grievances redressed by Central Ministries in April 2026 at an average disposal time of 13 days (DARPG, PIB, May 2026); a Review Meeting Module now enables Secretary-level scrutiny, with 331 review meetings held up to 30 April 2026.
- Social - mandatory social audit: the 2nd ARC recommended social audit for all programmes; Section 17 of MGNREGA makes Gram Sabha social audit statutory. Extending it to health, nutrition and housing schemes creates accountability that does not depend on the hierarchy auditing itself.

## Andhra Pradesh anchor
- AP's Grama/Ward Sachivalayam system places roughly ten functional secretaries within reach of every 2,000 rural households and 4,000 urban population, fixing named responsibility for named services at the cutting edge - the level at which the 2nd ARC said reform must occur.
- The Public Grievance Redressal System (PGRS) under the Real Time Governance Society auto-escalates a grievance to the next higher officer once the prescribed deadline lapses, and now accepts text, image and voice complaints through Mana Mitra - making delay itself the trigger for accountability rather than requiring the citizen to complain again.

## Conclusion

Accountability fails in India less from an absence of mechanisms than from the interval between act and consequence, and from authority that has been separated from responsibility. The remedy is convergent: assured tenure and Civil Services Boards to protect the honest officer, differentiated appraisal and social audit to expose the errant one, statutory service guarantees to give the citizen standing, and protected disclosure to surface what audit cannot see. Fusing authority with responsibility at every level, as the 2nd ARC urged, remains the single reform from which the others follow.

- 2nd ARC, 10th Report (Refurbishing of Personnel Administration): fuse authority with responsibility; introduce competency-based recruitment and appraisal; assured minimum tenure; two intensive mid-career reviews.
- T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013): minimum assured tenure for civil servants, Civil Services Boards for transfers and postings, and a bar on acting upon oral instructions - the leading judicial authority on bureaucratic insulation.
- Mission Karmayogi / NPCSCB: Central Sector Scheme under DoPT; Capacity Building Commission (2021) and Karmayogi Bharat SPV (2022); Karmayogi Competency Model; iGOT - 1.5 crore+ learners, 8 crore+ course completions, 4,600+ courses (PIB, April 2026).
- CPGRAMS benchmarks: 1,88,969 grievances redressed by Central Ministries in April 2026; average disposal 13 days in 2026 (16 days in April 2025); Grievance Redressal Assessment and Index (GRAI) ranks Ministries annually - a rare outcome-based accountability index.
- Legal comparators: Karnataka Sakala Services Act, 2011 (compensation for delay); Right to Public Services Acts in 20+ states; the central Right of Citizens for Time Bound Delivery of Goods and Services Bill, 2011 LAPSED with the 15th Lok Sabha - no central law exists.
- AP specifics: Grama/Ward Sachivalayam; PGRS with automatic escalation under RTGS; Mana Mitra voice and image grievance filing; AP e-Office.

Q106   Discuss the Indian experience of the Citizen Charter movement and suggest solutions to improve its impact in India. (APPSC, 2023)

A Citizen's Charter is a written declaration by a public organisation of the services it provides, the standards and timelines it commits to, and the remedy available on default. India adopted the instrument at the Conference of Chief Ministers in May 1997, adapting the United Kingdom's 1991 model with one distinctive addition - a statement of expectations from the client. Three decades on, the movement has succeeded in making service standards articulable but largely failed to make them enforceable.

## Design and the standard behind it
- DARPG is the nodal department and hosts charters on goicharters.nic.in. Its published baseline records 107 charters by Central Ministries/Departments/organisations and 629 by State Governments and UTs as of March 2005 (darpg.gov.in) - useful because it is a verifiable government figure rather than a circulated estimate.
- India became the first country in the world to publish a national standard for public service delivery, IS 15700:2005 of the Bureau of Indian Standards, which requires a charter to carry measurable service standards and the remedy for non-compliance - a point the Sixth Central Pay Commission specifically commended.

## What worked
- Standard articulation: departments were forced, often for the first time, to define what they deliver, to whom, and within what time. Railways, banking, passport and municipal services acquired publicly stated timelines against which citizens could argue.
- Institutional deepening through Sevottam: DARPG's Sevottam model assesses an organisation on three modules - Charter implementation, public grievance redress, and service delivery capability - shifting the focus from publishing a charter to sustaining it. Sevottam Guidelines 2025-26, with a model curriculum for capacity building of Grievance Redressal Officers, have been developed with the Administrative Staff College of India (DARPG, PIB, July 2025).

## What did not work
- Non-justiciability: a charter creates no enforceable right and carries no automatic relief for breach. The 2nd ARC's sharpest question to departments was whether the charter provides ANY automatic relief when norms are missed - for most, the answer is no.
- Failure to reach the cutting edge: the 2nd ARC found that most field formations either have no charter or adopt a generic one handed down by headquarters, so reform stops precisely where citizen interface is greatest.
- No consultation and no review: charters were drafted internally, rarely with civil society, and seldom revised, producing abstract commitments unconnected to what users actually expect.
- The central legislative gap: the Right of Citizens for Time Bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal of their Grievances Bill, 2011 - which would have made publication of a charter mandatory within six months and imposed penalties for default - LAPSED on the dissolution of the Fifteenth Lok Sabha. No central statute exists today.

## Solutions
- **Reform** — Content · Authority / example
- **Statutory backing** — Convert charter commitments into enforceable entitlements with penalty and compensation · Karnataka Sakala Services Act, 2011; 20+ State RTS Acts
- **Unit-level charters** — One charter per independent field unit under the organisation's umbrella charter · 2nd ARC, para 4.6.10 - 'one size does not fit all'
- **Participative drafting** — Wide consultation including civil society; firm, measurable commitments · IS 15700:2005; 2nd ARC nine principles
- **Independent evaluation** — End-user benchmarking, citizen report cards, external audit · 2nd ARC Seven-Step Model, Steps 5-7
- **Digital integration** — Link charter timelines to grievance dashboards for automatic breach detection · CPGRAMS; State RTS portal integration

- Convergence is now official policy: following the Prime Minister's direction at the PRAGATI meeting of 5 March 2025, DARPG is integrating State Right to Services portals with CPGRAMS through web APIs, on the finding that service-delivery efficiency and grievance volume are inversely related (PIB, March 2025). CPGRAMS itself redressed 1,88,969 grievances for Central Ministries in April 2026 at an average of 13 days (PIB, May 2026).

## Andhra Pradesh anchor
- AP has effectively operationalised the charter idea without waiting for a statute: the Grama/Ward Sachivalayam system commits doorstep delivery of notified services within stated timelines, and the Commissioner and Director of Municipal Administration publishes a departmental Citizen Charter (cdma.ap.gov.in).
- Crucially, AP's PGRS under RTGS auto-escalates an unresolved grievance to the next higher officer once the deadline lapses - supplying exactly the 'automatic relief on default' that the 2nd ARC found missing from Indian charters.

## Conclusion

India's Citizen Charter movement succeeded as a declaration of intent and failed as a guarantee. Its next phase must therefore be a transition from charter to entitlement - service standards backed by statute, unit-level charters drafted with users, automatic relief on default, and independent evaluation rather than self-assessment. Andhra Pradesh's model of doorstep delivery with automatic escalation shows that this transition is administratively feasible before it is legislatively complete. Until breach carries consequence, a charter remains a promise rather than a right.

- Six original principles of the UK Citizen's Charter (1991): Quality, Choice, Standards, Value, Accountability, Transparency. Re-launched by the Blair government in 1998 as 'Service First'.
- 2nd ARC, Citizen Centric Administration (12th Report), para 4.6.10 - nine principles: one size does not fit all; charter per independent unit; wide consultation with civil society; firm commitments; internal process reform; redressal on default; periodic evaluation; benchmarking through end-user feedback; hold officers accountable for results.
- 2nd ARC Seven-Step Model for Citizen Centricity (para 4.9.9), recommended as MANDATORY for all organisations with a public interface: Define - Set standards - Build capability - Perform - Monitor - Evaluate -Improve.
- IS 15700:2005 (BIS): India was the first country to publish a national standard for public service delivery; requires vision/mission, list of key services, measurable standards and remedies for non-compliance.
- Sevottam ('seva' + 'uttam'): three modules - Citizen's Charter, Public Grievance Redress, Service Delivery Capability; nine criteria; thirty-three assessment questions.
- Verifiable numbers: 107 Central and 629 State/UT charters as of March 2005 (DARPG); central Citizens Charter Bill, 2011 lapsed; CPGRAMS 1,88,969 redressals in April 2026 at 13 days average (PIB, May 2026).
- AP specifics: Grama/Ward Sachivalayam timelines; CDMA Citizen Charter; PGRS automatic escalation; Mana Mitra service delivery.

Q107   'The making of the Right to Information Act, 2005 in India has been largely attributed to the success of civil society movement.' Comment. (APPSC, 2023)

The RTI Act, 2005, which came into full force on 12 October 2005, is India's most widely invoked instrument of citizen oversight. The claim that it was 'largely' the achievement of civil society is substantially true as to origin and momentum, but incomplete as to authorship. The Act emerged from a triangular process -grassroots mobilisation supplied the demand and the design idea, the judiciary supplied the constitutional foundation, and the executive and legislature supplied the enforceable machinery.

## The civil society claim - and why it is strong
- The Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan, formed in Rajasthan in 1990, invented the Jan Sunwai - a public hearing at which muster rolls and bills were read aloud before the villagers named in them. The Beawar sit-in of 1996 turned a local wage-fraud grievance into a national demand, and gave the movement its formulation that information is the precondition of every other right.
- The National Campaign for People's Right to Information (NCPRI), formed in 1996, professionalised the demand - drafting model legislation, sustaining parliamentary lobbying and building the national discourse that made a central law politically unavoidable.
- State-level victories proved feasibility before the Centre acted: Tamil Nadu and Goa (1997), Rajasthan and Karnataka (2000), Delhi (2001), Maharashtra (2002). Each removed the argument that transparency was administratively impossible.

## What the claim omits - the judiciary
- The constitutional basis pre-dated the movement. In State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975) the Supreme Court held that the people have a right to know every public act of their functionaries; S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1982) located the right to know within Article 19(1)(a). Union of India v. ADR (2002) and PUCL v. Union of India (2003) extended it to candidates' criminal and financial antecedents, striking down the legislative attempt to reverse disclosure.
- This mattered because it converted a political demand into a constitutional obligation - the State was no longer merely being asked to legislate, it was being told that secrecy required justification.

## What the claim omits - expert committees and the State
- Institutional preparation ran in parallel: the Press Council's draft Right to Information Bill under Justice P.B. Sawant (1996), the Shourie Committee (1997), and the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2002), which recommended a statutory right. The Freedom of Information Act, 2002 was enacted but never brought into force - an instructive failure showing that legislation without machinery achieves nothing.
- The Act's follow-through was equally institutional. The 2nd ARC's very first report (June 2006) was titled Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance, and recommended repealing the Official Secrets Act, 1923 and substituting a chapter in the National Security Act - the State auditing its own secrecy regime.

## The same dynamic continues - the DPDP amendment
- Section 44(3) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 recast Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act; it came into force on 13 November 2025, with the DPDP Rules, 2025 notified on 14 November 2025. The Government's position is that the amendment codifies the privacy standard affirmed in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India and that the public-interest override in Section 8(2) of the RTI Act remains fully operative (PIB, November 2025); civil society contends that removing the express public-interest test from 8(1)(j) narrows disclosure of officials' information.
- Institutional health has meanwhile improved: after functioning with only a Chief and two Information Commissioners in late 2024, the Central Information Commission was restored to full strength when a new Chief Information Commissioner and eight Information Commissioners were sworn in on 15 December 2025 (PIB, 15 December 2025). Pendency nonetheless stands at 29,034 second appeals and 3,577 complaints as on 1 February 2026, while the rejection rate for RTI applications fell to 3.26% in 2024-25 from 7.21% in 2013-14 (PIB, February 2026).

## Andhra Pradesh anchor
- The Andhra Pradesh Information Commission was constituted on 2 March 2006 under Section 15 of the Act (sic.ap.gov.in), and the State runs its own online filing portal at rtionline.ap.gov.in - illustrating that the federal architecture of the Act, with parallel State Commissions, was itself a legislative design choice rather than a movement demand.

## Conclusion

Civil society deserves the primary credit: it identified the right, invented the method of asserting it, and generated the political pressure without which no Bill would have moved. But 'largely' should not be read as 'solely'. The judiciary had already made secrecy constitutionally suspect, expert committees supplied the drafting, and the State supplied the Information Commissions, penalties and appellate machinery that turned a right into a remedy. The current contest over Section 8(1)(j) shows that this collaboration - and this tension - is not a closed chapter of history but the Act's continuing condition.

- Milestones to date accurately: MKSS founded 1990; Beawar dharna 1996; NCPRI 1996; Press Council draft under Justice P.B. Sawant 1996; Shourie Committee 1997; state laws 1997-2002; Freedom of Information Act 2002 (never brought into force); RTI Act assent 15 June 2005, fully in force 12 October 2005.
- Judicial line: State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975) - right to know every public act; S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1982) - right to know under Art. 19(1)(a); Union of India v. ADR (2002) and PUCL v. Union of India (2003) -candidate disclosure; CPIO, Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019, five-judge bench) -CJI's office is a public authority.
- 2nd ARC, 1st Report, Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance (June 2006) - recommended repeal of the Official Secrets Act, 1923 and substitution by a chapter in the National Security Act; inclusion of Armed Forces in the Second Schedule with PIOs appointed even for Second Schedule bodies.
- Current institutional data: CIC restored to full strength with a Chief Information Commissioner and eight new Information Commissioners sworn in on 15 December 2025; pendency 29,034 second appeals and 3,577 complaints as on 1 February 2026; rejection rate 3.26% in 2024-25 against 7.21% in 2013-14 (PIB, Ministry of Personnel).
- DPDP Act, 2023 Section 44(3) amending RTI Section 8(1)(j) - in force 13 November 2025; DPDP Rules, 2025 notified 14 November 2025; Government position rests on Puttaswamy and the continued operation of RTI Section 8(2).
- AP specifics: Andhra Pradesh Information Commission constituted 2 March 2006 (sic.ap.gov.in); State RTI portal rtionline.ap.gov.in.

Q108   What is RTI? What rights are available under RTI Act 2005? If RTI is a Fundamental Right, then why do we need an Act to give us this Right? (APPSC, 2020)

The Right to Information is the legal entitlement of a citizen to access information held by or under the control of a public authority. Section 2(j) of the RTI Act, 2005 defines it in precisely those terms. Constitutionally it flows from Article 19(1)(a), as the Supreme Court held in State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975) and S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1982). The Act did not create the right; it created the machinery without which the right could not be exercised by an ordinary citizen.

## What is RTI
- Section 2(f) defines 'information' expansively - records, documents, memos, e-mails, opinions, advices, press releases, contracts, reports, papers, samples, models and data material in any electronic form, including information relating to any private body accessible under any other law.
- Section 2(h) defines 'public authority' to include bodies established by the Constitution, by law, or by government notification, and any body owned, controlled or SUBSTANTIALLY FINANCED by government, including NGOs so financed - a reach the constitutional right by itself could never have delivered against non-state actors.

## Rights available under the Act
- **Right** — Provision · Practical significance
- **Inspection of works, documents, records** — Sec. 2(j)(i) · Enabled villagers to verify MGNREGA muster rolls on site
- **Notes, extracts, certified copies** — Sec. 2(j)(ii)-(iii) · Certified copies are admissible evidence
- **Certified samples of material** — Sec. 2(j)(iv) · Verifying quality of road or construction material
- **Information in electronic form** — Sec. 2(j)(v) · Diskettes, tapes, printouts
- **Proactive disclosure without asking** — Sec. 4(1)(b) · 17 categories to be published suo motu
- **No reasons need be given** — Sec. 6(2) · Applicant need not justify the request
- **Reply within 30 days; 48 hours if life or liberty** — Sec. 7(1) · Free of cost if the deadline is missed - Sec. 7(6)
- **Two-tier appeal** — Sec. 19 · First Appellate Authority, then CIC/SIC
- **Penalty on the PIO** — Sec. 20 · Rs. 250 per day up to Rs. 25,000, plus disciplinary action
- **Overriding effect** — Sec. 22 · Prevails over the Official Secrets Act, 1923

## Why an Act was needed despite the right being fundamental
- A fundamental right defines an entitlement; it does not supply a procedure. Article 19(1)(a) tells a citizen she may know, but not whom to ask, in what form, at what fee or within what time. Sections 5, 6 and 7 create Public Information Officers, an application route and binding deadlines.
- Exemptions had to be defined with precision. Article 19(2) permits 'reasonable restrictions' but leaves their content to be settled case by case. Sections 8, 9 and 24 read with the Second Schedule specify what is withheld, converting unpredictable litigation into a knowable rule - with Section 8(2) retaining a public-interest override.
- Institutions had to be created. The Central and State Information Commissions under Sections 12 and 15 are specialised, accessible adjudicators. Without them, the only remedy for refusal would be a writ petition under Article 32 or 226 - costly, slow, and effectively closed to the rural applicant the Act was designed for.
- Consequence had to attach to refusal. A declared right without penalty invites indifference; Section 20's personal monetary liability on the PIO is what converts the entitlement into a remedy.
- Reach had to extend beyond the State. Fundamental rights are enforceable primarily against the State; Section 2(h) brings substantially financed non-government bodies within the disclosure regime.

## Current position and continuing challenges
- Section 8(1)(j) has been recast by Section 44(3) of the DPDP Act, 2023, in force from 13 November 2025, with the DPDP Rules notified on 14 November 2025. The Government's position is that this codifies the privacy standard of Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India while Section 8(2)'s public-interest override survives (PIB, November 2025); its practical effect on disclosure of officials' information is contested.
- Institutionally, the Central Information Commission was restored to full strength on 15 December 2025 with a new Chief Information Commissioner and eight Information Commissioners sworn in (PIB, 15 December 2025). Pendency remains substantial - 29,034 second appeals and 3,577 complaints as on 1 February 2026 - though the rejection rate has fallen to 3.26% in 2024-25 from 7.21% in 2013-14 (PIB, February 2026).

## Andhra Pradesh anchor
- The Andhra Pradesh Information Commission, constituted on 2 March 2006 (sic.ap.gov.in), hears second appeals and complaints within the State, while rtionline.ap.gov.in enables online filing - demonstrating the two-tier federal machinery that only a statute, not Article 19(1)(a) standing alone, could have established.

## Conclusion

RTI illustrates the distinction between a right and a remedy. Article 19(1)(a) established that citizens may know; the Act of 2005 established how, from whom, within what time and with what consequence for refusal - and extended the obligation to bodies substantially financed by the State. Its record includes bringing even the office of the Chief Justice of India within the definition of a public authority (Subhash Chandra Agarwal, 2019). The current tasks are to hold pendency down now that the Commissions are staffed, and to ensure that the recast Section 8(1)(j) is applied with Section 8(2)'s public-interest test intact.

- Section numbers examiners look for: 2(f) information; 2(h) public authority; 2(j) right to information; 4 proactive disclosure; 5 PIO/APIO; 6(2) no reasons required; 7(1) 30 days / 48 hours; 7(6) free if delayed; 8 and 9 exemptions; 8(2) public-interest override; 18 complaints; 19 appeals; 20 penalty; 22 overriding effect; 24 and Second Schedule exempt organisations.
- Exemptions under Section 8: sovereignty and integrity, security, strategic, scientific or economic interests; relations with foreign states; incitement to an offence; information barred by a court or amounting to contempt; breach of privilege of Parliament or a State Legislature; commercial confidence, trade secrets or intellectual property; fiduciary information; and information relating to a foreign government received in confidence.
- Case law: State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975); S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1982); PUCL v. Union of India (2003); Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v. CIC (2012) on personal information under Sec. 8(1)(j); CPIO, Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019, five-judge bench) bringing the CJI's office within 'public authority'.
- RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019: shifted the term, salary and service conditions of the Chief Information Commissioner and Information Commissioners from the statute to Central Government rules - criticised as diluting the Commissions' independence; a standard critical point.
- Current data: CIC restored to full strength on 15 December 2025; pendency 29,034 second appeals plus 3,577 complaints as on 1 February 2026; rejection rate 3.26% in 2024-25 versus 7.21% in 2013-14; rtionline.gov.in serves 2,200+ central public authorities (PIB, Ministry of Personnel).
- AP specifics: Andhra Pradesh Information Commission (constituted 2 March 2006, sic.ap.gov.in); rtionline.ap.gov.in for online filing.

Q109   |Section B, Q45 KEPT+ “The Right to Information Act is meant only for providing information but not grievance redressal.” Comment.

The Right to Information Act, 2005 is India's principal sunshine law, giving statutory shape to the right the Supreme Court had already read into Article 19(1)(a) in State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975) and Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002). Section 3 makes access to information a citizen's right; Sections 2(f) and 2(j) fix its boundary at material that already exists in a public authority's records. The statement is therefore substantially accurate: RTI is an architecture of disclosure, not of adjudication. Its constitutional worth lies precisely in that restraint — it arms the citizen with evidence, leaving redressal to forums designed for it.

## The Statutory Design Stops at Disclosure
- ‘Information’ is a closed category. Section 2(f) lists records, documents, memos, e-mails, opinions, advices, press releases, contracts and logbooks — all pre-existing material. Section 2(j)

confers only the right to inspect, take notes and obtain certified copies. Nowhere does the Act empower a Public Information Officer to resolve anything. IJudicial confirmation. In CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011) the Supreme Court held that a PIO is not obliged to create, collate, interpret or furnish non-existent information, and cautioned that treating RTI as an all-purpose remedy would paralyse administration. The Court expressly warned against RTI becoming a tool of ‘indiscriminate and impractical demands’ that divert scarce administrative time from governance itself.

## Grievance Redressal Has Its Own Statutory Architecture
- Separate forums exist by design. CPGRAMS handles Union-level grievances; the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 covers corruption complaints; State Right to Service Acts (Karnataka Sakala, 2011; Bihar RTPS, 2011) impose time limits with compensation; consumer fora and administrative tribunals cover service deficiencies. RTI feeds all of them — it does not replace them. IAP anchor — the division is visible in practice. Andhra Pradesh routes grievances through the Public Grievance Redressal System (pgrs.ap.gov.in) run by the Real Time Governance Society, escalating directly to the CMO, and through Mana Mitra, India's first WhatsApp-based governance platform, which now delivers 1,126 services across 35 departments to 58.2 lakh citizens with over 3.42 crore service sessions, with grievances registrable by text, image or voice under AI4PGRS (Government of Andhra Pradesh release, July 2026). Second appeals, by contrast, go to a wholly different body — the Andhra Pradesh Information Commission (sic.ap.gov.in), which decides only disclosure disputes.

## Yet RTI Powerfully Enables Redressal — the Data
- Disclosure is improving. The rejection rate of RTI applications across Central public authorities fell from 7.21% in 2013-14 to 3.26% in 2024-25, while pendency before the CIC stood at 29,034 second appeals and 3,577 complaints as on 01.02.2026 (PIB / DoPT reply, February 2026). Wider disclosure means better-evidenced grievances downstream — an RTI reply on a delayed pension becomes the annexure to the CPGRAMS complaint that actually secures it.

## Where the Statement Overstates — the Necessary Qualification
- Section 19(8)(b) empowers Information Commissions to award compensation for loss or detriment suffered; Section 20 imposes penalty of ₹250 per day up to ₹25,000 on an errant PIO. These are genuinely remedial powers, though confined to the information transaction itself, not the underlying grievance. ISection 4 changes the equation upstream. Suo motu disclosure of 17 categories of information pre-empts a large class of grievances by removing the information asymmetry that generates them — which the 2nd ARC's first Report, Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance (2006), identified as RTI's most under-used provision.

## The Emerging Constraint — Privacy vs Transparency
- Section 44(3), DPDP Act, 2023 substituted Section 8(1)(j), exempting all personal information and removing the earlier proviso that information which cannot be denied to Parliament shall not be denied to a citizen. The Government's position is that the amendment codifies K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) and that Section 8(2) remains fully operative, allowing disclosure where public interest outweighs protected harm (PIB, 2025). With the DPDP Rules notified on 14 November 2025, the balance between privacy and disclosure will now be settled case by case.
- **RTI Act CAN do** — RTI Act CANNOT do
- **Supply existing records [S.2(f), 2(j)]** — Resolve a service complaint
- **Compel proactive disclosure [S.4]** — Direct an authority to act on a demand
- **Penalise a defaulting PIO [S.20]** — Award relief on the underlying dispute
- **Compensate for detriment [S.19(8)(b)]** — Create or interpret new information

Alternative flow-diagram: Citizen → RTI application → Information → CPGRAMS / Lokayukta / RTS Act / Court → Redressal. Draw RTI as the *key*, the redressal forum as the *door*.

## Conclusion

The proposition is legally sound and administratively wise. RTI was designed as an instrument of transparency, and confusing it with an adjudicatory remedy would both overwhelm PIOs and blunt the Act's core purpose. The correct formulation is that RTI is the trigger of accountability, not its terminus: it converts an aggrieved citizen into an informed one, and an informed citizen into an effective claimant before the proper forum. A mature transparency regime therefore requires RTI to remain sharp and specialised, while parallel grievance institutions — CPGRAMS, Lokayuktas, Right to Service Acts and platforms such as Andhra Pradesh's PGRS — are correspondingly strengthened.

Q110   |Section B, Q46 REBUILT The promise of decentralisation of public service delivery is based on the hope that the local bodies will promote the required standards of accountability. Examine.

Decentralisation is the transfer of authority, resources and personnel from higher tiers to local self-government, resting on the principle of subsidiarity — that a function should be discharged at the lowest level competent to perform it. The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992-93) institutionalised this through Part IX and Part IXA, with Article 243G and Article 243W authorising States to devolve the 29 and 18 subjects of the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules. The underlying hope was that proximity would breed accountability. Three decades on, the record is one of substantial democratisation but only partial empowerment — local bodies have gained voice and money faster than they have gained authority.

## Why Proximity Should Produce Accountability
- Direct, continuous scrutiny. The Gram Sabha (Art. 243A) is the only constitutional body in India where the electorate itself, not its representatives, sits in session. Elected members live among those they serve, so a defective handpump or an absent teacher is visible daily — a form of oversight no district-level audit can replicate. IInclusion produces different priorities. Reservation of one-third seats for women (now raised to 50% by over 20 States) and proportionate reservation for SCs/STs has demonstrably shifted spending toward drinking water, sanitation and nutrition — goods the previously unrepresented value most. IAP anchor — institutionalised last-mile delivery. Andhra Pradesh operates 15,004 Village and Ward Secretariats under the AP Grama Sachivalayams and Ward Sachivalayams Act, 2023, one for roughly every 2,000 households, delivering around 500 services from 35 departments at the doorstep. This is decentralisation of administration — and the standing critique is that it strengthens the executive arm without correspondingly strengthening the elected Panchayat, illustrating that delivery and accountability are not the same thing.

## Examining the Record — What the Evidence Shows
- Devolution has risen, but unevenly. The Ministry of Panchayati Raj's Status of Devolution to Panchayats in States: An Indicative Evidence-Based Ranking, 2024 (released 13 February 2025) records overall devolution rising from 39.9% (2013-14) to 43.9% (2021-22), with the functionaries index climbing from 39.6% to 50.9% and capacity enhancement from 44% to 54.6% on the back of the Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (2018). IThe decisive finding — money without power. Over the same period financial devolution rose from 32.05 to 37.04, but functional devolution fell from 35.34 to 29.18 (MoPR, 2024). Panchayats are being funded to implement what others decide. Andhra Pradesh sits in the ‘medium devolution’ band (50-55), though its panchayats' revenue equals 2.42% of State Own Revenue — among the highest in the country, confirming that fiscal capacity alone does not translate into functional autonomy.

## The Accountability Deficit — Diagnosis by the 3Fs
- Funds: dependence and tying. The 15th Finance Commission awarded ₹2,36,805 crore to Rural and ₹1,21,055 crore to Urban Local Bodies for 2021-26 (PIB, February 2026). The 16th Finance Commission has recommended ₹4,35,236 crore for RLBs for 2026-31, of which the basic grant of ₹3,48,188 crore is split equally into tied and untied, the tied half earmarked for sanitation, solid waste and water management (PIB, 24 March 2026). Tied grants improve outcomes but narrow the very discretion on which local accountability depends. IFunctions: activity mapping incomplete. Devolution is often on paper. Line departments retain staff and budgets; parastatals and mission-mode societies bypass the Panchayat altogether. District Planning Committees under Article 243ZD — the constitutional device for integrating rural and urban plans — remain non-functional or nominal in most States, a failing the 2nd ARC's 6th Report on Local Governance (2007) flagged and sought to remedy through binding activity mapping. IFunctionaries and accountability tools. Gram Panchayat Secretaries are frequently multi-charge; State Finance Commissions are constituted late and their reports often untabled. Social audits and Citizens' Charters, the 2nd ARC's preferred accountability instruments, are unevenly implemented — the ARC recommended that “operational guidelines of all developmental schemes and citizen-centric programmes should provide for a social audit mechanism”, a recommendation still only partially adopted.

## The New Statutory Test — VB-G RAM G Act, 2025
- The Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025, which replaces MGNREGA with effect from 1 July 2026, vests planning, implementation and monitoring in Panchayats under Sections 16-19, strengthens Gram Sabha social audit under Section 20, and requires Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans integrated with PM Gati Shakti (PIB, December 2025 and February 2026). Whether accountability follows will depend on whether Gram Sabhas are given real records — muster rolls, measurement books, geo-tagged assets — as the Act requires.

- **Funds** — Own revenue + FC/SFC transfers · 32.05 → 37.04 (rising, but largely tied)
- **Functions** — 29 + 18 subjects (Sch. XI, XII) · 35.34 → 29.18 (declining)
- **Functionaries** — Own staff under Panchayat control · 39.6% → 50.9% (improving)

## Conclusion

The hope that local bodies would raise the standard of accountability has been partly vindicated and partly frustrated. Decentralisation has unquestionably widened participation and improved last-mile reach — Andhra Pradesh's 15,004 Sachivalayams and eGramSwaraj-linked online audits are evidence of that. But accountability requires the power to decide, not merely to deliver, and the constitutional record shows functions receding even as funds rise. The corrective is specific: statutory activity mapping under Article 243G, timely and binding State Finance Commissions, functional District Planning Committees under Article 243ZD, and genuine Gram Sabha social audit under the new VB-G RAM G framework. Only when the local body answers for decisions it actually took does decentralisation deliver its promise.

Q111   |Section B, Q47 REBUILT Social audit helps to narrow gaps between vision and reality. Examine the statement and also discuss the impediments in the institutionalisation of social audit in India.

Social audit is the statutory verification of a public programme by its own beneficiaries, in which the implementing agency places its records before the Gram Sabha for scrutiny in an open public hearing. It differs fundamentally from financial audit, which asks whether money was spent lawfully, and from performance audit, which asks whether it was spent efficiently: social audit asks whether the stated beneficiary actually received the stated benefit. Introduced through Section 17 of MGNREGA, 2005 and operationalised by the MGNREGA (Audit of Schemes) Rules, 2011 framed in consultation with the CAG, it is India's principal instrument for closing the distance between policy intent and lived outcome.

## How Social Audit Narrows the Vision-Reality Gap
- It converts paper into physical proof. Muster rolls, measurement books, bills, vouchers and geo-tagged asset records are read out and physically verified against the ground. Ghost beneficiaries, works recorded but never executed, machine use in labour-intensive works and inflated measurements surface only through this cross-check — precisely the deficiencies the Government itself acknowledged when introducing the new employment law, citing ‘work not found on the ground’ and ‘expenditure not matching physical progress’ (PIB, December 2025). IIt shifts accountability from vertical to horizontal. Departmental inspection is occasional and hierarchical; the Gram Sabha is permanent and peer-level. The 2nd ARC observed that social audit through beneficiary and civil-society groups is “a useful supplement to surprise inspections on the part of departmental supervisors” and recommended that the operational guidelines of all developmental and citizen-centric schemes provide for a social audit mechanism. IAP anchor — the model the country copied. Undivided Andhra Pradesh pioneered state-wide, institutionalised social audit of MGNREGA from 2006 through the Society for Social Audit, Accountability and Transparency (SSAAT), using trained village social auditors drawn from beneficiary households — an arrangement later adopted nationally as the independent Social Audit Unit model. Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal remain the only States conducting social audit of the National Social Assistance Programme (Ministry of Rural Development / PIB), giving AP a distinctive claim in any answer on this topic. IIt generates recovery and deterrence. Public naming in the presence of the village, followed by recovery orders and disciplinary action, imposes a reputational cost that departmental proceedings rarely match — the deterrent value often exceeds the sums recovered.

## Institutionalisation So Far — the Gains
- Statutory expansion. The Meghalaya Community Participation and Public Services Social Audit Act, 2017 remains India's only dedicated social audit legislation, mandating audit across 26 schemes in education, health and rural development. Eight States have extended social audit to eleven schemes including PMAY-G, Swachh Bharat Mission, ICDS and Mid-Day Meals (MoRD / PIB). IA new statutory footing. Under the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (in force from 1 July 2026), Section 20 strengthens Gram Sabha social audit, while Sections 23-24 mandate biometric authentication, geo-tagging and real-time dashboards, and the Centre may suspend fund release where serious irregularities are detected (PIB, December 2025). Central sanctions of ₹26,971 crore issued during the transition expressly include a Social Audit Unit component (PIB, 2026).

## Impediments to Institutionalisation — a Structural Diagnosis
- (i) The auditor is paid by the audited. Social Audit Units are funded out of scheme administrative costs released through the very departments they scrutinise. Salaries, vehicles and office space depend on departmental goodwill — a conflict of interest that no amount of training resolves. This is the single most serious impediment and should lead the answer. I(ii) Findings are recommendatory, not enforceable. There is no statutory obligation on the implementing agency to file a time-bound Action Taken Report, no prosecution power, and no appellate mechanism. Audits therefore accumulate findings without consequence, and repeated non-action erodes community willingness to participate. I(iii) The legal mandate is narrow. Outside the employment guarantee and Meghalaya's Act, most welfare schemes — NFSA, PMAY-G, health and nutrition programmes — carry social audit only in guidelines, which are administratively revocable. I(iv) Elite capture and reprisal. Gram Sabhas can be dominated by locally powerful interests; auditors and complainants face intimidation. The Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014, passed but never operationalised through rules, leaves them without statutory cover. I(v) Capacity and coverage deficit. Trained village resource persons are scarce, audit calendars slip, and coverage of the mandated audit cycle is uneven across districts. I(vi) The digital substitution risk. AI-based irregularity detection and biometric attendance under the 2025 Act are valuable, but if treated as a substitute for the public hearing they will restore the very vertical, opaque monitoring that social audit was designed to displace.
- **Stage** — Action · Weak link in practice
- **1. Disclosure** — Records placed before Gram Sabha · Records withheld or incomplete
- **2. Verification** — Door-to-door + site inspection · Shortage of trained auditors
- **3. Public hearing** — Jan Sunwai; findings read out · Elite capture, intimidation
- **4. Action Taken Report** — Recovery, disciplinary action · No statutory ATR duty

Alternative: a simple Vision → Gap → Reality bridge diagram, with ‘social audit’ as the bridge and the six impediments drawn as cracks in it.

## Conclusion

Social audit does narrow the gap between vision and reality, but only to the extent that its findings carry consequences. India has built the form of institutionalisation — Social Audit Units in every State, CAG-consulted rules, a new statutory mandate under Section 20 of the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 — without securing its substance: auditor independence and enforceable follow-up. The reform agenda is correspondingly precise: place Social Audit Units under the State Legislature or the CAG rather than the implementing department, make a time-bound Action Taken Report a statutory duty, extend the mandate by law to all major welfare schemes on the Meghalaya model, and use digital records to equip the Gram Sabha rather than to replace it. Andhra Pradesh, which gave the country its first working model through SSAAT, is well placed to lead that next phase.

- Meghalaya Community Participation and Public Services Social Audit Act, 2017 — India's only dedicated social audit statute, covering 26 schemes
- Section 4, RTI Act, 2005 as the disclosure precondition.
- Institutions: Social Audit Units (independent, in every State)

- NIRD&PR; (training)
- SSAAT, Andhra Pradesh — the original state-wide model

- NSAP social audit objectives (NSAP Guidelines, 2014): awareness generation; proactive disclosure; beneficiary verification; identification of ineligible and of eligible-but-excluded beneficiaries; recording of grievances for forwarding to the competent authority; identification of implementation bottlenecks. Only Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal conduct NSAP social audit.
- VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 — for use across Section B: replaces MGNREGA; guarantees 125 days (up from 100) under S.5(1); Ss.16-19 vest planning and implementation in Panchayats; S.20 social audit; Ss.23-24 biometric authentication, geo-tagging, real-time dashboards; Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans integrated with PM Gati Shakti; unemployment allowance payable after 15 days.

- Sharpening lines: Social audit answers the question financial audit cannot — did the named beneficiary actually receive the named benefit?
- Its power is reputational, exercised in the presence of the community
- Its fatal design flaw is that the auditor's salary is drawn from the audited programme.

Q112   |Section C, Q1 KEPT+ What is meant by 'International Ethics'? Explain the significance of ethics in international dispute resolutions and environmental cooperation among nations.

International ethics is the body of moral principles governing the conduct of States, international organisations and non-State actors toward one another and toward humanity as a whole. It is distinct from international law: law imposes obligation, ethics supplies legitimacy and voluntary compliance in a system that has no world police. Its concerns are the just use of force, human dignity, distributive fairness between rich and poor nations, and stewardship of the global commons. India's constitutional commitment to it is explicit — Article 51 directs the State to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage settlement of disputes by arbitration.

## Significance of Ethics in International Dispute Resolution
- It secures compliance where enforcement is absent. No mechanism can compel a sovereign State to honour an adverse award; compliance rests on the ethic of pacta sunt servanda. Example: in

The Bay of Bengal Maritime Boundary Arbitration (Bangladesh v. India), award of 7 July 2014 by an Annex VII UNCLOS arbitral tribunal (PCA as registry; UN Reports of International Arbitral Awards, Vol. XXXII), India accepted an outcome that awarded the substantially larger share of the disputed 25,000 sq km to a far smaller neighbour — a demonstration that a rising power's word can outweigh its immediate interest. IIt protects the weak through sovereign equality.Article 2(1) of the UN Charter gives every member equal standing irrespective of size or wealth, and the one-State-one-vote rule in the General Assembly operationalises it. Without this ethical premise, dispute settlement would simply register power. India's conduct in the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) framework and the India-Sri Lanka Maritime Boundary Agreements (1974, 1976) illustrate settlement by negotiated equity rather than by leverage. IIt supplies the humanitarian floor. The Geneva Conventions, the Genocide Convention and the doctrine of Responsibility to Protect place limits on what may be done even in lawful conflict. The global campaign against apartheid — sustained for decades by moral pressure long before it became legally enforceable — shows ethics acting as the vanguard of law. IThe necessary caveat — ethics without enforcement. The 2016 South China Sea award under the same Annex VII procedure was simply rejected by the losing party, and the veto in the Security Council routinely shields the powerful. Ethics therefore shapes international conduct but cannot guarantee it — an honest answer must say so.

## Significance of Ethics in Environmental Cooperation
- It resolves the fairness problem at the heart of climate action. The principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC), adopted at Rio (1992) and carried into the Paris Agreement (2015), recognises that those who caused the problem must lead in solving it. At UNFCCC COP30 in Belém, Brazil (10-21 November 2025), India welcomed the establishment of the Just Transition Mechanism, pressed for implementation of Article 9.1 — the legal obligation of developed countries to provide climate finance — and objected to unilateral trade-restrictive climate measures as violative of equity and CBDR-RC (PIB, 22-23 November 2025). IIt grounds intergenerational justice. Sustainability is an ethical claim on behalf of people who cannot vote or negotiate. Indian jurisprudence has internalised it: in M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024) the Supreme Court recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change as flowing from Articles 14 and 21, converting a global ethical premise into a domestic constitutional entitlement. IIt governs the global commons. The Antarctic Treaty (1959) reserves a continent for peaceful scientific use, demilitarised and unappropriated; UNCLOS treats the deep seabed as the common heritage of mankind. India joined Brazil's Tropical Forests Forever Facility as an Observer at COP30 (PIB, 2026), and leads the International Solar Alliance — headquartered in Gurugram — as an instrument of equitable technology access rather than commercial advantage. IIt extends accountability beyond States. Transnational corporations are now judged against ESG norms and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights; India's Mission LiFE shifts part of the burden to individual consumption ethics, and the G20 New Delhi theme ‘Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — One Earth, One Family, One Future’ (2023) framed the entire agenda in ethical rather than transactional terms. IAP anchor — why this is not abstract. With roughly 975 km of coastline, India's second longest, Andhra Pradesh bears the direct cost of decisions taken at Belém: cyclone frequency, saline ingress and coastal erosion make adaptation finance a fiscal question for the State, not a diplomatic abstraction. This is precisely the constituency on whose behalf India presses the Article 9.1 obligation.
- **Domain** — Ethical Principle · Instrument / Example
- **Dispute resolution** — Pacta sunt servanda · Bay of Bengal Award, 7 July 2014 (UNCLOS Annex VII)
- **Dispute resolution** — Sovereign equality · UN Charter Art. 2(1); Panchsheel, 1954

- **Domain** — Ethical Principle · Instrument / Example
- **Environment** — CBDR-RC / equity · Paris Agreement, 2015; COP30 Just Transition Mechanism
- **Environment** — Intergenerational justice · M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024), Arts. 14 & 21
- **Environment** — Common heritage of mankind · Antarctic Treaty, 1959; UNCLOS deep seabed

Alternative: a concentric-circle diagram — innermost ‘National Interest’, then ‘International Law’, outermost ‘International Ethics’ — showing ethics as the widest and least enforceable, yet the source of legitimacy for the inner two.

## Conclusion

International ethics is the moral infrastructure on which an anarchic international order rests. It cannot compel, but it explains why a State honours an adverse arbitral award, why a developing country's claim to differentiated responsibility is heard at all, and why the Antarctic remains unclaimed. Its record is uneven — the veto and the unenforced South China Sea award are standing reminders that power still resists principle. But India's own posture, from Article 51 and Panchsheel to its insistence at Belém that equity and CBDR-RC be operationalised rather than recited, illustrates the argument's practical force: in a world of shared risks, ethical cooperation is not idealism but the only durable form of self-interest.

Contrast with the South China Sea Arbitration (Philippines v. China), 12 July 2016, same procedure, award rejected by the respondent.
