Q125 | Section C, Q14 — Q. Define public service broadly. How do the virtues of trustworthiness and fortitude get manifested in public service? Explain with examples. Suggest three preventive measures of corruption. (APPSC, 2020)

Public service is best defined broadly, in three registers. As an institution it is the permanent civil service through which the State acts. As an activity it is the delivery of public goods and the exercise of delegated public power. As an ethic it is the treatment of that power as a trust rather than a possession — what the Constitution captures in the oath to discharge duties ‘without fear or favour, affection or ill‑will’. Trustworthiness and fortitude are the two virtues that sustain this trusteeship.

## Trustworthiness — the fiduciary virtue
- Meaning: reliability of word, record and rule, such that a citizen can predict how the State will behave. Its public value is systemic — where trust is low, intermediaries and rent‑seekers occupy the gap between citizen and counter.
- Manifestation: honouring the Citizen’s Charter timelines; recording reasons for decisions; suo motu disclosure under Section 4(1)(b) of the RTI Act, 2005. AP anchor — Mana Mitra issues QR‑coded, tamper‑proof certificates directly to the citizen’s phone, so caste, income and nativity certificates no longer require a visit, a request or a favour (Govt. of AP / RTGS, 2026).

## Fortitude — the virtue of courage
- Meaning: the cardinal virtue of persisting in the right course despite fear, pressure or personal cost. It has two faces — endurance (bearing transfers, harassment and isolation) and initiative (acting when inaction would be safer).
- Manifestation: recording honest dissent on file even when it displeases; refusing an illegal oral instruction and asking for it in writing; ordering an evacuation or a stop‑work on one’s own responsibility. Section 17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (inserted in 2018) requires prior approval before inquiry into official recommendations or decisions — designed to protect the honest officer, as the 2nd ARC urged in its chapter on Protecting the Honest Civil Servant, though it must not become a shield for the corrupt.

## Three preventive measures of corruption
- 1. Reduce discretion and re‑engineer the process (2nd ARC, Ethics in Governance, 2007, Ch. 6.7). Corruption is a function of monopoly plus discretion minus accountability; removing the face‑to‑face counter removes the rent point. AP anchor — Mana Mitra now delivers 1,126 services across 35 departments to 58.2 lakh citizens across 3.42 crore sessions, while Revenue One digitises land records with over 19,000 revenue officials on the platform (Govt. of AP / RTGS, July 2026). At the Union level, GeM does the same for procurement.
- 2. Preventive vigilance and integrity pacts (2nd ARC, Ch. 6.6 and 6.12). Instead of waiting for complaints, organisations must map corruption‑prone processes and audit them — the logic of the CVC’s annual Vigilance Awareness Week and its three‑month preventive vigilance campaign. The case for prevention is empirical: the CVC’s Annual Report 2024 records over 7,000 CBI corruption cases pending in courts, of which 379 have been pending for more than twenty years. Punishment is too slow to deter.
- 3. Citizen‑side transparency and social audit (2nd ARC, Ch. 5.4). RTI Section 4 makes disclosure a duty rather than a favour; Section 17 of MGNREGA mandates Gram Sabha social audit of works, with independent Social Audit Units in each State including Andhra Pradesh; Meghalaya’s Community Participation and Public Services Social Audit Act, 2017 remains the first State law to make social audit statutory across departments — a model worth generalising.

Inverted pyramid: broad base = SYSTEMIC REFORM (reduce discretion, IT, integrity pacts); middle = INSTITUTIONAL VIGILANCE (CVC, CVOs, Lokpal/Lokayukta); narrow apex = PROSECUTION. Caption: ‘Prevention is wide and fast; punishment is narrow and slow.’

Two‑column table: Virtue | Institutional expression — Trustworthiness: Citizen’s Charter, RTI s.4, Sevottam; Fortitude: written dissent, PIDPI channel, PC Act s.17A protection.

## Conclusion

Public service is the exercise of delegated power as a trust, and its two load‑bearing virtues are complementary: trustworthiness makes the State predictable, fortitude makes it incorruptible under pressure. But virtue cannot be the primary defence against corruption, because it is unevenly distributed. The durable answer is to design systems that demand less virtue — by reducing discretion, auditing preventively and opening the record to citizens. Andhra Pradesh’s digital service delivery illustrates the principle: the surest way to eliminate a bribe is to eliminate the counter at which it was demanded.

- 2nd ARC, 4th Report — Ethics in Governance (2007): Ch. 2.7 Code of Ethics for Civil Servants; Ch. 4.3–4.4 Lok Pal and Lokayukta; Ch. 5.4 Social Audit; Ch. 6.6 Integrity Pacts; Ch. 6.7 Reducing Discretion; Ch. 6.12 Risk Management for Preventive Vigilance; Ch. 7 Protecting the Honest Civil Servant.
- 2nd ARC, 12th Report — Citizen Centric Administration (2009): Sevottam framework and the seven steps to citizen‑centricity.
- Legal framework: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 as amended in 2018 (bribe‑giving made a distinct offence; Section 17A prior approval); Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013; Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 (yet to be fully operationalised); PIDPI Resolution, 2004; All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968.
- Institutions: Santhanam Committee (1964) → CVC (statutory under the CVC Act, 2003); CBI under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946; State Lokayuktas; Anti‑Corruption Bureaus — the 2nd ARC recommended bringing State ACBs under State Vigilance Commissions.
- International: India ratified the UN Convention against Corruption in 2011; Article 8 of UNCAC obliges States to adopt codes of conduct for public officials.
- Classic formulation worth quoting: corruption = monopoly + discretion – accountability (Klitgaard).

Q126 | Section C, Q15 — Q. The Constitution of India grants certain rights to citizens and also provides measures to safeguard them. What are the key constitutional arrangements to ensure the protection of these rights? (APPSC, 2025)

Part III of the Constitution (Articles 12–35) guarantees Fundamental Rights, but the framers understood that a right without an enforceable remedy is a moral claim rather than a legal one. The Constitution therefore builds protection in layers — textual, remedial, doctrinal, institutional and emergency‑proof — so that rights survive not only ordinary legislation but also executive excess and abnormal times. Ambedkar called Article 32 ‘the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it’ (Constituent Assembly Debates, 9 December 1948).

Layer 1 — Textual supremacy: Article 13

- Article 13(2) bars the State from making any law that abridges Part III, and any such law is void to the extent of inconsistency. This is what elevates Fundamental Rights above ordinary law; pre‑Constitution laws inconsistent with Part III are similarly void under Article 13(1).

Layer 2 — Remedial guarantee: Articles 32 and 226

- Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right — uniquely, the remedy is a right. The Supreme Court may issue habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. Article 226 gives High Courts a wider power (both fundamental and other legal rights, and over a larger territorial reach), but it is a constitutional, not fundamental, right and is discretionary.
- The remedy has been made real, not formal: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979) read speedy trial into Article 21 and secured release of undertrials; Article 39A with the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 and NALSA supply free legal aid so that indigence does not bar access; and public interest litigation, relaxed locus standi and epistolary jurisdiction (S.P. Gupta, 1981) open the court to those who cannot come themselves.

Layer 3 — Doctrinal protection: judicial review and basic structure

- Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) held that Parliament’s amending power under Article 368 cannot destroy the basic structure. L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) confirmed that judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 is itself part of that basic structure — meaning the remedy cannot be amended away.

## Layer 4 — Institutional protection
- An independent judiciary: security of tenure and removal only by special majority (Articles 124 and 217), salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund, and a bar on legislative discussion of judicial conduct (Articles 121 and 211).
- Rights commissions: NHRC and State Human Rights Commissions under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993; NCSC (Article 338), NCST (Article 338A) and NCBC (Article 338B, inserted by the 102nd Amendment, 2018); NCW and NCPCR. AP anchor — the Andhra Pradesh State Human Rights Commission, headquartered at Kurnool, exercises these powers within the State.

## Layer 5 — Emergency‑proofing
- Article 359 permits suspension of enforcement of rights during a National Emergency, but the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 expressly excluded Articles 20 and 21 — life, liberty and the safeguards of the accused can never be suspended. This was the constitutional correction of ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976), which the nine‑judge bench in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) expressly overruled.

## A living instrument — current expansion
- M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024 INSC 280, 21 March 2024) recognised a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21. Pragya Prasun and Amar Jain v. Union of India (2025 INSC 599, 30 April 2025) held inclusive digital access to be intrinsic to Article 21 and issued directions to RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and DoT to make e‑KYC accessible — directly consequential for States like Andhra Pradesh that now route the bulk of citizen services through digital channels.
- Rights are protected, not absolute: Article 19(2)–(6) permits reasonable restrictions; Article 33 allows Parliament to modify rights for the armed forces; Article 34 covers martial law; and Article 35 reserves to Parliament alone the power to legislate on certain Part III matters.

Five‑layer shield diagram: innermost core = FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS, then concentric rings outward — Art. 13 (voidness) → Arts. 32/226 (remedy) → Basic Structure (doctrine) → Judiciary + Commissions (institutions) → 44th Amendment (emergency‑proofing).

Comparison table — Article 32 vs Article 226: Nature of right | Whose rights | Territorial reach | Discretionary? | Can be suspended?

## Conclusion

The Constitution protects rights not by a single device but by a layered architecture: Article 13 makes them superior to law, Article 32 makes them enforceable, the basic structure doctrine makes the enforcement un‑amendable, independent institutions make it routine, and the 44th Amendment makes life and liberty proof against Emergency. Recent expansion into climate and digital access shows Part III functioning as a living instrument. The remaining challenge is not doctrinal but practical — judicial delay and unequal access mean the strength of the remedy still varies with the resources of the claimant.

- The five writs in one line each: Habeas Corpus — produce the body, tests legality of detention, lies against the State and private persons; Mandamus — command a public authority to do its legal duty, not against a private person or the President/Governor; Prohibition — stop a lower court exceeding jurisdiction, preventive only, issued against judicial bodies; Certiorari — transfer or quash, both preventive and curative, now available against administrative authorities too; Quo Warranto — by what authority do you hold this public office, lies only for substantive public offices.
- Article 32 vs 226: 32 is a Fundamental Right, 226 a constitutional right; 32 only for Fundamental Rights, 226 for fundamental and other legal rights; SC cannot refuse relief under 32, HC discretion under 226; 32 can be suspended under Article 359 (except for Articles 20 and 21), 226 cannot.
- 44th Amendment Act, 1978: removed the right to property from Part III (now Article 300A), substituted ‘armed rebellion’ for ‘internal disturbance’ in Article 352, and shielded Articles 20 and 21 from suspension.
- Key cases to carry: A.K. Gopalan (1950) → Maneka Gandhi (1978) — from ‘procedure established by law’ to ‘fair, just and reasonable’; Kesavananda Bharati (1973); L. Chandra Kumar (1997); Puttaswamy (2017) — privacy plus the overruling of ADM Jabalpur; M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024); Pragya Prasun / Amar Jain (2025).
- Statutory layer: Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (amended 2019); Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987; Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016.
- AP institutions to name: AP State Human Rights Commission (Kurnool); AP State Legal Services Authority; AP State Commission for Women; AP Lokayukta.

## Introduction
The **Women's Reservation Bill** — enacted as the **106th Constitutional Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam), 2023** — reserves **one-third of seats** in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies for women; its long, contested journey reveals the deep politics of gender and representation.

## The politics of the Bill
- **The long delay**: first introduced in **1996**, it repeatedly lapsed over three decades amid political resistance.
- **The 'quota within quota' demand**: several parties insisted on **sub-reservation for OBC and minority women**, arguing that a flat quota would benefit only elite women — a key fault line.

## Significance
- Builds on the success of **50% reservation in local bodies** (73rd/74th Amendments) in deepening women's political agency.

## Conclusion
The Women's Reservation saga shows how **gender justice contends with caste, party and power calculations**. The 2023 Act is a historic step, but its **delayed implementation** and the unresolved OBC-quota question keep the politics of representation alive.

## Introduction
The Constitution provides several **guarantees for women** — reflecting the vision of substantive equality — and the **National Commission for Women (NCW)**, a statutory body, is charged with safeguarding and advancing their rights.

- **Equality**: Article 14 (equality before law), **Article 15(1)** (no discrimination on sex) and **Article 15(3)** (special provisions for women — enabling protective legislation).
- **Equal opportunity in employment** (Article 16); **equal pay for equal work** and humane conditions/maternity relief (**Articles 39(a), 39(d), 42** — DPSPs).

- A **statutory body (NCW Act, 1990)** to:
  - **Review** constitutional and legal safeguards for women and recommend reforms;
  - **Investigate** complaints of rights violations and take up cases of deprivation;
  - Inspect jails/remand homes, fund litigation, and advise government on policy.
- It has powers of a **civil court** for inquiries.

## Limitations
- **Recommendatory powers**, resource constraints, and dependence on the government — prompting calls for greater autonomy and teeth.

## Conclusion
The constitutional guarantees and the NCW together form India's framework for gender justice; strengthening the Commission's **independence and enforcement capacity** is key to translating formal equality into real empowerment.

- Its recommendations are **advisory**, it lacks investigative machinery of its own, and it depends on government funding and cooperation — limiting effectiveness.

## Conclusion
The NCW is a vital institutional voice for women's rights; empowering it with **binding powers, autonomy and resources** would help it move from a largely advisory role to an effective guardian of gender justice.

## Introduction
The **National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)** is India's apex statutory watchdog for the protection and promotion of human rights, established under the **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993**.

## Composition
- A **chairperson** (a former Chief Justice or Judge of the Supreme Court) and members including a serving/former SC or HC judge and persons with human-rights expertise; the chairpersons of key national commissions are *ex-officio* members.

## Powers and functions
- **Inquiry**: into complaints of human-rights violations or negligence by public servants, *suo motu* or on petition.
- **Civil-court powers**: summoning witnesses, examining evidence, requisitioning records during inquiries.
- **Intervention** in court proceedings involving human rights; **visiting** jails and detention centres to study living conditions.
- **Review** of constitutional and legal safeguards, study of treaties, research, and **human-rights literacy**.
- **Recommendations**: to government for relief/compensation, prosecution, and systemic reform.

## Limitations
- Its role is largely **recommendatory**; it **cannot inquire into armed-forces violations** except through reports; a **one-year limitation** on complaints; and dependence on government for action — hence the tag 'a toothless tiger'.

## Conclusion
The NHRC is a crucial institution for accountability and dignity; giving its recommendations **greater enforceability and independence** would strengthen India's human-rights architecture.

**Mission Karmayogi** — the National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building (2020) — is a landmark reform aimed at transforming the Indian bureaucracy from a **rule-based** to a **role-based**, citizen-centric and future-ready civil service.

- **Continuous, on-demand learning**: the **iGOT-Karmayogi** digital platform delivers anytime-anywhere training across the officer's career.

- Effective only if paired with **structural reforms** — fixed tenures, insulation from arbitrary transfers (*T.S.R. Subramanian*, 2013), performance appraisal, and political will; risk of it remaining a training portal without cultural change.

## Introduction
**Decentralisation** — the transfer of authority, functions and resources from central to local levels — is widely regarded as a **necessary tool for good governance**, bringing decision-making closer to the people it affects.

- **Participation and responsiveness**: local bodies (PRIs and ULBs under the 73rd/74th Amendments) let citizens shape decisions, improving the fit between policy and local needs.

## Introduction
The critique that 'the **Right to Information Act** is meant only for providing information but not grievance redressal' identifies a real design limit — yet understates how transparency itself has become a powerful, if indirect, instrument of accountability.

## The RTI Act's core purpose
- The **RTI Act, 2005** operationalises the citizen's right to information under **Article 19(1)(a)**, mandating disclosure within **30 days** and creating Information Commissions as appellate bodies.
- Its stated object is **transparency and accountability** in public authorities — **access to information**, not the redressal of individual service grievances.

## The valid part of the critique
- RTI **cannot compel** the provision of a service or the correction of a wrong; it only compels **disclosure**. Grievance redress requires other mechanisms — **CPGRAMS**, Citizen's Charters, **Public Service Guarantee Acts**, ombudsman/Lokayukta, and courts.

## Why the critique is only partly true
- Transparency is a **precondition** for accountability: RTI exposes corruption, delays and arbitrariness, empowering citizens to seek redress and deterring wrongdoing.
- It complements, rather than replaces, redress mechanisms — and dilutions (the **2019 amendment**, the **DPDP 2023** carve-out to Section 8(1)(j)) threaten even this role.

## Conclusion
The RTI is fundamentally a **transparency law, not a grievance-redress law** — the critique is accurate as to design. But by making governance visible, it is an **enabler of accountability**; pairing it with strong service-guarantee and grievance mechanisms delivers the full promise of responsive government.

- **Incomplete devolution of the 3 Fs** leaves local bodies without the funds, functions or staff to deliver.

- Genuine devolution, capacity building, technology-enabled last-mile delivery (e.g., AP's **Village/Ward Secretariats and Volunteers**, DBT), and robust social audit.

## Introduction

Article 21 is drafted as a negative injunction — no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty “except according to procedure established by law” — and the Constituent Assembly consciously rejected the American “due process” formula on B.N. Rau’s advice. In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) the Supreme Court read it as a bare procedural check. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) reversed that, importing substantive review through the requirement that any procedure be “fair, just and reasonable”. Article 21 thereby became the reservoir from which almost every unenumerated Fundamental Right is now drawn.

## Procedural expansion — due process imported by interpretation
- Maneka Gandhi (1978) fused Articles 14, 19 and 21 into the “golden triangle”, so a liberty-restricting law must simultaneously survive non-arbitrariness, reasonableness and fairness review. This is the doctrinal engine — without it, every later expansion would have been textually impossible.
- The immediate payoff was Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979), which made speedy trial part of Article 21 and ordered the release of undertrials rotting without hearing. That principle is now statutory: Section 479, BNSS 2023 (in force 1 July 2024) mandates release of first-time undertrials who have served one-third of the maximum sentence — a judicial doctrine converted into an executable entitlement.

## Civil-libertarian expansion — dignity, privacy and autonomy
- K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017, nine judges) located privacy within Article 21, supplying the constitutional foundation for the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Its significance is structural: it also expressly overruled ADM Jabalpur (1976), closing the Emergency-era hole in Article 21.
- Autonomy has been the fastest-moving frontier. Navtej Singh Johar (2018) read down Section 377 IPC on dignity grounds; Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) recognised the right to die with dignity and the living will. Both were applied in Harish Rana v. Union of India (Supreme Court, 11 March 2026), permitting withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment after thirteen years in a persistent vegetative state — proof that Article 21 now governs the end of life as well as its conduct.

## Socio-economic and ecological expansion — Article 21 read with Part IV
- Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) made livelihood integral to life, protecting pavement dwellers from summary eviction. Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) converted emergency medical care into a State obligation. Unnikrishnan (1993) forced the 86th Amendment (2002) inserting Article 21A and the RTE Act, 2009 — the clearest instance of a DPSP migrating into Part III through Article 21.
- The current frontier is ecological. In M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (21 March 2024) the Court derived a distinct “right against the adverse effects of climate change” from Articles 21 and 14, read with Article 48A and Article 51A(g) — significant because Article 14 was invoked on the ground that climate harm falls unequally on the coastal and the poor.

## Andhra Pradesh anchor — the administrative translation
- AP’s Universal Health Policy under Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva — cover of ₹25 lakh per family per year, extended from BPL households to all State residents with effect from 1 April 2026 (AP Health, Medical & Family Welfare Dept./Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva Trust) — is the executive counterpart of Paschim Banga. AP is also a Fifth Schedule State where Samatha v. State of AP (1997) applied Article 21 dignity reasoning to tribal land.

## Conclusion

Article 21 has functioned as the Constitution’s engine of transformation, converting non-justiciable Directive Principles into enforceable entitlements and validating the “living Constitution” thesis. The caveat is essential to a full-marks answer: Article 21 is not absolute — it yields to a fair, just and reasonable procedure, and even privacy is subject to the legality–necessity–proportionality test in Puttaswamy. Judicial recognition has now outrun administrative capacity; the deficit today is in enforcement, not in interpretation.

## Introduction

A.V. Dicey framed rule of law in three limbs — supremacy of law over arbitrary power, equality before the ordinary law administered by ordinary courts, and a constitution that is the consequence rather than the source of individual rights. India adopts the first two and inverts the third: here the Constitution is the source, and rule of law flows from it. The Supreme Court settled its status in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), holding rule of law to be part of the basic structure and therefore beyond the amending power.

## Supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review
- Article 13 voids any law inconsistent with Part III and defines ‘law’ expansively to include ordinances, bye-laws and custom — the textual hook for judicial review. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) extended the constraint to the amending power itself, so that even Parliament acting under Article 368 operates under law.
- The doctrine remains live. In Special Reference No. 1 of 2025 (November 2025) the Court recalibrated the position on gubernatorial assent to State Bills, demonstrating that constitutional silences too are policed by law rather than by convention alone.

## Equality and the bar on arbitrariness
- Article 14 is the Indian version of Dicey’s second limb. E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) and Maneka Gandhi (1978) converted it from a classification test into a substantive prohibition on arbitrariness — “equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies”. Shayara Bano (2017) applied this to strike down instant triple talaq as manifestly arbitrary.

## Legality of coercion, taxation and deprivation
- Articles 20, 21 and 22 prohibit ex post facto criminalisation, double jeopardy and self-incrimination, and require grounds of arrest and access to counsel. The D.K. Basu (1997) arrest safeguards are now codified in Sections 35 and 47, BNSS 2023.
- Article 265 bars any tax except by authority of law and Article 300A bars deprivation of property except by authority of law — the fiscal and proprietary faces of legality, routinely litigated and easily forgotten in exams.

## Institutional guarantees
- Independent judiciary (Articles 124–147, 214–231: security of tenure, charged salaries, removal only by address); CAG (Article 148); Election Commission (Article 324); UPSC and State PSCs (Articles 315–323). Rule of law needs enforcement capacity, not merely norms — the central argument of the 2nd ARC’s 4th Report, Ethics in Governance.

## Where India departs from Dicey — the ‘examine’ core
- **Departure** — Provision / authority · Effect on Dicey’s equality limb
- **Official immunity** — Article 361 — President and Governors · No criminal proceedings during term
- **Separate adjudication** — Articles 323A/323B tribunals · Displaces ‘ordinary courts’; L. Chandra Kumar (1997) preserved HC review
- **Legislative privilege** — Article 105/194 · Narrowed by Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024), overruling P.V. Narasimha Rao — no immunity for bribery
- **Preventive detention** — Article 22(3)–(7) · Detention without trial permitted, unique among major democracies

## Andhra Pradesh anchor
- Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997) is the sharpest AP illustration: the Court held that State leases of Scheduled Area land to private mining companies violated the AP Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation — executive convenience subordinated to statutory text, which is rule of law in operation.

## EXAM-HALL DIAGRAM

## Conclusion

The Indian Constitution does not merely permit rule of law; it institutionalises it as an unamendable feature and gives it teeth through Articles 13, 32 and 226. Yet the guarantee is qualified — preventive detention, official immunity and tribunalisation are conscious deviations from Dicey’s model. The decisive variable today is enforcement: over four crore cases pending in the district judiciary (National Judicial Data Grid, Department of Justice) mean that legality exists in principle while access to it is rationed in practice.

The official Indian instruments are the National Judicial Data Grid and the eCourts Mission Mode Project Phase III (Cabinet approval, September 2023, ₹7,210 crore).
- Rule of law as basic structure: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975); reaffirmed in Minerva Mills (1980) on judicial review as an unamendable feature.
- The Emergency counter-example: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976) suspended habeas corpus; expressly overruled in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) — a rare instance of the Court repudiating its own worst decision.
- Rule of law is not merely formal. In Maneka the Court insisted on substantive fairness; contrast Joseph Raz’s thin (formal) conception with the thick conception the Indian Court has adopted.
- SDG 16 — targets 16.3 (rule of law and equal access to justice), 16.5 (reduce corruption) and 16.6 (effective, accountable institutions) are the international measurement frame; India reports on these through the NITI Aayog SDG India Index.

## Introduction

Part XVI (Articles 330–342A), read with Articles 15, 16, 17, 46, 244 and 335, forms the Constitution’s architecture of compensatory discrimination. Dr. Ambedkar defended it in the Constituent Assembly as reconciling formal equality with the reality of historic exclusion. The design is functional rather than uniform: each community receives a distinct combination of identification, protection, compensation, political representation and monitoring, calibrated to the disability it faces.

## Scheduled Castes — disability of untouchability
- Identification: Article 341 — the President notifies the list for each State by public notification; only Parliament may include or exclude a caste thereafter, insulating the list from State-level political pressure.
- Protective: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes its practice an offence, operationalised by the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC & ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 with its exclusive Special Courts.
- Compensatory: Articles 15(4) and 16(4); Article 16(4A) (77th Amendment, 1995) permits reservation in promotion with consequential seniority; Article 16(4B) (81st Amendment, 2000) removes carry-forward vacancies from the 50 per cent ceiling; Article 15(5) (93rd Amendment, 2005) extends reservation to private unaided institutions; Article 335 imports the efficiency caveat.
- Political and monitoring: Articles 330, 332, 243D and 243T — 84 Lok Sabha seats and 47 ST seats are reserved under the Delimitation Order, 2008, which is based on the 2001 Census, not 2011. Article 338 establishes the NCSC with civil-court powers of enquiry.
- Live development: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (1 August 2024, seven judges, 6:1) held sub-classification within the SC list constitutionally permissible under Articles 14, 15(4) and 16(4), provided there is intelligible differentia with a rational nexus — overruling E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2004).

## Scheduled Tribes — disability of geographic and cultural isolation
- Identification under Article 342; territorial governance under Article 244 — the Fifth Schedule for Scheduled Areas in ten States, with the Governor’s regulation-making power over land transfer and money-lending and a Tribes Advisory Council; the Sixth Schedule for Autonomous District Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
- Statutory extension: PESA, 1996 vests the Gram Sabha in Scheduled Areas with authority over minor forest produce, land alienation and consultation before acquisition; the Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognises individual and community forest rights. Article 275(1) provides grants-in-aid for tribal welfare; Article 338A creates the NCST (89th Amendment, 2003).
- AP anchor: Andhra Pradesh is a Fifth Schedule State — STs are 5.5 per cent of the State’s population (Census 2011) across 19 notified tribes including six PVTGs (Chenchu, Kondareddi, Savara, Gadaba, Porja, Kondh). The AP Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation, 1959 as amended by Regulation 1 of 1970 — the ‘1/70 Act’ — bars transfer of land to non-tribals; Samatha v. State of AP (1997) extended the bar to State mining leases.

## Backward Classes — disability of social and educational backwardness
- Articles 15(4) and 16(4) enable reservation; Article 340 empowers appointment of a Backward Classes Commission (Kaka Kalelkar, 1953; Mandal, 1979); Article 46 directs promotion of educational and economic interests as a DPSP.
- Implementation sequence matters. The Office Memorandum of 13 August 1990 implementing Mandal gave 27 per cent in central government services ONLY. Reservation in central educational institutions came later, via Article 15(5) (93rd Amendment, 2005) and the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006, upheld in Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (2008).
- Indra Sawhney (1992) fixed the 50 per cent ceiling, mandated creamy-layer exclusion, and barred OBC reservation in promotions. The 102nd Amendment (2018) inserted Article 338B (NCBC given constitutional status) and Article 342A (Central List of SEBCs); the 105th Amendment (2021) restored the States’ power to maintain their own SEBC lists. The 103rd Amendment (2019) added Articles 15(6) and 16(6) for 10 per cent EWS reservation, upheld 3:2 in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022).
- AP anchor: AP sub-categorises Backward Classes into Groups A to E, with Group E covering socially and educationally backward Muslim classes — an early instance of the sub-classification logic the Supreme Court endorsed in 2024. The AP Commission for Backward Classes is a statutory body under Article 340 jurisprudence.

## Anglo-Indians — disability of numerical dispersal
- Article 331: the President may nominate not more than two Anglo-Indians to the Lok Sabha. Article 333: the Governor may nominate one Anglo-Indian to a State Legislative Assembly. Articles 336 and 337 provided transitional reservation in certain services and educational grants, now spent.
- Article 334, as substituted by the Constitution (104th Amendment) Act, 2019 (in force 25 January 2020), extended SC and ST seat reservation to 25 January 2030 but did NOT extend Anglo-Indian nomination — which therefore lapsed on 25 January 2020. The Government cited the 2011 Census figure of 296 self-identified Anglo-Indians in the Lok Sabha debate of 10 December 2019.

## EXAM-HALL DIAGRAM

## Conclusion

The constitutional design is deliberately asymmetric: untouchability is met with prohibition, isolation with territorial autonomy, backwardness with quantifiable quotas, and dispersal with nomination. Its trajectory has been one of continuous constitutionalisation — commissions turned into constitutional bodies, quotas extended, and after Davinder Singh (2024), homogeneity within categories abandoned in favour of graded targeting. The unresolved tensions remain the 50 per cent ceiling, the absence of a caste census to update the empirical base, and the persistent gap between reserved posts and posts actually filled.

## Introduction

Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression to citizens. Justice Patanjali Sastri described it in Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950) as the foundation of all democratic organisation, since without free political discussion no public education, and hence no proper functioning of popular government, is possible. Its Indian development has been almost entirely judicial: the constitutional text is a single clause, but seven decades of interpretation have extracted from it a family of derived rights, each with its own limits under Article 19(2).

## Scope — rights derived from a single clause
- Freedom of the press has no separate mention and is read into 19(1)(a). Romesh Thappar (1950) struck down a circulation ban; Bennett Coleman v. Union of India (1973) held that even an indirect measure — a newsprint quota — is unconstitutional if its effect abridges expression, establishing the ‘effect, not form’ test.
- The right to know is the most consequential derivation. State of UP v. Raj Narain (1975) held citizens entitled to know what public functionaries do; Union of India v. ADR (2002) and PUCL (2003) made candidate antecedents disclosable; the RTI Act, 2005 is the statutory codification of this line.
- Also derived: commercial speech (Tata Press v. MTNL, 1995); the right to silence and against compelled expression (Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala, 1986 — the national anthem case); the right to cast a negative vote (PUCL, 2013 — NOTA); and the right to fly the national flag (Union of India v. Naveen Jindal, 2004).

## Nature — non-absolute, citizen-only, and closed-ground
- Kaushal Kishor v. State of UP (3 January 2023, Constitution Bench) is now the controlling authority on two points. First, the grounds in Article 19(2) are exhaustive — no additional restriction may be imposed by invoking Article 21 dignity as a competing right. Second, by 4:1 (Nagarathna J. dissenting), Articles 19 and 21 are enforceable horizontally against non-State actors, which matters enormously where private platforms mediate speech.

## Emerging dimensions — with the instruments that give them content
- Digital speech and intermediary liability: Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A, IT Act for vagueness and chilling effect and read down Sections 69A and 79. Regulation has since moved from post-facto takedown to ex-ante classification — the IT Rules, 2021, and the Ministry of Information & Broadcasting’s draft IT Rules of early 2026 proposing age-based classification and limits on explicit content across digital platforms.
- Internet as the infrastructure of speech: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) held indefinite suspension disproportionate, burdening both 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g), and required shutdown orders to be published, reasoned and periodically reviewed.
- Speech offences after the criminal-law overhaul: with the BNS, 2023 in force from 1 July 2024, promoting enmity moved from IPC Sections 153A/295A to BNS Sections 196, 197 and 299, and sedition under IPC 124A — kept in abeyance in S.G. Vombatkere (May 2022) — was recast as BNS Section 152 on acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity. In Imran Pratapgarhi v. State of Gujarat (March 2025) the Court quashed an FIR over a recited poem, holding that mens rea to promote enmity must be shown and that police must judge speech by the standard of a reasonable, strong-minded person, not the hypersensitive.
- Privacy, data and AI: Puttaswamy (2017) produced the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, whose amendment of Section 8(1)(j), RTI Act has itself been criticised as narrowing the right to know. MeitY’s India AI Governance Guidelines under the IndiaAI Mission now bring deepfakes and content provenance directly into the 19(1)(a) debate.

## Andhra Pradesh anchor — the right to know, applied
- The PUCL/ADR jurisprudence is not abstract in AP. In the simultaneous elections of May 2024, all 2,387 Assembly candidates and 454 Lok Sabha candidates in Andhra Pradesh filed Form 26 affidavits disclosing assets, liabilities, education and criminal antecedents (Election Commission of India, 2024) — a disclosure regime that exists solely because the Court read a right to know into Article 19(1)(a).

## EXAM-HALL DIAGRAM

## Conclusion

Freedom of speech in India has travelled from protecting the pamphlet and the newspaper to governing algorithmic amplification and synthetic media. Its nature has stayed constant — a citizen’s right, non-absolute, restrictable only on eight closed grounds — while its scope has expanded through derivation. The contemporary challenge is institutional rather than doctrinal: restrictions today operate through intermediaries, takedown orders and classification rules rather than through prosecutions, which makes the proportionality discipline of Anuradha Bhasin, and the exhaustiveness rule of Kaushal Kishor, the decisive safeguards.

## Value addition
- Amendment history of Article 19(2): the First Amendment (1951) added public order, friendly relations with foreign States and incitement to an offence, and inserted the word ‘reasonable’; the Sixteenth Amendment (1963) added sovereignty and integrity of India — eight grounds in all.
- Availability: Article 19(1)(a) is citizen-only. A company has no such right, though its shareholder-editors do — Bennett Coleman (1973).
- Hate speech has no statutory definition. Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan (2014) referred the gap to the Law Commission, which recommended new offences in its 267th Report (2017); the recommendation remains unimplemented.
- The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 creates a right to erasure (Section 12) but India still has no judicially settled ‘right to be forgotten’, and High Courts have taken divergent views.
- Obscenity standard: the Hicklin test of Ranjit D. Udeshi (1964) was replaced by the contemporary community standards test in Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal (2014).
- SDG 16.10 — ensure public access to information and protect fundamental freedoms — is the international benchmark; the 2nd ARC’s 1st Report (Right to Information) treats information access as the operational face of Article 19(1)(a).

## Introduction

The classification is not academic — it determines the remedy. A fundamental right is enforceable directly under Article 32 and can be curtailed only within Part III limits; a constitutional right is enforceable but shaped by constitutional design; a statutory right may be modified by ordinary legislation and is contested chiefly through election petitions. Indian courts have consistently classified the act of voting as statutory, while progressively constitutionalising the environment in which it is exercised.

## The orthodox position — a statutory right
- Article 326 mandates adult suffrage for the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies but confers no personal, enforceable right; it sets the franchise standard and leaves disqualification grounds — non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime, corrupt practice — to be defined by law. The operative right is Section 62, RPA 1951, exercisable only if the elector’s name appears on the roll prepared under RPA 1950.
- N.P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer (1952) held the right to vote and to stand are creatures of statute; Jyoti Basu v. Debi Ghosal (1982) put it most sharply — “a statutory right, nothing more, nothing less”; and Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006) reaffirmed this while upholding the open ballot in Rajya Sabha elections.
- The consequence is concrete. Section 62(5), RPA 1951 disenfranchises persons in prison or in lawful police custody, upheld in Anukul Chandra Pradhan v. Union of India (1997) on grounds of resource constraint and the ‘criminalisation of politics’ — a restriction that would face far stricter scrutiny if voting were a fundamental right.

## The constitutional-right counter-strand
- The periphery of voting is already constitutionalised. PUCL v. Union of India (2003) held the right to know candidates’ antecedents a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a) though the act of voting is statutory; PUCL (2013) held the right to cast a negative vote (NOTA) protected as expression under 19(1)(a) read with the secrecy guarantee in Section 128, RPA 1951. The manner of voting is thus a fundamental right even where the right itself is not.
- Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2 March 2023, Constitution Bench) went further. The majority anchored free and fair elections in the basic structure and prescribed an interim collegium for CEC and EC appointments; Justice Ajay Rastogi, concurring, held that voting is a constitutional right traceable to Article 326, its exercise protected by Article 19(1)(a). This is now the leading authority for the elevation argument.

## The 2025–26 revival — the roll becomes the battleground
- The Election Commission announced a nationwide Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls on 27 October 2025, with Phase I in Bihar completed in September 2025 and Phase II across nine States and three UTs completed in April 2026. Because the statutory right operates only through the roll, inclusion became the practical locus of the right.
- In its judgment of 27 May 2026 (Chief Justice Surya Kant, with Bagchi and Pancholi JJ.), the Supreme Court upheld SIR as within Article 324 read with Section 21(3), RPA 1950; applied the proportionality test and found the exercise not manifestly excessive; held the ECI competent to examine citizenship under Section 16, RPA 1950 for roll purposes; and clarified that exclusion from a roll affects only electoral entitlement, not citizenship, which remains for the competent authority under the Citizenship Act. The Court reiterated that free and fair elections are basic structure.

## Andhra Pradesh anchor
- Andhra Pradesh recorded 81.86 per cent turnout across its 175 Assembly constituencies in the simultaneous polls of 13 May 2024, against a national Lok Sabha turnout of 65.79 per cent (Election Commission of India, 2024), with roughly 4.13 crore electors on the roll. The contrast shows that the statutory character of the right has in no way diminished its democratic salience — and that roll accuracy, not legal status, is the operative constraint.

- **Fundamental** — Not in Part III · Rejected — Kuldip Nayar (2006) · No Article 32 remedy for denial of the vote itself

## Conclusion

The settled position is that the right to vote is a statutory right resting on a constitutional foundation: Article 326 supplies the mandate, the Representation of the People Acts supply the enforceable right, and

Article 19(1)(a) protects its informational and expressive periphery. But the direction of travel is towards constitutionalisation. Anoop Baranwal (2023) and the SIR judgment of May 2026 both locate electoral participation within the basic structure, and Justice Rastogi’s reasoning provides a ready foundation should a future bench reconsider the question.

## Value addition
- CORRECTION (booklet): Rajbala v. State of Haryana (2016) concerned educational and sanitation qualifications for CONTESTING panchayat elections, not the elector’s right to vote. It is not authority on the nature of the right to vote and should not be cited for that proposition.
- Article 325 is distinct from Article 326 and is genuinely enforceable: no person may be excluded from an electoral roll on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex. This is the constitutional guarantee most directly engaged by roll-revision litigation.
- The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18. Globally, Austria, Malta, Argentina and Brazil permit voting at 16, and the United Kingdom announced a move to 16 in 2025; a private member’s Constitution (Amendment) Bill, 2020 proposed 17 for India.
- Article 329(b) bars any court from interfering once the election process begins — the only remedy is an election petition to the High Court under Sections 80–81, RPA 1951 (Ponnuswami, 1952).
- ECI inclusion measures worth citing: home voting for electors aged 85 and above and for persons with disabilities, operationalised in General Election 2024; and the Remote Voting Machine prototype (ECI, 2023) for domestic migrants, still awaiting political consensus.
- SDG 16.7 — responsive, inclusive, participatory and representative decision-making — is the reporting benchmark; the 2nd ARC’s 4th Report (Ethics in Governance) and the Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) both treat roll accuracy as the precondition of a meaningful franchise.
