Q133  Section C | Booklet Q22 Discuss the scope of special provisions for Backward Classes and the test to determine Backward Classes. Discuss the difference in the scope of provisions under Article 15(4) and 16(4). (TGPSC, 2016)

Articles 15(4) and 16(4) are not carve-outs from the equality code but its enabling limbs. Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) settled that Article 16(4) is a facet of Article 16(1), not an exception to it — because formal equality among unequals entrenches disadvantage. Article 46 supplies the constitutional goal, Articles 15 and 16 the instruments, and judicially-crafted tests the discipline that keeps protective discrimination from becoming open-ended.

1. Scope of Special Provisions: An Expanding Architecture

- Article 15(4) — the founding enabler. Inserted by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 to overcome State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951), which had struck down communal reservation in education. It is enabling, not mandatory — the State may, but need not, act. This is why courts have consistently refused to treat reservation as a fundamental right of the beneficiary.
- Article 15(5) — reach into the private sector. Added by the 93rd Amendment, 2005, it extends reservation to private unaided educational institutions, excluding minority institutions. Upheld in Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (2008), which simultaneously read the creamy-layer filter into OBC reservation in central educational institutions — showing that widening reach was paired with tightening targeting.
- Articles 15(6) and 16(6) — the economic axis. The 103rd Amendment, 2019 created a 10% quota for Economically Weaker Sections, upheld 3:2 in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022). Its significance is doctrinal: economic disadvantage alone became a permissible ground of classification, and the 50% ceiling was held not to be inviolable for a quota drawn outside the SC/ST/OBC pool.
- Articles 16(4), 16(4A), 16(4B) — the employment cluster. Article 16(4) enables reservation in appointments for backward classes 'not adequately represented'. Article 16(4A) (77th Amendment, 1995) permits reservation in promotion for SCs/STs with consequential seniority; Article 16(4B) (81st Amendment, 2000) de-links carried-forward backlog vacancies from the annual 50% cap.
- Institutional scaffolding. The 102nd Amendment, 2018 inserted Articles 338B (constitutional NCBC) and 342A. The 105th Amendment, 2021 then inserted Article 342A(3), expressly restoring the power of States and UTs to prepare their own SEBC lists after Dr. Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil (Maratha quota, 2021) had read that power away — protecting roughly 671 State-listed communities (Constitution (105th Amendment) Act, Gazette of India, 19 August 2021).

## Tests to Determine Backward Classes
- Social and educational backwardness (M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore, 1963). Backwardness must be demonstrably social and educational; caste cannot be the sole determinant. Balaji also first articulated the 50% ceiling, reasoning that a 'special provision' that swallows the general rule ceases to be special.
- Creamy layer and the ceiling (Indra Sawhney, 1992). Caste may legitimately be the starting point for identifying a class; the economically advanced within OBCs must be excluded so that benefits reach the genuinely disadvantaged; and reservation must ordinarily stay within 50% except in extraordinary circumstances.
- Quantifiable data on inadequacy (M. Nagaraj, 2006; Jarnail Singh, 2018 and 2022). For promotion quotas the State must collect cadre-specific data on inadequacy of representation and weigh administrative efficiency under Article 335. Jarnail Singh clarified that no fresh proof of SC/ST backwardness is needed, but applied creamy layer to promotions.
- Sub-classification permitted (State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh, 1 August 2024). A seven-judge Bench held 6:1 that sub-classification within the Scheduled Castes is constitutionally permissible, expressly overruling E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2004) which had treated SCs as a homogeneous class.
- AP anchor. Acting on Davinder Singh, Andhra Pradesh constituted a One-Man Commission under Rajiv Ranjan Mishra, IAS (Retd.) (G.O.Ms.No.86, Social Welfare (CV) Dept., 15.11.2024) and enacted the Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Castes (Sub-classification) Act, 2025. It divides 59 SC sub-castes into three groups and splits the 15% quota as Group-I 1%, Group-II 6.5% and Group-III 7.5%, operated through a 200-point roster in two cycles, deemed effective from 17 April 2025 (AP Gazette, Part IV-A Extraordinary, 23 September 2025).

3. Difference in Scope: Article 15(4) vs Article 16(4)

- Field of operation. Article 15(4) covers 'advancement' generally, and above all education; Article 16(4) is confined to appointments and posts under the State. Fee waivers, scholarships and hostels are 15(4) measures; a reserved vacancy is a 16(4) measure.
- Trigger condition. Article 15(4) needs only social and educational backwardness. Article 16(4) adds a second, evidence-based threshold — inadequate representation in the services of the State — which is why employment quotas are more vulnerable to data-based challenge than educational ones.
- Beneficiary class and caveats. Article 15(4) names SEBCs, SCs and STs; Article 16(4) uses the wider phrase 'any backward class of citizens'. Article 335's efficiency caveat attaches to 16(4) claims, not to 15(4). Consequently 15(4) is broader in subject-matter, while 16(4) is deeper in evidentiary burden.

## Conclusion

The scope of special provisions has widened steadily — from education to private institutions, from caste to economic criteria, from appointment to promotion, and from the Union to the States. What has kept this expansion constitutional is the parallel tightening of tests: demonstrable backwardness, creamy-layer exclusion, quantifiable inadequacy and now calibrated sub-classification. Andhra Pradesh's 2025 sub-classification statute shows the model working as designed — a State using restored federal space to target benefits more finely, within judicially-set limits.

- NCBC: statutory since the NCBC Act, 1993 (Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment); constitutional since the 102nd Amendment, 2018 (Article 338B). Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three Members appointed by the President; reports laid before Parliament with an action-taken memorandum.
- Ceiling exceptions: Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation survives through insertion in the Ninth Schedule (76th Amendment, 1994), though I.R. Coelho (2007) made Ninth Schedule entries after 24 April 1973 open to basic-structure review.
- Mandal: the Second Backward Classes Commission (B.P. Mandal, 1979) reported in 1980; 27% central OBC quota implemented from 1990 and upheld in Indra Sawhney.
- AP's own history: the Anantharaman Commission (1968) produced the State's first SEBC list; AP later grouped BCs into Groups A–E, an early instance of the sub-classification logic the Supreme Court validated only in 2024.
- Article 371D: AP additionally operates a constitutionally sanctioned 'local area' classification for education and public employment under the Presidential Order, 1975 — a reservation-adjacent provision unique to the State.

Q134  Section C | Booklet Q23 Explain the Right to Equality guaranteed under the Constitution of India in the light of the doctrine of reasonable classification. (APPSC, 2012)

Article 14 carries two distinct guarantees. 'Equality before law' is Dicey's negative idea — no person is above the law and none enjoys special privilege. 'Equal protection of the laws', borrowed from the Fourteenth Amendment of the US Constitution, is positive — likes must be treated alike. As State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976) recognised, treating unequals equally is itself a form of inequality. The doctrine of reasonable classification is the judicial tool that keeps this distinction workable.

## The Classical Two-Pronged Test
- Origin and content.State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) struck down Section 5 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act because it let the executive send any case to a special court without any stated principle — uncanalised discretion is the paradigm Article 14 violation. Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice Tendolkar (1958) then systematised the test into two conditions.
- Intelligible differentia. The classification must rest on a real, identifiable distinction between those grouped in and those left out. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 treats persons under eighteen as a separate class because their culpability and reformability genuinely differ — the differentia is intelligible, not arbitrary.
- Rational nexus with the object of the law. The distinction must actually serve the statute's purpose. Progressive slabs under the Income-tax Act, 2025 (in force from 1 April 2026, replacing the 1961 Act) classify by income because ability to pay is rationally connected to the object of equitable revenue mobilisation. A differentia that is real but irrelevant to the object still fails.

2. From Classification to Arbitrariness: The Doctrinal Shift

- E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974). Justice Bhagwati held that equality is 'antithetic to arbitrariness' — Article 14 is not merely a rule for sorting people into valid boxes but a substantive guarantee against arbitrary State action. This freed Article 14 from the formalism of the classification test, which a cleverly drafted law could always satisfy.
- Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978). By requiring that any procedure be 'right, just and fair', the Court fused Articles 14, 19 and 21 into a single reasonableness enquiry — the golden triangle. Arbitrariness in substance, not just in classification, became reviewable.
- Manifest arbitrariness in practice.Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) struck down talaq-e-biddat as manifestly arbitrary because it permitted the irrevocable rupture of a marriage on caprice, without any attempt at reconciliation. Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) struck down Section 497 IPC for treating a wife as her husband's property, and Navtej Singh Johar (2018) read down Section 377 on the same reasoning.

## Where Classifications Fail — and Where They Survive
- Struck down. In Air India v. Nergesh Meerza (1981) the rule terminating air hostesses on first pregnancy was held 'callous and cruel' — the differentia bore no nexus with fitness to work. In Subramanian Swamy v. CBI (2014) Section 6A of the DSPE Act, requiring prior approval to investigate officers of Joint Secretary rank and above, was struck down: seniority has no rational connection to the object of detecting corruption.
- Upheld.Indra Sawhney (1992) sustained caste-based OBC identification as an intelligible differentia; Janhit Abhiyan (2022) sustained purely economic criteria under the 103rd Amendment. Both show that a classification serving substantive equality survives even where it produces unequal treatment on its face.
- AP anchor. Article 371D, operationalised by the Presidential Order of 1975, classifies Andhra Pradesh by 'local area' for admissions and State employment. But for Article 371D such residence-based preference would offend Article 16(2). It survives as a textbook classification — the differentia (historic regional imbalance between Coastal Andhra, Rayalaseema and the erstwhile Telangana districts) is intelligible, and the nexus (balanced regional development) is rational. The AP Administrative Tribunal, created under the same Article, is its adjudicatory forum.

## Conclusion

Article 14 does not demand uniformity; it demands justification. The classification test asks whether the State's line-drawing is rational, and the arbitrariness test asks whether it is fair even when rational. Read together, they let the State pursue substantive justice — through reservation, progressive taxation or protective labour law — while denying it any power to act on caprice. That combination is what makes Article 14 the operative guarantee of the rule of law in India.

- Exceptions to Article 14: Article 361 (immunity of President and Governors from court process during office); Articles 105 and 194 (parliamentary and legislative privileges); immunity of foreign diplomats and of the UN and its agencies under the United Nations (Privileges and Immunities) Act, 1947.
- Class legislation vs reasonable classification: the former is forbidden, the latter permitted — the distinction drawn in Anwar Ali Sarkar and still the standard opening line of any Article 14 answer.
- Dicey's three elements of the rule of law: absence of arbitrary power; equality before law; the Constitution as the result of ordinary law of the land. India adopts the first two; the third is inverted, since rights flow from the Constitution.
- Doctrine of legitimate expectation and non-arbitrariness extends Article 14 into administrative action — relevant to service and tender disputes and a frequent Section-B crossover.
- Recent:Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (nine-judge Bench, November 2024) confirmed that economic-governance choices are for the elected legislature so long as they clear the Article 14 reasonableness threshold.

Q135  Section C | Booklet Q24 Critically examine different models of Secularism in India. (TGPSC, 2024)

Indian secularism is not a wall of separation but a relationship of regulated engagement. The State neither has a religion nor privileges one, yet it may enter religious affairs to secure social reform. Although the word 'secular' entered the Preamble only through the 42nd Amendment, 1976, the Supreme Court in Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India (25 November 2024) dismissed challenges to that insertion, holding secularism to have been inherent in the constitutional scheme from the outset.

## Equal Respect / Neutral State Model (Sarva Dharma Sambhava)
- The State treats all faiths alike and privileges none. Its footing is Article 14, Article 15(1), Article 25 (freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation), Article 26 (management of religious affairs), Article 27 (no citizen compelled to pay taxes for promotion of any particular religion) and Article 28 (no religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions).
- Critique: neutrality assumes parity of social power. Where communities are hierarchically placed, formal even-handedness can freeze existing disadvantage — which is precisely why the framers refused to stop at neutrality and wrote Article 17 and Article 25(2)(b) into the same chapter.

## Principled Distance Model (Rajeev Bhargava)
- The State keeps a variable, principle-governed distance: it may intervene in one religion and abstain in another, depending on what constitutional morality requires. Article 17 abolishes untouchability; Article 25(2)(a) lets the State regulate secular activity associated with religious practice; Article 25(2)(b) permits throwing open Hindu religious institutions to all classes.
- AP anchor: the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987 (Act 30 of 1987, India Code) vests administration of temples and endowments in a State Endowments Department, which classifies institutions by income under Section 6 and appoints trustee boards under Section 15. The Dhoopa Deepa Naivedyam scheme funds poojas and archaka remuneration at low-income temples. This is principled distance in operation — the State manages the secular administration of religious property without professing the faith.
- Critique: the doctrine's flexibility is also its weakness. Because the State decides when to step in, uneven intervention across communities invites the charge of selectivity, and the Endowments model has no exact parallel for other faiths.

## Assertive / Reformist Secularism
- Here the State actively reforms practices that offend constitutional values. Shayara Bano (2017) invalidated instantaneous triple talaq, followed by the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019. Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (Sabarimala, 2018) held exclusion of women of menstruating age unconstitutional.
- Critique: the reference in Kantaru Rajeevaru (2020) to a nine-judge Bench, still pending, shows how contested this model is. It also depends on the essential religious practices test from Shirur Mutt (1954), which obliges judges to decide what a religion essentially requires — a theological enquiry courts are institutionally ill-suited to perform.

## Accommodative Secularism / Contextual Pluralism
- The State protects group-differentiated rights: Article 29 shields cultural and linguistic minorities, Article 30 guarantees minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions. In Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (November 2024) a seven-judge Bench overruled the test in Azeez Basha (1967), holding that statutory incorporation does not by itself defeat minority character.
- Critique: plural personal laws sustain identity but sit uneasily with Article 44's directive on a uniform civil code and can entrench gender-differentiated outcomes within communities.

## The Constitutional Floor
- In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) a nine-judge Bench held secularism to be part of the basic structure and made a State government's anti-secular conduct a valid ground for action under Article 356. Abhiram Singh v. C.D. Commachen (2017) reinforced this electorally by reading Section 123(3) of the RP Act, 1951 to bar appeals on grounds of the religion of the candidate or the voter.

## Conclusion

Indian secularism is best described not as one model but as a repertoire, selected contextually. Its coherence comes from a shared objective — that religion shall not determine citizenship, entitlement or dignity — rather than from a single rule of State-religion relations. The Supreme Court's affirmation in Balram Singh (2024) confirms that this contextual model is settled constitutional doctrine; the continuing task is applying it consistently across communities so that engagement never looks like partiality.

- Constituent Assembly: K.T. Shah's amendment to insert 'secular' into Article 1 was rejected; Ambedkar's position was that the Constitution's substantive provisions already secured secularism without the label.
- Article 25, Explanation II: reference to Hindus includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists — a textual point examiners test directly.
- Article 30(1A) (44th Amendment, 1978) requires that compensation for compulsory acquisition of minority educational institution property must not restrict the guaranteed right.
- Article 44 in practice: Uttarakhand became the first State to operationalise a Uniform Civil Code, brought into force on 27 January 2025 — a live test case for the tension between accommodative and assertive models.
- AP specifics: Endowments Act, 1987 (Act 30 of 1987); Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams governed by a separate statutory framework; Erragudi in Kurnool district carries Ashokan Rock Edicts whose message of respect across sects is India's earliest articulation of Sarva Dharma Sambhava — a distinctive AP-specific opening or closing line.

Q136  Section C | Booklet Q25 Analyse the effectiveness of the implementation of the Directive Principles of State Policy and suggest ways to improve it. (APPSC, 2016)

Articles 36–51 embody the socio-economic conscience of the Constitution. Article 37 makes them non-justiciable yet declares them 'fundamental in the governance of the country', binding the State to apply them in law-making. Their record is therefore best judged not by enforceability but by translation — how far directives have become statutes, statutes become entitlements, and entitlements become outcomes.

1. Legislative Translation: Substantial but Uneven

- Education (Article 45, later Article 21A). The 86th Amendment, 2002 converted a directive into a fundamental right, operationalised by the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009. This is the clearest case of a DPSP achieving justiciable status — the directive supplied the goal and the amendment supplied the remedy.
- Livelihood and food (Articles 41 and 47). The National Food Security Act, 2013 covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population. The employment guarantee, long carried by MGNREGA, 2005, is now recast: the Viksit Bharat–Gramin Rozgar Aur Aajeevika Mission Gramin (VB-G RAM G) Act, 2025 replaces it with effect from 1 July 2026 — an update every answer on Article 41 must now carry.
- Local self-government (Article 40). The 73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992 converted a Gandhian directive into constitutional obligation. In Andhra Pradesh the Grama and Ward Sachivalayam system, staffed by permanent functionaries and Volunteers, delivers over five hundred services at the habitation level — arguably the most literal institutional reading of Article 40 by any State.

## Structural and Institutional Constraints
- Fiscal dependence. Welfare directives compete with committed expenditure. The Sixteenth Finance Commission report, tabled in February 2026, retained vertical devolution at 41% but discontinued Revenue Deficit Grants — tightening the space within which States finance Article 41 and 47 commitments. AP's own social security outgo under the NTR Bharosa Pension Scheme illustrates the scale of the obligation.
- Non-justiciability and political cycles. Because no citizen can compel compliance, directives are vulnerable to short-termism. Article 47's directive on prohibition of intoxicating drinks is the sharpest illustration: AP's phased prohibition policy has repeatedly been calibrated against excise revenue, showing how a directive yields when it collides with fiscal necessity.
- Capacity and last-mile delivery. Article 47's health mandate is delivered through the National Health Mission, where outcomes vary widely by district. AP's Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva scheme and the AP Public Services Delivery Guarantee Act, 2017 attempt to convert directive-based welfare into time-bound, claimable service — a partial substitute for justiciability.

## Judicial Elevation
- Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) held that harmony and balance between Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure — neither has primacy. Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993), an AP-origin case, read the right to education into Article 21 and directly precipitated the 86th Amendment.
- Environment (Article 48A). In M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024 INSC 280) the Court read a right against the adverse effects of climate change into Articles 14 and 21, expressly drawing on Articles 48A and 51A(g) — the most recent example of a directive supplying the content of a fundamental right.
- Limits of elevation.Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (nine-judge Bench, November 2024) held that not every privately owned resource is a 'material resource of the community' under Article 39(b), signalling that judicial expansion of DPSPs has an outer boundary.

## Suggestions for Strengthening Implementation
- Selective statutory enforceability. Follow the RTE template for Article 47 health entitlements, converting directives into claimable rights with defined standards and grievance machinery.
- Outcome-linked monitoring. Map DPSP goals onto the SDG India Index framework, where India's composite score stood at 71 in 2023-24 (NITI Aayog, SDG India Index 2023-24, July 2024), and publish an annual DPSP progress statement alongside it — the Aspirational Districts Programme shows the method works.
- Service-guarantee legislation in every State. AP's Public Services Delivery Guarantee Act, 2017 makes specified services deliverable within stated timelines with penalties for default — a practical substitute for justiciability that other States can replicate.
- Legal literacy and demand-side pressure. NALSA's JAGRITI Scheme, 2025 links legal services institutions to local self-government bodies, equipping citizens to claim welfare entitlements rather than wait for them.

## Conclusion

The DPSPs have been substantially, though unevenly, realised. Their greatest successes came where a directive was converted into an enforceable right — Article 45 through the 86th Amendment, Article 40 through the 73rd and 74th Amendments. Their persistent weakness lies where implementation depends on fiscal room and administrative capacity alone. The way forward is not to make Part IV wholly justiciable, but to keep converting its most urgent directives into time-bound, claimable entitlements, as Andhra

Pradesh has attempted through its 2017 service-guarantee statute.

- Gandhian directives: village panchayats (Art. 40); cottage industries (Art. 43); prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs (Art. 47); organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry and prohibition of cow slaughter (Art. 48); promotion of SC/ST and weaker sections' interests (Art. 46).
- Added by later amendments: Article 39A (free legal aid), 43A (workers' participation in management) and 48A (environment) by the 42nd Amendment, 1976; Article 38(2) (minimising inequalities in income, status and opportunity) by the 44th Amendment, 1978; Article 43B (promotion of cooperative societies) by the 97th Amendment, 2011.
- Directives outside Part IV: Article 335 (SC/ST claims in services), Article 350A (primary education in the mother tongue) and Article 351 (development of Hindi).
- Ambedkar's defence: he described DPSPs as 'instrument of instructions' addressed to future legislatures, echoing the Government of India Act, 1935 — the framers' own answer to the charge that Part IV is unenforceable.
- AP figures: NTR Bharosa Pension Scheme rates were revised through G.O.Ms.No.43, PR&RD; (RD.I) Department, dated 13 June 2024, raising the base monthly pension to Rs. 4,000 and administered through SERP and the Village/Ward Secretariats.

Q137  Section C | Booklet Q26 Discuss the right to legal aid and whether it is a Fundamental Right or a Directive Principle of State Policy. (TGPSC, 2016)

The right to legal aid occupies both halves of the Constitution. Article 39A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, directs the State to secure that the legal system operates on a basis of equal opportunity and to provide free legal aid — but it sits in Part IV and is non-justiciable. Through successive readings of Article 21, the Supreme Court has converted that directive into an enforceable fundamental right, making legal aid the clearest illustration of the DPSP-to-FR migration.

## Textual Foundation
- Article 39A (Part IV). The directive is twofold — equal opportunity in the operation of the legal system, and free legal aid through suitable legislation or schemes so that justice is not denied by reason of economic or other disabilities. Being a directive, it creates a duty without a corresponding claim.
- Article 22(1) (Part III). Every arrested person has the right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice. This is a fundamental right but, standing alone, does not oblige the State to pay — which is exactly the gap the Article 21 jurisprudence closed.

2. Judicial Elevation: DPSP to Fundamental Right

- M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra (1978). Justice Krishna Iyer held that a prisoner unable to exercise the right of appeal for want of counsel may have counsel assigned under Article 142 read with Articles 21 and 39A, and must be furnished a free copy of the judgment in time. Legal aid first became a component of fair procedure here.
- Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979). Confronted with undertrials detained longer than the maximum sentence, Justice Bhagwati held free legal services to be an essential ingredient of the 'reasonable, fair and just' procedure Article 21 requires. Legal aid ceased to be charity and became a constitutional obligation.
- Khatri (II) v. State of Bihar (1981). The right attaches from the accused's first production before the magistrate, not merely at trial, and the State cannot plead financial or administrative constraint. This fixed the stage — the single most examinable proposition in this line.
- Suk Das v. Union Territory of Arunachal Pradesh (1986). A conviction without offering legal aid was set aside. The Court held it would make a mockery of legal aid to leave a poor, illiterate accused to ask for it; the presiding judge must inform him of the entitlement.
- Ashok v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2024 INSC 919, decided 2 December 2024). A three-judge Bench held that the right to legal aid is a fundamental right under Article 21 and that ineffective aid is no aid at all; the conviction was set aside and directions issued on the role of public prosecutors and the appointment of legal aid counsel. Read with Anokhilal v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2019), the standard has moved from availability to competence.

## Statutory and Institutional Machinery
- Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (in force from 9 November 1995) created NALSA, the State Legal Services Authorities, District Authorities and Taluk Committees, and gave Lok Adalat awards the force of a civil court decree. Section 12 fixes eligible categories; Section 22B provides for Permanent Lok Adalats in public utility services.
- Criminal procedure. Section 341 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (in force 1 July 2024, replacing Section 304 CrPC) obliges the court to assign an advocate at State expense where an unrepresented accused lacks means; Section 340 preserves the right to be defended by counsel of choice.
- Recent schemes. Under the Department of Justice's DISHA scheme, Tele-Law had delivered over 1.12 crore pre-litigation advices through about 2.50 lakh Common Service Centres across 777 districts as on 28 February 2026 (PIB, March 2026). The Legal Aid Defence Counsel System had disposed 7.86 lakh of 11.46 lakh assigned cases between 2023-24 and September 2025, and NALSA's SPRUHA (prisoners), Veer Parivar Sahayata Yojana (defence personnel) and JAGRITI (grassroots awareness) Schemes, all 2025, mark a shift from generic to segment-specific aid (PIB, February 2026).

## The Implementation Gap — and the AP Position
- The binding constraint is awareness, not architecture. Under Section 12(h) of the 1987 Act the eligibility ceiling in Andhra Pradesh is an annual income of Rs. 1,00,000, yet the bulk of eligible litigants never approach the system. The Andhra Pradesh State Legal Services Authority, headquartered at Amaravati with the Chief Justice of the AP High Court as Patron-in-Chief, operates through one High Court Legal Services Committee, 13 District Legal Services Authorities, 13 District Mediation Centres and 145 Mandal Legal Services Committees, supported by Para Legal Volunteers and Legal Aid Defence Counsel (APSLSA, NALSA portal). Density of institutions is therefore not the problem; conversion of eligibility into actual representation is.

## Conclusion

The right to legal aid is textually a Directive Principle under Article 39A and judicially an enforceable Fundamental Right under Article 21. The correct formulation is that Article 39A supplied the constitutional purpose and Article 21 supplied the remedy. Ashok (2024) marks the current frontier: the State's duty is no longer discharged by appointing counsel, but only by ensuring competent representation. Realising that standard now depends less on constitutional doctrine than on outreach, panel-lawyer quality and awareness at the mandal level.

- Committees behind the framework: the Justice P.N. Bhagwati Committee on Legal Aid (1971) and the Justice Krishna Iyer Committee on Processual Justice to the People (1973); CILAS (1980) preceded the 1987 Act.
- Lok Adalats: awards are deemed decrees of a civil court, final and non-appealable, though the underlying dispute may be litigated afresh if no settlement is reached — a favourite one-mark distinction.
- Section 12 categories include SC/ST members, women and children, victims of trafficking, persons with disabilities, industrial workmen, persons in custody and victims of mass disaster, ethnic violence or caste atrocity — irrespective of income in most of these categories.
- Article 39A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, alongside Articles 43A and 48A — a fact frequently asked as a standalone question.
- Comparative note:Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) performed the same function in the United States by reading State-funded counsel into the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments — a useful one-line comparative addition.
- AP institutional detail: APSLSA headquartered at Amaravati (Thullur Mandal, Guntur district); AP High Court at Amaravati established under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 with effect from 1 January 2019.

Q138  Section C | Booklet Q27 Analyse the concept and importance of Directive Principles of State Policy. Explain the relationship and difference between the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles. (APPSC, 2012)

The Directive Principles in Part IV (Articles 36–51) set out the socio-economic programme the framers could not make immediately justiciable. Borrowed from the Irish Constitution of 1937, which drew in turn on the Spanish Republican model, they were described by Dr. Ambedkar as an 'instrument of instructions' to future governments, and by Granville Austin — together with the Fundamental Rights — as the 'conscience of the Constitution'.

## Concept and Nature
- Article 37 makes the position exact: the provisions of Part IV are not enforceable by any court, yet the principles are 'fundamental in the governance of the country' and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws. Non-justiciability is therefore a statement about remedy, not about obligation.
- Purpose. Part IV was intended to convert political democracy into social and economic democracy. Ambedkar's warning in the Constituent Assembly — that India was entering a life of contradictions, equality in politics alongside inequality in social and economic life — is the clearest statement of what Part IV was meant to resolve.

## Importance of the Directive Principles
- They set the welfare-state agenda. Article 39(b) and (c) on equitable distribution of material resources and prevention of concentration of wealth supplied the constitutional basis for land reform, nationalisation and, more recently, redistributive regulation.
- They supply legislative direction. Article 45 produced the 86th Amendment, 2002 and the RTE Act, 2009; Article 40 produced the 73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992; Article 43B (97th Amendment, 2011) produced the cooperative-societies framework; Article 39A produced the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
- They supply interpretive content to fundamental rights. In M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024 INSC 280) the Court read a right against the adverse effects of climate change into Articles 14 and 21 by drawing on Articles 48A and 51A(g) — Part IV giving substance to Part III.
- They are a yardstick of government performance. Because Part IV states outcomes rather than procedures, it functions as a standing benchmark; the SDG India Index framework (NITI Aayog), on which India's composite score stood at 71 in 2023-24, is in effect a measurable restatement of the same goals.

## Relationship Between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs — Four Phases
- Phase I — Primacy of Part III.State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) held that DPSPs must run subsidiary to Fundamental Rights. Parliament responded with the First Amendment, 1951, inserting Article 15(4) and the Ninth Schedule.
- Phase II — Legislative assertion. After Golaknath (1967) restricted Parliament's power to abridge Fundamental Rights, the 25th Amendment, 1971 inserted Article 31C, immunising laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
- Phase III — Judicial settlement.Kesavananda Bharati (1973) upheld the first limb of Article 31C but struck down the clause ousting judicial review. The 42nd Amendment, 1976 extended Article 31C's protection to all directives; in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) the Court struck that extension down, holding that harmony and balance between Parts III and IV is itself part of the basic structure — neither has primacy. Waman Rao (1981) confirmed the surviving pre-1976 Article 31C.
- Phase IV — Contemporary boundary-setting. In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (nine-judge Bench, November 2024) the Court held that not every privately owned resource is a 'material resource of the community' under Article 39(b), departing from the wider view in Sanjeev Coke. The ruling marks the outer limit of DPSP-driven abridgement of property interests.

## Differences in Character
- Enforceability: Fundamental Rights are justiciable and enforceable through Articles 32 and 226; DPSPs are non-justiciable but politically and morally binding under Article 37.
- Object and orientation: Part III secures political democracy and is largely negative, restraining the State; Part IV seeks social and economic democracy and is positive, directing the State to act.
- Beneficiary and source: Fundamental Rights are individual-centric and, in origin, drawn from the US Bill of Rights; DPSPs are community-centric and drawn from the Irish Constitution. Certain rights (Articles 15, 17, 23, 24) operate against private persons as well; DPSPs bind the State alone.

## Conclusion

Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are not rival claims but two halves of one constitutional design — the first securing the individual against the State, the second obliging the State to act for the community. Minerva Mills settled that neither may be subordinated to the other, and that their balance is itself unamendable. Every significant social statute since — from the RTE Act to the legal services framework — has been produced by that interaction, which is why Part IV remains the operative engine of India's welfare constitutionalism.

- Classification of DPSPs: Socialistic (Arts. 38, 39, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47); Gandhian (Arts. 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48); Liberal-Intellectual (Arts. 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51). The Constitution itself contains no such heading — it is an analytical device, and saying so earns credit.
- Directives outside Part IV: Article 335 (SC/ST claims in services consistent with efficiency), Article 350A (primary education in the mother tongue for linguistic minorities) and Article 351 (development of Hindi).
- Amendments to Part IV: 42nd Amendment, 1976 added Articles 39A, 43A and 48A; 44th Amendment, 1978 added Article 38(2) and removed the right to property from Part III, relocating it as a constitutional right in Article 300A; 86th Amendment, 2002 substituted Article 45 and inserted Article 21A; 97th Amendment, 2011 added Article 43B.
- Article 50 (separation of judiciary from executive) is the directive behind the criminal-procedure reforms of 1973 now carried forward by the BNSS, 2023.
- AP anchor:Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) — an AP-origin case — read Article 45 into Article 21 and directly precipitated the 86th Amendment; AP's Grama and Ward Sachivalayam system and the AP Public Services Delivery Guarantee Act, 2017 are the State's institutional response to Articles 40 and 38.
