Q139  (Booklet Section C — Q28) Trace the genesis and development of the Uniform Civil Code in India. Cite authoritative judgments on this issue.

A Uniform Civil Code is a single secular body of law governing marriage, divorce, maintenance, adoption and succession for all citizens irrespective of religion. Its constitutional source is Article 44, which directs the State to "endeavour to secure" such a code. Placed in Part IV, it is non-justiciable under Article 37 — a deliberate framers' choice reflecting the tension between Article 14 equality and Article 25 religious freedom in a plural society.

## Constituent Assembly genesis (1948–50)
- Introduced as draft Article 35, adopted as Article 44. Muslim members led by Mohd. Ismail Sahib and Naziruddin Ahmad moved amendments to save personal law from its reach; all were defeated. K.M. Munshi and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar argued that uniformity in civil matters is not majoritarianism but a precondition of national integration, while Dr. Ambedkar assured that any future code could be made voluntary in its initial application.
- So what: its placement in the DPSP is not neglect but design — the Assembly chose persuasion over compulsion, which is precisely why every subsequent advance has come piecemeal, through legislature or court, rather than through one national statute.

## The legislative route
- Hindu Code Bills (1955–56) — four statutes codifying Hindu marriage, succession, minority and adoption law: the largest single act of personal-law reform, but applied to one community only.
- Special Marriage Act, 1954 — an opt-in secular code already available to any two Indians; the closest thing to a working UCC on the statute book, though under-used.
- Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 legislatively reversed Shah Bano; the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 criminalised instant triple talaq after Shayara Bano — showing Parliament moving in both directions across four decades.

## Judicial development — authoritative judgments
- **Case** — Year · Ratio / significance
- **Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum** — 1985 · Divorced Muslim woman entitled to maintenance under s.125 CrPC; the Court's first forceful call for a UCC as an instrument of gender justice and national integration.

- **Case** — Year · Ratio / significance
- **Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India** — 1995 · Conversion to Islam solely to contract a second marriage does not dissolve the first; such bigamy is void. Reiterated the Article 44 mandate.
- **Pannalal Bansilal Pitti v. State of A.P.** — 1996 · An Andhra Pradesh case. Held that a uniform law, though desirable, may be counter-productive if enacted in one stroke; piecemeal, gradual reform is constitutionally legitimate — the doctrinal foundation for today's state-by-state route.
- **John Vallamattom v. Union of India** — 2003 · Struck down s.118, Indian Succession Act, 1925 as violating Article 14; expressly regretted that Article 44 remained unimplemented.
- **Shayara Bano v. Union of India** — 2017 · Talaq-e-biddat set aside as manifestly arbitrary under Article 14; personal law practices are not immune from fundamental-rights scrutiny.
- **Jose Paulo Coutinho v. Union of India** — 2019 · Described Goa's uniform family law as a "shining example" and noted the framers' hope for Article 44 had yet to be realised.

## Contemporary state-level development (2024–26)
- Uttarakhand: the Uniform Civil Code of Uttarakhand Act, 2024 received Presidential assent on 12 March 2024 and came into force on 27 January 2025, making Uttarakhand the first State of independent India with a comprehensive UCC. It mandates registration of marriages and live-in relationships, prohibits polygamy, equalises inheritance, and expressly exempts Scheduled Tribes. A UCC (Amendment) Ordinance was promulgated under Article 213 on 27 January 2026 to strengthen registration, appeals and penalties (Prasar Bharati / Akashvani News, January 2026).
- Gujarat: following the Justice Ranjana Desai committee, the Gujarat Uniform Civil Code, 2026 was passed by the State Assembly on 24 March 2026, making Gujarat the second UCC State (Prasar Bharati / Akashvani News, March 2026). Goa continues under the Portuguese Civil Code, 1867 — a de facto UCC predating the Constitution.

## The Andhra Pradesh anchor — reform within personal law
- Long before the current debate, the Hindu Succession (Andhra Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1986 (A.P. Act 13 of 1986) inserted Section 29A, making a daughter a coparcener by birth with the same rights and liabilities as a son. Andhra Pradesh was among the first States to do so, and Parliament followed the same path nationally only in the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005. This demonstrates the alternative that the 21st Law Commission later endorsed: the substantive goals of a UCC — gender equality in property and family life — can be achieved by reforming personal laws from within, without a single code.

## Conclusion

The UCC's trajectory is not one of stagnation but of incremental convergence — the Assembly chose endeavour over enforcement, the Court has nudged rather than commanded, and the substantive gains have come through targeted statutes such as Andhra Pradesh's 1986 succession amendment and the 2019 triple-talaq law. With two States now legislating and challenges pending before the constitutional courts, the decisive question is no longer whether uniformity is desirable but whether it is achieved by a single national code or by continued reform within personal laws — a choice that must be settled by consensus rather than by fiat if Article 44 is to serve, and not strain, the pluralism of Article 25.

- 21st Law Commission Consultation Paper (August 2018): a UCC is "neither necessary nor desirable at this stage"; recommended codification and reform of personal laws instead. The 22nd Law Commission reopened public consultation in June 2023 — cite both to show the official position has not been static.
- Article 25(2)(b) expressly permits the State to make laws for social welfare and reform and to throw Hindu religious institutions open to all classes — the Explanation II includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists within "Hindu." This is the textual hook showing the Constitution itself contemplates State intervention in religious practice.
- Scheduled Tribe exemption in both the Uttarakhand and Gujarat codes reflects the protection of customary law under the Fifth and Sixth Schedules — an important federal-diversity caveat any UCC must accommodate.
- Personal law and Article 13:State of Bombay v. Narasu Appa Mali (Bombay HC, 1952) held uncodified personal law is not "law in force" under Article 13 and hence not testable against Part III — a precedent the Supreme Court has repeatedly doubted but not yet formally overruled.
- Goa exception: the Portuguese Civil Code, 1867, saved by the Goa, Daman and Diu (Administration) Act, 1962, is the only pre-existing uniform family law in India — but even it retains limited concessions to Catholic canon law and Hindu usages, showing that "uniform" rarely means absolute.

Q140  (Booklet Section C — Q29) Analyse the aims and objectives of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. Explain whether such objectives have been achieved.

The SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 — in force from 30 January 1990 — is the statutory arm of Article 17, which abolishes untouchability, read with the protective mandate of Articles 15(4), 46 and 335. Where the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 addressed untouchability as a civil disability, the 1989 Act treats caste violence as a distinct category of aggravated criminality demanding special procedure — its preamble promising prevention of atrocities, special courts, and relief and rehabilitation.

## Aims and objectives, read against the statutory machinery
- **Objective** — Statutory hook · What it actually does
- **Deterrence through specific criminalisation** — Section 3 · Enumerates atrocities that ordinary penal law does not capture — forcing consumption of obnoxious substances, garlanding with footwear, social and economic boycott, obstructing access to water bodies and public places, manual scavenging. The 2015 Amendment added new heads and the 2018 Amendment restored immediate arrest.
- **Accountability of the administration** — Section 4 · Punishes wilful neglect of duty by a public servant who is not an SC/ST member — a rare instance of Indian criminal law penalising official inaction, recognising that atrocities persist where local officials look away.
- **Speedy justice** — Sections 14, 14(3), 15 · Special Courts and Exclusive Special Courts with Exclusive Special Public Prosecutors; trial to be concluded within two months from the date of filing of the charge sheet.
- **Victim and witness protection** — Section 15A (2015 Amendment) · Confers a right to be heard, to be informed at every stage, to travel and maintenance expenses and to protection — shifting the victim from spectator to participant.
- **Relief and rehabilitation** — Rules 12(4) and 11, PoA Rules 1995 · Immediate monetary relief, ration, transport and legal aid within a fixed timeline following registration of the FIR.
- **Institutional oversight** — Rules 16 and 17, PoA Rules 1995 · State-Level Vigilance and Monitoring Committee chaired by the Chief Minister and a District-Level Committee chaired by the District Magistrate, meeting quarterly.

- **Objective** — Statutory hook · What it actually does
- **Stringency of process** — Sections 18 and 18A · Bars anticipatory bail under s.438 CrPC; s.18A (2018) removed the requirement of preliminary enquiry and prior sanction for arrest.

## Have the objectives been achieved? A three-part verdict

(i) Access to law — substantially achieved.

- Cases registered under the Act rose from 45,995 in 2020 to a five-year high of 53,372 in 2023, easing to 48,669 in 2024 (Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, Rajya Sabha reply citing NCRB, PIB, 30 July 2026). Rising registration in a stigmatised offence category signals improving willingness to report and reduced police refusal to record FIRs — an achievement, not a failure. Under the broader head of crime against SCs, the same NCRB series records 55,685 SC and 9,961 ST cases in 2024 (PIB, Rajya Sabha, July 2026).

(ii) Conviction — improving from a very low base.

- Convictions rose from 2,613 (2020) to 5,192 (2024), and persons convicted from 4,855 to 10,839 — more than doubling in five years (PIB, 30 July 2026). Charge-sheeting is comparatively strong at roughly 40,614 of 48,669 cases in 2024, indicating that investigation, not detection, is where the system holds up.

(iii) Speed — the objective has plainly failed.

- This is the sharpest indictment. Cases pending trial rose from 1,77,379 in 2020 to 2,87,694 in 2024 — the highest in the five-year series (PIB, 30 July 2026). Against a statutory two-month timeline in Section 14(3), a backlog growing by over a lakh cases in five years means the promise of speedy justice is a dead letter in practice. The cause is structural: Exclusive Special Courts have not been notified in every district, so most cases go to designated Sessions Courts already carrying a general docket.

## Judicial narrowing and restoration
- Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra (2018) diluted the Act by requiring preliminary enquiry and prior sanction before arrest. Parliament responded within months with the 2018 Amendment inserting Section 18A, which the Supreme Court upheld in Prathvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India (2020), holding that anticipatory bail is not an absolute right and its denial in this class of case is neither arbitrary nor violative of Article 14.
- Hitesh Verma v. State of Uttarakhand (2020) held that a caste insult must occur "within public view" to attract s.3(1)(r), narrowing the Act's reach in private-space humiliation.
- Shajan Skaria v. State of Kerala (2024) read Section 18 purposively: the bar on anticipatory bail operates only where the FIR discloses the necessary ingredients, protecting against frivolous invocation. In Kiran v. Rajkumar Jivraj Jain (Supreme Court, 1 September 2025), a Bench led by CJI B.R. Gavai clarified the converse — where the FIR does disclose a prima facie offence, the Section 18 bar is absolute. Together the two decisions calibrate the Act between protection and misuse.

## The Andhra Pradesh picture
- Andhra Pradesh operates 13 Special Sessions Courts for atrocity cases across its districts, with a dedicated Protection of Civil Rights Cell in the CID headed by an IGP/DIG for investigation and prosecution (Department of Social Welfare, Government of Andhra Pradesh). The A.P. State Commission for SCs and STs was constituted in 2016.
- On the economic limb, the A.P. Scheduled Castes Sub-Plan and Tribal Sub-Plan (Planning, Allocation and Utilisation of Financial Resources) Act, 2013 ring-fences budgetary outlays against diversion — recognising that penal deterrence alone cannot deliver the Article 46 promise of economic and educational advancement.

## Conclusion

The Act's objectives are partially achieved and unevenly so: it has succeeded as an instrument of access — more victims report, more charge sheets are filed, and convictions have doubled — but has failed as an instrument of timely justice, with pendency now approaching three lakh cases against a two-month statutory promise. The remedy is not further amendment but execution: notifying Exclusive Special Courts in every atrocity-prone district under Section 14, activating the Vigilance and Monitoring Committees under Rules 16–17, and pairing enforcement with the economic empowerment that Article 46 envisages. A law can prohibit an atrocity; only social transformation can prevent it.

- Section 21(4) obliges the Central Government to place an annual report on the implementation of the Act before both Houses of Parliament — a rare statutory accountability device; the July 2026 Rajya Sabha reply flows from this scheme.
- Rule 3(1)(i) read with Section 21(2) requires States to notify "atrocity-prone areas" (identified areas) for preventive deployment. Incomplete identification is a standing audit finding and a ready "way-forward" point.
- National Helpline Against Atrocities (NHAA) and the centrally sponsored scheme for implementation of the PCR Act, 1955 and PoA Act, 1989 — under which the Centre funds Exclusive Special Courts, relief and inter-caste marriage incentives — are the fiscal instruments behind the statute.
- State of Karnataka v. Appa Balu Ingale (1993) is the classic authority on untouchability as a continuing social reality, and Safai Karamchari Andolan v. Union of India (2014) on manual scavenging as its most degrading survival — both link the PoA Act to the wider Article 17 project.
- Post-1 July 2024, offences are read with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023; the PoA Act being a special law prevails over the general code by virtue of Section 20 (overriding effect). Mentioning this signals currency of legal knowledge.

Q141  (Booklet Section C — Q30) What do you understand by cyberstalking? What are the various other cyber offences recognised under the Information Technology Act, 2000?

Cyberstalking is the use of the internet, electronic mail or other electronic communication to persistently follow, monitor, contact or intimidate a person, causing alarm or distress. Its defining feature is not a single act but a "course of conduct" — repetition is the essence of the offence. India regulates it through a dual framework: the Information Technology Act, 2000, which is technology-specific and targets the misuse of computer resources, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which is person-specific and targets the harm to the victim.

1. Cyberstalking: constituent elements and the governing provision

- The correct current provision is Section 78 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (previously IPC s.354D), in force since 1 July 2024. It penalises any man who (i) follows a woman and repeatedly contacts or attempts to contact her despite a clear indication of disinterest, or (ii) monitors her use of the internet, e-mail or any other form of electronic communication. Punishment extends to three years on first conviction and five years on a subsequent conviction, with fine, and the offence is cognizable.
- Statutory defences are built in: conduct pursued for the prevention or detection of crime by a person entrusted by the State, pursued under any law, or reasonable and justified in the particular circumstances.
- Typical modalities: unsolicited persistent contact; covert monitoring via spyware or GPS; doxxing — publishing a home address, phone number or private images to expose the victim to risk; and threats or defamatory false accusations amplified by the reach of social media.
- Critical limitation worth stating: Section 78 is gender-specific — the offender must be a man and the victim a woman. Male, transgender and non-binary victims must fall back on Section 351 BNS (criminal intimidation), Section 356 (defamation) or IT Act provisions, which is a recognised gap in the law.

## Cyber offences recognised under the Information Technology Act, 2000
- **Section** — Offence · Nature and note
- **43** — Damage to computer, system or data · Civil liability — compensation to the affected person for unauthorised access, downloading, virus introduction or denial of access. Not an offence by itself; its criminal counterpart is s.66.

- **Section** — Offence · Nature and note
- **65** — Tampering with computer source documents · Concealing, destroying or altering source code required by law to be maintained. Up to 3 years and/or fine up to ₹2 lakh.
- **66** — Computer-related offences · Doing dishonestly or fraudulently any act referred to in s.43. Up to 3 years and/or ₹5 lakh — the workhorse hacking provision.
- **66B** — Dishonestly receiving a stolen computer resource or communication device · Up to 3 years and/or ₹1 lakh.
- **66C** — Identity theft · Fraudulent use of another's electronic signature, password or unique identification feature. Up to 3 years and ₹1 lakh.
- **66D** — Cheating by personation using a computer resource · The provision under which most phishing, vishing and "digital arrest" impersonation frauds are charged. Up to 3 years and ₹1 lakh.
- **66E** — Violation of privacy · Capturing, publishing or transmitting the image of a private area of any person without consent — gender-neutral, and therefore often the better charge in image-based abuse.
- **66F** — Cyber terrorism · Acts threatening the unity, integrity, security or sovereignty of India, or unauthorised access to restricted data. Punishable with imprisonment for life — the gravest offence in the Act.
- **67 / 67A / 67B** — Obscene, sexually explicit and child sexual abuse material · Escalating gravity; s.67B covers material depicting children in sexually explicit acts and is read with the POCSO Act, 2012.
- **69 / 69A / 69B** — Interception, blocking and traffic-data monitoring · Enabling powers, not offences; s.69A blocking was upheld in Shreya Singhal for having procedural safeguards.
- **70 / 70A** — Protected systems and critical information infrastructure · NCIIPC designated as the nodal agency under s.70A for critical sectors — power, banking, telecom, transport.
- **79** — Intermediary liability and safe harbour · Conditional immunity subject to due diligence under the IT Rules, 2021.

Essential caveat:Section 66A was struck down in its entirety in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) as vague, overbroad and violative of Article 19(1)(a), the restriction not being saved by Article 19(2). Any answer that lists s.66A as a live provision will lose credibility; conversely, noting its invalidation demonstrates precision.

## Enforcement architecture and recent developments
- The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) became an Attached Office of the Ministry of Home Affairs with effect from 1 July 2024, giving it institutional permanence. It operates the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal and the toll-free helpline 1930.
- Through the Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System (CFCFRMS), over ₹8,690 crore has been saved across more than 24.65 lakh complaints up to 31 January 2026; more than 12.94 lakh SIM cards and 3.03 lakh IMEIs have been blocked (Ministry of Home Affairs, PIB, March 2026). The Suspect Registry (launched 10 September 2024) and the Samanvaya and Pratibimb modules enable inter-State mapping of offenders.
- e-Zero FIR, piloted in Delhi from May 2025, automatically converts NCRP/1930 complaints above a ₹10 lakh threshold into a Zero FIR through CCTNS integration (PIB, May 2025) — directly attacking the delay that lets siphoned funds escape.
- The IT Rules were amended on 10 February 2026 to address synthetically generated information, requiring intermediaries to prevent unlawful AI-generated content, to ensure clear labelling and traceable metadata, and to remove unlawful content within three hours of a court order or reasoned government intimation (MeitY, PIB, March 2026) — the direct legislative response to deepfake-enabled stalking and impersonation.

## Andhra Pradesh anchor
- Andhra Pradesh hosts one of only seven Joint Cyber Coordination Teams (JCCTs) constituted under I4C — at Visakhapatnam — identified as a multi-jurisdictional cybercrime hotspot (Ministry of Home Affairs, PIB). The State's first dedicated Cyber Crime Police Station was inaugurated at Vijayawada in August 2018.
- The State recorded 66,507 cyber and financial crime complaints in 2024 with losses of ₹974.12 crore, and 64,048 complaints in 2025 with losses of ₹828 crore, as reported to the Conference of Collectors and Superintendents of Police at Amaravati (Prasar Bharati / Akashvani News, March 2026). Visakhapatnam City Police have produced 24 short awareness films covering 24 distinct fraud modalities including "digital arrest" scams — a citable example of prevention through public education rather than post-facto policing.

## Conclusion

Cyberstalking illustrates the central difficulty of cyber law: the harm is continuous, borderless and evidentially fragile, while criminal law is built for discrete, located acts. India's response is now reasonably complete on paper — Section 78 BNS for the conduct, the IT Act for the technology, and I4C with the 1930 helpline for redress. What remains deficient is capacity and conviction: trained investigators, forensic turnaround, and a gender-neutral stalking provision. Andhra Pradesh's shift toward preventive awareness campaigns points the right way, because in cyberspace deterrence by detection will always lag deterrence by digital literacy.

- Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) — struck down s.66A; distinguished discussion and advocacy (protected) from incitement (restrictable); read down s.79(3)(b) so intermediaries need act only on a court order or government notification. The single most important cyber-law judgment for this paper.
- K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) established informational privacy as part of Article 21, which is the constitutional foundation for treating monitoring and doxxing as a rights violation and not merely a nuisance.
- Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, with its Rules notified in November 2025, creates duties of purpose limitation and breach notification — the preventive layer sitting above the IT Act's punitive layer.
- Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 now governs the admissibility of electronic records (replacing s.65B of the Evidence Act, 1872) — decisive in cyberstalking prosecutions, where the case usually turns on the certification of screenshots and server logs.
- Institutional stack worth naming: CERT-In (s.70B) for incident response; NCIIPC (s.70A) for critical infrastructure; National Cyber Forensic Laboratory (Evidence) at Hyderabad; and the CyTrain MOOC platform for police and judicial capacity building.

Q142  (Booklet Section C — Q31) Explain the different types of cybercrimes and the importance of cyber laws in India.

Cybercrime covers unlawful acts in which a computer resource is the tool, the target or the place of the offence. Its scale in India tracks the scale of digitisation itself: with UPI, Aadhaar-linked services and DBT now embedded in everyday transactions, the attack surface has widened faster than the enforcement capacity. Cyber law — principally the Information Technology Act, 2000, now read with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 — supplies the legal architecture that makes the digital economy both possible and policeable.

## Types of cybercrime — classified by target
- **Target** — Types · Illustration and provision
- **Against the individual** — Cyberstalking, cyberbullying, doxxing, morphing and deepfakes, sextortion · Persistent monitoring or harassment through digital means. BNS s.78 (stalking); IT Act s.66E (privacy). Deepfake-enabled impersonation prompted the IT Rules amendment of 10 February 2026 mandating labelling of synthetically generated information (MeitY, PIB, March 2026).
- **Against property / financial** — Phishing, smishing (SMS-based), vishing (voice-based), ransomware, identity theft, "digital arrest" scams · Fraudsters extract OTPs, card details or net-banking credentials, or encrypt data for ransom. IT Act ss.66C and 66D. The CFCFRMS has saved over ₹8,690 crore in more than 24.65 lakh complaints up to 31 January 2026 (MHA, PIB, March 2026) — the scale of this head.
- **Against organisations** — Hacking, denial-of-service attacks, data breach, corporate espionage, source-code tampering · IT Act ss.43, 65 and 66. Breaches expose personal data, triggering the DPDP Act, 2023 obligation to notify the Data Protection Board and affected data principals.
- **Against the State** — Cyber terrorism, attacks on critical information infrastructure, cyber-espionage, election-related disinformation · IT Act s.66F (punishable with life imprisonment); s.70A designates NCIIPC as nodal agency for power, banking, telecom and transport. The Election Commission has required AI-altered campaign content to be labelled "AI-Generated" or "Synthetic Content" (ECI, PIB, 2026).

## Importance of cyber laws in India — four functional axes

(i) Enabling function — the foundation of the digital economy.

- Sections 4 and 5 of the IT Act, 2000 confer legal recognition on electronic records and digital signatures. This is the provision the original answer missed and the most important one: without it, an e-contract, a UPI mandate, a DigiLocker certificate or an e-Sign would have no legal standing. The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 now governs their admissibility in evidence. So what: cyber law is not merely restrictive — it is the enabling condition of e-governance itself.

(ii) Protective function — redress and asset recovery for victims.

- The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal and helpline 1930, operated by I4C — an Attached Office of the MHA since 1 July 2024 — allow a victim to freeze siphoned funds within the "golden hour." The ₹8,690 crore recovered up to January 2026 (PIB, March 2026) is money that punitive law alone would never have returned, illustrating that modern cyber law works as much through administrative process as through prosecution.

(iii) Regulatory function — privacy and platform accountability.

- K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) made informational privacy a facet of Article 21; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, with Rules notified in November 2025, operationalises it through consent, purpose limitation and breach notification. In parallel, the IT Rules, 2021 as amended with effect from 15 November 2025 tightened takedown procedure — an intimation to remove content may now be issued only by an officer of Joint Secretary rank or above, and in the case of police, not below Deputy Inspector General, and must specify the legal basis and the exact URL (MeitY, PIB, 2025). So what: this is a deliberate rebalancing of State takedown power against free speech under Article 19(1)(a), following the logic of Shreya Singhal.

(iv) Security function — protecting critical infrastructure.

- CERT-In (s.70B) issues threat advisories and mandates incident reporting; NCIIPC (s.70A) protects designated protected systems; the Cyber Swachhta Kendra provides botnet cleaning. The Union Budget 2025 allocated ₹782 crore to cybersecurity projects (PIB, October 2025), signalling that cyber defence is now treated as national-security expenditure rather than IT overhead.

## The global dimension and the Andhra Pradesh instance
- Global: the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime was adopted by the General Assembly by resolution 79/243 on 24 December 2024 and opened for signature at Hanoi on 25 October 2025, where 71 States and the European Union signed (UN Office of Legal Affairs / UNODC, October 2025). It enters into force ninety days after the fortieth ratification. India participated in the negotiations but has not signed, citing data-sovereignty and privacy concerns — a useful point on the tension between cross-border evidence-sharing and constitutional privacy standards.
- Andhra Pradesh: the State hosts one of seven I4C Joint Cyber Coordination Teams at Visakhapatnam, and recorded 66,507 cyber and financial crime complaints in 2024 (₹974.12 crore lost) and 64,048 in 2025 (₹828 crore lost) (Prasar Bharati / Akashvani News, March 2026). The decline in both complaints and losses between 2024 and 2025 is a rare positive data point and can be attributed to awareness-led prevention.

## Conclusion

Cyber law in India has moved through three generations — enablement (IT Act, 2000, giving electronic records legal force), criminalisation (the 2008 Amendment inserting ss.66A–66F and 43A), and now rights-based regulation (DPDP Act, 2023 and the IT Rules amendments of 2025–26 on takedown procedure and synthetic media). The persisting weakness is not the statute book but the enforcement chain: forensic capacity, trained investigators, and cross-border evidence access — the last being why India's position on the Hanoi Convention matters. As 2nd ARC observed of governance generally, a law is only as strong as the institution that administers it; in cyberspace, that institution must be as fast as the crime.

- Budapest Convention on Cybercrime (2001): India is not a signatory, objecting that it was drafted without Indian participation and that Article 32(b) permits trans-border access to data without host-State consent — a sovereignty concern. Pairing this with the Hanoi Convention gives a complete picture of India's treaty posture.
- National Cyber Security Policy, 2013 set the 5,00,000-professional target and created the 24×7 NCIIPC framework; a successor National Cyber Security Strategy has long been under preparation — a ready "way forward" point.
- Section 43A imposes compensation liability on a body corporate that fails to maintain reasonable security practices for sensitive personal data — the pre-DPDP data protection provision, and still the basis of several ongoing claims.
- Jurisdictional reach:Section 1(2) read with Section 75 gives the IT Act extra-territorial application where the offence involves a computer resource located in India — the provision that allows action against offshore fraud networks operating from South-East Asia.
- Capacity-building instruments to name: CyTrain MOOC for police and judicial officers; the Cyber Forensic-cum-Training Laboratories established in States under the CCPWC scheme; and the Suspect Registry launched on 10 September 2024, which by January 2026 had enabled the declining of transactions worth over ₹9,518 crore (MHA, PIB, March 2026).

Q143  (Booklet Section C — Q32) What is GST? Discuss the regulatory framework of GST in India, including Constitutional provisions applicable to GST.

The Goods and Services Tax is defined by Article 366(12A) as "any tax on supply of goods, or services or both except taxes on the supply of the alcoholic liquor for human consumption." Rolled out on 1 July 2017, it is a comprehensive, multi-stage, destination-based consumption tax that subsumed excise duty, service tax, VAT, octroi and entry tax. Its constitutional significance exceeds its fiscal significance: it is the first instance of the Union and the States exercising simultaneous taxing power over the same base, mediated by a joint constitutional body.

## Defining characteristics
- Destination-based: revenue accrues to the State of consumption, not production. This is a structural transfer from manufacturing States to consuming States and explains why compensation was politically necessary at the outset.
- Elimination of cascading: seamless Input Tax Credit across the chain removes "tax on tax," lowering the effective burden and creating a self-policing audit trail that widens the formal tax base.
- Dual model:CGST + SGST/UTGST on intra-State supply; IGST levied and collected by the Centre on inter-State supply and imports, then apportioned.
- Exclusions: alcoholic liquor for human consumption is constitutionally outside; the five petroleum products — crude, high-speed diesel, petrol, natural gas and ATF — are deferred under Article 279A(5) until the Council recommends a date.

## Constitutional provisions — the 101st Amendment Act, 2016
- **Provision** — Content and significance
- **Article 246A** — Confers concurrent but simultaneous power on Parliament and State legislatures to make laws on GST; Parliament has exclusive power in respect of inter-State supply. A special provision that operates notwithstanding Articles 246 and 254 — the architectural heart of the reform.
- **Article 269A** — IGST on inter-State supply and imports is levied and collected by the Government of India and apportioned between the Union and the States on the Council's recommendation; supply in the course of import is deemed inter-State.

- **Provision** — Content and significance
- **Article 279A** — Constitutes the GST Council within sixty days of commencement. Chair: Union Finance Minister; members: Union MoS (Finance/Revenue) and one Minister nominated by each State. Quorum: one-half. Decisions require three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting, with the Centre holding one-third and all States together two-thirds (Article 279A(9)) — so neither the Centre alone nor the States alone can carry a decision. Article 279A(11) requires the Council to establish a dispute-resolution mechanism.
- **Article 366(12A) & 366(26A)** — Define "goods and services tax" and "services" respectively — "services" meaning anything other than goods, a deliberately residual definition ensuring no supply escapes.
- **Article 279A(5)** — Petroleum products to be brought within GST from a date recommended by the Council — the constitutional hook for the unfinished agenda.
- **Seventh Schedule** — Entry 84 of List I recast to retain only petroleum and tobacco; Entry 52 (entry tax) and Entry 55 (advertisement tax) of List II omitted, and Entry 54 confined to the five petroleum products and liquor — the actual surrender of State fiscal autonomy.

## Institutional and administrative framework
- GST Council — the policy organ, recommending rates, exemptions, thresholds and model laws. GSTN provides the common IT backbone for registration, returns and e-invoicing; CBIC and State Commercial Tax Departments administer.
- Statutory scheme: CGST Act, IGST Act, UTGST Act and the GST (Compensation to States) Act, all 2017, with parallel SGST Acts enacted by each State legislature.
- Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) — launched on 24 September 2025, functioning through a Principal Bench at New Delhi and 31 State Benches across 45 locations, each comprising two Judicial Members, one Technical Member (Centre) and one Technical Member (State) (Ministry of Finance, PIB, September 2025). Its composition mirrors the Council's federal design; State benches such as Chennai became operational from January 2026. So what: until GSTAT, a taxpayer's only remedy beyond the Appellate Authority was a writ petition, clogging High Courts — its creation completes the dispute-resolution architecture the 101st Amendment had promised.

## Judicial gloss — the federalism question
- Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022) held that recommendations of the GST Council are recommendatory and not binding on the Union and the States; Article 246A confers simultaneous power, and both legislatures are equally competent. The Court described Indian federalism as a "dialogue" involving persuasion rather than hierarchy, and characterised the Council as a forum of collaborative, not co-operative-by-subordination, federalism. Citing this converts a descriptive answer into an analytical one.

## GST 2.0 — the rate rationalisation of 2025
- At its 56th meeting, the GST Council collapsed the four-slab structure into a two-rate system of 5% (merit) and 18% (standard), with a special 40% rate for luxury and sin goods, effective 22 September 2025 (PIB, September 2025). Rates on household essentials, life-saving drugs, cement, small cars and farm machinery were cut, and individual life and health insurance was exempted.
- Scale of the base: the GST taxpayer base grew from 66.5 lakh in 2017 to over 1.51 crore active registrations by 30 April 2025; gross collections reached ₹22.08 lakh crore in 2024–25 (+9.4%) (PIB, June 2025) and about ₹22 lakh crore in 2025–26, growing 8.3% despite the rate cuts (Ministry of Finance / Prasar Bharati, April 2026) — evidence that buoyancy has survived rationalisation.

## Andhra Pradesh anchor
- Andhra Pradesh's post-settlement SGST up to December 2025 stood at ₹25,045 crore against ₹24,505 crore in the corresponding period of 2024–25 (GSTN monthly State-wise data, January 2026). As a revenue-deficit State, Andhra Pradesh is doubly exposed under the new dispensation: the compensation guarantee under the 2017 Act lapsed in June 2022, and the Sixteenth Finance Commission report, tabled in February 2026, retained devolution at 41% while discontinuing

Revenue Deficit Grants. This makes own-tax buoyancy and enforcement — rather than transfers — the State's principal fiscal lever, which is why the A.P. Commercial Taxes Department's analytics-driven compliance drive is a live governance example.

## Conclusion

GST is best understood not as a tax reform alone but as a constitutional experiment in shared sovereignty: Article 246A dissolved the neat Union–State division of the Seventh Schedule, and Article 279A created an institution to manage what the division no longer could. Mohit Minerals confirmed that this arrangement rests on persuasion rather than command. With the two-slab structure of September 2025 easing rates and GSTAT completing the appellate chain, the framework is now largely mature. The unfinished agenda — bringing petroleum within the fold under Article 279A(5), and securing the fiscal position of revenue-deficit States such as Andhra Pradesh after the lapse of compensation — will test whether cooperative federalism can survive without a compensation guarantee to hold it together.

- Nomenclature precision: GST was introduced as the Constitution (122nd Amendment) Bill, 2014 and enacted as the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016 — the commonest factual slip in answers on this topic.
- Anti-profiteering: Section 171 CGST Act was administered by the NAA, then the Competition Commission of India, and cases now lie before the Principal Bench of GSTAT; the Council fixed 1 April 2025 as the sunset date for receiving new applications.
- Compensation architecture: the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 guaranteed States 14% annual growth over the 2015–16 base for five years, funded by a cess. The guarantee ended in June 2022; the cess continued only to service back-to-back borrowings raised during the pandemic.
- Reverse charge and e-invoicing: Section 9(3)–(4) CGST Act shifts liability to the recipient in notified cases; mandatory e-invoicing above prescribed turnover, plus the e-way bill, are the two compliance instruments that made GST self-enforcing through data matching.
- Comparative note: India's is one of very few dual GST models globally (Canada being the closest analogue). The Kelkar Task Force (2003–04) and the Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers under Asim Dasgupta are the institutional antecedents, and the First Discussion Paper (2009) is the founding policy document — worth naming to show historical depth.

## Introduction
The Constitution permits **special provisions for the advancement of Backward Classes** as an exception to formal equality — an instrument of **substantive equality** — with the courts evolving a **test to identify** who qualifies as backward.

## The scope of special provisions
- **Article 15(4)** (added by the 1st Amendment after *Champakam Dorairajan*) and **Article 16(4)** enable reservations and special measures for **socially and educationally backward classes**.
- **Article 340** provides for a commission to investigate their conditions (the **Kaka Kalelkar** and **Mandal** Commissions).
- Reservation in education extended by **Article 15(5)** (93rd Amendment); EWS by the **103rd Amendment**.

## The test to determine backwardness
- **Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)** — the foundational ruling:
  - Backwardness is **primarily social**, with caste a relevant but not sole criterion;
  - Introduced the **'creamy layer'** exclusion for OBCs;
  - Capped total reservation at **50%** (barring extraordinary circumstances);
  - Barred reservation in promotions for OBCs (later modified for SC/STs via amendments).
- Later rulings refined economic criteria (*Janhit Abhiyan*, 2022, upholding EWS) and permitted **sub-classification** (*Davinder Singh*, 2024).

## Conclusion
Special provisions for Backward Classes reflect the Constitution's **compensatory-justice** vision; the **Indra Sawhney** framework — social backwardness, creamy-layer exclusion and the 50% ceiling — remains the guiding test for balancing equality with affirmative action.

## Introduction
The **Right to Equality (Articles 14–18)** is a cornerstone of the Constitution, and its meaning has been transformed by the **doctrine of non-arbitrariness** — a shift from a formal to a substantive understanding of equality.

## The classical doctrine — reasonable classification
- **Article 14** guarantees 'equality before the law' and 'equal protection of the laws'.
- The traditional test permits **reasonable classification** if it rests on an **intelligible differentia** having a **rational nexus** with the object of the law — equality means treating equals equally and unequals unequally.

## The doctrine of non-arbitrariness
- **E.P. Royappa (1974)** and **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** expanded Article 14: equality is **antithetical to arbitrariness**; any arbitrary state action violates Article 14, regardless of classification.
- This 'new doctrine' widened judicial scrutiny of executive and legislative action, linking Articles 14, 19 and 21 (the **golden triangle**).

## Wider equality provisions
- **Article 15** (no discrimination + special provisions for women, children, SC/ST/OBC/EWS), **Article 16** (equality of opportunity in public employment + reservations), **Article 17** (abolition of untouchability), **Article 18** (abolition of titles).

## Conclusion
The Right to Equality has evolved from **formal equality (classification)** to **substantive equality (non-arbitrariness and affirmative action)** — making Article 14 a dynamic guarantee against arbitrary power and a vehicle of social justice.

## Introduction
**Secularism** is a basic feature of the Indian Constitution, but India's model differs markedly from Western conceptions — a distinctive approach best understood by comparing the different **models of secularism**.

## The models compared
- **Western/American model — strict separation ('wall of separation')**: the state stays entirely aloof from religion; no state interference and no support.
- **French model — laïcité (assertive secularism)**: the state actively keeps religion out of the public sphere.
- **Indian model — 'principled distance' (Rajeev Bhargava)**: the state maintains **equal respect for all religions (*sarva dharma sama bhava*)** rather than strict separation. It **can intervene** — to ban untouchability (Article 17), reform religious practices (temple entry, triple talaq), or support all faiths even-handedly.

## Features of Indian secularism
- **No state religion**; freedom of conscience and religion (**Articles 25–28**); the word 'Secular' added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**.
- Held to be part of the **basic structure** (*S.R. Bommai*, 1994); the **essential religious practices** test regulates the state–religion interface.

## The critical examination
- Indian secularism enables **reform and equal treatment** but faces tension between **religious freedom and reform**, majoritarian pressures, and debates over 'appeasement' versus genuine even-handedness.

## Conclusion
India's **'principled distance' secularism** is a contextual innovation suited to a deeply religious, plural society — neither a wall of separation nor hostility, but engaged even-handedness. Its resilience depends on the state's fidelity to equal respect for all faiths.

## Introduction
The **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs, Part IV, Articles 36–51)** are non-justiciable goals meant to guide the State toward a **welfare state and social and economic democracy**; their implementation record is substantial though uneven.

## Nature and purpose
- **Non-justiciable** (Article 37) but 'fundamental in the governance of the country' — a moral and political mandate.
- Classified as **socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual** principles.

## The record of implementation
- **Legislative fulfilment**: land reforms and abolition of zamindari (Article 39); **Panchayati Raj** (Article 40 → 73rd Amendment); **equal pay and maternity/labour laws** (Articles 39, 42); **free and compulsory education** (Article 45 → Article 21A, RTE 2009); **MGNREGA, NFSA** (Article 41, 47); **environmental protection** (Article 48A); **UCC efforts** (Article 44).
- **Judicial elevation**: courts read DPSPs into Fundamental Rights (*Unnikrishnan*, *Olga Tellis*), and *Minerva Mills* (1980) held the **harmony between FRs and DPSPs** to be basic structure.

## Effectiveness and gaps
- Real progress on welfare and rights, but **incomplete** on the UCC, prohibition, cottage industries, and health/education spending targets — constrained by resources and political will.

## Conclusion
The DPSPs have been a **powerful compass** transforming India into a welfare state; their non-justiciability has not prevented substantial implementation, though realising the unfinished directives remains a continuing constitutional obligation.

## Introduction
The **right to legal aid** — ensuring that no one is denied justice for want of means — occupies a distinctive place, straddling the **Directive Principles** and the **Fundamental Rights**, and is now firmly recognised as an enforceable right.

## Its constitutional status
- **As a Directive Principle**: **Article 39A** (added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976) directs the State to provide **free legal aid** and ensure justice is not denied by economic or other disabilities.
- **As part of a Fundamental Right**: the Supreme Court has read free legal aid into **Article 21** (life and personal liberty) and **Article 14** (equality):
  - *Hussainara Khatoon* (1979): legal aid is an essential ingredient of a **'reasonable, fair and just' procedure** under Article 21.
  - *M.H. Hoskot* and *Khatri v. State of Bihar*: the state must provide counsel to the indigent accused.

## The statutory framework
- The **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** created **NALSA, State and District Legal Services Authorities**, **Lok Adalats**, and legal-aid clinics — operationalising the right.

## Conclusion
Though originating as a **Directive Principle (Article 39A)**, the right to legal aid has been **elevated to a Fundamental Right** as an inseparable part of Articles 21 and 14 — making access to justice a genuine constitutional guarantee, not merely an aspiration. It is a prime example of DPSPs enriching Fundamental Rights.

## Introduction
The **Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36–51)** embody the Constitution's vision of a **welfare state** and, together with the Fundamental Rights, form what Granville Austin called the Constitution's 'conscience'.

## Concept and importance
- **Non-justiciable** goals (Article 37) that are nonetheless **'fundamental in the governance of the country'** — guiding the State toward **social and economic democracy**.
- **Classification**: **socialistic** (Articles 38, 39, 41–43 — welfare, equitable distribution, living wage), **Gandhian** (Articles 40, 43, 46, 47, 48 — panchayats, cottage industries, weaker sections, prohibition, cattle), and **liberal-intellectual** (Articles 44, 45, 48A, 50, 51 — UCC, education, environment, judicial separation, international peace).
- **Importance**: they set standards for governance, inform judicial interpretation, and are a **yardstick** to judge government performance.

## Relationship with Fundamental Rights
- Initially seen as **subordinate** to FRs (*Champakam Dorairajan*, 1951), the two were later **harmonised**:
  - *Kesavananda Bharati* (1973) and especially *Minerva Mills* (1980) held that the **harmony and balance between FRs and DPSPs is part of the basic structure** — 'the two are like two wheels of a chariot'.
  - Courts read DPSPs **into** FRs (education, environment, livelihood) to enrich rights.

## Conclusion
The DPSPs are the **socio-economic soul** of the Constitution, complementing the Fundamental Rights. Read together in harmony, they translate political democracy into **social and economic democracy** — the founders' vision of justice in full.

## Introduction
The **Uniform Civil Code (UCC)** — a common set of personal laws governing marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption for all citizens regardless of religion — is envisaged in **Article 44** of the Directive Principles, and its trajectory reveals the tension between **national integration and religious freedom**.

## Genesis and constitutional basis
- **Article 44**: 'The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a **uniform civil code** throughout the territory of India' — a non-justiciable directive.
- The **Constituent Assembly** debated it fiercely; it was placed among the DPSPs as a goal, not an immediate mandate, balancing reform against minority apprehensions.

## Judicial development
- **Shah Bano (1985)**: the Court granted maintenance to a divorced Muslim woman and urged a UCC — sparking the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986.
- **Sarla Mudgal (1995)** and **John Vallamattom (2003)**: reiterated the call for a UCC to promote national integration and gender justice.
- **Shayara Bano (2017)**: struck down **instant triple talaq**, advancing gender justice within personal law.

## The contemporary debate
- **Uttarakhand enacted a State UCC (2024)** — the first — reviving the national debate; the **22nd Law Commission** sought fresh views.
- Arguments: UCC promotes **equality, gender justice and integration**; critics fear it threatens **religious freedom (Articles 25–26)** and pluralism.

## Conclusion
The UCC remains an **unfulfilled directive** at the heart of the equality-versus-diversity debate. A **consensual, gender-just and consultative** approach — reforming discriminatory practices across communities — is the path most consistent with both Article 44 and India's pluralism.

## Introduction
The **Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989** is a landmark social-justice legislation enacted to protect the most vulnerable communities from caste-based violence and humiliation, giving teeth to the constitutional promise of dignity and equality.

## Aims and objectives
- To **prevent atrocities** against SCs and STs and punish offences of caste-based violence, humiliation and exploitation not adequately covered by ordinary law.
- To provide for **special courts** for speedy trial, **relief and rehabilitation** of victims, and **preventive measures**.
- To give effect to **Articles 17 (abolition of untouchability), 15, 46 and 21** — securing dignity and protection.

## Key features
- A detailed list of **offences of atrocity** (social boycott, forced labour, denial of access to public resources, sexual exploitation, humiliation).
- **Special/Exclusive Courts and Special Public Prosecutors**; enhanced punishments; provisions against public servants' neglect of duty.
- **Victim and witness protection**, monitoring by the National Commissions, and the **2015/2018 amendments** strengthening it.

## Assessment
- **Strengths**: a strong deterrent and rights-affirming framework.
- **Challenges**: **low conviction rates, delays, under-reporting, and misuse concerns** — the Supreme Court's *Subhash Kashinath Mahajan* (2018) dilution was reversed by a legislative amendment restoring the Act's rigour (upheld in *Prithvi Raj Chauhan*, 2020).

## Conclusion
The Act is a vital instrument of **substantive equality and dignity** for SCs and STs; its effectiveness depends on **sensitised enforcement, speedy trials and social change** — law reinforcing the constitutional commitment to a caste-free, just society.

## Introduction
An **office of profit** is a position under the government that yields a financial gain, salary or perquisite; holding one can **disqualify a legislator** under Articles 102(1)(a) and 191(1)(a), a bar designed to preserve the **separation of powers** and prevent conflicts of interest.

## The concept
- A legislator holding an office of profit **under the Union or a State government** (other than an office exempted by law) is **disqualified** from membership.
- **Rationale**: to keep legislators independent of executive patronage and free from any clash between duty and personal gain.
- **Tests** evolved by the courts: whether the government **appoints and can remove** the holder, pays remuneration, and whether the office carries powers or patronage — not merely whether profit is actually received.

## Developments in India
- The **Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959** exempts a list of offices from the bar.
- **Jaya Bachchan v. Union of India (2006)**: the **potential** for profit, not its actual receipt, attracts disqualification.
- The **2006 controversy** (dozens of MPs holding such offices) led to a retrospective expansion of the exempted-offices list — criticised as diluting the safeguard.
- The **2017 disqualification of 20 AAP MLAs** (Delhi parliamentary secretaries) by the ECI kept the issue alive, though later set aside on procedural grounds.

## Conclusion
The office-of-profit bar is a vital guarantee of **legislative independence and probity**. But the ever-expanding list of exemptions risks hollowing it out — a clear, uniform statutory definition of 'office of profit' is needed to restore its purpose.

## Introduction
The **Rajya Sabha (Council of States)** and the **Lok Sabha (House of the People)** together constitute Parliament, but their relative positions are **unequal** — the Constitution deliberately gives primacy to the directly elected Lok Sabha while assigning the Rajya Sabha distinctive federal and revising roles.

## Where the Rajya Sabha is subordinate
- **Money Bills (Article 110)**: introduced only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha can merely **recommend** changes within 14 days, which the Lok Sabha may reject — it cannot amend or reject a Money Bill.
- **Executive accountability**: the **Council of Ministers is responsible only to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3))**; a no-confidence motion lies only there.
- **Financial control**: the Budget and demands for grants are effectively decided by the Lok Sabha.
- **Joint sitting (Article 108)**: on a deadlock over ordinary bills, the larger Lok Sabha usually prevails by numbers.

## Where the Rajya Sabha is equal or superior
- **Equal powers** on ordinary bills, constitutional amendments, and in electing/removing the President and Vice-President and impeaching judges.
- **Exclusive powers**: **Article 249** (authorising Parliament to legislate on a State-List subject in the national interest) and **Article 312** (creating a new All-India Service) — reflecting its role as guardian of States' interests.
- As a **permanent House** (one-third retiring every two years), it provides continuity and a revising, deliberative check.

## Conclusion
The Rajya Sabha is a **co-equal in legislation but subordinate in financial matters and executive accountability** — a second chamber that represents the States and revises legislation, while ultimate democratic authority rests with the popularly elected Lok Sabha.
